News.title: School protests send shivers down French government's spine
News.content:
It is a piece of wisdom that all French leaders take care to heed: young people on the street equals trouble.

Since the student protests of May 1968 â memorably described by President De Gaulle as chienlit (bed defecation, in other words chaos) â every government has run scared of angry French youth.

Why? Because youth movements are unpredictable and shapeless, often with no clear structure to negotiate with. Because when they protest, other groups join in.

Also: because as they're young, the public tends to sympathise. And because if the police mess up and cause injury or worse, then the consequences are incalculable. And presidential elections are only months away.

For all these reasons, when la jeunesse en colÃ¨re (angry youth) is at the barricades governments tread very carefully indeed.

Right now, French teenagers are at the barricades and if they are not visibly angry (the mood is more excitement), they certainly have the government of President Emmanuel Macron in what Le Monde called on Friday "the cold sweats".

A movement that started nearly two weeks ago in the low-income Seine-Saint-Denis area of northern Paris has in the last few days spread across the country.

News.title: Watch: 'I was not going to let others die' - pilot of Flydubai flight describes cockpit attack by co-pilot
News.content:
An Indian pilot who was attacked by his co-pilot on an Israel-bound Flydubai plane has received a call in his hospital bed from India PM Narendra Modi.

Visibly emotional, Capt Smit Machchhar said he fought back because he could not allow everyone on the flight to die.

He has been hailed a hero for opening the cockpit door, allowing passengers to overpower the attacker.

The flight, which had departed from Dubai, landed safely in Saudi Arabia. All on board survived.

Read more about this story.

News.title: Woman who killed abusive partner has murder conviction overturned
News.content:
A west Belfast woman who stabbed her abusive partner to death while he slept has had her conviction for murder overturned.

The Court of Appeal ruled that jurors were misdirected on Julie Ann McIlwaine's loss of control defence to the killing of James Joseph Crossley in March 2022.

Senior judges quashed the guilty verdict and gave the prosecution two weeks to decide if it is to seek any retrial.

"We cannot be satisfied that the conviction is safe," said Lady Chief Justice Dame Siobhan Keegan.

McIlwaine, 35, who has been serving a minimum 12-year jail term, wept on the videolink from Hydebank Prison as the ruling was delivered.

She admitted killing her partner but denied murder, claiming to have suffered a temporary loss of control as a victim of domestic abuse.

Crossley, 38, was stabbed up to 10 times in the chest and abdomen as he lay sleeping beside the couple's young child at McIlwaine's former home in Dunmurry.

The pair had been in a relationship marred by emotional manipulation and coercive control.

At the time of his death, Crossley was on bail for an alleged assault against McIlwaine and subject to a restraining order prohibiting any contact with her.

Despite a period of separation, they had re-established their relationship by the night of the killing.

The court heard Crossley took medication and went to sleep after arguments in which he issued an ultimatum for McIlwaine to choose between him and her family.

News.title: Tories aim to be election-ready ahead of party conference
News.content:
Welfare spending is increasingly seen by the Conservatives as a core battleground with Labour.

During Labour conference they derided the event as the "Welfare Party Conference". Whereas Sir Keir Starmer sought to cut welfare spending before backing down in the face of a rebellion by his own MPs, Burnham has made clear that he believes the way to reduce the benefits bill in the long-term is more up-front investment in support for those out of work.

This is a clear ideological difference which both parties are happy to embrace. Conservative strategists believe there is a broader lesson there.

"The differences between the parties have been quite muddled for a while," one says. "Now that Burnham is prime minister we have a more traditional left-right split."

Another area where Badenoch will embrace that divide in the coming days is the pensions triple-lock.

The policy currently guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% â whichever is the highest.

Badenoch will make clear that the Conservatives continue to support that policy in its current form, breaking with some generally supportive think tanks and policy experts who believe Badenoch should follow Burnham's lead.

In his conference speech on Tuesday, Burnham set out plans to end the existing triple lock from 2030, so the state pension increases at least by inflation or 2.5% - but remove the automatic annual link with average earnings.

The Conservatives hope the sharpening left-right split leaves Reform UK in a strategic bind, occupying a less obvious place on that spectrum.

A year ago some senior Conservatives feared being usurped by Reform as the leading party of the right was a near-inevitability, but now they are optimistic that Nigel Farage's party is on an inexorable slide.

That bullishness is fuelled in large part by the difficulties Reform has faced over Nigel Farage's Â£5m gift from Christopher Harborne and the fallout - including a police inquiry - from the recent Channel 4 News investigation.

"I find more and more voters raise concerns about Reform with me - people who weren't previously giving us the time of day," one MP said.

"These are successful people with big garages and good jobs who do not necessarily pay that much attention but want a small-c conservative government.

"They were switching to Reform because they were fed up with us and thought Farage was now the main option on the right. But they are starting to come back."

Others are less positive, pointing out that Reform still often record higher shares than the Conservatives in the polls â and more importantly have now won far more votes than them in successive years of local and national elections.

News.title: Dolly Parton sings Jolene in Welsh in recording released after her death
News.content:
A new version of Dolly Parton's Jolene is set to be released, with parts of the song sung in Welsh by the legendary country artist.

The song was recorded before her death on 25 August, and is a collaboration with Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis as well as Parton's niece, Jada Star.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote more than 3,000 songs.

The single will come out on 9 October, and is the second posthumous release from Parton - who was of Welsh descent.

In a teaser video released on social media, Star and Lewis explained how the song came to light.

As a proud Welsh speaker, Lewis, from Neath, had started translating some of her favourite tunes, and soon landed on the Parton classic, Jolene.

"Two years ago I posted a video of me singing the Dolly Parton classic Jolene in Welsh, external," said Lewis.

"I never expected it would go viral and definitely didn't expect it to attract the attention of Dolly's family - especially her niece Jada."

News.title: What does Man City guilty verdict mean for their squad?
News.content:
The looming punishment certainly complicates City's plans in the transfer market.

"This isn't the players' failing, it's on the club. Potential new signings aren't even in the building and joining City without knowing what the punishment would be represents an undeniable risk, so any new contracts would have to have indemnities," said one leading agent.

It was acknowledged that writing eventualities into new registrations is very difficult, though City players do have release clauses in their deals should the club enter into administration.

Until a post-appeal verdict over sanctions is made, making new signings will certainly become more complicated, though it is still likely they will be able to attract big players as they still have the financial muscle to do so.

For example, one potential method of persuading a player to join would be to offer them a contract on big money with no pay decreases if the club are relegated, and then include a fixed fee release clause if City don't return to the top flight within a set period.

If sanctions ensure relegation and include further points deductions that stretch over multiple seasons, attracting top players will of course be harder.

City could make a wage package hard to resist for elite players, but it seems inconceivable that a footballer of that ilk would join with demotion a possibility as there are likely to be other top options elsewhere.

The same logic can be applied to the retention of their current squad.

There is almost certainly going to be interest in their top players from other elite clubs across Europe. It will be very difficult for City to keep that level of player in the coming months and years while the saga plays out.

So with all that said, particularly if relegation is confirmed, City will have to rebuild their squad to some extent, though the prospect of a transfer embargo as one of the sanctions would prevent them from making any signings at all.

Such a rebuild may include the promotion of some of the club's best academy players, who stand to benefit if the first-team squad disbands.

When Chelsea were placed under a transfer embargo in 2019, the likes of Mason Mount, Tammy Abraham, Fikayo Tomori, Billy Gilmour and Callum Hudson-Odoi all emerged as senior players.

And while City may look to rebuild with a profile of player they believe will be adept at being successful in the EFL, you will likely see a number of their younger players fast-tracked.

With that said, a number of clubs are already working on seeing if they can capitalise on the current uncertainty by luring City's best academy talent.

News.title: First minister demands 'new deal' from Andy Burnham to make Wales equal with Scotland
News.content:
First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth has demanded a "new deal" for Wales from the UK government that would put the country on an equal footing with Scotland.

In a letter he said powers over policing, justice, rail and the Crown Estate should be transferred to Cardiff.

Speaking at Plaid Cymru's conference in Llandudno, the party's leader said Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised him he would not undermine Wales.

Ap Iorwerth is expected to meet the prime minister, along with the first ministers of Scotland and Northern Ireland, at the end of the month.

The UK government said it was "committed to building a stronger and fairer Wales in a stronger and fairer United Kingdom".

Plaid Cymru is gathering in Llandudno's Venue Cymru for the first time since it won a historic victory at the Senedd election in May.

The party had won power for the first time, ending Labour's 27 year control of the Welsh government.

Ap Iorwerth said the result amounted to a "new dawn" for Wales, and "the beginning of our work to give flight to a nation whose wings have been clipped for far too long."

But he warned that the upcoming Welsh government budget process would be "tough", and said he would have to "find savings where we can".

News.title: K-pop giants Stray Kids join BTS in boycotting the Grammys
News.content:
One of the world's biggest K-pop groups, Stray Kids, are joining BTS in boycotting the 2027 Grammy Awards.

The move comes after the introduction of a controversial new category for Asian pop music, which critics fear will ghettoise genres like K-Pop and J-Pop.

BTS announced they would not submit songs for consideration in any category in July, saying they hoped their music "can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language".

Stray Kids, who recently scored their ninth US number one album, have now followed suit. In a short statement, their record label JYP simply said: "Stray Kids did not submit for the Grammys."

Stray Kids had previously refrained from giving a direct answer to questions about the awards.

During a press conference for their latest album, This and That, in August, singer Hwang Hyun-jin said: "We have never once set award results or records as our goal.

"Our top priority is for our fans to be happy and satisfied," he added.

The news will come as a blow to the Recording Academy, which organises the Grammys.

Stray Kids are phenomenally popular in the US, and recently headlined the Governor's Ball festival in New York, sharing the bill with Lorde and A$AP Rocky.

In the album chart, only one other band has scored more number one albums: The Beatles.

Earlier this year, all eight members of the band were given voting privileges at the awards, which gives additional weight to their decision to withdraw. BTS are also voting members of the Academy.

News.title: Man City verdict has 'significant implications for integrity of the game', says FA
News.content:
Manchester City have confirmed they have lodged an appeal after an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

In a short statement, the club said the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".

Asserting its innocence, the club added it had filed "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions" on Thursday evening.

Earlier on Friday, the Football Association said the verdict against City has "significant implications for the integrity of the game".

In a statement, English football's governing body added: "We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate."

It was confirmed on Tuesday that City were found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

"As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage," the FA added.

"We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely."

The overarching powers the FA has could see the governing body launch its own investigation into the matter with the threat of further sanctions.

Sources told BBC Sport that City were expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than Â£830m.

The Premier League says City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

News.title: Chaos, coffins and 'Claudiapatra' steal the show in Celebrity Traitors
News.content:
Ex-BBC journalist Amol Rajan swooped the following day, asking Grant: "What happened last night?"

But instead of sowing clever seeds of doubt, Grant said he'd been so "blatant" about wanting to be a traitor that he simply responded he was one, when he was asked.

It was an odd reply, perhaps because he was flustered.

Rajan labelled him the "Lord of Chaos", but Hall stayed loyal.

"I just don't believe Richard's a traitor, I've known him 30 years and he's my neighbour," she said.

"He says and does eccentric things, he's an amazing guy, but I think he's acting out because he's not been chosen."

Hall's loyalty could be tested though, given Alan Carr murdered Paloma Faith in series one by touching her face.

Comic and writer Miranda Hart also thinks Grant could be a faithful, but admitted she is confused.

Winkleman told the press launch she thought Grant blurted out his identity in error, because he was so thrilled to be a traitor.

"He was giddy, wasn't he? He's just laughing at what's happening. Fantastic," she said.

Ed Gamble, the host of BBC One and BBC Sounds spin-off show Uncloaked, added: "It felt like he'd been given the lead role in a film and he just had to tell everyone. It's such an insane moment."

Stephen Lambert, the head of Studio Lambert, which produces the show, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday: "It's a strange way to be a traitor. To be a traitor on the show is all about keeping the fact that you're a traitor a secret.

"He had to row back quite quickly because he remembered that actually the point of being a traitor is not to tell anyone."

Grant may find that no-one tells him a secret ever again.

He did eventually decide to let the much more cool, calm and collected Jama take the lead in their subsequent decision making.

News.title: Crypto thieves attack man in home and threaten to kill pregnant wife's baby in 'horrific' robbery
News.content:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

A businessman was beaten with hammers by masked men who broke into his home and threatened to kill his heavily pregnant wife unless he transferred hundreds of thousands of pounds of cryptocurrency.

Speaking to the BBC, the couple, who want to remain anonymous, described the attack as "horrific" and said they feared for their unborn baby's life.

The attackers left in a car driven by a getaway driver after the man transferred his crypto savings.

Crimestoppers are offering a Â£10,000 reward for information in the attack, which was captured on home security footage and is being investigated by the police.

Experts say it is one of a growing type of violent theft known as a "wrench attack" targeting cryptocurrency investors.

As crypto coins have risen in value, reports of these violent robberies linked to digital assets have emerged in the UK, France and the US.

Once funds are transferred, recovering them can be extremely difficult.

The man, who the BBC is calling James, said three intruders forced their way into their Solihull home before launching an assault which lasted 45 minutes.

"The door gets pushed open, I can see gloves coming in, balaclavas," he said.

James tried to fight the men off but they hit him in the face, head and ribs with hammers.

His wife, who was seven months pregnant, was held down on the sofa by one of the criminals.

"He's got a pillow over her face," James said. "He's literally suffocating her on the sofa. I can hear her screaming, 'I can't breathe'."

The couple still had no idea what the criminals wanted until one of the men demanded James unlock his phone and hand it over.

James said the attackers appeared to know he owned cryptocurrency, but had little understanding of how to access it.

Instead, they were taking instructions from someone else connected via a live video call.

"I can hear the guy on FaceTime saying: 'Show me everything on his phone. Show me what apps he's got'," he said.

News.title: Olivia Dean accused of copying Bill Withers' Just The Two of Us
News.content:
British pop star Olivia Dean has been accused of copying the melody of Bill Withers' soul classic Just The Two of Us in a legal case filed in California.

The complaint centres around Dean's song I've Seen It, taken from her Brit Award-winning 2025 album The Art of Loving.

Just The Two of Us was a hit for Withers in 1981, and the publishers of the late singer's catalogue allege that the two songs "share musical features" that are "so striking" they cannot have arisen by coincidence alone.

The lawsuit names Dean's record label Capitol Records, parent company Universal Music Group and her publishing companies as the defendants. It does not seek damages from the singer herself or her co-writers Bastian LangebÃ¦k and Max Wolfgang.

In legal documents seen by the BBC, Mattie Music Group, which looks after Withers' back catalogue, said it hired a musicologist to review the two songs.

He concluded "that the works contain substantial similarities" including the "repeated copying" of the melody from Just The Two of Us, the documents said.

The publishers claim they notified Dean's record label of the potential infringement in August, but the music was not pulled from distribution.

To prove plagiarism, Mattie Music Group would have to prove that Dean and her co-writers had previously heard Withers' original composition.

In the lawsuit, they allege that his song's "extraordinary and sustained" commercial success, including "decades of radio play", would mean the musicians had "reasonable opportunity" to have encountered Just The Two of Us before writing I've Seen It.

The defendants have yet to respond to the lawsuit. The BBC has contacted them, and Dean's representatives, for a comment.

News.title: Greens can move Labour in the right direction, says Polanski
News.content:
Zack Polanksi has urged voters to back the Greens to force changes from Andy Burnham, arguing his party has the power to move Labour in "the right direction".

In his speech to the party's annual conference, the Green leader said that "sustained pressure" from his party had made forced Labour into changing its stance on issues including climate and its stance towards Israel.

He told activists in Brighton that Labour had failed to take action on housing, as he called for a three-year cap to limit rent rises in the private sector.

And he said that voting for the Greens would force changes from the government, telling members: "Vote Green, and watch Labour move".

Polanksi arrived in Brighton facing questions over how he would seek to position the party to respond to Labour's change of leadership under Burnham, amid signs the Greens' rise in national polls last year may have waned.

He began his address by celebrating his party's surge in membership since his election as party leader a year ago, and electoral successes including the hundreds of councillors it gained in May's local elections in England.

In his half-hour address, he did not mention the Conservatives or Reform UK but launched repeated attacks on Labour's record in office.

He criticised Labour for making "slogans without action" on the cost of living and vowed only his party would end "Rip Off Britain".

And he was particularly critical of Labour's record on housing, where he accused the party of failing to take on the "powerful vested interests of developers and big landlords".

Instead, he urged the government to enact an "emergency brake" on private rents, under which they would be prevented from rising above the lowest of consumer price index measure of inflation, wage growth or 2%, for three years.

News.title: Man jailed for 15 years over Ulez camera blast
News.content:
A man who blew up a ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) camera in south-east London has been sentenced to 15 years in jail at the Old Bailey.

Kevin Rees, 63, of Harcourt Avenue, Sidcup, detonated the explosives in the Ulez camera in Wellesley Avenue, Sidcup, at about 18:45 GMT on 6 December 2023.

The device damaged cars and houses up to 100m away, with shrapnel hitting outside of a a child's bedroom. Rees was convicted in January at Woolwich Crown Court of causing an explosion likely to endanger life.

During the trial, Rees told the Woolwich Crown Court he "strongly opposed" the Ulez scheme and the mayor of London, Lord Sadiq Khan.

The Metropolitan Police said Judge Anthony Bate ruled that the offence had a "terrorism connection", resulting in a tougher sentence and stricter controls after Rees's release.

"It was miraculous that nobody was killed or seriously injured in the large explosion caused by Rees," said Det Ch Supt James Derham, who leads local policing in the Bexley area.

"He showed a complete disregard for the welfare and safety of the people who live in, or were travelling through, the area at the time of the explosion â all because he was unhappy with the Ulez scheme."

News.title: No more cereal at the end of the aisle? New rules in Scotland's supermarkets
News.content:
Price promotions on those items - such as "three for the price of two", "three for Â£10" or "buy five and save 20%" - are no longer allowed.

Multi-buy offers, including extra loyalty points, are also banned.

Another type of deal that falls foul of the rules is those offering a free high-sugar, fat or salt product alongside another purchase - for example, a free chocolate bar with a newspaper.

There are no restrictions on discounts such as half-price or "save Â£1".

Online retailers also face restrictions - including a ban on advertising some foods on their homepage.

Similar restrictions are already in place in England and Wales.

In England, price or multibuy promotions on unhealthy food and drink were banned in October 2025.

Wales followed in March, external when it brought in its rules preventing medium and large retailers promoting less healthy products.

Restrictions on advertising junk food, external across the UK were also introduced in January.

News.title: LFB named in Met's evidence file on Grenfell fire
News.content:
London Fire Brigade (LFB) has confirmed it is among those facing possible criminal action over the Grenfell Tower fire.

Prosecutors were handed an evidence file on 20 organisations and firms and 54 individuals from the Metropolitan Police earlier this week.

The force is seeking charges including corporate manslaughter, gross negligence manslaughter, health and safety offences and fraud-related offences relating to the deaths of 72 people in the disaster.

London fire commissioner Jonathan Smith said he welcomed the progress in the investigation.

The Met's investigation - Operation Northleigh - began soon after the fire in June 2017 and has involved hundreds of investigating officers.

The CPS said any charging decisions would be made before the 10th anniversary of the disaster in 2027.

In a statement, the LFB said: "The London fire commissioner has been notified by the Metropolitan Police Service that, following its investigation into the events surrounding the Grenfell Tower fire, a file has been submitted to the CPS for its consideration in respect of London Fire Brigade.

"The London fire commissioner welcomes the progress in the investigation process and reaffirms his commitment to providing the CPS with full cooperation, as LFB has sought to do throughout Operation Northleigh."

Smith said: "We remember the 72 people who lost their lives, and our thoughts remain with the bereaved, survivors and everyone whose lives were changed forever by that night.

"LFB accepted the findings of the Grenfell Tower Inquiry and has now implemented all the recommendations from both phases.

"We continue working with our partners across government and the fire and rescue sector to ensure the lessons of the Grenfell tragedy are learnt, and this continues to shape everything we do."

Andy Burnham should publish all details of his meetings with Manchester City’s owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), and declare all hospitality he has accepted at the Etihad Stadium, the Liberal Democrats have said.

The prime minister was roundly criticised this week for saying he would be “really concerned” if City’s Abu Dhabi owners sold the club after the club was found to have breached the Premier League’s financial rules by an independent commission, crediting them with being “a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”.

Downing Street was forced to issue two clarifications of his position on Thursday, with a spokesperson for the PM insisting the guilty verdict against Manchester City is “serious”.

Mr Burnham’s comments drew criticism on social media and shadow sports minister Louie French called for the government to “keep politics out of football”, with the case set to proceed to an appeal board and a sanctions hearing.

Now, the Liberal Democrats have drafted a strongly-worded letter to the prime minister, criticising his defence of City as “extraordinary”.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham speaks to Manchester City Chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak prior to the Vincent Kompany Testimonial at the Etihad Stadium in 2019 ( PA )

In the letter, seen by the Guardian, the party’s spokesperson for culture, media and sport, Anna Sabine, wrote: “As you will know, an independent commission has found Manchester City guilty of 114 charges of breaching financial rules over a timeframe of nearly a decade, including the use of ‘sham contracts’ and schemes to disguise more than £830m of funding.

“Despite this, your response was to thank the club’s owners for their work and describe the findings as ‘contested’ and that it was ‘wrong to jump to a conclusion’. It is extraordinary that a prime minister would use his position to call into question the findings of the independent investigation, and risk undermining trust in the Premier League’s processes.

“This has been a difficult year for football’s reputation. Fifa’s conduct around the World Cup has already raised serious questions about integrity in the game we love. At a moment like this, fans expect their prime minister to stand up for the rules in place, not to appear to side with a club found guilty of breaking them.”

Ms Sabine told the Guardian that the prime minister’s ties to ADUG should be looked at, saying she is planning to write to Downing Street and the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to demand details of their meetings.

“Football fans up and down the country deserve to know that the rules apply to everyone, however rich and powerful they are,” she said. “When the prime minister leaps to the defence of a club’s owners within hours of a verdict, people are entitled to ask what their relationship is.

“Andy Burnham must come clean and publish details of every meeting and conversation he has had with City Football Group, Abu Dhabi United Group or UAE government representatives, going back to his time as mayor – and that includes any hospitality freebies received.”

A Downing Street spokesman said on Thursday: “As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgement is serious and there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules.

open image in gallery The then Manchester mayor joins Prince Harry at Manchester City's training ground ( PA )

"He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.”

Former City and FA chairman David Bernstein said he was “concerned” about Mr Burnham’s comments and the issue was “something that politicians should be seen to be staying well away from”.

He told BBC Newsnight: “It is absolutely vital that this independent regulator can perform independently and without political interference and I think there are issues coming out of all this in terms of the board of directors, possibly the owners as well, where the independent regulator will need to get involved.”

City confirmed on Friday that they have lodged an appeal against the guilty verdict, having claimed the commission’s decision contained “clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”.

Downing Street has been contacted for comment.

News.title: FTSE 100 tumbles amid bond market sell-off
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. House prices fell unexpectedly last month as mortgage borrowers prepare for a jump in interest rates.

Typical property values declined by 0.2pc during September, reversing 0.2pc growth in August, according to the Nationwide house price index.

The figure was much worse than analysts had forecasts, with most expecting prices to remain steady.

Over the course of the year to September, the rate of house price growth halved from 1.6pc to 0.8pc, which was the weakest rate since December 2025.

The value of the average home has fallen to £274,251 over concerns the Bank of England is on the cusp of raising interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for mortgage holders.

Money markets indicate there is an 84pc chance policymakers will raise rates from 3.75pc to 4pc in November in an effort to bring down inflation caused by the Iran war energy shock.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:“Market activity and house prices have remained subdued in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop.

“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns.

“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank Rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Polanski urges Miliband to block Rosebank oil field over Israel links | Green leader claims North Sea project is a test of Foreign Secretary’s proposed sanctions regime

2) Netherlands ditches wealth tax over exodus fears | Dutch PM scraps plan to target paper profits, instead introducing a more convention capital gains levy

3) Diesel crisis deepens as UK’s biggest refinery shuts for 10 weeks | Fears of squeeze on supplies after fuel costs rise higher than £2 per litre

4) Debt-ridden France branded ‘the new sick man of Europe’ | Investors hope the European Central Bank sees the struggling country as ‘too big to fail’

5) Britain blocks foreign lawyers after surge in south Asian applicants | Bar Standards Board halts scheme unless candidates have already secured a position

What happened overnight

The cost of government borrowing edged higher in Asia as soaring energy costs sparked inflation fears.

Bond yields, a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money, surged in September as investors brace for a period where interest rates stay higher for ​longer.

The yield on benchmark US 10-year Treasury notes hit 5.31pc, the ‌highest level since mid-June 2007. The 10-year yield gained 87 basis points in the July-September quarter, the biggest quarterly rise since 1994.

Market focus has been on how long US Treasury yields stay above the psychologically important 5pc level, while some investors even contemplate the possibility of yields breaching 6pc.

Yields in Japan have climbed to multi-decade highs too, while those in Germany, France and Britain have all hit 17 to 19 year peaks.

On Thursday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government ​bond yield was at 3.11pc, not far from the 30-year high it hit last week.

Asian technology stocks rose after a boost from AI chipmaker Micron, ​although US bonds struggled ‌after their sharpest quarterly sell-off in more than three decades as inflation risks from elevated energy prices linger.

Stalling peace talks between the US and Iran to end the seven-month-long war in the Middle East have kept crude prices aloft.Brent futures surged 42pc in the July-September quarter.

The high-stakes earnings from Micron, a key supplier to AI bellwether Nvidia, signalled strong demand for AI memory chips, with financial commitments under long-term supply agreements at $32 billion, up from $22 billion in June.

That helped push tech-heavy stock markets in Asia higher. Japan’s Nikkei jumped over 3pc, and South Korea’s Kospi reversed earlier losses to gain 1.7pc. Taiwan’s stock benchmark was 0.8pc higher.

News.title: Chewing tobacco killed 250,000 people in one year, study shows
News.content:
Chewing tobacco killed around a quarter of a million people in 2023, with use of the product remaining stubbornly high, according to research.

The smokeless tobacco is particularly popular in south Asia that is placed between the cheek and lower gum. It is flavoured and sometimes sweetened, and users often spit out unwanted juices while chewing. It is often viewed as safer than smoking but it is a major cause of stroke, as well as head and neck cancer.

Chewing tobacco is different to white snus or nicotine pouches, which contain no tobacco. These white pouches are also made up of flavourings and sometimes sweeteners, and deliver a hit of nicotine through the lining of the mouth.

Despite a successful fight against smoking over the last few decades, rates of chewing tobacco use have fallen little and it has often been overlooked in tobacco control efforts, researchers point out. In a study published in the Lancet Global Health, researchers from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation in the US estimate that 241 million people aged 15 years and older used chewing tobacco in 2023.

Researchers looked at data on use in 204 countries between 1990 and 2023 and found that there was no significant decrease in the number of users of chewing tobacco over that period. And in 24 countries there was a significant uptick in the number of people using the product. Researchers estimate that about one in five men and one in 10 women in south Asia chewed tobacco in 2023.

Bangladesh has seen the biggest increase in the number of people using the product with 15 million new users between 1990 and 2023. Nepal, Madagascar and Yemen also saw increases in the number of users.

In India 105 million people chew tobacco regularly, accounting for just over two thirds of users globally. Historically, Indians would chew paan, tobacco in its raw form which was mixed with betel leaf and areca nut, a mild stimulant. But the use of chewing tobacco exploded in the 1980s when manufacturers began grinding these into a powder and selling them in packets known as gutkha. This was banned in 2012 but is still widely available. Chewing tobacco is also popular in Pakistan, China and Vietnam.

News.title: Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
News.content:
Dame Esther was a vocal supporter of the Assisted Dying Bill, claiming in March that most people “want and need” the right to end their own lives.

When the bill was defeated in the House of Commons in September, as MPs voted 286 to 270 against the legislation, she called it a “tragic day”. The bill would have allowed those with less than six months to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives.

In 2024, she said that she had joined the Dignitas assisted-dying clinic in Switzerland.

Writing for The Telegraph at the beginning of September, Rebecca Wilcox, Dame Esther’s daughter, said her mother was “too ill now to travel to Dignitas as she had planned and paid for”.

Earlier this month, Dame Esther said in a statement that it was too late for her to “buzz off” to the clinic in Switzerland and said Britain’s current laws on assisted dying are “messy and cruel”.

In a final message shared by her family, the presenter said she had been “immensely lucky” for the support she had received from the public, which she said had enabled her “to live such a long and happy life”.

She added: “Sadly, all good things come to an end, as they say. So I particularly wanted to say goodbye and thank you so very, very much. Perhaps I will see you eventually, on the other side. I do hope so. With very good wishes, as ever, Esther.”

News.title: Eight tips for improving your laptop’s performance (and save your sanity)
News.content:
MacBooks and Windows laptops both have modes intended to maximise battery life. Low Power Mode (Mac) and Power Saver (Windows) should be avoided if you want peak performance.

On a Mac, you’ll find the Low Power Mode switch in Settings > Battery. For the best experience, set this to Never, but remember to change it back if you need your MacBook to last longer.

On a Windows laptop, there are two controls you need to consider. Both are found in Settings > System > Power & Battery.

Energy Saver mode uses multiple tactics to reduce battery consumption, including lowering maximum power. Switch this off, and you have access to Power Mode controls.

Your options are Best Power Efficiency, Balanced and Best Performance. While Balanced is the default, I was able to unlock up to 33 per cent more power by playing around with these settings using my own laptop.

To make matters more complicated, some laptops have their own performance modes. Many Asus laptops have MyAsus or Armory Crate, for example. Lenovo has the Vantage app, Dell has MyDell, and MSI laptops have MSI Center.

3. Stop applications from opening on start-up

If your laptop is slow when it first starts up, it may be because a whole bunch of apps have been given the green light to wake up with it.

Some applications such as antivirus software are critical, but most can be toggled off. As an example, I make sure apps such as Spotify, Steam and WhatsApp don’t open on startup; I only launch them when I need them.

On a MacBook, you can see which apps have this permission in Settings > General, under Open at Login. Select an app entry and click the “minus” button to remove it.

On a Windows laptop, you’ll find the list of start-up apps in Settings > Apps > Startup. Each entry has a little on/off slider.

4. Free up storage space

News.title: Why the UK medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks
News.content:
The UK’s medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks, experts have warned, with the NHS dependent on a system where much of the world relies on a handful of countries for its drug supplies.

India and China are the backbone of the global medicines market, manufacturing around two-thirds of the world’s active pharmaceutical ingredients. This leaves countries exposed to factory shutdowns, natural disasters, geopolitical tensions, shipping disruption and sudden changes in the price or availability of raw materials, experts told The Telegraph.

“We rely now more than ever on other countries to make sure we can get access to the medicines that the vast majority of people take,” said Dr James Davies, director of research and insights at Community Pharmacy England.

Nearly all the active ingredients in the UK’s most widely used medicines are made overseas, around 80 per cent of them in China and India, leaving the NHS exposed to shocks thousands of miles beyond its control.

The resilience of Britain’s medicine supply has eroded gradually in recent years, as global instability has placed growing strain on the supply chains it depends on.

“We’ve seen more global turbulence in general,” said Dr Davies. “It’s not unique to the UK, but it’s affecting countries across Europe, across the Western world, with the Iran war, with difficulties flying things over Ukraine and Russia, and challenges with shipping in the Red Sea.”

In the UK, shortages have been reported across a wide range of products, including antibiotics, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder medicines, epilepsy treatments, hormone replacement therapy, and some diabetes medicines.

The drugs most at risk are the cheapest and most widely used – statins, blood pressure pills and antibiotics – taken by millions of people and manufactured in China and India at huge scale and minimal cost.

“Some antibiotics are almost exclusively made in China,” said Dr Davies. “For some of the blood pressure medicines, they’re more likely to be made in India. But across the board, those two are where most of the raw ingredients for those active pharmaceutical ingredients come from.”

News.title: Fraudster jailed for 41 years over Pakistani nurse scam in Saudi
News.content:
A fraudster who sent 92 Pakistani nurses to Saudi Arabia on fake documents in an elaborate scam to provide workers for short-staffed Gulf hospitals has been jailed for 41 years.

Ghulam Zulfiqar Ali used forged experience certificates, created fake verification QR codes and phoney employment platform IDs.

Ali was being paid by the Saudi authorities to find staff, but also charged genuine Pakistani nurses who wanted a job overseas, in a racket that has caused major embarrassment to the Pakistan’s authorities.

Gulf nations including Saudi Arabia are experiencing a severe shortage of nurses, compounded by rapid population growth, a rising burden of chronic diseases, and heavy dependence on nurses from abroad.

The World Health Organization (WHO) forecasts a global shortfall of 4.5 million nurses by 2030, and recruiting nurses for developed countries is a lucrative trade.

The 91 women were all genuine nurses, but did not meet the criteria for the “Nurse Highly Qualified” visa category under which they were sent.

When the Saudi authorities realised the fraud they deported all the nurses.

Syed Shehzad Nadeem Bukhari, director of Pakistan’s Federal Investigation Agency, told the Telegraph: “They lost both their money and their employment, and the incident caused serious embarrassment to Pakistan internationally.”

Investigators found that between October 2022 and September 2023, a Pakistani employment firm called M/S Sahou Manpower obtained permissions for the recruitment of 108 nurses for a Saudi-based manpower company, to work in hospitals under the visa category “Nurse Highly Qualified”.

The investigation found the Saudi employer bore all recruitment costs, including visa processing fees and air tickets.

It paid the Pakistani recruiting firm between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,100 (GBP 830) per candidate. However, Ali was also demanding between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,000 (GBP 750) from each nurse.

Investigators found the candidates were genuine nurses, but did not meet experience requirements and were given fake certificates.

Meanwhile Ali had not uploaded their details to Saudi systems designed to verify and check qualifications and give each applicant a QR code. Instead he provided them with faked QR codes and verification platform IDs.

Ali was convicted of cheating, two counts of forgery and emigration offences.

He was given 41 years imprisonment by the special court in Rawalpindi. He was also fined £1,904 and ordered to pay £25,031 compensation – £272 to each of the 92 nurses.

His accomplice, Ghulam Fareed, was given three years’ imprisonment and a £544 penalty.

Nasreen Begum, one of nurses, told the Telegraph: “We are thankful to FIA for compensation. Most of us have genuine qualifications as nurse-midwives, licenced practical nurses, clinical nursing assistants and a lady health visitor but our documents weren’t verified and that landed us in a difficult situation.”

Zeenat Khan, another victim of the fraud, said she had opted to take a job in Saudi Arabia because she was jobless despite having nursing qualifications.

She said: “I have three kids and wanted to give them a good education. Now, I hope to get back my money,” she said.

Swera Ali said she had been working in a private hospital in her native Lahore, Punjab province, but received only £50 a month and performed 16 hours duty.

She said: “My parents took a loan from relatives to facilitate me, but my hope of making money from an overseas job was short-lived when they deported us after less than a month.”

Mr Bukhari added: “The investigation established that their nursing diplomas were genuine. The fake QR codes and fake [employment platform] IDs were created by the accused, and the experience certificates were forged by the visa agent without the knowledge of the nurses.”

News.title: How vaccines and antibiotics can beat some cancers
News.content:
At least one in eight cancers worldwide are caused by viruses and bacteria, according to a new study published in The Lancet.

An estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 – out of a total of 20 million recorded worldwide – were caused by common infections, almost all of which could have been prevented with treatments such as antibiotics or vaccines.

Almost half of infection-linked cancers, around 760,000 cases, were caused by H. pylori, a bacterium that infects the stomach, researchers from the International Agency for Research on Cancer found.

The pathogen, which is typically ingested through contaminated food and water and is carried by around 60 per cent of the world’s population at any given time, can remain relatively undetected in the gut for between 20 and 40 years without causing any symptoms.

If left untreated, it can trigger chronic inflammation in the stomach and cellular mutations that, in some cases, lead to gastric cancer.

Cases of stomach cancer linked to H. pylori are particularly common in East Asia, where roughly 80 per cent of the population carries the bacterium. This is due in part to the prevalence of a more aggressive strain of the pathogen, known as CagA, which is endemic to the region.

East Asian diets – which typically include salty, pickled or smoked foods – can also damage the stomach’s protective lining and accelerate the inflammatory processes that can contribute to stomach cancer, researchers have found.

While H. pylori infection is treatable with a course of antibiotics, its symptoms often mimic those of other digestive problems and can be difficult to distinguish without testing.

This means the infection can remain undetected for years, allowing inflammation and damage to progress.

Sports.title: Man City charges LIVE: Appeal confirmed in new statement taking aim at the Premier League
Sports.content:
Manchester City have formally confirmed they have launched an appeal after being found guilty of 114 breaches of Premier League financial rules

Manchester City have confirmed that they have lodged an appeal against 'the opinion' of the Premier League independent commission to find them guilty of 114 breaches of financial rules

The club said in a statement: "The club's firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.

"The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

"We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete."

The Premier League announced earlier this week that City had been found guilty of 114 charges brought against them for financial breaches.

Their top-flight rivals are said to be readying legal action against them to the tune of £800million, while a cross-party group of MPs have urged HMRC to investigate the tax implications of the Premier League's charges. The FA have also now put out a statement, their first on the matter since the Premier League verdict was revealed.

It now remains to be seen what punishment is given to City, with reports claiming that chiefs at other football clubs want a sanction to be imposed before the end of the season.

City are now set to argue that the government of Abu Dhabi - not the club's owners - part-funded the "sham" sponsorship deals that contributed to them breaching Premier League financial rules.

Sports.title: 'I had to leave Man Utd because I wasn't wanted - it wasn't good for me'
Sports.content:
'I had to leave Man Utd because I wasn't wanted - it wasn't good for me'

A former Manchester United star lambasted the club for their treatment of him

View 2 Images Romelu Lukaku's tenure at Manchester United lasted just two years (Image: Gareth Copley/Getty Images)

Romelu Lukaku remains on track to reach 100 international goals in an extraordinary national team career with Belgium. The Fenerbahce striker could feature in the country's Nations League clash against Turkey on Friday night (October 2) and has long been the go-to man for his nation, for whom he's scored 93 goals in 133 games.

‌



‌



It's form he never quite managed at Manchester United. The 33-year-old joined the Old Trafford outfit from Everton in a £75million deal in 2017. Despite many expecting Lukaku to lead the line for United for years to come, especially after coming off a career-best 25-goal season for the Toffees, the striker lasted just two years at Old Trafford.

‌



His goalscoring record of 42 goals in 96 across all competitions for United was a respectable tally, but not what United were likely expecting for the fee they invested in him. He clinched a £74m move to Inter Milan in the summer of 2019 and claimed he didn't feel protected by the club after reports of his uncertain future were constant.

‌



Lukaku appeared on NBA champion Josh Hart’s LightHarted podcast in an interview that was recorded before his move to Italy. He said: "A lot of stuff has been said where I didn’t feel protected. I felt like a lot of rumours, ‘Rom going there’, ‘They don’t want Rom’, and nobody came out to shut it down.

"It was for a good three, four weeks. I’m waiting for someone to come out and shut it down. It didn’t happen. I had my conversation, told them it was better to go our separate ways. If you don’t want to protect somebody, all these rumours come out.

Portuguese media deliver damning Cristiano Ronaldo verdict as players refuse to discuss him READ MORE :

"I just wanted you to say: ‘Rom is going to fight for his place,’ but it never happened for four, five months. If you’re happy, you find a way. It doesn’t matter if you’re on the bench or starting but nobody told me that was the situation, so I thought for two, three weeks to analyse, see all this s*** coming out in the media."

‌



The ex-Chelsea and Everton striker appeared to suggest he knew where leaks about his future had originated from and claimed he was among the scapegoats at United when the side had lost games.

View 2 Images Romelu Lukaku didn't reach the heights expected of him at Old Trafford (Image: Getty Images)

He explained: "Who leaks it? Not me. Not my agent. I see it on my phone come out of nowhere. I told them it’s not good for me to be at a place where I’m not wanted. We’re not stupid. They consider us dumb but we are not dumb. We know who is doing leaks and stuff.

‌



"I told them, you can’t be working like this, it’s better for me to go now. They have to find somebody [to blame]," he said. "It is Pogba, it is me or it is Alexis. It’s the three of us all the time. For me, I just see it in many ways."

Lukaku reinvented himself at Inter Milan with 64 goals scored in 95 games while leading the Italian giants to the Serie A title in 2020. His exploits saw him clinch a return to Stamford Bridge in 2021 for £90m, but his reunion with Chelsea was disastrous.

Article continues below

In his three years in west London, he spent just one of them at the club, with two seasons spent on loan, first back at Inter Milan and another with Roma. He secured a permanent move to Napoli in 2024 and won his second league title in his debut campaign in Naples. After an injury-ravaged second season at the club, he joined Fenerbahce this past summer.

Sports.title: Premier League appeal deadline could change after Man City tear into 'unsafe' verdict
Sports.content:
Premier League appeal deadline could change after Man City tear into 'unsafe' verdict

Manchester City have appealed a guilty verdict regarding breaches of the Premier League's financial rules, with officials now working to conclude the case

View 3 Images Manchester City have lodged an appeal to the Premier League (Image: Getty Images)

The Premier League, in theory, face a strict deadline following Manchester City's appeal against a guilty verdict on financial breaches, though the situation could yet change. City were incensed when an independent panel ruled that the club had made infractions between 2009 and 2018.

‌



‌



A damning statement further alleged that the Abu Dhabi United Group club had 'artificially inflated' revenue to the tune of £900million in order to comply with regulations, and accused them of "sham" sponsorship deals. City have since confirmed they have challenged the panel's findings, as they look to establish the innocence they have maintained throughout the entire saga.

‌



A statement released on Friday morning read: "Manchester City Football Club can confirm that at 7pm on Thursday 1st October 2026 the Club lodged its comprehensive Appeal against the opinion of the Premier League Commission, in relation to the Premier League disciplinary matter.

‌



Man City charges LIVE: Appeal confirmed in new statement taking aim at the Premier League READ MORE :

"The Club's firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe. The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

"We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete.

The FA also issued a statement of their own on Friday, writing: "The Independent Commission's decision has significant implications for the integrity of the game. We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate.

‌



"As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage. We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely."

View 3 Images The Football Association have issued a statement on Manchester City's charges (Image: Kevin Hodgson/MI News/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

FOLLOW OUR MAN CITY FB PAGE! Follow our Manchester City Mirror Football Facebook page

‌



As a consequence of the appeal, the Premier League now theoretically has a limited window to deliver a final verdict. That's because the rules and regulations stipulate that any appeal hearing must occur within 12 weeks of a challenge being lodged.

A verdict is also required from the appeals board no more than 30 days after the hearing concludes. Taking everything into account, it means that the Premier League ought to deliver a final decision no later than January 23, 2027.

However, reports indicate that another section of the Premier League code outlines how the regulation can be set aside if necessary. It is also suggested that said rule was only drafted this summer.

‌



View 3 Images Manchester City have been ruled guilty of financial breaches (Image: Gary Oakley/PA Wire)

If accurate, it means the Premier League could ultimately take as long as they deem necessary to scrutinise every aspect of the case in minute detail. That would once again leave football supporters and rival clubs enduring a prolonged wait to finally discover City's fate.

The club are, however, unable to take the case to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), owing to a separate Premier League ruling. The English top flight's regulations stipulate that all disputes and appeals must be handled within England and Wales.

Article continues below

Given that CAS is headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland, City will find themselves unable to call upon the governing body should they be unhappy with the league's conclusions.

Sports.title: Unai Emery makes bombshell claim about Premier League rivals after Man City verdict
Sports.content:
Unai Emery makes bombshell claim about Premier League rivals after Man City verdict

Manchester City have launched an appeal after being found guilty of serious financial breaches, including 'sham' sponsorship deals, and Unai Emery has given a worrying response

View 2 Images Unai Emery has spoken about the Manchester City case (Image: Marc Atkins/Getty Images)

Aston Villa manager Unai Emery has responded to the Manchester City scandal by shockingly claiming that "many other clubs" have "inflated their budgets".

‌



‌



City have launched an appeal after a Premier League commission found them guilty of 114 of the 115 charges against them. The club was found to have used a "disguised funding scheme" between 2009 and 2018 to hide secret funding of more than £830million.

‌



They are expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were not "sham" arrangements used to "disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities", but were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners.

‌



The bombshell news is still being processed, with rival Premier League clubs reportedly keen for City to be punished harshly, given the extent of their financial breaches. Aston Villa boss Emery has now become the first Premier League manager to comment publicly on City's case, giving a worrying response.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Man City charges LIVE: Appeal confirmed in new statement taking aim at the Premier League READ MORE :

Asked by Diario de Sevilla what the impact would be on the Premier League, Emery replied: "It's an issue that was already known. Because we all have our restrictions, we have to sell players to comply with Financial Fair Play, we have to figure out how to draw up contracts with new people.

‌



"Financial Fair Play seeks a financial balance so that what you generate is spent and there isn't inflation. Yes, many other clubs have inflated their budgets, and now it's coming to light, and naturally there's a decline.

"That's something that the courts and those responsible will have to decide. I feel sorry because how that team played. With [Pep] Guardiola, there were times when they were unmatched."

View 2 Images Manchester City owner Sheikh Mansour has been put under the spotlight (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Back in June, Aston Villa were fined £19.4m by European football's governing body, UEFA, for a "significant breach" of its squad-cost rule for 2025. Chelsea, Nottingham Forest and Newcastle were all also fined for breaches of UEFA's rules, which differ to the Premier League's.

Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules are designed to keep club's spending in check and ensure their expenditure is broadly in line with what they are earning. By artificially increasing sponsorship deals, City were able to cheat the system.

City claim that the money in question came from the Abu Dhabi government, not owners Abu Dhabi United Group. ADUG is a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour.

‌



The club has always strongly denied wrongdoing, claiming to have 'irrefutable evidence' and their decision to launch an appeal means the case will continue for much longer.

But they could be forced to face up to very serious consequences, with the commission having the power to impose heavy fines, points deductions or even relegation. There have also been calls for the titles City won during the nine-year period in question to be stripped, although that is unlikely.

Sports.title: Man City's 'irrefutable evidence' and brutal reality in bid to appeal Premier League verdict
Sports.content:
It's the scandal which has rocked the Premier League to its very core.

Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges which were levied against them back in February 2023, a verdict which has immediately tainted the trophy-laden era overseen by their owners.

Talk of asterisks and the stripping of titles has been rife in the days following the verdict and court of public opinion has already spoken. But while people are speculating over City's potential - and substantial - looming punishment, the club have already made it clear that they will fight the damning verdicts until the bitter end by launching an appeal.

With the next stage of the saga now pending, Mirror Football asks the question: where do things stand right now?

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

The verdict

View 3 Images Manchester City have enjoyed a trophy-laden period (Image: Getty Images)

It was just over one week ago that the football world was rocked to its very core: Manchester City had been found guilty of all but one of the serious charges laid against them.

‌



That included an elaborate 'Disguised Funding Scheme', which was instigated between 2009 and 2018 to improperly declare £949.94m worth of commercial sponsorship revenue. Just £119.25m of that sum was proven to be legitimate base fee payments courtesy of Abu Dhabi sponsors, meaning City banked just under £830.7m direct from their owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).

Not only did City's grossly inflated revenue figures from that period help finance the run of domestic dominance they enjoyed, there were other damning revelations laid out in black and white along with the ruthless takedown of City's 'sham' contracts.

The commission brutally dismissed the accounts given by some of City's witnesses, who are said to have given evidence 'that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest'. The scathing statement redacted the details of such individuals, plus lawyers and other names.

Confirmation of another redacted individual receiving secret payments beyond their initial contract was also outlined in a 40-page document which has absolutely torched both Manchester City's reputation and their lengthy list of accolades.

‌



City's 'irrefutable' evidence

View 3 Images Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Ferran Soriano have both spoken in the wake of the verdict (Image: Robbie Jay Barratt - AMA/Getty Images)

In the aftermath of the Premier League's seismic ruling, Manchester City have been remarkably calm. City's chairman, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, even released a statement the day after reports revealing the guilty verdict, illustrating that the club were still steadfast in their belief that they would be proven innocent.

Ferran Soriano, City's chief executive, went one further in a video message to staff after the Premier League verdict was published, shedding light on the club's 'irrefutable evidence' which had been previously referenced by Al Mubarak.

We now know City's explanation for the figures referenced above: that the funding came from the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners.

‌



“The whole Premier League case against us is based on a single false accusation – that the owner’s personal money was somehow and secretly put into the club via some sponsors from Abu Dhabi. This is just not true,” said Soriano.

“Irrefutable evidence has been provided to the Premier League commission that shows that it could not happen and that it did not happen. This includes bank statements, money transfers, witnesses and everything necessary to categorically demonstrate the money did not come from the owner.”

The appeal - and what's next

We now know what the appeal is likely to be largely based on. Whether it will be Manchester City's silver bullet is up for debate, though - particularly as that explanation has already been rejected in the Premier League's 40-page verdict.

So, not only is City's explanation that the money came direct from Abu Dhabi nothing new in terms of the initial hearing, it was dismissed as “untrue” in the ruling, meaning City will have to convince any appeal panel that such a verdict was incorrect.

‌



Whether that is plausible is, again, up for debate. It is worth noting the strong language that was used to dismiss City's explanation, which the commission felt was “concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the disguised funding scheme”.

View 3 Images City's title triumphs have come into question (Image: Getty)

It feels like it would require a pretty seismic turnaround for City's name to be cleared on that front. And whether or not people would accept it after the revelations laid bare in this verdict is another matter altogether.

City confirmed on Friday that they had officially lodged their appeal on Thursday night. Per the updated Premier League rules in the summer, this would need to be concluded within 12 weeks. The new three-person panel would then have 30 days to make their decision, which would put a timeframe for an undisputed outcome towards the end of January.

‌



However, there is another potential twist in the saga: City could argue that as this process started well before the implementation of said new rules at the start of this season, such a timeframe should not apply. And that is why nobody really knows how much longer this saga will drag on for - some Premier League clubs even fear the saga will stretch well beyond the end of the 2026-27 campaign.

Manchester City's hierarchy insist the battle is far from over. On that front, at least, they may very well be right.

Sports.title: We handed Man City the ultimate punishment and simulated 10 seasons – here's how bad things got
Sports.content:
We handed Man City the ultimate punishment and simulated 10 seasons – here's how bad things got

What would happen if Manchester City were kicked down to non-league? We asked Football Manager to find out

View 7 Images Imagine Enzo Maresca managing in the National League (Image: Molly Darlington/Getty Images)

Manchester City are set for another trophy-laden era, even if they receive the worst possible punishment after being found guilty of 114 Premier League rule breaches.

‌



‌



At least according to everyone's favourite management game, Football Manager. City, who continue to deny any wrongdoing and have appealed against the independent commission's verdict, and the rest of football are waiting to see what punishment will be meted out to the eight-time Premier League champions.

‌



Potential sanctions include expulsion from the top flight, a points deduction and a huge fine. The most severe penalty could see City booted all the way down to the National League, leading to matches against the likes of Boston United, Hornchurch and a derby with Altrincham.

‌



An awful prospect for City fans - certainly for the ones who have only known Premier League glory - but a fascinating one for everyone else. We turned to Football Manager 26's pre-game editor to simulate 10 City seasons ahead from the fifth tier.

FOLLOW OUR MAN CITY FB PAGE! Follow our Manchester City Mirror Football Facebook page

Setting up the FM experiment

After demoting City four consecutive times, we granted the highest-placed club in each division a reprieve from relegation. That handed a lifeline to West Ham United, Oxford United, Exeter City and Harrogate Town in their respective leagues.

‌



Following that, we tweaked a number of behind-the-scenes statistics to mirror the club's decline in reputation and morale, taking into account how players such as Erling Haaland, Enzo Fernandez and Gianluigi Donnarumma would react if they were suddenly expected to compete in the fifth tier.

Using a custom database refreshed with the summer's most significant transfers, we set about our task. With everything loaded up and ready to go, we simulated 10 seasons to discover whether City could fight their way back to the summit.

View 7 Images Erling Haaland was quickly on his way out of the club (Image: Getty Images)

‌



National League reality

The player exodus was instant. Six of City's top earners, including Haaland, demanded a move. The likes of Fernandez and Donnarumma had little appetite to stick around for fixtures against Southend United or Gateshead, either.

Haaland secured a move to Barcelona, with Rayan Cherki following him to the Catalan capital. Real Madrid swooped for Fernandez, while Donnarumma and Jeremy Doku headed to Newcastle, and Antoine Semenyo left for Atletico Madrid. The remainder of the squad surprisingly stayed intact.

View 7 Images City had to make do with derbies against Altrincham in the National League (Image: Getty Images)

‌



City were utterly dominant in their first season in the National League. The Citizens won 44 of their 46 matches, drawing two, and stormed to the title with 134 points. Despite holding on to a host of big-name stars, however, the club were dumped out of the FA Cup by MK Dons.

There was cause for celebration, as the club lifted the FA Trophy, though this triumph stood in stark contrast to the European night supporters had grown accustomed to.

Enzo Maresca remained at the helm and oversaw a remarkable transformation in Nico O'Reilly, who emerged as the club's leading scorer that campaign with 23 goals. Unsurprisingly, City opted against dipping into the transfer market, and none of their star names departed until the summer.

‌



Back in the EFL

City's return to the EFL also got off to a flying start. Another commanding league campaign saw City cruise to the League Two title, though they did suffer two defeats and draw eight times, clinching the championship with a staggering 34-point margin over runners-up Chesterfield.

Further FA Cup misery followed, with a third-round exit at the hands of Bolton Wanderers. Season two brought no additional silverware, as Norwich City knocked the Sky Blues out of the League Cup, while Millwall triumphed in a penalty shoot-out in the FA Cup quarter-finals.

New free signing Milan Smit from Stoke City was City's leading marksman with 19 goals as City finally opened their chequebook again. On this occasion, it was a comparatively modest outlay for James Justin from Leeds United at just £5.5m that represented their biggest expenditure.

‌



View 7 Images Enzo Maresca was sacked after failing to get City out of the Championship (Image: Getty)

The departures before the season kicked off were equally noteworthy. Elliot Anderson, O'Reilly and Josko Gvardiol were amongst the high-profile names who had remained at City despite the club languishing in the fourth tier. All three eventually moved on during the summer.

Anderson departed for Bournemouth for £29.5m, while O'Reilly switched to Spurs for £26.5m. Gvardiol reunited with Haaland at the Camp Nou in a staggering £88m transfer.

‌



Further glory followed in the third year of exile. Another league title was clinched in League One, as the Citizens swept past runners-up Salford City by 25 points, amassing 107 points from 33 victories and eight draws, although that was the sole piece of silverware in season three.

Maresca's time runs out in the Championship

Back up to the Championship, then, with just one promotion standing between City and a Premier League return. In theory, at least.

However, the City train ran out of steam upon entering the world's toughest domestic non-top-flight division. Having raced through the lower reaches, City couldn't break free of mid-table mediocrity in year four and finished 11th.

‌



Maresca was eventually dismissed, with legend Richard Dunne stepping in for the remainder of the campaign as caretaker boss before making way in the summer for Regis Le Bris. The Frenchman didn't deliver instant success, guiding City to 10th place. But in their third year of Championship action, five years after being booted out of the Premier League, they finally reached the promotion play-offs.

View 7 Images Regis Le Bris was handed the reins (Image: James Gill - Danehouse, Getty Images)

The Blues overcame West Brom in the semis to set up a nail-biting final against Coventry City, which ended in disappointment for Le Bris' troops in a 3-2 loss. It wasn't the end of City's suffering.

‌



Twelve months later, they were back in the play-offs. After disposing of West Brom once more in the semi-finals, Wolves crushed City's dreams of returning to the top tier with a 1-0 victory at Wembley.

Determined to put things right, Le Bris invested heavily in the summer. A whopping £88m was splashed on Porto's Brazilian forward William Gomes, while a combined £95m secured Marc Pubill from Bayern Munich and defensive midfielder Marc Cascado from Sunderland.

At last, City secured their return to the Premier League. Le Bris masterminded a league campaign that clinched the Championship crown at the fifth attempt with 86 points.

‌



Back in the big time

Having cemented his status as a City cult hero, Le Bris' next challenge was to climb the Premier League standings as rapidly as possible. Opting to place faith in the majority of his current squad, the City manager decided against lavish spending upon returning to the top division.

Striker Defari Richardson proved the marquee acquisition in a £20m switch from Aston Villa. Le Bris' judgment proved largely sound as his team finished seventh to secure Europa League qualification at the first opportunity. The following year, City invested a combined £75m on fresh talent ahead of European competition. However, it proved insufficient.

City crashed out of the Europa League at the quarter-final stage, succumbing to eventual runners-up Real Betis. Chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak was in an unforgiving mood as Le Bris was dismissed in January 2036 after five years at the helm with City 14th in the table.

‌



Fellow Frenchman, Julien Stephan, who had captured the Championship, League Cup and FA Cup with Ipswich Town in our simulation, assumed control. He guided City to a modest 11th place.

View 7 Images Julien Stephan took over from Le Bris (Image: PA)

What about Man United and the wider football landscape?

City's expulsion created a void at the summit of English football. Manchester United supporters could scarcely dream of a more satisfying scenario than their club stepping up to fill it.

‌



But would United turn that golden opportunity into tangible success? Sadly for the red half of the city, not quite.

Instead, Arsenal tightened their grip on the division, forging a new dynasty. The Gunners claimed the league title six consecutive times in our simulation, adding two more championships after arch-rivals Spurs and Liverpool each won the Premier League.

United were far from disgraced over the 10-year period, although Michael Carrick was dismissed in December 2026. His successor, PSG chief Luis Enrique, took the reins at the close of that season, and the transformation was striking. He remained at the helm throughout the entire simulation, overseeing 510 matches across a nine-year spell.

‌



View 7 Images Mikel Arteta and Arsenal kept lifting Premier League titles (Image: Getty)

He emerged victorious in 309 of those outings, collecting three trophies for the Red Devils along the way. Two FA Cup triumphs were complemented by a Europa League crown, as league finishes fluctuated between third and sixth.

The Premier League even witnessed the same trio of sides occupying the top positions for three successive seasons. Arsenal, runners-up Liverpool and third-placed Newcastle dominated the standings for three years on the trot.

‌



On the European stage, Arsenal finally got their hands on the Champions League trophy by defeating Liverpool in the final during season four. Barcelona, PSG, Liverpool and Real Madrid all lifted the prestigious prize at least once during the simulation.

Haaland guided Barca to three Champions League titles, while Pep Guardiola went on to manage both Portugal and Germany before making a dramatic return to club football. His surprise appointment as Chelsea boss nearly produced a Champions League title, only for them to fall short against PSG in the final.

City's starting XI 10 years after relegation to the National League: Zion Suzuki (GK), Marc Pubill (RB), Jaydee Canvot (CB), Abdukodir Khusanov (CB), Daniel Svensson (LB), Mamadou Coulibaly (DM), Marc Casado (DM), Cole Campbell (RW), Allan (CAM), William Gomes (LW), Hamza Abdelkarim (ST).
