World.title: The U.S. Senate is up for grabs. Can this Ohio Democrat win back working class votes?
World.content:
The U.S. Senate is up for grabs. Can this Ohio Democrat win back working class votes?

toggle caption i Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly.

COLUMBUS, PAINESVILLE AND AKRON, Ohio — It was a raucous homecoming for Sherrod Brown.

AC/DC's "Thunderstruck" blared from ballroom speakers. Union stalwarts representing steelworkers, utility workers, construction workers and others greeted the 73-year-old Democrat with resounding cheers and endless handshakes.

This was the biennial gathering of the Ohio AFL-CIO, a crowd Brown has kept at the forefront of his agenda throughout his 50 years in public office, including 32 years in the U.S. Congress.

And these are the people Brown is counting on to send him back to Washington after suffering defeat at the polls two years ago.

Sponsor Message

"I want you to talk to people, because people will listen to you," he implored. "I want you to share information — how I spent my whole career fighting for workers."

If you're a pipefitter, he told the room, other pipefitters will listen to you, as will your friends at church and school and in your neighborhood.

"Tell them how important this election is, and how important it is that they get out and vote," he said.

A pivotal race

Brown's appeal to labor unions comes two years after the three-term U.S. senator was unseated by GOP businessman Bernie Moreno, losing in a year when President Trump won the most votes of any presidential candidate in Ohio history.

Now, Brown is hoping to regain a U.S. Senate seat by defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill JD Vance's seat early last year. The race remains a toss-up, one that could determine control of the Senate for Trump's final two years in office.

With early voting set to begin Oct. 6, union members are knocking on doors, phone banking and showing up at rallies for Brown. They're hoping to drum up enough support to overcome a shift that took hold in Ohio in 2016, when Trump ran on a promise to revitalize factories and put people back to work. That year, Trump won 54% of union households in the state, while Hillary Clinton won just 41%.

Sponsor Message

"Back when Hillary was running, so many people just — they wanted change," says Dave Janiszewski, a Democrat who split his working years between a steel plant and a paper plant before retiring nine years ago.

toggle caption i Andrea Hsu/NPR

Now, donning a navy and gold United Steelworkers Political Action Committee jacket, Janiszewski is spending his days canvassing middle class neighborhoods around Columbus, doing exactly what Brown called for: knocking on the doors of union households, trying to persuade voters who aren't sure about Brown, or about voting in the midterms at all, that he's their guy.

"I've personally met him, know him — I've been around him since 2012," Janiszewski tells one young man who comes to the door. "He's always been there for working people."

A Democrat in an increasingly red state

Initially, Brown withstood Ohio's electoral shift to the right, winning re-election to a third Senate term in 2018, two years after Trump was first elected president. Aside from judges, Brown was the only Democrat still winning statewide races in Ohio.

Janiszewski says Ohio workers were clear on what Brown stood for. People knew him as the guy who vehemently opposed NAFTA, who showed up on picket lines, who only wore suits made in Ohio. In 2021, Brown pushed through legislation that saved the pensions of millions of union workers from insolvency. It was called the Butch Lewis Act , named after an Ohio truck driver who died while working to protect retiree benefits.

"Anything that we needed, he was there for us," says Janiszewski.

Still, by 2024, conditions proved insurmountable. At the top of the ticket, Trump defeated then-Vice President Kamala Harris by more than 11 percentage points. Brown lost to Moreno by less than 4 percentage points.

Dorsey Hager, executive secretary-treasurer of the Columbus/Central Ohio Building and Construction Trades Council, says those numbers are telling.

"It's no secret that President Trump won the state in '16, '20, and '24. A lot of that was due unfortunately to our members voting and supporting him and supporting some downballot Republicans, too," says Hager, noting that the council has supported Republicans in the past but has endorsed Brown this fall.

Sponsor Message

Hager is hopeful many of his members will follow that endorsement. Even though jobs are plentiful, he says many construction workers have told him they're suffering from high gas and diesel prices, high food prices and overall inflation.

"They're feeling it very hard," he says.

A split among labor

It's often said that union voters are not a monolith, and that's ever apparent in the U.S. Senate race in Ohio this fall. While most labor organizations have endorsed Brown, the building trades councils in Cleveland and Toledo have endorsed Husted, calling him a "friend and advocate" for construction workers. The Boilermakers union is also backing Husted, citing his support for union jobs in power plants, refineries and shipbuilding.

toggle caption i Andrew Harnik/Getty Images North America

On the campaign trail, Brown is trying to counter those narratives, arguing that Husted is only looking out for Wall Street, drug companies, and the tech companies now building data centers across Ohio, thanks to massive tax breaks Husted championed as lieutenant governor.

But in Lake County, one of eight Ohio counties that abandoned Brown in the last election, Republican commissioner John Plecnik is confident union members will choose Husted this fall if only because Husted supports Trump.

"People aren't stupid. They know that the borders were wide open during President Biden's term, and it was hurting labor. It was hurting salaries," Plecnik says. "Now that we see strong border security, you're starting to see salaries tick back up again, jobs tick back up again."

A boost from public employees

While the phrase "union voter" often calls to mind a blue-collar worker, the Brown campaign is also focused on the state's unionized teachers, local government workers, and other public sector workers.

As part of his stump speech, Brown is reminding them of his final act in the Senate. Weeks after losing the 2024 election, Brown, along with Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins, pushed through the Social Security Fairness Act, restoring full social security benefits to millions of public employees, including a couple hundred thousand in Ohio.

Sponsor Message

One of them is Patty Taylor, who worked in IT for the Akron Housing Authority for almost 30 years. To supplement her income, she sometimes took seasonal work with employers like UPS, FedEx and the department store Kohl's, and then worked a full-time job for a private company after retiring from the government. Those private sector jobs earned her social security benefits. But under a decades-old provision, those benefits would have been significantly reduced because she also has a government pension from her housing authority job, where she didn't pay Social Security taxes.

toggle caption i Patty Taylor

Brown and his cosponsors called it an unjust penalty. Their bill cleared the Senate by a vote of 76 to 20. Taylor, who's now 69, credits Brown with saving her retirement.

"He stood up for me, and he didn't even know me," she says. "If it wasn't for me getting the [full] Social Security, I would really, really be hurting right now."

So now, she's giving back.

In her retirement, Taylor is serving as secretary-treasurer for the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees Retiree Chapter 1184. This fall, she's been spearheading a postcard writing campaign for Brown and the Democrat running for Ohio governor, Amy Acton. She has handwritten hundreds of postcards urging AFSCME members to vote and recruited other retirees to do the same.

Along the way, she's made sure to talk up Brown's last vote in the Senate.

"It has changed some of the people's lives that are in our subchapter," she says. "They said, 'We'll do postcards. How many postcards can I do?'"

World.title: Cornell probe: Governor vows to change N.Y. rape law that makes reporting hard when intoxication present
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Letitia James, attorney general of New York, says her office will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses and, 'if warranted, pursue prosecutions' after a civil suit revealed allegations of a 2024 gang rape of a woman attending Cornell University and sparked questions about how the initial investigation was handled.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul says she intends to "close the loophole" in her state's law that currently makes it difficult for sexual assault survivors to claim they were mentally incapacitated during an assault if they were voluntarily intoxicated.

Hochul and the state attorney general spoke with reporters Friday morning about the criminal investigation into a woman's allegations that she was gang raped at a Cornell University fraternity house.

"Voluntary intoxication is not a licence for sexual assault or gang rape. Period," Hochul said.

WATCH | Investigation into 'Cornell 7' reopened: U.S. prosecutors reopen alleged gang rape investigation at Cornell University | Duration closed caption 5:08 Prosecutors in New York state are reopening an investigation into an alleged gang rape at Cornell University in 2024. The alleged victim, identified as Jane Doe, filed the lawsuit earlier this month saying she was drugged and raped by seven fraternity members, who have since been dubbed the 'Cornell 7.'

"If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol."

Hochul announced Thursday she appointed the office of Attorney General Letitia James as the special prosecutor to oversee the investigation, saying she had lost faith in the local district attorney's ability to handle the case.

The attorney general will oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury.

"What we learned yesterday raised even more troubling questions," Hochul said on Friday.

"According to news reports, she [Jane Doe] could not have been clearer that she was 100 per cent confident that she had been raped," Hochul added. "Shockingly, those words didn't make it into the account that police sent to prosecutors."

The investigation had initially been closed without charges in 2024.

Last month, the woman filed a lawsuit and Tompkins County district attorney Matthew Van Houten reopened the investigation. He has since been bombarded by criticism that he abandoned the original investigation too quickly.

"In what world would police learn from a victim that she had been literally gang raped... and not elevate that to the district attorney?" Hochul said. "In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved or request the full transcript?"

Messages left for Van Houten were not immediately returned late on Thursday.

Hochul reiterated concerns that the survivor didn't get the support she deserved when she first reported her allegations.

"At every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her," Hochul said.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, left, speaks with New York Attorney General Letitia James during a news conference on Friday in New York. (Yuki Iwamura/The Associated Press)

The case has roiled the Ivy League campus and raised questions about its response and the larger issue of how sexual assaults are handled on college campuses. Specifically, new reporting throws Cornell's Title IX investigation into the spotlight.

In the U.S., Title IX is a civil rights law meant to address complaints of sex-based discrimination, harassment and/or sexual violence at educational institutions that receive federal funding.

CBS News New York obtained transcripts from Cornell's Title IX investigation, which include interviews with Jane Doe, six of the seven accused men, as well as 20 witnesses.

Doe's roommate reportedly said she heard Doe tell one of the accused, "You had penetrative sex with me. I had so much ketamine, my eyes were crossed, and you still had sex with me."

Meanwhile, Doe said she neither consented nor showed "excitement and enthusiasm, which is kinda the basis of consent."

According to CBS News, the men gave their accounts, too. One said he was only in the room for five minutes and didn't see her naked, while another said she consented to him taking ketamine from her body.

For its part, Cornell University has said it can't share information about its Title IX investigation, citing privacy concerns.

When asked on Friday about Cornell's decision not to share its Title IX investigation, Hochul called the law "deeply flawed."

Students express anger, frustration, grief on campus

Over more than two hours on Thursday, students and other members of the Cornell community expressed anger, frustration and grief over the school's handling of sexual assault allegations in general, with several speakers sharing their own experiences of sexual violence.

Many criticized Cornell president Michael I. Kotlikoff and the university's administration, calling for greater transparency and accountability in the handling of the case, stronger sexual assault prevention efforts and changes to fraternity life.

The woman told campus police in November 2024 that she was assaulted, then discussed it with the university's internal investigators as part of Cornell's disciplinary process.

The lawsuit against seven fraternity brothers, the university, the Chi Phi fraternity and others alleges that she was plied with drugs and alcohol, then subjected to sex acts by a group of men while she was partially or entirely incapacitated.

One of the men sent a social media message to other fraternity members alerting them to what was happening, and inviting people to take part, according to the lawsuit.

Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they participated in a sexual assault. One said his client hadn't touched the woman. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful.

World.title: It's the biggest Alberta separatist account on the internet. It has links to a movement leader
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One of the most influential voices on Alberta separatism is not a politician or even a clearly-identified person at all, but a combination social media account and merchandise line that is among the independence movement’s breakout stars.

The RiseOfAlberta account was created in the spring of 2025 and describes itself as “accelerating Alberta’s journey towards independence.” Since then it has amassed almost 100,000 X followers with a firehose of shareable clips and AI-generated memes about Alberta.

“They’ll depict, for example, eastern Canadians as very bureaucratic, government loving people, whereas Albertans are these Wild West people that hate government and love building,” says Chris Ross, a senior analyst at the Media Ecosystem Observatory, a research initiative that studies Canada’s online world and recently released a report into the dominance of separatist influencers.

“It’s a very idealistic, utopian perspective of what their idea of an Albertan is.”

In between separatist talking points, the account dabbles in the conspiratorial side of the movement, posting images of Alberta workers standing up to “globohomo,” derogatory online slang for the 2SLGBTQ+ movement, echoes Donald Trump’s call to see “mass immigration” as an “existential threat to Western civilization" and refers to climate change as “fake and gay.”

Many points are punctuated by an ad for an Alberta-branded blanket or hat.

Some of the items available for purchase on the Rise of Alberta online store, which is associated with a X account that drives the most engagement 'by far' on the topic of Alberta independence, according to researchers from the Media Ecosystem Observatory. (Alex Boyd/CBC)

Distrustful of mainstream institutions, some in Alberta’s separatism movement have constructed their own online world populated by independence-minded influencers. Within that, Rise of Alberta is a behemoth, driving four times the engagement of the second-most popular account, according to the report. (The account is aware of this, based on a response to a curious American back in January: “I’m the biggest Alberta Independence account on X,” it wrote. “Happy to chat.”)

But as the account has grown its influence, the person behind the curtain has remained a mystery. The account has not responded to curious social media users, nor did it respond to direct messages sent by CBC News and Radio-Canada asking about the account’s identity.

It’s also not clear where the money from the premium camo hoodies and charcuterie boards is going, though the account has said that the proceeds help cover the costs of the “tools” used to make its graphics.

Now, CBC News has found that the account has links to another heavyweight figure in the separatist movement, Keith Wilson, a lawyer who leads the Alberta Transition Council.

According to an analysis by CBC News and Radio-Canada, the same email address was used to set up the Rise of Alberta website, the site where merchandise is sold, and the website for one of Wilson’s companies and the site for the Alberta Transition Council.

When asked by CBC News, Wilson said that he was pleased that the account was so successful, and that it had come up with some “incredible, interesting and funny ads.” But he was clear he was not the one behind the account: “Not everybody’s interested in being famous, right?” he said.

“I can tell you, it’s not me.”

In a followup call and email, Wilson acknowledged that he knows the person behind the account, explaining that it was run by the person who had set up his websites — “a website designer and webmaster” — which was why the same email had been used.

He “clearly” had a relationship with the person, he said, but he declined to provide more detail or to identify the person.

“The individual has chosen to engage in political commentary anonymously,” he wrote. “I respect that choice.”

Wilson stressed he had no say over the content Rise of Alberta posted and had "nothing to do with" the money the store was making.

He does provide some assistance to the person running the Rise of Alberta account, he said, including listing its merchandise on the “store” tab of his personal YouTube channel.

“I let him do that,” he said. “It doesn’t cost me anything and helps him.”

Returns of unwanted Rise of Alberta merchandise are also sent to the mailing address for his law firm, he said, though he added there weren’t many. (“Those blankets are amazing,” he said. “I have three.”)

While the person posting on the Rise of Alberta account remains unclear, they frequently share video clips of Wilson, and comment positively on his activities in the separatist movement. With the launch of Let Alberta Decide in June, the account posted that it was “incredibly encouraging” that Wilson was helping lead a “serious campaign.”

Keith Wilson with the third-party advertiser Let Alberta Decide sits behind a series of computer screens in his office, which he calls the 'war room.' (Nathan Gross/CBC)

Wilson, who has publicly debated former premier Jason Kenney on the topic of independence, is also very active online, but strikes a different tone. He tweets clips of his own commentary and links to articles from the news sites dismissed by Rise of Alberta as “fake news.” The post pinned to the top of his page quotes the French Enlightenment philosopher Voltaire.

Rise of Alberta “constantly amplifies Keith Wilson’s posts, essentially acting as a campaign tool, but without any of the normal consequences,” says Ross, who was the lead author of the Media Ecosystem Observatory’s recent report on separatism influencers.

This is particularly notable because Rise of Alberta is “by far” the most influential account driving the conversation about separation, Ross said. The recent report found the account is single-handedly driving 11.8 per cent of all online engagement about the upcoming referendum, he said.

One in five of the images posted by the account is an ad for merchandise, according to an analysis by researchers from Common Ground at the University of Alberta.

The second most influential account, according to the report, is Keith’s personal X account, meaning the two accounts get almost 15 per cent of the online shares, likes and comments on separatism-related content.

In a normal election, party leaders would be scrutinized over their online campaign materials, Ross said. But because there are no elected politicians championing the separatist side, that vacuum has been filled by highly active, anonymous social media accounts, he said.

“The movement is structurally revolving around the Rise of Alberta account online, but no democratic form of scrutiny can interface with it,” he said. “It is bizarre, but the result of a modern campaign organized outside of party politics.”

(Wilson disagrees with this characterization, pointing out that he has more than 80,000 followers and many other big accounts interact with his posts. Besides which, he says, the separatism movement predates the Rise of Alberta account.)

WATCH | University researchers study AI videos promoting Alberta separatism: ‘Slopaganda’: University researchers study AI videos promoting Alberta separatism | Duration closed caption 2:09 New research has identified a rise in AI-generated YouTube videos promoting Alberta separatism. The content is targeting Albertan audiences ahead of a potential referendum on separation. The research paper, titled “Slopaganda,” found that this content is part of a larger network of online fake news. Emily Fitzpatrick has more.

Last November, a social media user pointed out the similarities between something Wilson and Rise of Alberta posted, and questioned whether they were the same person. Both accounts denied it.

“It’s not, but I am flattered,” Rise of Alberta posted with a cowboy emoji.

“I am too,” Wilson responded.

CBC News and Radio-Canada were able to link the Rise of Alberta website and Keith Wilson via the emails used to set up their respective websites by using DomainTools, a web analytics tool. An archived version of the Rise of Alberta website also listed the same mailing address as Wilson’s law firm in St. Albert, Alta.

While Rise of Alberta’s website was registered anonymously, meaning the identity of the owner is not publicly displayed, the company hosting it provides an anonymized email address to contact the website’s owner.

That same email address was first used a decade ago to register the website for Veritas Litigation Support, a company founded by Wilson. Starting last year, it has since been used for 16 other websites, most of which are related to Alberta independence.

It was also used for the websites for the Alberta Transition Council, an independence group led by Wilson, and Let Alberta Decide, a registered third-party advertiser co-chaired by Wilson.

The email has also been used to register a site called Rise of Saskatchewan, which is not active.

Wilson said the person behind Rise of Alberta sets up all of his websites, and he’s not sure why the sites all list the same email.

“I have been using the services of the person who runs that account for my websites for many years, and I don’t track all of the other stuff that they do,” he said. “I just know the stuff they do for me and they’re very good at it.”

The origin story on the Rise of Alberta website says the account began in the spring of 2025 because the person behind the account “had become convinced that Alberta would be better off as an independent country, and [they] wanted somewhere to say it.”

Things really took off after Prime Minister Mark Carney was elected last year, and soon posts were reaching millions of people, the site says. A few months later, followers started asking for merchandise and the store was born. (CBC News sent messages to the Rise of Alberta website and Facebook page, asking about the person running the account, and did not receive a response.)

Wilson says the person behind Rise of Alberta is “highly skilled” and “very creative.” Wilson also said he hadn’t seen the posts in which Rise of Alberta referred to climate change as “fake and gay” or referenced “globohomo,” and reiterated that he had nothing to do with what that account posted.

There’s a cost to being a public separatist in Alberta, Wilson says. There’s the risk to your career, to say nothing of the physical risk, he says. He gets hate mail and death threats, he adds.

“There’s a logical explanation as to why someone would want to remain anonymous, and I’m going to go as far as to suggest it’s almost admirable that the person’s not seeking personal fame, unlike every other social media influencer.”

World.title: Hidden cameras show some stores unlocking speed limits on e-bikes, selling e-scooters that go up to 120 km/h
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Whether it's children cruising down a suburban street, drivers delivering food downtown or a daredevil taking their need for speed to the highway, electric bikes and electric scooters are becoming more common across Canada.

A new hidden camera investigation by Marketplace shows how some stores are selling e-scooters and e-bikes with top speeds much higher than provincial speed limits and with recommended rider ages younger than provincial regulations allow.

Most provincial traffic laws limit e-bikes and e-scooters to 32 kilometres per hour or less. Age restrictions, meanwhile, vary across the country, ranging from 12 to 18. The territories and some provinces have no minimum age to ride.

That means it is mostly up to local police services to enforce these rules at a time when the number of injuries caused by these vehicles is climbing yearly, and public calls are growing for stronger, consistent rules nationwide and better enforcement .

Marketplace visited some of Canada's most well-known big box and specialty shops in the Greater Toronto Area — Amego, Emmo, EZbike, Best Buy, Canadian Tire and Costco — that sell popular brands. The undercover journalists tested how easy it is to find an e-bike or e-scooter that either had a maximum speed or age recommendation contravening Ontario limits.

In Ontario, e-scooter and e-bike riders must be at least 16. E-scooters cannot travel faster than 24 km/h on a flat surface, and e-bikes cannot travel faster than 32 km/h, according to provincial laws.

10 of 12 stores exceeded Ontario limits

Of the 12 stores journalists visited undercover, salespeople at six stores told us or showed us how to bypass built-in speed limits.

While most stores reminded us of Ontario rules, 10 stores sold e-bikes or e-scooters with maximum speeds beyond Ontario limits.

Stores are allowed to sell the e-bikes no matter how fast they go, but Michael Pasquali, founder of the Canadian Electric Bicycle Association (CEBA), says it's "heartbreaking."

"Shops that are selling products that are way beyond the legal limit, they're putting a lot of people in danger."

Seven stores also had e-scooters for sale with manufacturer-recommended rider ages under 16, though some medical experts say e-bikes and e-scooters are too unsafe for anyone under 16.

Watch the full Marketplace investigation on Friday, Oct. 2, on CBC-TV and YouTube.

"It's not just a toy; it's a motorized vehicle," said April Kam, an emergency physician at McMaster Children's Hospital in Hamilton.

"We're seeing kids who are presenting with brain bleeds, with abdominal injuries, solid organ injuries."

Recently released data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information shows 150 people ages 15 and under were hospitalized for falls involving an e-scooter in the 2025-2026 fiscal year across Canada, compared to 54 the year prior. That's an increase of roughly 178 per cent — and reflects a steady year-over-year increase for the last three years.

The number of head injuries related to e-scooters has also increased, from 50 in the 2022-2023 fiscal year to 157 in the 2025-2026 fiscal year. Fractures, dislocations and or muscle and tendon injuries have more than doubled in that same period, with 544 last fiscal year.

The Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program released its own survey in August and found 10 children have died from using devices like e-scooters and e-bikes in 2025.

Meanwhile, sales for the electric rides have more than quadrupled in Canada since 2019, with roughly 372,000 e-bikes and 76,000 e-scooters sold so far this year, according to Statista.

Marketing to kids 'deceiving' parents, doctor says

The youngest age recommendation the Marketplace journalists found was at Canadian Tire — a Razor e-scooter that hits a maximum speed of 16 km/h and is recommended for children who are eight or older.

"That just boggles my mind. Kids at this age don't necessarily have the developmental ability to maneuver these motorized vehicles," said Kam, who is also president of the Canadian Paediatric Society's emergency medicine section.

"It's very concerning that there's this huge market for selling children these motorized vehicles, essentially, and deceiving the parents and family, marketing them as toys."

WATCH | Doctor says kids 16 and under shouldn't ride e-bikes, e-scooters : Doctor says kids 16 and under shouldn't ride e-bikes, e-scooters | Duration closed caption 1:51 April Kam, an emergency physician at McMaster Children's Hospital in Hamilton, says e-bikes and e-scooters are vehicles, not toys.

Razor, the manufacturer of that particular e-scooter at Canadian Tire, said in a statement its device meets U.S. safety guidelines that say eight-year-olds can operate slow-moving motorized vehicles.

The company said its e-scooter is safe when properly used, isn't meant to be on public roads and that riders should follow local laws.

In statements to Marketplace, Best Buy, Canadian Tire and Emmo said customers should follow local laws. Best Buy said rules for e-bikes and e-scooters are evolving and that it tries to keep product information updated.

Costco didn't comment on Marketplace's findings.

E-bike stores can modify speed controls

At an EZbike location in Richmond Hill, a salesperson told undercover journalists it sells e-scooters that can reach 120 km/h — a speed that could get you a ticket on most highways.

At other stores, some e-bikes have their speed limited to 32 kilometres, adhering to Ontario's rules. But when asked if they modify vehicles, a salesperson at an Emmo location in Toronto said yes, they could modify a bike to go up to 150 km/h for off-road use.

"That's horrible," said Pasquali, of CEBA, who owns his own e-bike store in Hamilton.

Emmo and the company that operates the Emmo stores Marketplace visited said in a statement that a product's technical capabilities should not be confused with what's allowed on the roads.

But as an employee at an Emmo in Vaughan, Ont., described it: bypassing the speed limiter is "just like a toggle switch."

WATCH | E-bike stores can modify speed control: E-bike stores can modify speed control | Duration closed caption 2:53 Undercover CBC journalists visited 12 stores selling e-bikes and e-scooters across the Greater Toronto Area. Salespeople at six stores told them or showed them how to bypass built-in speed limits on the vehicles.

Passing on that kind of advice is "extremely unethical," Pasquali said.

"If you're showing consumers how to push a button and make it faster or offering to modify it to go faster with the caveat that you keep it off road, well, that's technically right. But most consumers aren't doing that, right?"

A salesperson at an Amego store in North York, Ont., went a step further, unlocking the 32 km/h speed limit in front of undercover journalists and revving the motor, showing the e-bike exceeding the speed limit and saying it could hit a top speed of roughly 50 km/h.

Amego said in a statement it does not offer or perform modifications, and its salesperson likely exaggerated the top speed.

EZbike didn't comment on Marketplace's findings.

Mom wants change after son's devastating injury

Amy Richards, of St. John's, became one of those parents pleading for change after watching her son spend 102 days in the hospital after losing control of his e-scooter.

Jayden King, 14, was riding his e-scooter on a quiet street in May when he hit a speed bump and lost control.

King's mom says he was wearing a helmet at the time of the accident but suffered a traumatic brain injury. He spent 21 days in a coma and had to have part of his skull surgically removed due to brain swelling. Once he's healthier, King will have to undergo another surgery to get the rest of his skull put back in place, Richards said.

WATCH | Mom wants change after son's devastating e-scooter injury: Mom wants change after son's devastating e-scooter injury | Duration closed caption 2:30 Amy Richards of St. John's wants stronger e-bike and e-scooter legislation after her 14-year-old son crashed an e-scooter in May.

He learned to walk, talk and eat again but still lives with a long list of issues, including memory loss.

"I can't remember nothing in my whole life," King said. He says there's not a chance he'll ride an e-scooter again.

Newfoundland and Labrador has no rules governing e-bikes or e-scooters, but a spokesperson for Government Services said in a statement that it has consulted the public and is looking at changes to the Highway Traffic Act to include micro-mobility devices.

Richards said it should have happened a long time ago, and no one under 16 should be able to ride one.

"We need to protect our children. That should come first and foremost," she said.

Pasquali says the federal government needs to step in and stop the sale and importation of e-bikes and e-scooters that can be modified with the flick of a switch.

Safety is top priority, federal minister says

Canada's Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon told Marketplace in an interview in late September that he has heard stories of people being injured riding e-bikes and e-scooters, and he wants to talk to his provincial counterparts about how to respond.

Most of the legislation governing e-bikes and e-scooters is provincial, he said, and there is "impetus" for provinces and municipalities to act.

But, MacKinon also said the federal government needs "to absolutely consider what we will do in terms of regulating the safety of those devices."

"We'll always work with safety in mind. Safety is our principal priority."

World.title: Why your Habs tickets cost more than any other NHL team's this season
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Move over, Toronto.

Following a successful year that saw the Montreal Canadiens reach the Eastern Conference final, tickets to see the Habs play at home this season will be the most expensive in the NHL — a new feat for the historic franchise.

According to sports betting and online casino research firm Bookies.com and TicketData.com, a website devoted to tracking resale ticket prices, Canadiens fans will pay an average of over $220 for cheapest tickets — more than double the league average — to see their team in action this season.

Montreal is one of the biggest markets in the NHL, and the Canadiens consistently rank in the top five among priciest tickets in the league, with the Toronto Maple Leafs leading the pack most seasons over the past decade.

Moshe Lander, a sports economist and associate professor at Concordia University, says although Habs fans might not be happy about the high ticket costs, they shouldn’t be surprised.

“Unfortunately for Montreal Canadiens fans, a little bit of success is the type of thing that reawakens a lot of dormant fans.”

WATCH | 2026-27 NHL season gets underway: 3 things fans should know about the Montreal Canadiens this NHL season | Duration 1:03 NHL hockey is back — and there are a few noteworthy points to know about the Habs as the regular season gets underway.

After starting a rebuild in 2021 that saw the Canadiens finish at or near the bottom of the standings three years in a row, Montreal reached the playoffs in each of its last two seasons, and a skilled young core is driving a renewed sense of excitement around the team.

Lander says it is also driving ticket prices up.

“It’s in demand like anything else,” he said.

'It used to be more accessible,' fan says

Habs fan Melissa Plett has been attending games at the Bell Centre since she moved from Manitoba to Montreal 15 years ago, but current prices are making her think twice about buying a ticket this season.

Plett says she understands why ticket prices are going up, but as the team continues to improve, she worries die-hard fans will be priced out of the rink.

“I feel like it used to be more accessible,” Plett said. “Even when you go down [to the boards] for warm-up and then you have to leave because the ticket owners come down. It definitely feels like it’s the elites or whatever you want to call them that can afford that down there.”

Plett says playoff tickets are even more inaccessible.

“You keep wondering which game you should pay for because these tickets are so expensive,” Plett said. “It’s become such a gamble on your money.”

WATCH | Habs ticket prices soared during last season's playoff run: Is it cheaper for Montreal Habs fans to make the trip to Buffalo than the Bell Centre? | Duration closed caption 1:55 Playoff tickets in Montreal could set you back several hundred or even thousand dollars. For some Canadiens fans, it makes more sense to head south of the border to Buffalo, N.Y., to watch the Habs battle the Sabres.

For other fans, like Sunil Peetush, it’s worth the gamble.

“It is the hottest ticket in town. It is the big show in Montreal, so you’re expected to pay a premium,” he said.

Peetush, who is a season ticket holder, says he maintains that it is a good deal to see the Habs play in Montreal — if you can get tickets before they hit the resale market.

His season tickets come out to less than $200 per game. “I see them selling on the aftermarket sometimes $600 to $1,000 a seat where I am sitting,” Peetush said.

While the team doesn’t have any say in resale prices, Canadiens owner Geoff Molson wrote in a statement to CBC News that the organization aims to make games accessible to as many fans as possible.

At the start of each season, it releases thousands of tickets to the public, including discounted options for families and students. A limited number of tickets for upcoming games are also released on the 15th of each month.

The same seats sold directly by the organization are consistently cheaper than those on the resale market, but Plett says they go so quickly, she doesn’t even bother trying to get into online ticket queues.

“Even if I tried to get on that… chances are I'm not going to be the one to buy them and then I forget about it and I miss out,” she said.

Secondary market booming

Earlier this year, Quebec cracked down on resale markets when it passed a law requiring platforms to disclose when tickets are being resold.

But critics say it still comes up short in lowering prices for consumers on the secondary market.

Unlike similar legislation in Ontario, the Quebec law doesn’t include a price cap on resale tickets, which allows resellers to charge inflated prices much like an unregulated market.

When faced with criticism, Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette defended his government’s decision to stop short of introducing a price cap on resale tickets, arguing that it would create an illegal market.

In the Canadiens’ case, the law, which came into effect Sept. 12, has so far done little to limit illegal resale markets.

Although the organization’s terms and conditions state holders must resell their tickets exclusively through Ticketmaster, the team’s official marketplace, fans looking for seats can still find them on a number of other ticketing sites or through social media groups dedicated to reselling and buying Canadiens tickets.

High interest paired with a healthy resale market means the price to see the Habs play at home likely won’t decrease any time soon.

Still, Peetush says this season’s high get-in price at the Bell Centre will be worth it most nights.

“The team is so dynamic, it’s so young, the building is just topping… I guarantee you if they win, you’ll be hyped for a week."

World.title: LNG Canada to use Chinese steel on $33-billion expansion project in Kitimat, B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LNG Canada will once again use Chinese steel for the "specialized fabrication capability" it says it requires for its $33-billion Phase 2 expansion project in Kitimat, B.C.

When the proposed expansion led the list of early projects referred to the new federal Major Projects Office in September 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters these ambitious building projects would be "at the heart of our new, comprehensive Buy Canadian policy."

In fact, the joint venture will buy more components from the state-owned China Offshore Oil Engineering Co., Ltd. (COOEC), which also manufactured its first two liquified natural gas processing units, known as trains, now in operation.

On Tuesday, LNG Canada announced an expansion of the facility’s production capacity, adding two more trains for a total of four on the site, increasing its production from 14 to 28 megatonnes per year once Phase 2 construction is complete, likely in the early 2030s.

At the event marking the final investment decision, CBC News asked the prime minister if the expansion would be built with Canadian or Chinese steel.

"It’s a great question for the proponents of Phase 2," Carney said. "I’ll leave it to them."

"There will be full opportunities to buy Canadian steel, and we'll continue to invest in the Canadian steel industry to make sure that's the case. But it will be for them to decide," the prime minister said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks at an event earlier this week where LNG Canada said it will go ahead with the Phase 2 expansion project at its LNG terminal in Kitimat, B.C. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

Accordingly, CBC News asked LNG Canada where it intends to source steel for its expansion.

"For the plant construction in Kitimat, the challenge is not a preference for offshore steel, but the specialized fabrication capability required for modules of this scale and complexity," LNG Canada spokesperson Paul Hagel wrote in an email.

"There are no fabrication yards in Canada that can manufacture and deliver the additional modules required for Phase 2. Only five fabrication yards globally have the combination of space, capacity, quality systems and marine access required for this scope of work, including COOEC in China, which successfully fabricated modules for LNG Canada’s Phase 1."

Chinese state-owned producer holds 15% stake

Shell Canada Energy is the majority operator and project leader in Kitimat, holding a 40 per cent stake in LNG Canada.

State-owned PetroChina, the largest oil and gas producer, supplier and global investor in China, is a 15 per cent shareholder. The other three partners in the joint venture are Malaysia’s Petronas (25 per cent), Japan’s Mitsubishi Corporation (15 per cent) and the Korea Gas Corporation, or KOGAS (five per cent).

LNG exported from Kitimat is distributed by these five energy giants to Asian markets, based on their relative stake in the project.

Prior to a final investment decision for Phase 1 of the Kitimat facility in 2018, the joint venture sought and received an exemption from steep anti-dumping and countervailing duties that had been levied on fabricated industrial steel from China to protect Canada’s steel industry.

Canada is among many countries that implement safeguards based on threats identified by its domestic steel producers. State-subsidized Chinese steelmakers produce more than China’s domestic economy requires. The surplus ships overseas, undermining the cost-competitiveness of steel manufactured in countries like Canada that have higher-paid, unionized workers and higher environmental standards.

The value of the concession the federal government made to LNG Canada for Phase 1 was estimated at $1 billion.

The 2019 remission order published in the Canada Gazette said that LNG Canada, as well as the Singapore investors behind the Woodfibre LNG project in Squamish (slated to come online in 2027), had told the finance department there was no Canadian capacity to produce what they needed.

They also framed the cost impact of these duties as having a "negative impact on investment decisions."

In other words: without it, the deal may not have gone ahead.

However, the duties in effect when the use of Chinese steel first drew negative attention in 2018 expired after five years and have not been renewed.

LNG Canada told CBC News there are no tariffs now on importing steel components from its Chinese supplier.

The office of Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told CBC News that the Canada Border Services Agency determines whether additional levies are required on Chinese steel to avoid predatory dumping. In this case, the measures were dropped and Canadian producers have not objected, because these particular components don’t directly compete with what they make.

In 2024, other surtaxes and tariff rate quotas (volume restrictions) were placed on a list of specific Chinese steel products that could threaten the viability of Canada’s domestic industry. That list, however, does not include what LNG Canada is importing.

Compressor stations target 70% Canadian steel

Other aspects of the Kitimat expansion may, however, use Canadian steel. For example, in order to expand storage and production at the export terminal, Coastal GasLink needs to expand the volume of gas moving in its pipeline network to Kitimat.

The new compression stations required along the pipeline will be "targeting almost 15,000 tonnes of steel from Canadian suppliers or mills, representing approximately 70 per cent of the steel required for that work," the LNG Canada spokesperson wrote.

That apparent prioritization of Canadian supply chains would be more consistent with the assurances the prime minister gave in September 2025, when LNG Canada’s Phase 2 expansion led the first list of priority referrals to the new federal Major Projects Office.

"These major projects will be at the heart of our new, comprehensive Buy Canadian policy," Carney said in his remarks a year ago. "To strengthen Canada’s independence, resilience and security, we will build with Canadian steel, lumber, aluminum, and by Canadian engineers and tradespeople. We will be our own best customer."

Unlike public purchasing contracts now subject to the federal government’s Buy Canadian procurement guidelines, the supply chains used by private sector energy companies are, as Carney noted Tuesday, up to them to decide.

World.title: 'Prepared ourselves for the worst': FlyDubai passenger recounts moments during cockpit attack
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Almog Italie and his family were on the final leg of their trip home following a vacation in Japan when they felt FlyDubai flight FZ1073 plummet.

"Suddenly we were moving like a roller-coaster without any notice ... I thought it was turbulence," Italie said, adding that after several seconds, the plane stabilized before it started diving again.

He quickly realized something was amiss.

"We understood something is wrong and something is going on in the cockpit, because that wasn't normal at all," he told CBC News.

WATCH | The FlyDubai flight survived against impossible odds. Here's how: How a FlyDubai flight survived a hijacking attempt against impossible odds | About That | Duration closed caption 11:52 A FlyDubai flight bound for Tel Aviv plummeted more than 17,000 feet through the air after the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain in the plane's cockpit. Andrew Chang breaks down the attack and how the plane managed to land safely despite the odds. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Italie was one of 174 people on board the plane earlier this week when one of the pilots stabbed the other in an attempt to crash the plane. The flight plunged 17,000 feet.

"It was very fast," Italie said of the situation.

He recounted how crew and passengers ran to the cockpit to foil the attempt.

A spokesperson for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later revealed how the stabbed pilot, Indian national Smit Machchhar, was covered with blood and on the floor when he managed to open the cockpit door, allowing others to rush in, subdue the perpetrator and let a second pair of FlyDubai pilots take over the flight.

Those involved resurfaced several minutes later to update the other passengers and confirm that they were looking for a safe place to land.

"So, what needed to be done was to maintain calm, stay in the seats and do nothing else that would cause chaos," Italie said. "And this is exactly what saved our lives. Nobody panicked and we controlled the situation."

"We didn't know how the landing was going to go, so we prepared ourselves for the worst," he added.

Ultimately, the plane landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where Italie said authorities warmly welcomed passengers and crew, even providing food.

"They were very, very nice," Italie said. "Much appreciated."

'Unity' saved everyone's life: passenger

Hours later, passengers were on board a different flight and made it to Tel Aviv. But passengers continue to recount those terrifying minutes.

"I just can say that it was a miracle. It was awful, crazy, and we thank God that we survived it. We didn't think we will make it, but thank God we are in Israel. We are back home. And we are happy to see everyone here," said another passenger, Lital Shachaf.

For Italie, the "unity" on board saved everyone's life.

Yaniv Hayun, 50, was one of four passengers who rushed to the cockpit during the chaos to overpower the unidentified co-pilot behind the attack. He said he learned what to do thanks to an aircrash television show. Another, a dentist, treated Machchhar's wounds.

"The people united. We helped each other," Italie said. "That's a message I want to share."

World.title: What I learned from North America's top meteorologists at Climate Week
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hi, it's Johanna. For almost two decades, I've been talking about climate change through the weather we experience every day. But after spending Climate Week in New York with fellow meteorologists from across North America, one thing is clear: this job is getting deeply personal.

This week:

What I learned from North America's top meteorologists at Climate Week

The Big Picture: Progress on the world's nature goals

Mycelium with your meatballs? How one Vancouver company is farming fungi to combat meat costs

What I learned from North America's top meteorologists at Climate Week

Grabbing a quick moment outside the WNYC radio studio before heading in to record. (Johanna Wagstaffe/CBC)

I was invited to join a closed-door workshop in New York City during Climate Week called "Beyond the Forecast: How Trusted Weather Voices Can Help Communities Understand Climate and Extreme Weather." Hosted by the Clinton Global Initiative in partnership with the Eleven Eleven Foundation, the session offered a rare space to talk openly with other broadcast meteorologists about how we communicate climate change.

I mean, this is my bread and butter. For almost two decades, I've been talking about climate change through the everyday weather we experience. I've been grateful to have the support, platforms and formats at CBC to do just that.

Even so, there is a distinct weight to this work — seeing the data play out in real time, knowing the severity of a storm's impact before it hits, and navigating how politicized the term "climate change" has become. Stepping into my new role as the host of CBC's climate podcast What on Earth?, the timing couldn't have been better for this gathering.

Finding common ground in New York

Arriving in New York, I loved being recognized by fellow Canadians at Newark Airport — climate advisers from Vancouver headed to the same gathering. It was a nice reminder of why these conferences matter. Bringing people together (despite the carbon footprint of travel) creates a momentum you can't replicate virtually.

Walking from the subway up 5th Avenue toward the conference centre on my first day, I instinctively fell into the fast-paced ebb and flow of the city street. I credit my former Toronto days for my defensive walking skills, but adopting that rhythm makes you feel immediately plugged in. This trip was going to be all about feeling part of something bigger.

Fuelling the Climate Week hustle with an essential New York slice. (Johanna Wagstaffe/CBC)

The workshop itself was one I won't soon forget. Nearly every major meteorologist I've watched on U.S. networks was there (plus Bill Nye!). Our scheduled two-hour session ran long — after all, we talk for a living — but it was deeply cathartic. Hearing forecasters from Fox News to CNN to ABC, alongside scientists and policy-makers, open up about the shared challenges of communicating climate risk felt like a rare moment of unity.

Here are a few takeaways I can share:

1. The connection between weather and climate is undeniable — but the pushback is real

Underlying every discussion in that room was one overarching reality: we are all trying to talk about climate change as station scientists.

The science behind extreme weather is indisputable. But for television forecasters attempting to bring that science into daily broadcasts, the pushback from audiences can be tough — and deeply emotional. While I've been lucky enough to avoid the absolute worst of it, let's just say you never truly develop a thick skin. And knowing what lies ahead when forecasting a devastating storm carries a real weight.

Between sessions, I raced from Midtown down to SOHO to record in the studios at WNYC (New York public radio) — a fun moment of solidarity, hopping from one public broadcaster's home base to another. But the conversation I recorded hit home sharply. I spoke with forecaster Chris Gloninger, who made the difficult decision to leave his TV news career after facing severe harassment and a death threat simply for explaining climate links on air.

But Chris's story was a stark reminder that serving as a trusted voice often comes at a high personal cost. To go "beyond the forecast," weather communicators need more than just thick skin — we need strong community support to keep having these vital conversations safely.

Connecting with forecaster Chris Gloninger during Climate Week in New York. (Johanna Wagstaffe/CBC)

2. U.S. and Canadian TV live in different broadcast universes

I attended the workshop alongside only one other Canadian: my friend Mark Robinson from The Weather Network, who I went to meteorology school with! Being there together highlighted how much the U.S. and Canada have in common, and also just how differently our two media markets operate.

American broadcast TV remains deeply traditional, with millions of viewers still tuning in to local 6 o'clock newscasts every night. For U.S. forecasters, that means trying to cram complex climate attribution science into a lightning-fast, two-minute weather window between commercial breaks.

Reunited with fellow Canadian weather broadcaster and storm chaser Mark Robinson from The Weather Network. (Johanna Wagstaffe/CBC)

At CBC, as the media landscape has shifted, we've chosen to experiment with meeting audiences where they are. Beyond dedicated space on podcasts like What On Earth? and digital platforms, our local TV markets frequently carve out extra airtime specifically to connect the dots between severe weather and climate change. Having that room to explain why a heat wave or atmospheric river is happening is something I was reminded not to take for granted — because in a tight TV hit, context is often the first thing left on the cutting-room floor. But as more U.S. newsrooms experiment with climate-dedicated segments and digital extras, the potential to inform communities is huge. It shows that when we give trusted weather voices room to breathe, audiences gain a far better understanding of the world shifting around them.

Stepping out of those closed-door rooms in New York, I was reminded that connecting those dots on air isn't always easy, and it certainly isn't always comfortable — but as extreme weather becomes our daily reality, it's a conversation we're more committed than ever to having.

— Johanna Wagstaffe

Old issues of What on Earth? are here . The CBC News climate page is here .

Check out our podcast and radio show. In our latest episode : When a meteorologist took a job in Iowa, he was excited to make his forecasts matter to viewers by bringing in climate impacts that were relevant to their lives, like rising costs and energy independence. But then the backlash began, escalating to a death threat.

He's not the only one. At climate week in New York City, a group of meteorologists gathered to share stories about speaking to often polarized audiences. When facts become political, how can climate change's frontline communicators stick to the science?

What On Earth? drops new podcast episodes every Wednesday and Saturday. You can find them on your favourite podcast app or on demand at CBC Listen . The radio show airs Sundays at 11 a.m., 11:30 a.m. in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Check the CBC News Climate Dashboard for live updates on record-breaking weather and current conditions across the country. Set your location to find out how today's temperatures compare to historical trends.

Reader feedback

Last week, we told you about a unique air quality meets wearable art project that's trying to bring awareness about dangerous pollutants especially when we can't see them.

Edwina Hylton wrote in with an important point: "In the eventuality that the device shows serious pollution, what is the person wearing the device supposed to do? Fine to know things are bad, but if there isn't a reasonable alternative, what is the point in collecting the information?"

While not always equitable or within reach, some experts we've spoken to over the years have said awareness gives a power of choice to take action , like wearing a mask or moving indoors.

And, for some, like reader Maureen Moffat, awareness is a click away. She writes, "I check the air quality daily on the net. Easy."

Got questions, comments, or just want to share something? Write us at whatonearth@cbc.ca (and send photos there, too!)

The Big Picture: Progress on the world's nature goals

Four years ago, Canada welcomed negotiators from around the world to strike a historic deal on protecting nature. The conference was supposed to be in China, but it was 2022 and the COVID-weary government there had decided not to host.

So the meeting reverted to Montreal, which hosts the secretariat of the UN treaty that governs biological diversity, and I jumped on a train to go cover it. Canada led negotiations to land a new global target : protecting 30 per cent of lands and oceans by 2030. And it decided to lead by example by embarking on its own ambitious conservation agenda.

Here's a map of Canada's protected spaces. Canada has protected about 14 per cent of its lands and 15.5 per cent of its oceans so far.

And a new assessment says there's progress internationally — the world will reach 27 per cent protection on land by 2030. For oceans, protection will only reach 12 per cent. I spoke to Steven Guilbeault, Canada's former environment minister and the guy who helped land that deal in Montreal, about why we are falling short — and also why he's still optimistic countries will ramp up the fight against biodiversity loss.

— Inayat Singh

Hot and bothered: Provocative ideas from around the web

A man in Squamish, B.C., has put his Halloween zombie decoration out early — to keep bears out of his garbage bins. See how the bears are responding in this CBC News video .

Kids are being toilet trained later and later. That's costing parents in money spent on diapers and time spent on additional gross diaper changes. But it's also creating a lot more plastic waste. A new study calculates the environmental cost, and offers some solutions .

Mountainous, densely populated Japan doesn't have many places to put large solar farms, but it has found a solution in a type of infrastructure that proliferated in the economic boom of the 1980s and is now disused .

A new study shows electric trucks are becoming cheaper to operate than their diesel counterparts and how quickly the savings can outstrip the higher up-front cost in some European countries .

Canada's Building Canada Strong Act is supposed to speed up infrastructure projects. But it could also dismantle environmental safeguards that protect Canadians and prevent wildlife from extinction, despite the federal government claiming otherwise , environmental groups tell CBC's David Thurton and Olivia Stefanovich.

Mycelium meatballs? How one Vancouver company is farming fungi to combat meat costs

Vancouver-based company Maia Farms has figured out a way to grow and harvest mycelium — the hidden, underground root-like networks of fungus that give rise to mushrooms. (Monia Blanchet/Radio-Canada)

If fermented liquid fungus from a bioreactor doesn't sound like your idea of a delicious meal, the folks at Maia Farms say, don't knock it 'til you've tried it.

The Vancouver-based company has figured out a way to grow and harvest mycelium — the hidden, underground root-like networks of fungus that give rise to mushrooms.

"The bioreactor allows us to control the environment in which the mycelium are grown," said chief innovation officer Sean Lacoursiere.

"It allows us to keep everything moving and grooving and it also allows us to aerate and provide all the oxygen that the mushroom will need."

WATCH | Company argues mushrooms could help lower skyrocketing meat costs for restaurants: Company argues mushrooms could help lower skyrocketing meat costs for restaurants | Duration closed caption 2:02 Meat is one of the biggest costs facing restaurants and data shows prices are only going up. Diners are increasingly seeing those expenses being reflected in menu prices. A Vancouver company is trying to make meat go further by blending it with mushrooms.

The result is a food product that can be mixed with different protein sources to add bulk and enhance a meal's nutritional profile.

While mushroom products are often used in meat substitutes, one of Maia's target markets is the meat industry itself.

"We can add a lot of nutritional, taste and texture benefits while reducing the amount of meat that's required," Lacoursiere said.

The offering couldn't be timelier for restaurateurs and other food retailers struggling to keep costs down as the price of meat soars.

According to Canada Beef, retail beef averaged $28 per kilogram in April, up 15 per cent from a year ago and close to a record high.

Maia Farms' director of food science and innovation Karen McAfee said mycelium could replace between 25 and 40 per cent of the meat in items like sausage rolls, meatballs and burger patties.

"It can help retain moisture… it can also help with the high level of umami flavour," she said.

Better for the planet

The benefits of hiding mushrooms in your meat go beyond the financial.

"From our estimates, we produce around two kilograms of carbon dioxide per kilogram of material," Lacoursiere said.

According to a 2024 report by the Canadian Roundtable for Sustainable Beef, one kilogram of consumed boneless beef in Canada produces 32.8 kilograms of carbon dioxide.

The same amount also requires 1,912 litres of water, almost four times the 500 litres Maia reports in its process.

"I don't think people really comprehend just how much of a difference this type of product can make," he said.

Finding consumers

While meat alternatives are readily available in Canadian supermarkets, sales in the sector have been declining for several years .

Lacoursiere is hoping Maia has what it takes to buck the trend.

"The whole goal of our company here is to produce mycelium at large scales, at a very cost competitive level. And we're already seeing that," he said.

As for the "ick" factor?

"It's an oyster mushroom. It's been eaten for hundreds, if not thousands of years. It's delicious. We just found a way to grow it in a submerged liquid state."

— Ruby Cornish

World.title: Why are B.C. firefighters still using wildfire data from the 1990s?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Neal McLoughlin, superintendent of predictive services with the B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS), is trying to get one of B.C.'s most challenging fires, the Bald Range wildfire, to behave in his modelling software the way it did on the ground in the Okanagan Valley on Aug. 7.

On his computer, he's turning up the dials for extreme fire behaviour, replacing the forest fuels with more flammable types, programming a stronger wind from the west and swapping local topography of a downward sloping hill with a flat landscape.

Only with those interventions do his simulations get close to what actually happened on the ground that night in Summerland, when more than 12,000 people were forced to flee as flames rushed toward the town in mere hours. One woman died in the chaos.

"Observed fire behaviour is doubling what our models would otherwise predict," said McLoughlin.

It's partly because the data that informs these computer models was collected at least 30 years ago, when extreme fire behaviour, driven by events like prolonged drought — a feature of climate change — was less common.

The challenge is especially pronounced in B.C.'s Southern Interior region, officially the driest place in Canada, according to the Canadian Drought Monitor , in a wildfire season that saw less area burned than average, yet was one of the most devastating seasons on record for property destruction.

McLoughlin says his team has learned to be skeptical of their fire modelling software's predictions during hot and dry days because the models can underperform. (Georgie Smyth/CBC)

BCWS specialists look to their model predictions the way most of us consider a weather forecast. In their case, they're co-ordinating a response to a wildfire, thinking about how quickly it might spread and how their tactics and safety plan should change around that. It's part of the larger toolbox, on top of human resources, BCWS uses to evaluate and dedicate resources to wildfires.

While it's a conceptually robust prediction system, based on more than 100 years of data collection and analysis, even its website states it "was last updated in the early 1990s."

Trusting the models

In practice, McLoughlin says, his team have learned to become more skeptical of the model's predictions on those exceptionally hot and dry days, when even decades of high-grade data cannot overcome their own instincts that a wildfire could be significantly worse than the models say.

Ultimately it's people that make decisions about how to respond to a wildfire, not models, and on those fire-prone days McLoughlin has begun training his team to really apply their lived experience of past extreme fires. On some days, he says: "I don’t trust the models on this day. I expect it's going to do something very different."

"Black swan events" is what Chelene Hanes, a research scientist with the Canadian Forest Service (CFS), calls those unpredictable fires, which fall outside what years of fire science has taught practitioners like her.

The hills of Prairie Valley outside Summerland, B.C., were first affected by a compounding years-long drought, the worst in Canada according to the federal drought monitor, before being met with an extreme out of control wildfire in August. (Georgie Smyth/CBC)

The basis of the prediction software is the Canadian Forest Fire Danger Rating System (CFFDRS), which forms the foundation of how agencies across the country evaluate the potential of wildland fires.

Hanes says updates to the Fire Behaviour Prediction System, part of the modelling that forecasters use, could be rolled out by 2029, but including new data from these more aggressively burning fires is unlikely because it's both very expensive and dangerous to collect.

"A lot of it is reanalysis of data that was collected over numerous decades because it is really good data," she said. "But we do need to collect more information because we are trying to stretch our capabilities with the models with our knowledge of physics and math in the fire environment."

Deeper and hotter

McLoughlin took us close to the ignition point of B.C.'s largest wildfire this summer, the Pear Lake Wildfire, near Clinton — a fire that had the hallmarks of behaviour that needs to be more accurately modelled.

The fire, which eventually scorched an area larger than Greater London, burned through more than 100 structures and, from where we stood, seemingly all the pines on the hill across from us, leaving a strange landscape of thousands of blackened stumps, standing like tiny spent matchsticks.

The hills near Clinton, B.C., after the province's largest wildfire this season. So-called 'leopard or cheetah trees' were common here, signs of a fire so intense the bark explodes off the trunk. (Georgie smyth/CBC)

There's a lot of evidence of the impacts of drought, McLoughlin said as he walked through some of the burn scar. He pointed to 30-metre-tall trees that had burned from the top right down to the root plates, leaving huge holes in the ground, and other trees spotted black and yellow — so-called "leopard or cheetah trees," a phenomenon also observed in the Jasper wildfire — when a fire burns so hot bark explodes off the trunk in patches.

Persistent drought means fires burn deeper and hotter, he said.

These are the kinds of conditions that can lead to a convective or column-driven fire, best known by their distinctive tall pyrocumulonimbus clouds that can look and act like huge thunderstorms as superheated gases and debris are pushed skyward, sometimes mixing in air from the upper atmosphere.

It used to be something you'd see once in your career, said McLoughlin. B.C.'s 2023 season had close to 100.

Pyrocumulus clouds, seen from more than 100 kilometres away in Coquitlam, B.C., are pictured forming above the Boston Bar wildfire on July 21. (Submitted by @Brad604/X)

The fire ground we were standing in had multiple pyrocumulus events, one of them with lightning, which started a new fire that eventually merged together.

"Those were not the conditions we collected data for," says McLoughlin.

Predicting the behaviour of a column-driven fire is simply "not part of our old systems," he said, as opposed to a more horizontal wind-driven fire where the models "do a great job."

Lack of data on extreme conditions

The last time that modelling software had a major update was 1992, but it's not as straightforward as putting some newer numbers in a spreadsheet said Hanes, from the CFS.

The capacity to do the kind of science where a timer could be put in the ground to measure the spread of a fire or infrared cameras could be used to look at the intensity of a fire is hard to imagine occurring in a life-threatening situation like the Bald Range or Pear Lake wildfire.

McLoughlin says their underlying modelling tools have very little data that informs extreme fire behaviour. (Georgie Smyth/CBC)

Even experimental burns — which is how scientists studied fires that informed the prediction systems used today — are too dangerous under the extreme conditions they're experiencing, according to Hanes.

"We don't have a lot of data on the extreme end," Hanes said, because the risk of an experimental blaze getting out of control during extreme conditions is just too high.

So, Hanes says they're often "piggybacking" their research on prescribed burns, though she admits many didn't happen this year because the season got too busy. They're also collaborating with some research groups like NASA whose planes can fly through fire storms to collect data.

McLoughlin says he's been asked multiple times about BCWS using artificial intelligence to help predict these new, seemingly unpredictable wildfires, but for him it still comes back to collecting more contemporary data.

"If we're not making an effort to collect that data on the ground to inform these models, they're not going to make good predictions," he said. "It's as simple as that."
