World.title: How Assisi marks 800 years since St Francis's death and why he still embodies peace
World.content:
In 2026, on 4 October, the day dedicated to Saint Francis, became a national holiday. In Assisi the celebrations are entering their peak in these very days and the epicentre will be the Upper Basilica. At 23:59 on Saturday 3 October the bells will ring out in celebration, marking the start of the official ceremonies.

 

From this year, 4 October has once again become a national holiday to celebrate the universal values of peace, fraternity, solidarity and respect for the environment embodied by Saint Francis of Assisi.

On Sunday, the first national holiday dedicated to the saint, the ceremony will be attended by President of the Republic Sergio Mattarella and ambassadors from all over the world because, as Euronews is told by Friar Giulio Cesareo, director of the Communications Office of the Sacred Convent of Assisi, "Francis is not a gift only for Italy but for the world".

But who was Saint Francis and why does his appeal remain so powerful 800 years after his death?

Tradition has handed down several different images of Francis that in one way or another continue to engage with today's world. As Professor Antonio Musarra, professor of Medieval History at Sapienza University in Rome and Harvard fellow who has recently published The world according to Francis of Assisi (Il Mulino, 2026) (source in Italian), explains to Euronews:

"Francis has been reread over the course of history in completely different ways. Already in his own time, in the 1200s, biographies and hagiographies accumulated that portray him differently, but the Francis we have today, the one we have inherited, is the one that begins to emerge after the First World War: he is Francis of peace, Francis of diplomacy, Francis who tries to reconcile the factions."

And indeed, when we ask him how relevant the saint is and what he could teach the world today, the professor has no doubts: it is his modus operandi, his "style". "A style that we see clearly in his relationship with the Mediterranean, with other cultures, with what is different," the professor continues.

He offers two examples: "The different at home, for instance the leper from whom his conversion springs, but also the religious other, as when he met the sultan." This meeting was the one that Giotto chose to include in the cycle on the life of Saint Francis with which, at the end of the 13th century, he frescoed the lower part of the single nave of Assisi's Upper Basilica.

Why the meeting between Francis and Saladin's nephew is so important

The encounter between Saint Francis of Assisi and the sultan of Egypt al-Malik al-Kamil took place during the Fifth Crusade in Damietta, Egypt. It is a meeting from which we can still learn today.

As Father Paolo Nicelli, lecturer in theology at the Catholic University of Milan and expert on the relationship between Islam and modernity, explains to Euronews: "Damietta is a port, a major commercial centre and therefore of interest to both Christians and Muslims, so the dispute is not spiritual but clearly of an economic and military nature."

He goes on: "On one side we have Francis, a profoundly spiritual man, on the other we have a man of state, as is often the case in Islam." Saint Francis is a man of faith and leaves the crusaders' camp to cross enemy lines, convinced that he will succeed in converting Saladin's nephew.

The conversion never came about, but Francis was received with respect by the sultan. Hagiographic tradition also tells of the legendary 'ordeal of fire', in which Francis declared himself ready to walk into the flames together with Muslim clerics to demonstrate the truth of his faith. The sultan refused the challenge, but was impressed by the courage of the poor man of Assisi.

The meeting with a representative of Islam based on dialogue rather than weapons thus became in the following centuries a model of peace and interreligious dialogue.

"An example of mercy and forgiveness," Nicelli adds. "A forgiveness that is even more necessary today, especially in a globalised society like ours. In this sense Francis's model is certainly countercultural, because it goes directly against today's dominant values: ambition, individualism, selfishness, self-centredness, self-glorification and so on."

And perhaps this is why, 800 years after his death, his figure is still so celebrated and significant today.

World.title: Beyond K-pop and cinema: Major Korean exhibition brings centuries of art and belief to London
World.content:
Long before K-pop filled stadiums and Korean films won global acclaim, the peninsula’s artists were casting temple bells, shaping delicate ceramics and capturing mountains in ink.

 

That older cultural world takes centre stage in ‘Korea’, the British Museum’s first major exhibition on Korean art and history in more than 40 years.

Spanning from 300 BC to the present, its 100 exhibits explore the beliefs and traditions that shaped Korean art.

The display includes 10 national treasures and 13 other treasures, official Korean designations recognising their cultural and historical importance, according to Samsung, the exhibition’s corporate partner.

Incense burner with the mythical creature, Girin, from AD 1100-1200, on display at new ‘Korea' exhibition at the British Museum. AP Photo

Among the objects on display are a 900-year-old incense burner crowned with a mythical creature and a huge Buddhist temple bell around 1,000 years old.

The exhibition moves from the luminous blue-green ceramics of the Goryeo dynasty to the restrained porcelain of Joseon, shaped by Confucian ideals, according to the British Museum and Samsung.

Together, they show how Buddhism and Confucian ideas shaped Korean art over the centuries.

For the exhibition’s curator, Yoojin Kwak Choi, the “absolute star exhibit” is Jeong Seon’s Clearing After Rain on Mount Inwang.

Jeong Seon is an 18th-century Korean painter of the Joseon dynasty who helped shift landscape painting from idealised Chinese-style scenes towards Korea’s actual scenery, Choi explains.

Mountain Spirit, 1960, Pak Nosoo AP Photo

But there are modern examples of Korean craftsmanship too.

Yeesookyung’s 2018 vase combines ceramic shards from North and South Korea. In Korean artisanal tradition, imperfect work is destroyed, so the artist has taken broken shards from that destruction and glued them together with gold leaf.

Most exhibits come from the collection of the late Samsung chairman Lee Kun-Hee.

The billionaire amassed a vast collection over his lifetime, and after his death in 2020, his family donated more than 23,000 works to South Korean national museums.

“Some people might think that Korean culture is new, but it is thousands upon thousands of years old,” said Benjamin Braun, Samsung Europe’s chief marketing officer.

For visitors drawn to Korea through its music and cinema, the exhibition opens a door onto that longer history.

‘Korea’ runs at the British Museum until 31 January 2027.

World.title: Spanish Congress rejects housing laws despite Sánchez's warning: 'They'll be judged sooner than they think'
World.content:
Spain's parliament on Friday rejected two housing decree-laws promoted by the government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, aimed at tackling a housing crisis that has spurred nationwide protests.

 

The two votes are a heavy political blow to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and went ahead as hundreds of protesters gathered outside parliament.

These rejections, delivered in a voice vote, represent a parliamentary setback for the executive and came after a sitting marked by last-minute negotiations and uncertainty over the support of its parliamentary partners. Sánchez spoke for a few minutes before the vote to urge MPs to "do the right thing or history will judge you sooner than you think and more harshly than you can imagine."

After the first of the decrees was rejected by 172 votes in favour and 178 against, a demonstration marched to Madrid's central Puerta del Sol square, chanting "General strike!" The second decree was then also voted down.

Housing affordability crisis

The government decrees were intended to quell a public uproar following the televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman last week in Madrid that sparked protests and a camp-in that has occupied Madrid’s most important square ever since. Barring a surprise, the progressive coalition of Sánchez will suffer a costly legislative defeat that will likely fan the flames of the protests.

The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the past 10 years. The average price per square meter has risen from €8.20 in 2016 to €15.1 this year, according to the real estate website Idealista.

The elderly woman whose eviction sparked the protests, Maricarmen Abascal, has become a symbol for the fight for lower housing costs in the southern European country, where many people are priced out of buying a home and are being squeezed by a small rental market.

The company that evicted her finally caved under immense public and political pressure this week and said that she can return to the apartment. Abascal is currently in a hospital since being removed from her home on a stretcher, but her lawyer said she is happy to know she will be going home.

Crushing votes

The vote came after a morning of speeches in which the housing minister, Isabel Rodríguez, urged the different groups to back the measures, having explicitly asked Junts per Catalunya to vote in favour or abstain, after the pro-independence party announced on Thursday night that it would oppose both texts and submit its own proposal to the government. In the end, Sánchez's PSOE, Spain's social democratic party, refused to withdraw the two decrees, as the Catalan party had demanded.

Rodríguez told the chamber that one of the two decrees incorporated many of the proposals (source in Spanish) put forward by Junts. "Ninety per cent of what they handed to the prime minister is now set out in the Official State Gazette," said the housing minister, who pledged to process the decrees as a bill so that "clarifications or technical corrections" requested by the groups could be incorporated later.

The minister also warned in her speech about the consequences of the vote and appealed to MPs' sense of responsibility. "With this vote, we are deciding whether we do not want another eviction or are willing to face the next one," Rodríguez said, while hundreds of people gathered outside the Congress of Deputies, Spain's lower house of parliament, to demand a solution to the housing crisis gripping the country.

Diverging positions

The sitting began at 11:00, after Sánchez was greeted with an ovation from the socialist benches on his arrival at Congress. During the debate, the groups stuck to the positions they had set out in the preceding hours, albeit with different nuances.

The PNV, the Basque Nationalist Party, announced that it would support one of the decrees "with many doubts". Its spokesperson, Maribel Vaquero, lamented that it had not been possible to reach the minimum agreement her party had called for.

The Canarian Coalition party, a regionalist centre to centre-right party, for its part, confirmed its favourable vote on the first decree because it sees it as "a starting point."

Spain's far-left party Podemos confirmed its four votes in favour of both texts, although its secretary-general, Ione Belarra, criticised the government for having "chopped up" the measures. "It's just another excuse. People don't want excuses; they want solutions," she argued during the sitting.

EH Bildu, another Basque nationalist party leaning left, also expressed its displeasure during the debate. Its MP Oskar Matute said he was "deeply angry" at the prospect of particular interests prevailing over the measures proposed to tackle the housing problem, brought into sharp focus by Maricarmen's eviction and which culminated last weekend in a protest camp in the central Puerta del Sol square.

Opposition from conservative parties PP and Vox, together with Junts' rejection, had left the government facing particularly tight parliamentary arithmetic. The coalition executive needed to win support from different parties to get the initiatives through a chamber in which socialist parties PSOE and Sumar do not have an absolute majority.

Possible early election

The vote on the housing decrees had also sparked, within the PSOE and the government, a debate about the possibility of bringing the elections forward if Congress rejected the initiatives.

Sánchez's office insists that no decision has been taken, although government and PSOE figures had floated the possibility of Sánchez calling elections if the decrees were voted down. At the same time, other socialist leaders have urged caution and argued that the consequences of any eventual call need to be carefully weighed.

The issue is therefore tied to the outcome of a vote the government has presented as a test of the chamber's ability to reach agreements on one of the main problems facing Spanish society. Sánchez had already urged the parliamentary groups to show "a sense of perspective" in backing the measures and argued that housing should be kept out of "partisan confrontations."

While the sitting was underway, around a hundred people gathered outside Congress, mobilised by the Tenants' Union. Protesters chanted slogans against PP, Vox, and Junts and also held a banner critical of PSOE and Sumar. Police had deployed a large security operation around the chamber.

World.title: Iconic London hotel Dukes is set to reopen in mid-2027
World.content:
As legendary watering holes go, Dukes Bar is right up there.

 

Known for its martinis, which are said to be what inspired Ian Fleming to create James Bond’s signature beverage order, the saloon has welcomed some very famous guests, and even royalty, over the years.

The hotel the bar is in – Dukes London at 35 St James's Place – is currently undergoing renovations, and now we have a rough reopening date: Q2 of 2027, when it will become Dukes London, Minor Reserve Collection.

The 85-key property in the UK capital is being transformed by Russell Sage Studio, and will reopen with 13 executive suites and five signature suites inspired by past guests.

“Few hotels capture the character and heritage of London quite like Dukes,” William E. Heinecke, chairman and founder of Minor International, parent company of Minor Hotels.

“Together with our trusted partner Seven Tides, we look forward to the hotel’s next chapter, preserving Dukes London’s unique identity while expanding its reach through Minor Hotels' global luxury platform.”

The Delany Drawing Room will offer afternoon tea in its conservatory and garden space Minor Hotels

The transformation is being led by Russell Sage Studio Minor Hotels

What’s new at Dukes London?

While Dukes Bar has stayed open throughout the renovations, the hotel reopening will see the addition of a new lounge and bar, The Delany Drawing Room.

Whiskies are to The Delany Drawing Room what martinis are to Dukes Bar, with 160 different types available (alongside Champagne and cocktails). Featuring a conservatory and secluded garden, The Delany Drawing Room will also open for afternoon tea.

Minor Hotels is also partnering with The Wolseley Hospitality Group, responsible for well-known eateries including The Wolseley and The Delaunay, on a new restaurant.

World.title: Iran accused of blocking SIM cards, digital access to silence dissent
World.content:
DW has spoken with several Iranians who say their SIM cards, bank access and online accounts were blocked until they deleted critical content or pledged to stop activism.

In Iran, cell phone numbers are a key tool for digital identity verification and access to banking, judicial, administrative and insurance services, as well as many everyday activities.

As a result, disconnecting a SIM card can do more than block calls and text messages. It can also cut off access to a wide range of digital services.

Some Iranians said the restrictions on their cell phones were accompanied by the blocking of user accounts and access to banking and government services. They said access was restored only after they deleted critical content or pledged to stop participating in protest-related activities.

DW spoke to three people in Iran about the issue. They have used pseudonyms out of concern for their safety.

'Six hours of interrogation'

Sina told DW that he realized his SIM card had been disconnected while returning from university and trying to book a taxi by phone.

The 25-year-old said that after visiting a telecommunications center, he received a call from someone claiming to be from the Intelligence Organization of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IO-IRGC), who instructed him to go to a specified location to have his SIM card reconnected.

A message on Instagram stating: 'The activities of the page are in accodance with the laws of the Islamic Republic of Iran' Image: unbekannt

Sina said he was interrogated for about six hours and that his mobile phone was confiscated.

He said the return of his SIM card and phone was made conditional on signing a pledge expressing "remorse" for his activist activities and online "propaganda against the system." He said he was also required to publish posts supporting the Islamic Republic to "prove his brotherhood with the system."

Several hours later, he said, his family discovered that posts on his Instagram account had been deleted. Only one remained, stating that "the activities of the page are in accordance with the laws of the Islamic Republic of Iran."

A month later, he said, he had still not received his SIM card or mobile phone back and was unable to access his social media accounts.

Sorour, a 41-year-old translator at an official translation office in Tehran, said that after her SIM card was disconnected, she went to a location designated by the IO-IRGC, where she was interrogated for hours about her activities on Instagram and X.

Revolutionary Guard has 'massive' role in clampdown: expert To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sorour said she was told to make her account private and pledge to refrain from activities critical of the authorities, including advocating for political prisoners, protesting executions and supporting demonstrators during nationwide anti-government protests that began in late December 2025.

Mina, who lives in Isfahan, said she was summoned by an institution she identified as the IRGC Intelligence Organization after posting a comment supporting one of the country's political currents under a post by a foreign-based news outlet.

The 63-year-old said her SIM card and national identification card were blocked after she refused to comply with the summons.

According to Mina, the restrictions disrupted her access to bank transfers, administrative systems, online purchases and services that require electronic identity verification and one-time passwords.

She told DW she had also been denied access to Sana, the judiciary's electronic system, and was therefore unable to determine whether a case or charges had been filed against her.

SIM cards: the key to digital life in Iran

Several other Iranian citizens also posted similar complaints on social media.

Zia Nabavi, a former political prisoner, said in an Instagram post that his SIM card had been suddenly disconnected.

He said he discovered the issue while at a doctor's office, where he needed access to his mobile phone and banking text messages.

"For a long time, I have come to the conclusion that the government's policy toward critics and opponents is to apply pressure that pushes them toward obedience or withdrawing from their activities," Nabavi wrote.

Regime 'taking the Iranian people hostage' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Reyhaneh Saeedi, a physician and activist, also said on Instagram that her SIM card has been blocked for months and that this is the second time she has faced such restrictions.

She said the measure has effectively prevented her from practicing medicine, issuing prescriptions and renewing her Medical Council and medical office licenses.

Saeedi said her identification card had also been deactivated. She added that no ruling had been formally served on her, she had not been informed of any charges or judicial proceedings, and her efforts to determine the reason for the restrictions had yielded no results.

Actress Shaghayegh Dehghan said on Instagram that her SIM card had been blocked and that she did not know which institution or authority was behind the move.

Cutting communications

The disconnection of SIM cards and other digital restrictions has become part of a broader set of tools that the Islamic Republic has used over the past four decades to exert pressure on opponents, critics, journalists, and civil and human rights activists.

The Defending Free Flow of Information (DeFFI) organization reported in 2025 that journalists and activists had their SIM cards blocked without judicial orders.

The measures have raised concerns about the powers exercised by security institutions to deny citizens access to communication tools and essential services.

They have also highlighted the absence of a clear accountability mechanism, leaving those affected with no obvious avenue to challenge the restrictions or seek an explanation.

World.title: Trump, Macron confirm Europe will release diesel stockpiles after US requests
World.content:
The US leader asked European countries to release some of their diesel reserves to ease the rising prices. The issue has damaged Trump's popularity back home.

US President Donald Trump announced on Friday that Europe will release parts of its diesel reserves with immediate effect.

"Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil," Trump posted on his Truth Social account, adding that the process will begin "immediately."

This comes as the US leader faces growing pressure at home due to mounting prices of oil and other goods as a result of the Iran war and his trade policies.

According to the American Automobile Association (AAA), the average price of a diesel gallon in the US was 6.37 dollars (5.65 euros).

Trump has argued the soaring prices are worth it in order to make sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons, with the prices supposedly coming down after the war's end.

Russia's ban on exports, which came due to Ukraine's attacks on its refineries, also contributed to the hit in diesel supply around the world.

Macron confirms move

French President Emmanuel Macron, who is also the G7 chair, confirmed the news by saying that the G7 will release up to 100 million barrels over the next four months.

Macron also committed to refraining from any trade-limiting measures when it comes to petroleum and energy products between partner countries.

"Our citizens' concerns about energy prices remain a top priority," G7 leaders said in a joint statement published by Macron.

"We will monitor developments closely and stand ready to adjust measures as needed."

Diesel prices have also risen sharply in Germany Image: Robert Michael/dpa/picture alliance

This comes after a call between Macron and Trump on the issue took place overnight, the French Embassy in the US said.

The US had demanded France, Germany and other European countries to release 100 million diesel barrels within a 20-day window, Reuters reported, citing sources.

World.title: Germany's Franz Reindl elected new IIHF president
World.content:
Franz Reindl has been elected president of ice hockey's world governing body. The former forward was a member of West Germany's Olympic bronze medal-winning team.

Franz Reindl came from behind to narrowly beat Petr Briza of the Czech Republic in a run-off vote to become the International Ice Hockey Federation's new president on Friday.

Reindl had trailed Briza 48-36 in the first round of voting but picked up crucial votes after Aivaz Omorkanov of Kyrgyzstan was eliminated. He then beat Briza 60-57 in the runoff held on the Spanish island of Tenerife. Six of a total of nine candidates had withdrawn prior to the election.

The 71-year-old German, who had been a member of the IIHF Council since 2016, succeeds Canadian-born Frenchman Luc Tardif, who had announced in March that he would not seek a further term in office. Reindl's election comes 5 years after he had finished as runner-up to Tardif. His term runs until 2030.

Wealth of experience

Reindl has done it all in German ice hockey, having been a player and coach, as well as serving as the first CEO of the top-flight professional league, the Deutsche Eishockey Liga (DEL), from 1994 to 19<96. He also headed the organizing committees for three World Championships — in 2001, 2010 and 2017. From 2014 to 2022 he served as president of the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB), overseeing an upturn in the fortunes of the men's national team, which won the silver medal at the Pyeongchang Winter Olympics in 2018.

Franz Reindl served as interim coach of the men's national team, here during the 2004 World Cup of hockey Image: Christof Koepsel/Bongarts/Getty Images

"Franz Reindl has shaped German ice hockey for decades—as a player, but above all through the various key roles he has held within our federation," the current DEB chairman, Frank Lutz, said.

"The fact that the international ice hockey family is now entrusting him with the leadership of the IIHF is a great tribute to his work."

Successful playing career

Like Briza, who was a goalie for the Czechoslovakia team that won bronze in Albertville in 1992, Reindl was also an Olympic bronze medalist, having been a member of the 1976 West Germany team who beat the United States and Finland to finish third in Lake Placid.

Domestically, Reindl played 669 games and scored 423 goals for SC Riessersee and SB Rosenheim over 16 seasons in the Eishockey-Bundesliga, the predecessor to the DEL.

Tardif's years as IIHF president were marked by two major events: the return of National Hockey League players to the Olympic tournament in Milan Cortina this year, and the exclusion from international play of Russia in 2022 over the country's full-scale war on neighboring Ukraine.

Reindl is the second German to be elected IIHF president after Günter Sabetzki, who held the post from 1975 to 1994.

World.title: Argentina launches cash-for-citizenship scheme
World.content:
Investors seeking the fastest but most costly route to Argentine citizenship can choose between a non-refundable gift of $350,000, or buying a government bond for $800,000, if they think that will pay off in the end.

Argentina's government launched a scheme it hopes will attract wealthy investors and simultaneously "further strengthen the Argentine Republic's fiscal and financial position," offering people the chance to apply for citizenship via investment and thus bypass the more typical procedures.

Economy Minister Luis Caputo and Cabinet chief Diego Santilli launched the citizenship-by-investment program amid the "Argentina Week" business event in Paris, saying it would start accepting applications during the fourth quarter of 2026.

"This announcement is part of Argentina's drive toward international openness and integration, accompanied by reforms aimed at strengthening the investment climate and attracting capital," the Economy Ministry said in a statement .

Argentina's President Javier Milei has tried to portray himself as a cost-cutting pro-business leader restoring stability to one of the world's most fragile economies, which has defaulted on or restructured parts of its national debt multiple times just this century. Its most recent emergency loans scheme from the IMF and World Bank was approved last April.

Luis Caputo announced the move amid the 'Argentina Week' event in Paris trying to drum up business and investment Image: Teresa Suarez/AP Photo/picture alliance

What are the details of the citizenship-by-investment program?

The program plans to offer "two simple and transparent mechanisms" to the primary investors seeking citizenship for themselves and perhaps for their immediate family.

The first is "making a direct, non-refundable contribution of $350,000 (roughly €310,000) to the National Treasury," the Economy Ministry said. The other higher risk, higher reward approach will be "subscribing to a $800,000 public bond created specifically for this program."

The principal applicant's spouse and children aged 25 or under can then also apply, albeit themselves having to pay smaller fees. Spouses and childless children aged 18-25 would be charged $100,000 each, and minors would have to contribute $25,000 each.

"Under this scheme, a typical family unit consisting of a principal applicant, their spouse, and two minor children could apply for Argentine citizenship for a total of $500,000," the ministry said, referring to a sum equating to well over a century earning Argentina's nominal median wage.

Argentina loses 33 companies a day under Javier Milei To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Argentina said it would incorporate recommendations from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) to ensure the adoption of international best practices and "comply with applicable standards regarding the prevention of money laundering, terrorist financing, and financial transparency."

"We continue working to strengthen Argentina's ties with the world, project the value of our citizenship internationally, and consolidate the country as an open and reliable nation," Economy Minister Caputo said online.

World.title: Can there be solar for all, everywhere by 2030?
World.content:
Prominent climate leaders have called on governments, businesses, institutions and the public to make a push for solar power before the decade is out, repowering the world with cheap, clean energy. Is that possible?

In a world set ablaze by war and global warming, with ever worsening climate disasters such as wildfires in Europe and collapsing glaciers in Nepal, solar energy provides the solution of clean, affordable power, prominent climate leaders wrote in an open letter pushing for more solar.

Signed by prominent climate figures such as author Bill McKibben, former UN Climate Secretary Christiana Figueres and Canada's former Minister of Environment and Climate Change Catherine McKenna, the letter makes a clear call. It urges governments, businesses, institutions and the public to come together to provide clean, affordable energy to "everyone, everywhere by 2030" — from the close to one billion people who still lack access to reliable electricity, to the billions more who pay too much for dirty fossil fuels.

Close to 1 billion people don't have access to reliable electricity — solar power could change that Image: Moritz Wolf/imageBROKER/picture alliance

With just a little over three years to go until the decade is out, how realistic is this push?

"It's an ambitious target, but we've blown away in terms of where we thought we would be on solar and renewables," McKenna told DW. "So let's just keep on going."

Where are we currently with solar?

According to global energy think tank Ember, solar power has grown at its highest rate in eight years. In 2025, it increased by a record 30% over the previous year and has risen more than tenfold since 2015.

Solar is the cheapest form of electricity in the history of the world, said McKenna, who founded the climate advisory firm Climate and Nature Solutions, and the global coalition Women Leading on Climate.

"It is scaling way faster than anyone ever imagined."

As is battery technology used to store excess renewable energy.

"The cost of batteries have as well come down as the cost of solar modules," said Eicke Weber, a physicist and former director of Germany's Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems who went on to found the European Solar Manufacturing Council, among other things.

"We have the technologies available and we have enough money to finance it," he said, of a transition to widespread solar access.

In 2025, for the first time in 100 years, renewable energy sources overtook coal power in the global electricity mix, Ember's most recent analysis showed.

Where do we need to get to with solar?

At the moment, installed solar capacity around the world stands at 3 terawatts. 1TW equals 1000 gigawatts, and a single nuclear power plant has a capacity of 1GW.

Currently, the world produces about 1TW of new photovoltaic capacity each year, most of it in China. Weber says in order to fully change global energy supply to renewables, we would need about 50TW, adding that "we have more production capacities than we are selling."

Roughly 655 million people still lack access to electricity.

"The pace of electrification in Sub-Saharan Africa has to triple to achieve universal access by 2030," McKenna said, pointing out how quickly this gap could be closed with solar.

Areas without electricity have the opportunity to leapfrog straight into clean technologies, she says, bypassing the fossil fuels that are heating the planet. Rising global temperatures are fueling extreme weather events such as drought, storms and flooding around the world.

"And there's a misunderstanding, which is often propagated intentionally by fossil fuel companies, that it's expensive, it's hard, it's unreliable. And that just isn't the case anymore," she said. "To be honest, the most unreliable thing is if you're trying to pass fossil fuels through the Strait of Hormuz."

Is solar for all, everywhere really doable in that short amount of time?

Hans-Josef Fell is used to the argument that certain things cannot be done. Widely known as a pioneer of renewable energy, he drafted Germany's Renewable Energy Sources Act which established feed-in tariffs that catalyzed clean energy growth at home and beyond.

"The Renewable Energy Sources Act unleashed exponential growth that shattered every assumption about what was achievable. It overturned the scenarios and projections that policymakers and experts had considered realistic. In the end, reality outperformed all expectations," said Fell, who now heads the think tank Energy Watch Group.

Fell, who has lived off grid for five years, says achieving a global energy transition requires political and societal will that is "currently lacking around the world because public debate is dominated by fossil fuel interests."

Solar power has been growing exponentially over the past years Image: Thomas Imo/photothek/picture alliance

According to calculations by his think tank, if global energy demand were met entirely by renewables, solar energy would account for roughly 60-70% of the supply. The rest would come from wind power, and other sources, such as bioenergy and hydropower.

Where to go from here?

Countries like China and Pakistan have already pushed ahead.

"It is in our hands right now in the year 2026 to say we drop everything, we concentrate on this problem. We don't need to wait for new research," Weber said.

"It is possible to achieve this, but it would require a very kind of moonshot program," he added, saying it would need serious political backing.

He says while it might be possible for Germany to pull off such as transition in two or three years, if the political will were there, it would likely take longer to achieve on a global scale. "We would need probably till 2040 to say that we have a goal of a worldwide 80%, 90% electricity from renewables."

How countries are skipping 200 years of carbon emissions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"I would sum it up this way: if we as a global society tackle this properly, we might actually be able to make it happen," Fell said. "And even if we achieve only 90% of that goal, it would still be a remarkable accomplishment."

McKenna points to the need for blended finance, calling on governments, the World Bank, the African Development Bank and the private sector to put in money.

"What is irrational is continuing down the road of fossil fuels," she said. "That's irrational on the costs, the risks, the impacts. It's an old technology."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

World.title: North and South Korea trade accusations over landmines that injured three soldiers
World.content:
A mine blast that injured three South Korean soldiers has renewed scrutiny of North Korea's actions along the border and raised questions about its strategic goals.

Pyongyang and Seoul are trading increasingly hostile accusations across the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that divides the peninsula, 10 days after three South Korean soldiers were injured by a land mine on the South's side of the border.

The latest tensions may reflect a broader North Korean effort to test South Korea's resolve while extending its control to the outer limits of its territory, including an area that has effectively been a no-man's land for more than 70 years, according to a professor of foreign policy at South Korea's Kyung Hee University.

"The North revised its constitution in March this year and officially stated that they intend to define the absolute geographical limits of the nation, and that includes within the DMZ," said Choo Jae-woo.

"They want to maximize their territory and it is my sense that they would like to push the Military Demarcation Line [MDL] — the half-way point in the DMZ — further south," he told DW.

"I see the placing of landmines on the South's side of the line as a purely political act by the North, an attempt to threaten and intimidate the South."

Why Seoul blames North Korea

The three men were part of an 18-strong patrol clearing a new route through the DMZ as part of an investigation into the activities of North Korean troops in the western sector of the zone. The four-kilometer-wide strip of land has divided the peninsula since the Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953.

The DMZ is a fortified buffer zone between the two Koreas that has been in place since 1953 Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

Shortly before 11 a.m. on September 21, the patrol was around 10 meters south of the MDL when a staff sergeant detonated a mine. A second mine went off as the unit commander approached to provide assistance. Both men were successfully evacuated and have undergone surgery, with a third soldier treated for minor wounds.

The South Korean military has conducted an investigation with the United Nations Command, which administers the armistice on the border, and concluded in a report released this week that the mine was of North Korean origin.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff on Wednesday accused the North of sowing mines to the south of the MDL, a breach of the armistice agreement, and demanded an apology from Pyongyang and a commitment to halt the construction of further fortifications along the border.

"This constitutes a blatant violation of the Armistice Agreement and undermines the spirit of existing inter-Korean agreements and must be halted immediately," Kang Hyun-woo, chief director of operations, said in a press briefing.

"North Korea must immediately cease activities that heighten tensions on the Korean Peninsula, such as its so-called 'border fortification.' We strongly demand an apology and responsible measures from the North," Kang added.

In a statement, the UN Command said it had "determined that an Armistice Agreement violation occurred. UNC is addressing the violation through established Armistice mechanisms."

Prisoner swap: From North to South Korea via Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Many in the South are demanding more resolute action on the grounds that failure to respond will be taken as a sign of weakness in Seoul.

Na Kyung-won, a politician from the conservative opposition People Power Party (PPP), has demanded that the South Korean military carry out exercises simulating a "decapitation attack" against North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

She has also called for the restart of propaganda broadcasts from loudspeakers on the border and for dissident groups to be allowed to launch balloons carrying propaganda into the North.

A pattern of border confrontations

Yu Yong-weon, also of the PPP, told reporters on Wednesday that North Korean troops had crossed the MDL around 20 times in August and on 30 occasions in September. On each occasion, South Korean troops fired warning shots when the incursions were detected.

An editorial in the Korea JoongAng Daily on Thursday said North Korea must be "held accountable" for the incident, arguing that Pyongyang's denial of responsibility "demands a firm response, clear accountability and stronger border enforcement."

Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong has accused Seoul of conspiracy after it blamed Pyongyang for the blast in the DMZ Image: Yuri Smityuk/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

The North is not backing down, however, with Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, accusing the South of staging a provocation and threatening to retaliate.

In a statement published by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on Wednesday, Kim Yo Jong dismissed the South's allegations as a "self-staged farce" and accused the "South Korean armed gangs" of using the incident to justify political and military provocations against Pyongyang.

Accident or calculated provocation?

Andrei Lankov, a professor of history and international relations at Seoul's Kookmin University, is more willing to view the landmine detonations as an accident.

"It makes no sense to me for North Korea to do this deliberately," he said. "At the moment, the North wants to keep a low profile and do nothing that could provoke the South. There is no gain in a deliberate attack like this."

Lankov believes a more likely scenario is that the mines were shifted from the northern side of the MDL in heavy rain or natural movements of the terrain, meaning that the North's protestations of innocence are genuine.

"I also do not think the South Korean government has any interest in escalating the situation further and that they will hope this is quickly forgotten," he said. "They will want to brush it under the carpet."

Choo, however, is less convinced and senses a growing anger in South Korean society that the government is not standing up to provocations from north of the border.

"I believe that resuming the propaganda broadcasts over the border would be an effective response, but I do not believe this government will do that," he said. "This government is trying very hard to connect with the North, but I see a failure to take a firm line this time being interpreted in the North as a sign of weakness in Seoul.

"Not responding would give Pyongyang a green light to push a little more and then a little more again," he said. "There is a lot of anger here that the government is not doing enough to protect soldiers who are serving on the DMZ, to protect the people and to protect our territory."

World.title: Manchester City Premier League charges: What do they mean?
World.content:
Since being bought by the UAE in 2008, Manchester City have become one of the world's most successful football clubs. A raft of serious financial charges threatens to undermine this and bring chaos to the Premier League.

Manchester City has won the English Premier League eight times over the last 14 years. Whether those titles will remain is one of a plethora of issues at stake after England's top division charged one of its most high-profile clubs with more than 100 breaches of its financial regulations.

On Tuesday, the Premier League announced that an independent commission had found City had drawn up "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs." These contracts, dubious sponsorships and a number of other methods were, according to the commission's report , used to inflate the club's revenue to the tune of about £900 million (€1.05 billion) over the period between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

The case has been ongoing for eight years after initial revelations from Der Spiegel, a German magazine, and Rui Pinto of the 'Football Leaks' website. City continues to deny any wrongdoing.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case," read a club statement . "Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe."

On Friday, the club issued a further statement saying it had lodged a "comprehensive Appeal."

What was the Premier League verdict on the Manchester City charges?

The 750-page report was damning, accusing City of inflating contracts and sponsorship deals, running secondary contracts off the books, making "concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation" and signing off inflated image rights deals to artificially boost their earnings. The report says all this enabled them to pass both Premier League and UEFA financial spending limits.

The Premier League's chief ­executive, Richard Masters, described the case "as the most significant in Premier League history," adding that the club "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade."

Although the Premier League, the world's most commercially successful football league, has drawn some praise for its actions, others point out that it took Pinto leaking emails and media reports to take action. The report shows that Manchester City, which had won the league once in 71 years before being taken over by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in 2008, were consistently posting revenues way higher than any of their more established and successful rivals.

Who are the key figures at Manchester City?

In this context, its the owners. The Abu Dhabi United Group, essentially an investment vehicle for the UAE royal family, bought the club in 2008. Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, know simply as Sheikh Mansour, fronted the takeover. He is a member of the ruling Al Nahyan family and the UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister. Khaldoon Al Mubarak, who also holds several government positions in the UAE, was brought in as chairman.

Nation-state ownership of this type is controversial in European football. Manchester City's owners have long been criticized for the country's human rights record and using the club for sportswashing. Similar criticisms have been made of European champions Paris Saint-Germain, which Qatar owned and City's Premier League rivals Newcastle United, which is owned 85% by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

As well as huge domestic success, City won the Champions League under Pep Guardiola in 2022-23 Image: Jose Breton/NurPhoto/IMAGO

City's CEO, Ferran Soriano, joined in 2012 as City expanded their ownership into foreign leagues, buying up clubs in the US, Japan and Australia. He replaced former head coach Roberto Mancini with fellow Spaniard Manuel Pellegrini before former Bayern Munich and Barcelona coach Pep Guardiola took over in 2016, ushering in the club's most successful period.

How did Manchester City's system work?

The club immediately started splashing out on big-money transfers after the UAE investment arrived. At the time, neither UEFA nor the Premier League had the tight financial rules they now have. UEFA introduced its Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules for the 2011-12 season, while the Premier League followed with its Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) in 2013-14.

City's free spending and relatively low commercial income meant they were likely to fall foul of such rules. The club was handed a conditional €60 million UEFA fine for losses in the 2011-12 and 2012-13 seasons. They would later be banned from the Champions League on similar grounds in 2020 before being reinstated on appeal.

In an attempt to try and comply with these financial rules, City set up a system they called "Project Longbow" in 2012. The commission said much of this was genuine, but one arm of it was an agreement with a third party called Fordham that was, according to the ruling, "little more than a front." Essentially, it reads, the club's UAE owners "would be used (and were used) to enable Fordham to acquire from the club (at a sizeable, artificially inflated price) the club's entitlement to benefit financially from its players' image rights."

In other words, City's owners were pumping money into their own club through vastly inflated sponsorship and image rights deals so their income looked higher and they could spend more, particularly on player transfers and wages. The report also claims that City paid three individuals, whose names are redacted, through a third party to keep them off the books.

What happens next?

That's the question on everyone's lips. So far, no sanctions have been imposed on City, and the appeal will likely drag proceedings out even longer. Meanwhile, the club, which is top of the Premier League, faces Liverpool on October 11, after the international break.

While there is no precedent for such a tranche of charges, clubs have previously fallen foul of the Premier League's PSR regulations. Everton were handed a 10-point penalty for a £19.5 million breach over a period ending with the 2021-22 season. This was based on a Premier League tariff of six points for the initial breach, plus an additional point for every £5 million the club overspent. Given that City's overspending is close to a billion pounds, applying that would certainly relegate them, though the Premier League does not operate England's second-tier league, the Championship.

For now, it looks like City and the league will play on under a cloud. But if the verdict remains after appeal, clubs and individuals whose careers and honors stand to be impacted will likely come forward and litigate. City themselves could be relegated, docked points over successive seasons, face transfer bans or any combination of those things. The titles won in the relevant period could also be stripped.

This article was originally published on September 30, 2026. It was updated on October 2, 20206 with Manchester City's statement confirming that it had lodged an appeal.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: Half of Europe witnessed record heat stress this summer — EU
World.content:
The EU's climate monitor said this summer was third-warmest for the continent on record. European rivers also registered their lowest average flows since records began in 1992.

A record 52% of Europe witnessed "very strong" heat stress by the end of this summer, the EU's Copernicus Climate Service (C3S) said in new research published on Friday.

What did Copernicus say in its findings?

According to Copernicus, "very strong" heat stress is characterized by temperatures which feel higher than 38 degrees Celsius (100.4 degrees Fahrenheit).

Around 80% of Europe witnessed "strong" heat stress by the end of the summer. "Strong" heat stress is when temperatures feel like more than 32 degrees Celsius (89.6 degrees Fahrenheit).

Heat stress is when temperatures and humidity are so high that the body cannot cool itself through perspiration.

This summer was the third-warmest on record on the European continent and the hottest on record in Western Europe.

"One of the things that stands out for 2026 is that the heat was not only remarkable for its intensity, but also for its geographical extent," Samantha Burgess, the deputy director of the C3S, said.

The Rhine River in western Germany saw record lows during the heat waves this summer Image: Hesham Elsherif/Anadolu/picture alliance

Copernicus also said that European rivers registered their lowest average flows since records began in 1992. In addition, the service said that "56% of the European ocean was much warmer than average, with 22% experiencing record-high summer sea surface temperatures."

Burgess said that drought impacted almost half of Europe by the end of this summer.

"That's one of the defining characteristics of summer this year, that it was not a single record. It was the way that multiple records appeared together across the climate system," she said.

What was the impact of the European heat waves this summer?

Tens of thousands of people died in heat waves in Europe this summer, which also impacted economic activity and agricultural harvests.

Some cities such as Paris even temporarily restricted alcohol sales as temperatures frequently spiked above 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) on parts of the continent.

Air conditioning is uncommon in some parts of Europe, with many Europeans staying home or going out to the pool to cool off.

France's firefighters on the wildfire frontline To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In addition, the frequent heat waves and dry conditions this summer also led to wildfires in southern France and the southern Spanish region of Andalusia, among other locations.

The biggest wildfire in history in Germany's most populous state, North Rhine-Westphalia, triggered evacuations in August before it was brought under control.

Wildfires not only damage buildings but also create harmful air pollution in the environment.

World.title: Votación de los decretos de vivienda y las acampadas, en directo | El Congreso tumba los decretos de vivienda y abona el terreno para un adelanto electoral
World.content:
Bustinduy asegura que votar “no” a los decretos de vivienda es “traicionar a su pueblo para servir a la bandera del rentismo”

El ministro de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030, Pablo Bustinduy, ha asegurado este viernes en el Congreso que votar “no” a los decretos de vivienda es “traicionar a su pueblo para servir a la única bandera del rentismo”. Así se ha pronunciado al defender el segundo texto impulsado por el Ejecutivo, después de que la ministra de Vivienda, Isabel Rodríguez, defendiera el primero y todos los partidos del arco parlamentario manifestaran su intención de voto. “Yo creo que hoy van a cometer un error político del que se van a arrepentir durante mucho tiempo (…) Les puedo asegurar que el pueblo va a tener memoria y va a recordar quiénes les ha traicionado”, ha dicho a PP, Vox y Junts.

Bustinduy ha reconocido en su turno de palabra que coincide con el diputado de ERC Gabriel Rufián, que intervino minutos antes, en que los diputados y diputadas que voten “no” este viernes a los decretos de vivienda impulsados por el Gobierno deberían “revelar con quién se han reunido” en los últimos días. En esta línea, ha criticado la negativa de PP, Vox y Junts a apoyar las medidas presentadas por el Ejecutivo de Pedro Sánchez. En el caso de los populares, ha hecho especial referencia al ático que compró la Comunidad de Madrid, presidida por Isabel Díaz Ayuso, valorado en unos seis millones de euros.

“Lo de hoy no va de aritmética parlamentaria. No va de negociaciones entre grupos políticos. Lo de hoy es un conflicto de clase, es defender a una oligarquía internacional que está extrayendo las rentas y el salario de las clases trabajadoras para repartírselas como dividendos y no tributar en España”, ha señalado el ministro.

Durante su intervención, Bustinduy ha reivindicado la necesidad de que las viviendas sean para los ciudadanos y no para los “fondos buitres” o grandes tenedores que, ha recalcado, expulsan a los vecinos de los barrios en los que han vivido toda la vida. Y, antes de cerrar su turno de palabra, ha espetado: “Ustedes no defienden a los españoles. Defienden a los ricos. No tienen bandera ni vergüenza”. “Son unos vende patrias”, ha añadido.

World.title: La estafa del falso empleado de banca
World.content:
Recibir un SMS que alerta sobre un movimiento sospechoso en nuestra cuenta bancaria puede evitar que seamos víctima de un robo, excepto si no ha sido el banco quien realmente lo ha emitido

En la estafa del falso empleado de banca el delincuente primero envía un mensaje con una alerta sobre un movimiento sospechoso en la cuenta y facilita un enlace o un número de teléfono al que llamar. Ya en la conversación, intenta convencer a la víctima de que su dinero está en peligro para que autorice operaciones que resultarán fraudulentas

En 2025, Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad (INCIBE) registró 25.133 casos de phishing. Durante los dos últimos años, tanto la Policía Nacional como la Guardia Civil y el Banco de España han emitido alertas sobre el aumento de las llamadas de falsos empleados bancarios.

TÉCNICAS DE MANIPULACIÓN

Autoridad Suplantan a profesionales pertenecientes a bancos a los que la víctima concede poder y confianza Urgencia Crean la sensación de que hay poco tiempo para actuar, lo que evita que la víctima reflexione o consulte con alguien Sobrecarga de información técnica Emplean jerga bancaria para intimidar y hacer creer que dominan una situación compleja Aumento gradual de las peticiones Incluye a la víctima en grupos de aplicaciones de mensajería para hacerle creer que mucha gente ya está ganando dinero

CIBEREXPERTO NOMBRE Jordi Sánchez CARGO Experto en fraude de CaixaBank “Durante la llamada, el estafador te hace creer que te está guiando para solucionar tu problema, pero en realidad, está intentando que tu hagas exactamente lo que necesita, emitir operaciones bancarias, descargar aplicaciones o facilitar información, como códigos o datos de tarjetas” Play / Pause CÓMO EVITAR LA ESTAFA DEL FALSO EMPLEADO DE BANCA 1 Sospechar de mensajes inesperados. No clicar en ningún enlace que aparezca en el mensaje ni llamar al número que ofrecen. Ante la duda, siempre se debe llamar a los números oficiales del banco 2 Desconfiar de la urgencia y de las amenazas.Mensajes como “Su cuenta será bloqueada” buscan que se actúe sin pensar 3 No compartir claves ni códigos de verificación. El banco nunca solicitará contraseñas u otros códigos de seguridad 4 No descargar archivos ni instalar aplicaciones. Los estafadores pueden pedir que se descarguen programas que en realidad les están dando acceso al teléfono de la víctima

Una estafa que ha evolucionado. Este fraude comenzó como un SMS y una llamada, pero hoy se dan variantes como la que busca robar información de las tarjetas bancarias mediante el uso de la tecnología NFC del teléfono móvil. Este sistema de comunicación inalámbrica permite compartir información entre otros, tarjetas y móviles, y realizar pagos sin contacto. Los estafadores solicitan a la víctima que se descargue una aplicación maliciosa y que acerque la tarjeta al smartphone. Así, sus datos son enviados a otro teléfono de los atacantes, donde crearán una tarjeta de forma virtual con la que intentar sacar dinero o comprar en comercios.

El teléfono puede parecer auténtico. Los estafadores pueden hacer que en la pantalla del móvil de la víctima figure el mismo número que utiliza el banco para atender a sus clientes o que el SMS aparezca en el mismo hilo que las comunicaciones legítimas mediante una técnica que se conoce como spoofing (que significa suplantación).

Conocen datos personales de su víctima. En muchos casos, disponen de información de su objetivo, como el banco del que es cliente, parte del DNI o la dirección de correo electrónico.

Si ya se ha caído en la estafa. Se debe poner en conocimiento del banco de inmediato para que se puedan adoptar las medidas operativas oportunas. También es muy importante guardar las evidencias, como capturas de pantalla, SMS, correos y registro de llamadas. Presentar una denuncia ante la Policía Nacional o la Guardia Civil.

OTROS CASOS DEL FALSO EMPLEADO DE BANCA

Cada semana aparecen noticias con nuevas maneras de embaucar a ciudadanos con una estafa de este tipo:

World.title: Soy presidente de mi comunidad y el administrador se niega a entregarme el acta de la última junta. ¿Qué puedo hacer?
World.content:
Pregunta. Somos una comunidad de cuatro portales y cuatro presidentes. Yo soy uno de ellos. El 12 de mayo tuvimos reunión general donde se acordó el cambio de presidentes y otras cuestiones, como los arreglos de los tejados. Pedí a la administradora cuatro veces el acta de la reunión general, tanto por WhatsApp como por email y no hay manera de que lo mande. ¿Qué puedo hacer? R. Calzada Gútiez

Respuesta. La Ley de Propiedad Horizontal (LPH) establece en su artículo 19 que el acta debe quedar cerrada con las firmas del presidente y del secretario al finalizar la reunión o dentro de los diez días naturales siguientes. Asimismo, dispone que el acta debe remitirse a los propietarios conforme al procedimiento previsto en la ley. Además, el secretario está obligado a custodiar los libros de actas y a conservar durante cinco años las convocatorias, comunicaciones, apoderamientos y demás documentación relevante de las reuniones.

Estas disposiciones implican que, una vez celebrada la junta, los acuerdos deben formalizarse mediante la correspondiente acta, firmada por el presidente y el secretario dentro del plazo legal, y comunicarse a los propietarios en el domicilio designado a efectos de notificaciones. Por tanto, el secretario-administrador tiene la obligación de remitir a todos los propietarios, incluidos los miembros de la junta, copia del acta con los acuerdos adoptados.

Además, el artículo 20 de la LPH establece entre las funciones del administrador actuar como secretario de la junta y custodiar, a disposición de los propietarios, la documentación de la comunidad. Entre esta documentación se encuentran las actas de las reuniones de los últimos cinco años, que el administrador debe conservar y poner a disposición de los propietarios, junto con cualquier otra documentación comunitaria que pueda solicitarse.

Por ello, si el administrador no ha remitido el acta con los acuerdos aprobados o no facilita el acceso a documentación de interés comunitario, puede exigírsele su entrega mediante un requerimiento fehaciente, como un burofax con certificación de texto y acuse de recibo, fijando un plazo para su cumplimiento.

Si, pese a ello, no atiende el requerimiento, su conducta podría considerarse contraria a sus obligaciones legales y profesionales. En ese caso, podría presentarse una queja ante el Colegio de Administradores al que pertenezca, reclamar los daños y perjuicios que, en su caso, se hayan ocasionado o acordar en junta de propietarios la resolución del contrato de prestación de servicios y el nombramiento de un nuevo administrador.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Fries with that? Homes near Amsterdam TikTok queue sell for less
World.content:
Homes near Fabel Friet, an Amsterdam chip shop whose TikTok-fuelled queues have become one of the city’s more unlikely tourist attractions, sell for less than comparable homes just streets away, according to a TU Delft study.

The research, reported by local broadcaster AT5, came out this week at the same time as the city council and the shop’s owners faced off in court over the queue and how to deal with public nuisance caused by it.

PhD researcher Rosa van der Drift compared the sale prices of 6,233 Amsterdam homes between 2015 and 2023, taking account of factors such as size and condition. Homes within 500 metres of the shop sold for 4.88% less on average, or about €41,000.

Within 70 metres, the gap widened to 11.4%. The study does not establish any correlation with causation.

Old licence

The court case was made by a group of residents against the city council, not the business. They argue the council did not properly weigh their interests when it granted Fabel Friet an operating licence, and want the licence withdrawn or its conditions tightened.

In 2024, a judge suspended a council rule limiting the queue to 10 people after Fabel Friet called it unworkable.

On Tuesday, one resident told the court there were people eating chips outside “every day, from 11 in the morning until 9 in the evening”, AT5 reported. The residents’ lawyer said a serious accident on the crowded bridge was only a matter of time.

The owners told the court their crowd managers keep the queue safe, the street is cleaned 4 times a day and crowds are down 23% since they opened other branches. For a while they hired a falcon 3 times a week to scare off the gulls, but stopped when residents began using it as evidence against them.

A representative of mayor Femke Halsema acknowledged that the old licence had not been effective enough, and said stricter conditions had been added to the current one about 6 months ago. “It is complicated,” the representative said, according to AT5. “You are so successful, is that not allowed?”

The judge urged both sides to find common ground, reminding the residents of the Dutch saying that a good neighbour is better than a distant friend. She will rule within 6 weeks, but only on the old licence, because objections to the current licence have yet to be decided.

World.title: Cabinet backtracks on box 3 tax plans for small savings
World.content:
The cabinet has promised to rewrite part of its new tax plan for savings and investments, just two days after announcing it, so that fewer people with modest savings are impacted.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen, of the right-wing liberal VVD, made the commitment in parliament on Thursday after MPs from both opposition and coalition parties attacked the plan.

“I have discussed this with the prime minister and with the coalition,” the Financieel Dagblad reported him as saying. “We are prepared to make changes. There will be a proposal to spare small savers.”

Under the plan presented on Tuesday, people would pay 36% tax on returns above €1,000 a year from 2028, down from €1,800 in the earlier version of the reform. Heinen also said he still believed the plan would exempt couples with up to €100,000 in savings.

No funding yet

The minister said he did not yet know how the cabinet would make up the shortfall. Small savers were the main source of funding for the box 3 overhaul, which reports say could cost up to €20 billion.

“We don’t have many levers to pull,” Heinen said. “And every choice you make is enormously complicated.”

The cabinet will send the bill to the Council of State, the government’s senior advisory body on legislation, without an alternative source of funding. Heinen said he would come up with proposals by October 12, when MPs debate the cabinet’s annual package of tax changes.

He also said he would look again at a temporary measure for next year, which would cut the tax-free allowance from €59,357 to €30,846 per person and raise the tax rate. You can find out more about how the changes would affect you in our box 3 explainer.

World.title: Dutch royal house earned nearly half a billion from slavery
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Dutch royal family, the House of Orange-Nassau, earned an estimated €576 million from slavery, mostly in the former Dutch East Indies, according to a new investigation into the monarchy.

The research was commissioned by king Willem-Alexander, who granted access to the royal archives and funded the inquiry.

“All stadtholders, kings, and queens, at least up to and including Wilhelmina, were convinced of the legitimacy of colonialism and its importance for the Netherlands,” lead researcher Gert Oostindie said during a ceremony on Friday to present the findings.

The 2,000 page report has been published into five books and was presented to the king. Willem-Alexander described the conclusions as “heartbreaking and confronting” during the gathering at the Academy Building in Leiden.

“I cannot change the past, but I can make a positive contribution to the present and the future to the best of my ability,” he said.

According to the research, the royals earned very little from the transatlantic slave trade, not because they were opposed but because they were unsuccessful.

Oostindie’s work found that while monarchs voiced support for the institution, few had a direct impact on policy.

Only King William I, who was in power from 1813 to 1840, had a direct hand in colonial slavery. Prior to that, leaders left it to the States General, the country’s early administrative assembly, or to the powerful Dutch East India Company (VOC).

After the reign of William I, monarchs were forced to share power with an increasingly important parliament, which made most of the policy decisions.

Willem-Alexander asked Oostindie, a former professor of colonial history, to conduct the investigation in 2022. Sixty researchers were involved in the nearly four year project.

In 2023, the king formally apologised for the Netherlands’ slave trading history during an annual commemoration for the abolition of the practice.

The monarch also stopped using a ceremonial golden coach which has repeatedly come under fire for a painted panel that depicts scenes of colonialism.

Research by the home affairs ministry in 2023 came to a similar conclusion. That study, carried out following a 2021 parliamentary motion, involved some 30 academics and historians and was published as the book Staat en slavernij (State and slavery).

World.title: Rivers too low for depth checks, leaving ships to risk stranding
World.content:
Rivers in the east of the Netherlands have fallen so low that the authorities can no longer measure whether ships can pass safely, leaving skippers to decide for themselves whether or not to sail and risk getting stranded.

Rijkswaterstaat, the transport ministry department that manages the waterways, told broadcaster NOS its survey boats can no longer reach the shallowest stretches of the IJssel, the Nederrijn, the Pannerdensch Kanaal and much of the Waal.

In certain places the channel is less than 125cm deep, leaving only three agency boats that are shallow enough, but they are also needed in other regions.

Without them, Rijkswaterstaat cannot publish its daily shipping readings of the depths, which barge operators use to avoid getting stranded. Commercial firms collect and sell similar data, but not every skipper has or can pay for a subscription.

Transport under pressure

“This is very worrying,” Fiona Oomen, of inland shipping association Koninklijke Binnenvaart Nederland, told NOS. “All transport is under pressure, on the roads and on the waterways. What if the water drops even further? Where is everything supposed to go?”

The flow of the Rhine at Lobith, where the river enters the Netherlands, is now around 545 cubic metres per second. That is well below the record low of 614 set in August.

Last weekend a Dutch cruise ship carrying 140 passengers became stuck at Cologne as the Rhine dropped to new lows in Germany.

On the IJssel, a one-way system imposed last week has forced some vessels to take a detour of up to 300km.

Freight carried on Dutch waterways fell by 19% in August, according to CBS figures, with cross-border traffic with Germany worst hit.

The infrastructure ministry lifted the national water shortage in early September, but warned that river levels could stay low until the end of the year. The cabinet has ruled out compensation for businesses hit by the drought.

Rain needed

Rijkswaterstaat could not say how long the situation would last. “We need rain in the catchment area,” a spokesman told NOS, adding that it would have to fall mainly outside the Netherlands. Current forecasts suggest the flow will not get worse, but will not improve much either.

He warned that a different problem would follow. “When it’s over, we get the next problem,” he said. “Then we’ll have high water again.” The North Sea is currently exceptionally warm, which could mean a very wet autumn.
