New numbers from the Dutch statistics agency CBS show the inflation rate rose slightly in August.

The preliminary estimate from the Central Agency for Statistics shows a 0.1% rise from August, putting September’s inflation rate at 3.4%.

The final numbers will be released on October 13.

Fuel and energy prices account for most of the increase. The cost of petrol and gas for heating is was up 13.9% in September over the same month the year before.

Grocery prices, however, have dropped slightly for the second month in a row. Food staples were down 1.3% over the year before, after dropping 0.5% in August.

World.title: The Netherlands had its first TV broadcast 75 years ago
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Seventy-five years ago today, the Dutch had their first opportunity to watch a television broadcast: a performance of the play De Toverspiegel, live from a studio in Bussum.

The Royal Family watched the 90-minute production from the Soestdijk Palace.

Concerns about television’s corrupting influence on society and a focus on post-war reconstruction meant that the Netherlands entered the television era only in 1951, later than the United Kingdom or the United States.

The BBC had begun broadcasting in 1936.

The country had around 500 television sets at the time. Radio was the much more widely consumed medium, with around 250,000 devices in homes across the Netherlands.

A television set cost 785 guilders, about a third of the average annual salary, putting the luxury good far out of reach for most of the country.

Media historian Huub Wijfjes told the NOS that initial television broadcasts simply copied whatever was on the radio. “TV took a dominant position and reached its peak in the 60s, 70s, and 80s. The medium displaced radio,” he said.

By 1956, there were 75,000 television sets in the country.

On the website for the Netherlands Institute for Sound and Vision, you can watch the early broadcasts.

World.title: Israeli group disrupts Delft screening of Gaza documentary Naza
World.content:
A premiere screening of the documentary Naza, which investigates the killing of civilians by the Israeli military in Gaza, was interrupted in a Delft cinema on Thursday afternoon by a woman taking a microphone and addressing the audience about the October 7 massacres.

She stood in front of the screen midway through the film and began describing how her family members were murdered during the Hamas attacks that sparked the Gaza war in 2023.

The crowd booed her off stage, the microphone was disabled, some shouted “shame on you”, though some applauded her. The woman’s name is Sabine Taasa, a French-Israeli citizen from a town near the Gaza strip and who lost her husband and a son during the attacks.

An Israeli activist group Ad Kan accompanied Taasa to the screening. The group describes itself as former army and intelligence officers who infiltrate and obstruct what they say are anti-Israeli and anti-Semitic activities in foreign countries.

Another member tried to project footage from the October 7 attacks in the cinema while Taasa spoke, according to broadcaster NOS.

Naza, which has been lauded by critics, consists of anonymous interviews with 24 members of Israeli intelligence and military services. They describe how they attacked Gaza, how AI systems were used to select targets, and the policies toward collateral damage and loss of innocent life.

Some describe killing hundreds of civilians at a time to target single military figures; others describe using surveillance techniques to wait for militants to be at home with their families before striking – a tactic known as “where’s daddy”.

Israeli officials have condemned the film, with prime minister Netanyahu pledging to strip the film makers of their citizenship. Other military figures have disputed the claims made in the film and branded it propaganda.

Dutch-Israeli relations have been strained recently over the decision to ban imports of goods from illegal settlements in occupied Palestinian territories. Dutch diplomats have had their status stripped in response.

World.title: Polish coal mining giant JSW to shed 4,200 jobs – 21% of its workforce – this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish state-owned mining firm Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa (JSW), which is the EU’s largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland’s biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year. The plans come as JSW seeks to turn around its finances after years of large losses, as well as a broader shift in Poland away from reliance on coal. Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa do końca 2026 r. zwolni ponad 4,2 tys. osób. – Musimy kierować się interesem spółki – mówił na konferencji prasowej prezes JSW. Więcej: https://t.co/7Sxrhuuaja pic.twitter.com/evJoQal0c3 — Gazeta.pl (@gazetapl_news) October 1, 2026 On Wednesday, JSW’s management board announced that it expected the size of its workforce to decline by 4,248 by the end of this year, bringing it below 16,000, down from 20,135 at the end of March. “We anticipate that approximately 2,200 people will leave in the third quarter, and about 1,400 in the fourth quarter,” adding to those who have already left, said the firm’s CEO, Bogusław Oleksy, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Last year, Poland introduced a new law making it easier for coal companies to close mines and reduce their workforce. It provides for large severance payments and other measures intended to soften the blow for those who lose their jobs. News service Strefa Inwestorów says that, on this basis, more than 3,000 JSW employees have the option to take so-called mining or mineral-processing leave while just under 1,200 can opt for one-off severance payments. President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill that makes it easier to close down coal mines and provides severance pay of 170,000 zloty to miners. The measures are seen as a key part of Poland’s transition towards cleaner forms of energy https://t.co/vH6MU4nBsv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 The workforce reduction is part of JSW’s recovery plan for 2026-2035, announced this week. Other key objectives include cutting costs and investment without decreasing production while increasing the share of coking coal in output. When asked how the workforce reduction would affect production, Oleksy said the company would optimise its operations to make more efficient use of employees and equipment. He noted that most of the losses would be administrative positions rather than staff directly involved in production. In February this year, the company reached an agreement with unions to reduce labour costs in order to help stabilise the company’s financial position. JSW employees almost unanimously supported the agreement, reported broadcaster TVN. The initial results of the cost-cutting measures are beginning to show. In the first half of 2026, the cost of extraction per tonne fell to 609 zloty (€139) from 778 zloty a year earlier. JSW’s long-term goal is to bring the cost down to around 560 zloty per tonne. The company is still posting heavy losses, though those have also fallen this year. JSW posted a net loss of just over 1.0 billion zloty in the first half of 2026, around half the 2.1 billion zloty figure from the same period a year earlier. For the full year 2025, the company recorded a loss of 6.3 billion zloty, which was down from a record figure of 7.3 billion zloty in 2024. Polish state-owned mining giant JSW, the EU's largest producer of coking coal, has reported a record annual loss of 7.3bn zloty. It attributed the results to falling coal prices, lower production volumes, and the impact of a one-off write-off https://t.co/vrSgRu630b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 11, 2025 JSW’s announcement comes just as some officials and industry representatives are warning that the energy crisis caused by conflict in the Middle East could increase demand in Poland for coal, which is still used to generate around half of electricity and to heat almost a fifth of homes. Polish coal is among the most expensive in the world to extract, and the industry survives largely due to heavy public subsidies. In 2026, the state is expected to spend 5.5 billion zloty propping up the sector, after an outlay of 9 billion zloty last year. Successive governments have been seeking to move away from coal, which went from producing 87% of Poland’s electricity in 2015 to 52.2% in 2025. Meanwhile, between 2015 and 2024, the proportion of households using hard coal for heating fell from 40% to 17%, while those using natural gas doubled from 10% to 21%. However, the energy crisis prompted by US and Israeli attacks on Iran this year has resulted in natural gas prices soaring. As a result, Poland’s state assets minister, Wojciech Balczun, said last month that the geopolitical situation meant coal’s role this year would be “larger than we anticipated”. “We are currently increasing output at coal companies and are aware of the energy sector’s demand for coal as a stabilising factor,” he said, quoted by news service Money.pl. World.title: Polish president backs down and approves government’s windfall tax on fuel companies
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has reversed course and signed into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits that he had previously blocked. The government had been pushing the president to approve the measures amid soaring fuel prices. In announcing his decision on Thursday, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, insisted that he now expected the government to move to lower fuel prices for consumers. A few hours later, the government confirmed that it would do so, and on Friday morning it announced cuts in VAT and excise duty on fuels. Nie pozwolę rządowi dłużej odsuwać od siebie odpowiedzialności za tę trudną sytuację. Podpisałem ustawę dotyczącą nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych i zakończę proces ustawiania Polaków w roli politycznych zakładników. To rząd ponosi pełną odpowiedzialność za ceny paliw -… pic.twitter.com/7AX8v4a9Q0 — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) October 1, 2026 The windfall tax will levy a one-off charge of 60% of excess profits from liquid fuel sales, calculated as the amount that would have been generated using a company’s average 2025 fuel sales margin, increased by 20%. It is expected to raise around 4 billion zloty (€914 million). When announcing the plans, the finance ministry said the levy was justified by this year’s “exceptional economic and geopolitical conditions that have led to above-average financial results in a specific segment of the fuel sector, not resulting from improved operational efficiency…but from a supply shock”. The tax was intended to offset some of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by cutting VAT and excise duty and introducing a maximum daily price. Those measures were initially in place from March to June. However, in July, Nawrocki announced that he would not sign the windfall tax into law. He instead sent it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) for assessment. That process can take years, effectively killing off the bill. The president argued that the proposed measures “raised serious constitutional concerns”. In particular, he criticised the fact that the tax would be retroactive, applying to revenue earned from the beginning of March. Since then, he and the government have been locked in a dispute over the issue, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk arguing that measures to reduce fuel prices, which were briefly reintroduced in the last two weeks of August, can only be restored if Nawrocki signs the windfall tax. Nawrocki’s office, however, has argued that fuel companies would pass the costs of the tax onto consumers, therefore actually increasing prices. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 In September, the government’s majority in parliament passed the windfall tax bill a second time. And Nawrocki has now backed down, announcing in a recorded speech on Thursday evening that he would sign the bill into law. However, he has still asked the TK to assess its constitutionality. Nawrocki declared that he was seeking to call the government’s bluff. He claimed that they were actually hoping the windfall tax would fail so that the treasury could continue obtaining normal tax revenue from high fuel prices, as well as dividends from state oil giant Orlen. By signing the bill, the president said he was “ending the process of holding Poles hostage”. He now expected the government to “immediately” reintroduce measures to bring down prices at petrol stations, as well as the cost of fuel for farmers. To nie ja wygrałem. Wygrali Polacy, którzy już w weekend zapłacą mniej za paliwa. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 1, 2026 In response, government spokesman Adam Szłapka told broadcaster TVN that they were ready to make the necessary decisions to reduced prices on Friday and that the measures could be in force already by the weekend. “It’s good that the president has stopped blocking this,” he said. On Friday morning, the government announced that it would reduce VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and cut excise duty – both measures it also used earlier this year. The new policies will be in place until 31 December. Energy minister Miłosz Motyka told Polskie Radio that maximum daily prices would also be reintroduced. Earlier, on Thursday evening, finance minister Andrzej Domański announced on social media that he estimated fuel costs would be reduced by 1.2-1.3 zloty per litre once the subsidies were reintroduced. According to price monitoring service ePetrol, diesel prices are currently averaging around 9.14 zloty per litre while PB95 petrol is at 8.19 zloty. Those are both record highs. Ustawa o podatku od nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych właśnie wpłynęła do RCL. Jeszcze dziś będzie ogłoszona. Oznacza to, że już w weekend ceny na stacjach paliwowych będą niższe. Szacunkowo o około 1,2-1,3 zł na litrze. I po co były te gierki, Panie Prezydencie? — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) October 1, 2026 The dispute over financing fuel price cuts comes at a time of growing concern over Poland’s public finances, something Nawrocki referred to in his address on Thursday. Poland has been running one of the EU’s highest deficits, despite the government committing to bringing it down after being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. Public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time this year. Last month, Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3, pointing to a “deteriorating” fiscal situation and the “limited willingness or ability” of the authorities to take necessary action. The last time the country was at A3 level was in 2002. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A group of prominent Polish businesspeople have announced that they are investing in a project to develop small modular nuclear reactors being led by the country’s richest man, Michał Sołowow. Among them are Rafał Brzoska, founder of delivery giant InPost, and Mati Staniszewski, CEO of ElevenLabs, a leading artificial intelligence firm. The group is investing 500 million zloty (€114 million) in Sołowow’s Synthos Green Energy (SGE), which, together with 1.35 billion zloty from foreign investors, will secure the company’s financing for the next two years as it seeks to roll out BWRX-300 reactors in Poland, Central and Eastern Europe and the UK. As a European SMR development platform headquartered in Warsaw, Poland’s energy security is of special importance to us. We are proud to announce that today our founder, Michał Sołowow, unveiled a PLN 500 million investment by a group of leading Polish entrepreneurs in SGE’s… pic.twitter.com/J2SerVjIlG — SGE (@SGE_Nuclear) September 30, 2026 The investment, which was formally announced at a business conference in Warsaw on Wednesday, comes as Sołowow seeks to expand his nuclear project beyond SGE’s troubled partnership with Polish state energy giant Orlen, where disagreements have delayed plans to build SMRs in Poland. Alongside Brzoska and Staniszewski, the other new investors are Dariusz Gałęzewski, co-founder of drinks maker Oshee; Krzysztof Pawiński, CEO of food company Maspex; Michał Brański of media group Wirtualna Polska; and Michał Wypychewicz of ZPUE, the largest manufacturer of transformer stations in Europe. “They invested their own private funds because they understood the problem and then believed in the concept and the solution,” Sołowow told Business Insider Polska. SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed on site, are seen by their proponents as a fast and cost-effective way of installing nuclear capacity. In July, SGE announced plans to build 14 BWRX-300 reactors with a combined capacity of 4.2 gigawatts (GW) across three sites in the UK, which it said would generate enough electricity to meet 11% of the country’s demand. The company also hopes to deploy up to 26 reactors across six locations in Poland. The BWRX-300 is a 300-megawatt water-cooled small modular reactor. Construction of the first ever unit began in Canada in 2025, with completion planned for 2029 and commercial operation expected in 2030. Synthos Green Energy, a firm owned by Polish billionaire Michał Sołowow, has announced plans to build 14 small modular nuclear reactors in the UK. It says that the £35 billion project could deliver enough power to meet 11% of the UK’s demand https://t.co/YTMIzYERuJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 Brzoska said that developing SMR technology “is an investment in Poland’s future”, because without “reliable, predictable and competitively priced energy…it is difficult to talk seriously about further growth in industry, data centres, artificial intelligence, automation or modern logistics”. Staniszewski, whose company recently received an $11 million investment from Poland’s state-owned National Development Bank (BGK) to establish an AI development centre in Poland, said lower electricity prices were important for the sector. SGE notes that demand for electricity is set to rise 40% in Poland over the next 14 years, according to grid operator PSE. Electricity prices have risen rapidly in recent years and are now the second most expensive in the European Union in relation to the cost of living. Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year. The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025 Poland remains the EU’s most coal-dependent country, with more than half of its electricity generated from coal. Over the past decade, however, the country has diversified its energy mix, with the share of renewable energy sources tripling to nearly 30% in 2025. Poland plans to reduce its reliance on coal further, including through the construction of its first nuclear power plant (of the traditional type, not an SMR). The 3.75-gigawatt project is scheduled to be commissioned in 2036. Sołowow has also been pursuing the deployment of SMRs in Poland through Orlen Synthos Green Energy (OSGE), a joint venture between SGE and state energy giant Orlen, Poland’s largest company, to develop BWRX-300 reactors in Poland. OSGE is seeking a so-called contract for difference (CfD) framework, an agreement with a state that guarantees a fixed price for electricity and helps shield developers from market swings, covering 14 reactors at three sites. Polish state energy firm Orlen has announced an agreement to build the country’s first small modular nuclear reactor (SMR). It says Poland will be the first country in Europe to deploy an SMR developed by US-based firm GE Hitachi Nuclear Energy https://t.co/MPWXS3qZ1d — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2025 The project, however, has been delayed by disagreements between the two shareholders. Sołowow told Business Insider Polska that they reached an agreement last month that would allow construction of two reactors to move forward, but said he regretted entering into the partnership with Orlen. “I find it deeply regrettable, because it is precisely due to Orlen’s unnecessary involvement that we are discussing this project in political terms, even though it is not a political project,” he said. Sołowow has argued that a private-sector model can shorten construction times and improve cost control compared with traditional state-led nuclear projects. At the same time, he has highlighted the importance of the state’s role in implementing the project, saying its success depends on coordination between private investors and state policy. This includes contracts for difference, administrative procedures and the preparedness of the nuclear regulator. World.title: Activists launch world’s first abortion pill delivery locker in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Activists in Poland have launched what they say is the world’s first delivery locker that provides women with abortion pills, access to which is normally tightly restricted. They have placed the device opposite parliament in Warsaw, a location intended to send a message to the politicians who have made Poland’s abortion laws among the strictest in the world. The locker (called an “abortomat” in Polish, combining the words aborcja, meaning abortion, and automat, meaning an automatic machine) has been launched by Women Help Women (WHW), a global organisation that provides “self-managed abortion”, and Abortion Dream Team (ADT), a Polish activist group. They emphasise that the installation “is completely real [and] not an artistic performance”. It consists of 22 numbered lockers and a numeric keypad. Women who have contacted WHM seeking an abortion are given a six-digit PIN code that opens one of the doors, inside which is a package containing the pills. Recipients can either take the pills at home or do so in a specially prepared space opened last year by ADT and where the locker is located. The activists emphasise that such delivery mechanisms for abortion pills are particularly important in Poland because of the country’s highly restrictive laws. Abortions are only allowed in two circumstances: if pregnancy is the result of a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. As a result, only 851 legal terminations took place in Poland last year. However, activist groups such as WHW, ADT and Women on Web (WOW) say that they help tens of thousands of women in Poland obtain abortions each year through other means, in particular by providing pills. But they face legal risks for doing so: assisting someone in obtaining an unlawful abortion is a crime punishable by up to three years in prison. In 2023, ABW activist Justyna Wydrzyńska was convicted of that offence. Two years later, the sentence was annulled on a technicality and a new trial was ordered. Polish activist Justyna Wydrzyńska, who was convicted for providing abortion pills to a pregnant woman, has succeeded in having the conviction overturned on appeal. However, the case will now return to the lower court, where it will be heard again https://t.co/U3J5FmXdMw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 14, 2025 “The abortomat transforms a closely guarded, criminalised procedure into something as simple as picking up a package,” wrote ADT. “A door that opens when all others have slammed shut.” They say that the machine is intended for women who have an urgent medical need that means they cannot wait for the several days it takes to deliver pills by post, or who are in abusive, controlling relationships that make postal delivery unsafe. Wydrzyńska’s conviction came after the husband of a woman she helped obtain abortion pills found them and reported the case to the police. However, although assisting a woman in obtaining an unlawful abortion is an offence, the woman who had the abortion is not criminally liable. “The abortomat is not a human being, and the person collecting the pills, in accordance with the regulations, is not breaking the law,” said Wydrzyńska, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. WHW and ADT do not collect any personal information from women using the service. The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that Poland violated the rights of a pregnant woman who had to travel abroad to obtain an abortion after her foetus was diagnosed with a birth defect https://t.co/TgckusMxmJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 13, 2025 Under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which ruled from 2015 to 2023, the abortion law was tightened and was strictly enforced. In December 2023, a new, more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk came to power, promising to liberalise the abortion law. However, it has so far failed to pass any such legislation. In 2024, a move to decriminalise abortion assistance up to the 12th week of pregnancy was rejected by parliament, after the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition joined the right-wing opposition in voting against it. Tusk subsequently admitted that it would be impossible during the current parliament to soften abortion laws. Instead, his government issued guidelines on when and how abortions can be carried out, with the aim of ensuring that doctors and prosecutors “take the women’s side” when making decisions on the issue. World.title: Fugitive opposition politician granted safe passage to return to Poland against prosecutors’ wishes
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Warsaw court has approved a request from Marcin Romanowski, a fugitive former government minister who has been on the run for almost two years, to receive safe passage back to Poland. Romanowski is believed to currently be in the pro-Russian Moldovan breakaway region of Transnistria. Although Polish prosecutors have long been seeking Romanowski’s return, they opposed his request for safe conduct, arguing that he cannot be trusted to comply with its terms given that he has repeatedly sought to evade the law. Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, has already announced that prosecutors will appeal the court’s decision, which he claims was issued by an illegitimately appointed judge and in violation of regulations. Nie ma i nie będzie bezkarności dla ludzi Zbigniewa Ziobry. Prokuratura złoży ZAŻALENIE na decyzję o wydaniu listu żelaznego dla Marcina Romanowskiego. Spójrzmy prawdzie w oczy: kto jednoosobowo próbuje zapewnić nietykalność człowiekowi podejrzanemu o gigantyczne nadużycia w… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 30, 2026 Romanowski served as deputy justice minister in the former Law and Justice (PiS) government between 2019 and 2023. After PiS lost power, prosecutors sought to bring charges against him for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served in government, including participating in an organised criminal group. However, Romanowski fled Poland in December 2024 and was granted asylum by Hungary, which was then ruled by Viktor Orbán, a conservative ally of PiS. When Orbán lost power earlier this year, Romanowski went on the run, and for months his location was unknown. In August, it emerged that Romanowski had sent a letter to Poland requesting safe passage to return. The document indicated that he was in Tiraspol, the capital of Transnistria, a region that sought to break away from Moldova in the 1990s and is now effectively under Russian control. Prime Minister @donaldtusk says that, based on intelligence sources, Poland is now “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia https://t.co/mdvmJpkFf7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 18, 2026 At the time, the spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, Przemysław Nowak, said that there were “no grounds whatsoever” to approve Romanowski’s request for safe passage to Poland. He noted that “the suspect has evaded legal proceedings, questioned the legality of the authorities’ actions, left Poland and then Hungary to avoid arrest, and publicly declared his lack of intention to return to the country due to the ongoing criminal proceedings against him”. However, on Wednesday, Warsaw’s district court approved Romanowski’s request. A spokeswoman for the court said that the decision had been made as “previous methods used [to secure Romanowski’s return] were ineffective” and safe passage would “allow the case to be clarified”. The politician’s lawyer, Bartosz Lewandowski, said that safe passage meant his client could not be detained in Poland and that a European Arrest Warrant against him, which applies in other EU countries, would no longer be valid. ❗️Sąd Okręgowy Warszawie wydał @RomanowskiPL list żelazny, uchylając środek zapobiegawczy w postaci tymczasowego aresztowania od momentu uprawomocnienia się orzeczenia❗️ Mój Klient na terytorium Polski nie będzie mógł być zatrzymany i tymczasowo aresztowany, a ENA „upada”, jeśli… — Bartosz Lewandowski (@BartoszLewand20) September 30, 2026 In a subsequent justification for the ruling, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily, judge Konrad Mielcarek wrote that Romanowski had pledged to “voluntarily return to the country”. Conditions for his safe passage include Romanowski reporting to the court and prosecutors at designated times and places, not leaving his declared place of residence, and not seeking to obstruct the criminal proceedings against him. The judge said that prosecutors had failed to provide adequate arguments as to why Romanowski’s request should be denied. He also found that Romanowski had not obstructed proceedings against him, but had merely exercised available legal remedies. The fact that Romanowski had fled Poland does not count against him, argued the judge. In fact, “the very nature of safe passage is to provide a person residing abroad with a legal guarantee…in exchange for voluntarily submitting to the jurisdiction of Polish authorities”. The judge also clarified that safe passage is neither a “reward” nor a “privilege” and that, given that evidence in the case is already secured and Romanowski no longer has influence over justice ministry officials, the risk of tampering is low. The National Prosecutor’s Office immediately issued a statement declaring its opposition to the ruling and its intention to appeal. It noted that there had been no confirmation that Romanowski really is in Tiraspol and that the suspect had repeatedly sought to evade the law. “These circumstances do not provide assurance that the suspect will comply with the conditions of the letter of safe conduct,” wrote the prosecutors, who also pointed to the fact that Romanowski had admitted to using travel documents issued under a false identity. Żurek, meanwhile, noted that Mielcarek is one of the so-called “neo-judges”, appointed by a judicial body rendered illegitimate by PiS’s reforms. There are legal doubts about the status of such judges and the rulings issued by them, some of which have been overturned on that basis. In his statement, the justice minister also argued that, under the law, safe passage cannot be issued without a prosecutor’s consent. Lewandowski, however, cited examples of case law that he said disproved this. He also noted that prosecutors had not filed any motion to recuse Mielcarek from the case. Prokurator ocenia dzisiejsze postanowienie Sądu o wydaniu podejrzanemu Marcinowi Romanowskiemu listu żelaznego jako niezasadne. Na postanowienie to prokurator złoży zażalenie. Sąd może wydać list żelazny, jeżeli podejrzany przebywający za granicą złoży oświadczenie, że stawi… — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) September 30, 2026 Romanowski served in the justice ministry when it was led by Zbigniew Ziobro, a deputy leader of PiS, who is also wanted by the Polish authorities on suspicion of 26 crimes relating to his time in office. Like his deputy, Ziobro also obtained asylum in Hungary. When Orbán lost power, Ziobro fled to the United States, reportedly with help from a senior Trump administration official. Poland has requested that Ziobro be extradited, though that process could take years. Both Ziobro and Romanowski deny committing the crimes they are accused of and claim that they are being pursued as an act of “political revenge” by the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. World.title: Speaker of Polish parliament signs off on service dog’s retirement after eight years of “exemplary” service
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. After eight years of service, Cobra, one of the first dogs to serve in the security force of Poland’s parliament, has retired. To mark the occasion, the speaker of the lower-house Sejm, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, personally informed Cobra of the decision. “An application for transfer to retirement?” said Czarzasty, sitting opposite the extremely well-behaved Cobra in a video published by the Sejm. “Impeccable reputation. No disciplinary punishments. You’ve never barked in the Sejm,” he read from her files. “OK, signed. As of tomorrow, you are free.” Cobra idzie na emeryturę! 🐕‍🦺 Decyzję o przejściu w stan spoczynku przypieczętował podpisem Marszałek Sejmu @wlodekczarzasty. 😉 Psy Straży Marszałkowskiej to ważny element systemu ochrony Sejmu. Czuwają nad bezpieczeństwem wszystkich osób w gmachach pozostających w zarządzie… pic.twitter.com/dKRvHOlKxe — Sejm RP🇵🇱 (@KancelariaSejmu) September 30, 2026 On a more serious note, the Sejm pointed to the vital role played by dogs in the so-called Speaker’s Guard (Straż Marszałkowska), which is responsible for security in parliament. “They watch over the safety of all people in the buildings managed by the chancellery of the Sejm,” they wrote, thanking Cobra for eight years of “exemplary” service and wishing her well on her “well-deserved retirement”. Two weeks ago, the Sejm announced the arrival of a new dog, Otik, who would serve as part of the Speaker’s Guard. He has worked alongside Cobra and another canine colleague, Hela, until now. State broadcaster TVP reports that Cobra was one of the first dogs to enter service in the Speaker’s Guard. It notes that dogs serving in the force are eligible for retirement after reaching the age of nine. Their handler has the option of taking in the dog after it retires, or they can nominate another person to care for the animal. The chancellery of the Sejm then continues to cover the costs of any veterinary care that the dog requires. It has not been revealed where and with whom Cobra will spend her retirement. In 2021, Poland’s government moved to introduce retirement benefits for dogs and horses who had served in the police force, border guard and fire service, providing them with support after they finished working. The following year, that was extended to the prison service. World.title: Inflation hits 4% in Poland as fuel prices surge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s inflation accelerated to an annual rate of 4.0% in September, up from 3.4% a month earlier, driven primarily by higher fuel prices amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the end of Polish government subsidies that kept down prices at the pump. The development means that inflation has now risen above the upper bound of 3.5% set by the National Bank of Poland (NBP), which aims to keep the figure at 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Analysts say that an interest rate hike by the NBP is now more likely. The new preliminary inflation figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that prices in September were 4% higher than a year earlier, the fastest rise since June 2025. On a monthly basis, prices in September were up 0.7% from August. The rise was caused in particular by the price of fuel for private transport, which was up 36.1% on a year earlier and 9.2% from the previous month. Energy prices also rose, with electricity, gas and other fuels up 4.9% year-on-year and 0.9% month-on-month. To shield consumers from the energy crisis triggered by US and Israeli attacks on Iran, Poland has twice introduced temporary measures to curb petrol station prices, including daily price caps and cuts in VAT and excise duty. The system was in place from March to June and again during the the last two weeks of August. The government has been under pressure from the opposition and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to reintroduce the subsidies. However, it argues that Nawrocki’s decision to block a proposed windfall tax on fuel companies makes the measures harder to fund Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices provided some offset, falling 0.5% from a year earlier, although they edged up 0.1% from August. Analysts, however, expect food prices to rise later in the year to reflect lower agricultural yields. According to GUS’s own estimates, also published on Wednesday, the grain harvest came in 5% lower compared to the last season. This will, in turn, “push the CPI index higher in the coming months”, wrote Erste Bank. The breach of the upper end of the central bank’s inflation target and the 4% threshold could influence the stance of the NBP’s Monetary Policy Council (RPP), prompting it to hike rates, added Erste Bank analysts. Inflacja CPI we wrześniu w górę do 4,0%r/r (ING: 4,2%; konsensus: 4,1%). Wyraźny wzrost cen paliw (36,1%r/r) odpowiada już za ok. połowę wzrostu cen w ujęciu rocznym. Zahamowanie spadków cen żywności m/m. Inflacja bazowa prawdopodobnie w dół do 3,0-3,1%r/r, co oznacza że wciąż… pic.twitter.com/AqdIXBthFl — ING Economics Poland (@ING_EconomicsPL) September 30, 2026 Economists at ING Bank Śląski, meanwhile, expect the first rate hike – after a series of nine cautious cuts between September 2023 and March 2026 – to come in early 2027. “The RPP may opt to wait, leaving interest rates unchanged in October, with discussions on potential monetary policy tightening beginning in November following the release of the NBP’s new projections,” they wrote on X. Poland’s benchmark interest rate currently stands at 3.75%, down from a peak of 6.75% reached during the country’s last tightening cycle in 2021-2022, when policymakers were grappling with persistent inflation fuelled by the post-pandemic recovery and the war in Ukraine. Inflation peaked at 18.4% during that period.

World.title: US ambassador inaugurates planned Polish-American Centre at Kraków’s Kościuszko Mound
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The US ambassador to Poland, Thomas Rose, has launched a planned new Polish-American Centre to be established in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city. Rose symbolically laid a cornerstone for the new facility and announced a $150,000 (577,000 zloty) grant to restore and preserve the site. The centre, whose website describes it as a “home for all Polish-American initiatives in Poland”, will be established alongside the famous mound in Kraków created in honour of Tadeusz Kościuszko, a hero of both the Polish and American struggles for independence in the 18th century. Proud to announce a $150,000 AFCP grant to help restore and preserve the future site of the Kościuszko Mound’s Polish American Center — a living symbol of the friendship between our two nations. Under @POTUS, we remain committed to preserving the shared history that binds the… pic.twitter.com/5atStUIid2 — Ambassador Tom Rose (@USAmbPoland) September 29, 2026 “This is a tremendous opportunity for me, on behalf of President Donald Trump and the American people, to celebrate what I consider the most important relationship the United States has with Europe today,” said Rose at the ceremony on Monday. “America is fortunate to have many, many good friends around the world. But we have no better friend in Europe,” he added, quoted by broadcaster RMF. Together with Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska, the speaker of Poland’s Senate, he laid a cornerstone for the new centre and announced the $150,000 grant, which comes from the Ambassadors’ Fund for Cultural Preservation, a programme run by the US State Department. “Tadeusz Kościuszko is a symbol of the historical bond between Poland and the USA,” declared Kidawa-Błońska. “There is no better place for the Polish-American Centre than Kraków and the mound commemorating a hero of both nations.” Tadeusz Kościuszko to symbol historycznej więzi między Polską i USA. Nie ma lepszego miejsca dla Centrum Polsko-Amerykańskiego niż Kraków i kopiec upamiętniający bohatera obu narodów. Niech powołane dziś Centrum dobrze służy naszym relacjom, które budujemy od 250 lat 🇵🇱🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/8nOkCYDLfD — Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska (@M_K_Blonska) September 29, 2026 Kościuszko’s Mound was established in Kraków in 1823, following the pattern of two prehistoric mounds that already existed in the city. It honours Kościuszko, a military officer who had fought against Russian rule over Poland and in the Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War. Construction of the new Polish-American Centre is being supported by the Kościuszko Mound Committee in Kraków in partnership with USA250PL, the platform for celebrations in Poland of this year’s 250th anniversary of the American Declaration of Independence. The Kościuszko Mound Committee has long been engaged in efforts to preserve the mound against partial collapses caused by heavy rain. Polish hydraulics manufacturer PONAR Wadowice is also listed as a partner of the new centre. The facility says it “will serve as a living symbol of friendship, understanding, and transatlantic cooperation”, providing “a welcoming space for dialogue, creativity, and exchange”. The centre will house event spaces, conference rooms, and offices. In June, the centre acted as a patron of a United States–Central and Eastern Europe Connection Weekend at Kraków’s Jagiellonian University. Next year it plans a commemoration of the Battle of Saratoga, where Kościuszko designed fortifications that contributed to the American victory. Poland has long looked to the United States for support and as an example during its struggle for independence over the last two centuries, including during the period of partitions in the 19th century, the reestablishment of the Polish state after the First World War, and during the later decades of communist rule. Since the fall of communism, the US has become Warsaw’s most important security partner – including establishing its first permanent military garrison, named Fort Kościuszko, in Poland in 2023. The US has opened its first military garrison in Poland, and its first anywhere on NATO's eastern flank. "This is a historic moment," says Poland's defence minister. "We have been striving for years for this word 'permanent' and it has now become fact" https://t.co/knJEcqv4MB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 21, 2023 Last week, President Donald Trump, in a virtual address to the Polish-American Congress (an entity unrelated to the new centre in Kraków), praised his Polish counterpart Karol Nawrocki, a close Trump ally, and described himself as a “great friend of the people of Poland”. Shortly before that, Nawrocki had expressed confidence that a planned new US military base in Poland would soon be confirmed, and suggested that it would be named Fort Trump. World.title: Prague Passengers Can Now Request Czech or English Speaking Bolt Drivers
World.content:
Bolt has introduced two new ride categories in Prague that allow passengers to request drivers who speak either Czech or English.

The new options are available at the same price as a standard Bolt ride.



They are open to drivers of any nationality who can communicate in the relevant language at a level suitable for everyday conversation.

Czech-speaking passengers who are less comfortable communicating in English can request a Czech-speaking driver, while foreign residents, tourists and business travellers can choose a driver who speaks English.

Bolt already provides automatic translation for communication between passengers and drivers within its app. Booking information, addresses and messages can therefore be translated automatically. The new categories are designed to cover situations in which communication takes place outside the app, particularly during the journey itself.

The company said the new options are already available in Prague, where it has enough partner drivers who meet the language requirements.

Drivers can choose whether to participate in the new categories. They may offer rides in Czech, English, both languages or continue driving exclusively in the standard category.

Participation is voluntary.

Passengers will see the two new options directly in the Bolt app. The Czech-speaking category is identified by an icon featuring the Czech flag, while the English-speaking option uses an English flag icon.

World.title: Pegasus Airlines Completes Acquisition of Czech Airlines and Smartwings
World.content:
Pegasus Airlines has completed its acquisition of Czech Airlines and the Smartwings Group, marking a major change in the ownership of one of the Czech Republic’s most established aviation businesses.

The Turkish low-cost carrier announced the completion of the transaction on Thursday, October 1, following the approval of the relevant regulatory authorities and the fulfilment of the required closing conditions.



The deal brings together Pegasus Airlines and the Czech-based Smartwings Group, creating an aviation group with a combined fleet of more than 175 aircraft.

The two airlines also have firm orders for a further 140 aircraft.

For passengers in Prague and across the Czech Republic, Smartwings will continue to operate under its existing brand. Its day-to-day operations, customer relationships and service are expected to remain in place, while the company will gain access to new opportunities for expansion and development through its new ownership.

Pegasus expands further into Central Europe

Founded in 1990, Pegasus Airlines has operated as a low-cost carrier since 2005. The airline currently serves 161 destinations in 57 countries from its main hub at Istanbul Sabiha Gökçen Airport and other bases in Türkiye.

Its network covers Europe, the Middle East, North Africa and Asia, making the acquisition an opportunity to strengthen Pegasus’ presence in Central and Eastern Europe.

Smartwings, meanwhile, operates a network of around 80 destinations across 20 countries. The group has a particularly strong position in the Czech leisure travel market, with scheduled and charter services as well as private flights and special flights for international companies and organisations.

The Czech airline has been operating under the Smartwings name since 1998, while the Czech Airlines (ČSA) brand is one of the oldest names in European aviation.

The combined business is expected to benefit from the complementary networks of the two airlines. Pegasus brings a large international network and experience with the low-cost model, while Smartwings has an established customer base and strong relationships with tour operators in the Czech Republic and wider Central European market.

Pegasus said that Smartwings will continue operating under its established brand following the completion of the acquisition.

Pegasus carried a record 43.3 million passengers in 2025 and operates one of Europe’s younger aircraft fleets.

World.title: Ibiza Is Coming to Prague: A Night of DJs, Lasers and Tropical Vibes
World.content:
On April 17, 2027, OX Club in Prague will transform for one night into an Ibiza-inspired party featuring DJs, immersive visuals and tropical-themed spaces.

The Sound of Ibiza event will bring British DJ and producer Daxson, Dutch DJ and producer Laura Van Dam, Czech DJ Lucca and DJ TiGi to one stage.



The night will combine electronic music with a full immersive laser show, acrobatic performances above the dancefloor and Ibiza-inspired décor throughout the club.

There will also be a dedicated Sunset Experience for photos and social media, as well as a Chillout Zone with its own DJ programme and mentoring by Pavel Bidlo.

Daxson has performed at major festivals and clubs including Creamfields, EDC, UNTOLD and Ministry of Sound, while also creating several anthems for Transmission Festival. Laura Van Dam has appeared at Tomorrowland, Ultra, EDC, Sziget and Ushuaïa Ibiza and has built a following with her melodic techno and trance sound.

DJ Lucca, one of the country’s best-known electronic music artists, has performed alongside international names including Carl Cox and Paul van Dyk.

The event will also feature competitions for an iPhone and other prizes. An Ibiza Beach Outfit is suggested, although the dress code is optional.

With a capacity of 1,000 people, Sound of Ibiza aims to recreate the atmosphere of the famous Mediterranean party island in the centre of Prague for one night.

Tickets went on sale on October 1. Party packs are also available.

The event has no age restriction. Tickets are available through GoOut.

World.title: The Prague Post’s First Issue Goes Online 35 Years Later
World.content:
The Prague Post has launched a digital archive marking 35 years since the publication of its first issue.

October 1, 2026, marks the 35th anniversary of the newspaper’s debut.

Founded in 1991, The Prague Post was Czechoslovakia’s longest-running English-language weekly newspaper.



The newly launched archive begins with that very first issue, which is available to read in full, browse online and search by text.

A new issue will be added each week, corresponding to the same week 35 years earlier.

The project will allow readers to follow the political, social and cultural changes of the early 1990s through the newspaper’s coverage, much as readers did at the time.

The Prague Post Archive is also active on Facebook and Instagram, where updates about newly digitized issues and the project will be shared.

The archive is administered by Modrá sova z.s., a nonprofit English-language library and learning center in Loužnice, where The Prague Post’s physical archives are housed.

Issues published between 1991 and 1994 have already been scanned and processed.

Around two decades of additional issues remain to be digitized, making the project a long-term and costly undertaking. Modrá sova has independently funded the digitization work since the project began and is now inviting organizations and individuals interested in supporting the project to contribute through the archive’s website.

The archive will also continue to handle requests from people looking for specific articles and welcomes visitors by appointment.

For more information, contact Mimi Fronczak-Rogers at [email protected] or +420 721 518 385.

World.title: Halloween Trick-or-Treat for Charity to Return to Prague on October 22
World.content:
A Halloween charity event will bring children and families to several Prague neighbourhoods on October 22, combining trick-or-treating with fundraising for SOS Children’s Villages.

The Halloween Trick-or-Treat for Charity will take place from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. across Vinohrady, Vršovice, Žižkov, Prague 15, Holešovice and Barrandov.



The concept is simple. Children dressed in Halloween costumes and accompanied by their parents will visit participating host locations, which can include cafés, restaurants, shops, confectioneries, schools, children’s centres and other businesses or organisations.

The participating locations will remain a secret until children register for the event and receive a special map showing where they can go trick-or-treating.

At each location, children will make a contribution of at least CZK 10 to a sealed collection box supporting SOS Children’s Villages. In return, they will receive a sweet treat before continuing to the next location.

Last year’s event attracted more than 1,100 registered participants and raised CZK 296,157 despite rainy weather.

The entire amount was donated to SOS Children’s Villages, which has supported children, families, young people and foster carers in the Czech Republic for more than 50 years.

How it started

Dinah Spritzer-Richter and several of her friends organized the first American Halloween in Prague for her two children in 2017. The event has supported charity from the very first year, with the proceeds going to help children in SOS Children’s Villages.

Dinah sees the charity side as just as important as creating a joyful and memorable experience for the kids.

How to take part

Families who want to participate can register in advance and then use the secret map to find the participating locations on October 22.

Children are encouraged to come in costume and bring enough coins to make contributions at the individual stops.

Businesses and organisations can also join the event as hosts. Each host is asked to prepare sweets, add some Halloween decorations and wear at least part of a costume or Halloween accessory.

Hosts must be available for at least two hours between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m.

The organisers will provide the collection boxes, while hosts provide the sweets for visiting children.

World.title: Prague Study Reveals How Much Waste Tourists Leave in the City Center
World.content:
Specialists from Prague City Hall and the Institute of Circular Economy (INCIEN) have analyzed the contents of public waste bins in central Prague, finding that about one ton of rubbish is discarded on Wenceslas Square every day.

The latest analysis was carried out to examine how the composition of waste changes with the seasons and fluctuations in tourist traffic.

A similar measurement was conducted during the winter, providing a basis for comparison.



Beverage packaging made up roughly one-third of the waste collected from bins on Wenceslas Square. Cans and plastic bottles were among the most common items.

Another third consisted of disposable food-service items, particularly cups. The remaining third was made up of general household waste.

Researchers also found waste originating from businesses in the surrounding area, including cafes and shops. Some household rubbish appeared to have been left by tourists staying in apartments rented through short-term accommodation platforms.

Food waste was another recurring part of the findings. Partially eaten food was frequently found in the bins, with trdelník pastries among the more common examples.

The summer analysis gives Prague authorities a clearer picture of the waste generated in one of the city’s busiest public spaces during the peak tourist season and allows them to compare the results with the winter survey.

World.title: Prague Hospitals Warn of Critical Blood Shortages
World.content:
Several hospitals in Prague are reporting critically low blood supplies, prompting the Czech Ministry of Health to urge people to donate blood in the coming days.

The shortage is affecting more than individual blood groups. Hospitals and transfusion centers in several parts of the Czech Republic are reporting a broader decline in available supplies, with some facilities nearing the minimum levels needed to maintain safe operations.



The situation differs from one region to another. Some transfusion centers still have adequate reserves, while others are short of particular blood groups or are approaching critical levels.

The shortage also extends to individual blood components. In Prague, the Institute for Clinical and Experimental Medicine (IKEM) is currently seeking more platelet donors regardless of blood type.

People planning to donate are advised to check the latest information on the website or social media channels of their chosen transfusion center before visiting.

Why hospitals need more donors

Hospitals depend on regular blood donations not only during emergencies but also for planned medical treatment.

Blood is routinely needed for surgery, childbirth and the treatment of patients who require repeated transfusions. This includes some cancer patients whose treatment can interfere with the body’s production of blood cells.

Blood donations are also essential in cases of severe complications during childbirth. Heavy blood loss can become life-threatening within a short period, and an adequate supply of donated blood can be critical to saving the lives of mothers and newborns.

The demand for blood can increase during the summer and holiday period, when hospitals continue to perform scheduled procedures while also dealing with more injuries and traffic accidents. At the same time, the number of people coming to donate tends to fall as residents leave the country or travel elsewhere.

Number of donors continues to decline

Official figures indicate that the Czech donor base has been shrinking. Around 348,000 people donated blood last year, down from 362,000 the previous year.

Transfusion centers are also losing older regular donors as they reach the age limit, while the number of younger people replacing them has not been sufficient.

In the Czech Republic, adults can generally donate blood until the age of 65, provided they weigh more than 50 kilograms. Additional eligibility restrictions may apply, including for people who have recently travelled to countries where certain infectious diseases are present.

Donating blood in the Czech Republic is voluntary and free of charge. Donors are entitled to time off work on the day of their donation, while some health insurance companies provide additional benefits or rewards for regular donors.

World.title: Bangkok Gears Up for the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings
World.content:
All eyes are on Thailand as the country prepares to host the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG) Annual Meetings, also known as the 2026 Annual Meetings or AM2026 Thailand.

Running from 12-18 October 2026, at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center (QSNCC) in Bangkok, the event will mark Thailand’s second time hosting the meetings, following its first in 1991. This will make Thailand one of only three nations to have hosted the IMF–WBG Annual Meetings twice.



The IMF–WBG Annual Meetings, held for two consecutive years in Washington D.C. and every third year in one of the 191 member countries, serve as a gathering of top economic figures from around the world. By covering a broad range of issues, the meetings aim to strengthen global financial stability, combat poverty, and ensure inclusive economic growth and job creation.

Thailand’s selection to host again in 2026 highlights how the country has advanced over the past three decades in terms of its institutional progress, economic resilience, and sustained engagement with international partners. As host, Thailand brings decades’ worth of experience in economic transformation and regional leadership to the table.

The “Olympics of Finance”

Often dubbed the “Olympics of Finance,” the meetings are set to attract more than 15,000 participants, including finance ministers, central bankers, economists, business leaders, civil society representatives, and journalists from the IMF and World Bank’s 191 member countries, including the Czech Republic.

The Annual Meetings will be held under the theme of “Thailand’s New Horizons: Empowering People, Building Resilience”. Therefore, the meetings will focus on enhancing people’s potential and creating opportunities, with the goal of fostering a financial and economic system that is safe, sustainable, and inclusive.

Under the theme, the government plans to showcase four policy priorities it believes are increasingly relevant in an era marked by geopolitical fragmentation, economic volatility, and demographic change. These are indeed the issues that warrant serious conversation and sincere collaboration among the global community and all stakeholders to address them in the most efficient way:

Digital Transformation : The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems.

The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems. Connected Economy : A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored.

A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored. Climate Finance : The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change.

The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change. Longevity Economy: The final priority seeks to turn the challenges of ageing populations into new sources of economic growth.

Alongside these focus areas, the Bank of Thailand plans to unveil the “Bangkok Blueprint,” an international framework developed jointly with the IMF and the World Bank aimed at combating digital financial fraud and strengthening trust in the digital economy.

Readiness in All Aspects

According to the Fiscal Policy Office, Thailand’s overall readiness has been assessed at “Grade A” following months of coordination between the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Thailand, and the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings Secretariat.

Preparations extend beyond the conference venue. Authorities have developed contingency plans for traffic management, emergency responses, and arrangements for high-level foreign officials. A working group has also been established to address cybersecurity matters.

Beyond Tourism: A Regional Economic Capital

Beyond its long-established reputation as a world-renowned tourist destination, the 2026 Annual Meetings offer Thailand an excellent opportunity to present another dimension of the Kingdom to the international community.

AM2026 reinforces Thailand’s standing as a trusted international partner while highlighting its growing role as a regional economic capital and a hub for finance, investment, policy innovation, and multilateral dialogue in Southeast Asia. Having said that, countries and companies vying for economic and business opportunities cannot overlook Thailand and its potential to become an important impetus for their long-term prosperity and growth.

(Source material and reporting courtesy of Thailand NOW)

World.title: Mineral water springs: 3 levels that set property value
World.content:
My previous article explained why Hungary’s geothermal and mineral water resources represent untapped natural capital and why property prices do not yet reflect their full potential. This article moves one step closer: it examines how a water-law permit and official recognition as natural mineral water can affect the value of a specific property, and why two neighbouring plots that appear identical may command very different prices simply because one is associated with an officially recognised, lawfully exploitable source and the other is not. The value of a property with mineral water springs is shaped not only by market demand, but also by the combination of permits, official recognition and restrictions on use.

Author: Emese Széll, Private Real Estate Advisor to Premium Clients in Hungary

Recognition as natural mineral water: a condition for market access

Natural mineral water is not merely a quality category; it is a legally regulated designation. In Hungary, the Government Office of the Capital City Budapest recognises water as natural mineral water, on application, under Joint Decree 65/2004 (IV. 27.) FVM–ESzCsM–GKM. Only water recognised through this procedure may be marketed under the designation “natural mineral water”. Recognition requires evidence of compliance with the prescribed chemical, microbiological, source-protection, extraction and bottling conditions.

It is not an exclusive market right or a legal monopoly. Rather, recognition is a condition for the lawful use of the designation and for placing the product on the market, while the geological characteristics of the source and the site-specific permits may create commercial scarcity.

According to the case files available to me, hydrodynamic modelling for one of the sources examined demonstrated an adequate degree of protection for the water base, while tritium analysis supported the conclusion that the water originated in deeper strata. The Government Office of the Capital City Budapest recognised the water as natural mineral water. That recognition, together with the relevant water-law permits and protection measures, may have substantial market value, but it does not create a statutory monopoly.

The Börzsöny case: mineral water springs, 150 metres and a decade-long process

I know the case of a mineral water source in the Börzsöny hills well. According to the documentation available to me, the well was drilled in 1979 to a depth of approximately 150 metres and produces high-quality aquifer water. Hydrodynamic modelling was prepared for the operating permit, using numerical simulation to examine the vulnerability of the water base and the origin of the water. Over the 50-year assessment horizon, the model indicated no recharge from surface sources; the calculation used a recharge zone with a radius of 448 metres, and the tritium content was negligible.

Official recognition of the water as natural mineral water, together with the completion of the related permitting process, materially strengthened the property’s market position. The point at which the recognition decision became final was the key legal milestone affecting value.

The protection system as both a value driver and a constraint

The protection of water bases is governed by Government Decree 123/1997 (VII. 18.). The system provides for inner and outer subsurface protection zones, hydrogeological zones A, B and C, and corresponding surface protection areas where a subsurface zone reaches the surface. The inner protection zone must be designated. Whether outer and hydrogeological A and B surface protection areas must also be designated depends in part on whether the corresponding subsurface zones reach the surface, while a hydrogeological C zone is not mandatory in every case.

Not every restriction appears on the land-registry title sheet. Inner and outer surface protection areas must be entered in the land register, while rights, obligations and prohibitions associated with hydrogeological protection zones are also recorded in the water-law register (vízikönyvi nyilvántartás). The protection system may restrict certain uses of surrounding land while reducing the risk of contamination of the water base.

A source with a properly established protection system may therefore embody two forms of value. The first is the verified water use authorised by a valid operating water-law permit. Ownership of the property and entitlement under the permit do not necessarily belong to the same person, however, and purchasing the property does not automatically transfer the permit. A change in the permit holder or the owner may require an authority review and an amendment to the permit. The second source of value is the protection of the water base, which may restrict certain uses of neighbouring properties and thereby help preserve water quality over the long term.

The Great Plain case: value held in suspension

A different situation arises where the resource exists, the well has been drilled and the water has been chemically tested, but exploitation has not begun. I am also closely familiar with a thermal well on the Great Hungarian Plain. It draws thermal water from a depth of nearly 950 metres at a temperature above 50 °C. According to the laboratory report available to me, its silicic-acid content, expressed as SiO2, is approximately 341 mg/l, nearly four times the silica content of Fiji Water, a frequently cited global premium benchmark.

The chemical profile alone, however, does not establish eligibility for recognition as natural mineral water or medicinal water, nor does it demonstrate suitability for beverage or therapeutic use. Separate testing and authority procedures are required. The well has not operated since it was drilled in 2007, not because of its geological characteristics, but because parallel permitting procedures became protracted.

This is a case in which the theoretical value of a property associated with mineral water springs or a thermal water resource may be high, while the market price does not yet reflect it. From an investment perspective, this may be the entry point, but only for a buyer who understands what is required to turn geological promise into a legally exploitable asset.

What is a spring actually worth in the property price?

The answer depends on the stage reached in the permitting and recognition process. The following three levels are not statutory categories, but a practical due-diligence model.

Level one: speculative. The presence of the water resource is suspected on geological grounds or has been documented, but no valid authority permit exists; any water-related premium is therefore largely speculative. Level two: permitted but not recognised. The well has been completed and has a valid operating water-law permit, but the recognition procedure required for the intended commercial or therapeutic use has not yet been completed. Level three: fully resolved. The relevant recognition decision has become final, the applicable subsurface protection zone or surface protection area has been designated, and all permits required for the intended bottling or other use are in place.

At that third stage, the property’s value can be assessed according to a different logic from that applied to ordinary land or buildings.

What comes next

Reaching the third level requires a complex process involving several authorities and overlapping fields of law. The next article examines this path in detail, including the roles of the regional water-management and water-protection authority, the mining authority where applicable, and the nature-conservation, agricultural-land-protection, building and land-registry bodies; it also considers Natura 2000 implications and the long-term sustainability of permits, drawing on direct experience of the two projects described here.

Legislation cited

This article provides general market and legal information only and does not constitute individual legal, water-law or food-law advice. The project-specific data described above should be verified against the original laboratory reports, permits and authority decisions. The English titles of Hungarian legislation are descriptive translations; the Hungarian-language legal text is authoritative. Legislation checked as at 3 September 2026.

World.title: Danube water levels could fall way below 200-year low
World.content:
The Danube has fallen to a historic low in Budapest, with water levels expected to decline further over the weekend as persistent dry weather continues across the river’s catchment area.

What do negative water levels mean?

On Wednesday, the Budapest water gauge recorded -1 centimetre, breaking a record that had stood for almost 200 years. The level had previously fallen to zero in early September, but continued drought has since pushed the river below that mark.

The gauge’s zero point corresponds to the lowest water level recorded during the 1834 low-water period. A negative reading does not mean that the riverbed is dry; rather, it indicates that the water level has fallen below the historic reference point.

Regular state measurements in Budapest began in 1823, and the river had never previously fallen below today’s zero mark. According to water-management authorities, the latest reading therefore represents an unprecedented low in the modern measurement record.

Danube water levels are expected to decline even further

Hungary’s General Directorate of Water Management predicts that the situation could deteriorate further, with the Danube potentially reaching -8 centimetres in Budapest by the weekend. The continuing lack of rainfall across the river’s catchment area is the main factor behind the decline. Little significant precipitation is expected in the Alps and along the upper reaches of the Danube, meaning there is currently no clear source of increased water flow, writes Időkép.

The effects are being felt elsewhere in Hungary as well. At Paks, the river could fall to around -113 centimetres, although an earlier record low of -140 centimetres is not currently expected to be challenged. A riverbed threshold constructed there in August has helped maintain water levels.

The exceptionally low conditions are also creating growing difficulties for river navigation, as sandbanks and obstacles on the riverbed come increasingly close to the surface. With little rainfall forecast, Budapest and other sections of the Danube may continue to experience unusually low water levels in the coming days.

World.title: Major step for the Hungarian minority in Ukraine as educational bill submitted to parliament
World.content:
Ukraine has taken a significant legislative step towards strengthening the educational rights of its Hungarian minority, submitting a bill to parliament that would expand protections for minority-language schooling. The move has been welcomed by Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán, although the legislation still needs parliamentary approval.

The bill, registered in Ukraine’s Verkhovna Rada on 1 October, is expected to be considered later this month. It follows a June agreement between Budapest and Kyiv concerning the linguistic, educational and cultural rights of Hungary’s ethnic Hungarian community in Ukraine.

What would change?

Under the proposed legislation, Ukrainian would remain the language of the education system. However, schools with classes or groups teaching in the language of an indigenous people or an EU-official minority language would be guaranteed the right to use that language. The bill would also create a formal status for secondary schools serving national minorities. Institutions where more than half of pupils receive education in a minority language could qualify for this status.

For Hungarian-speaking pupils, the proposed framework could allow schools to teach national history and preserve elements of their material and cultural heritage, including traditions, symbols and customs. Official educational documents could also be issued in the minority language at parents’ request. Parents would have the right to request an expansion of subjects taught in Ukrainian, provided that at least two-thirds of parents in the relevant class or group submit a written request.

A dispute stretching back years

Minority-language education has been one of the principal sources of tension between Budapest and Kyiv since Ukraine introduced changes to its language and education policies in the late 2010s. The June 2026 agreement was reached following several weeks of expert-level negotiations involving Hungarian and Ukrainian officials, as well as representatives of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia. The details of the agreement were not initially published, but its stated objective was to expand linguistic, educational and cultural rights.

The issue has also become linked to Ukraine’s European Union accession process. Hungary had previously opposed the opening of parts of the negotiations, while Magyar has said that progress on minority rights is a condition for Budapest’s support for further steps. Reuters reported that Ukraine’s latest bill is therefore closely connected to efforts to advance the accession process.

Budapest welcomes the move

Anita Orbán said the bill followed recent bilateral consultations and discussions with representatives of the Transcarpathian Hungarian community. Magyar likewise said it would strengthen the legal guarantees surrounding Hungarian-language education and the network of educational institutions.

The legislation nevertheless marks only the next stage of the process. Its final wording could still change during parliamentary debate, and its practical impact will depend on how the new provisions are implemented. For the Hungarian-speaking community in Ukraine, the parliamentary process will therefore be closely watched as a test of whether the commitments made in recent months become lasting legal protections.
