World.title: What will be Vic Rodriguez’s arguments in his fight vs impeachment threshold?
World.content:
In his appeal, Rodriguez says he will reiterate his 'intergenerational sovereignty' argument

The Supreme Court (SC) junked on Wednesday, September 30, the petitions challenging the adjusted threshold for conviction in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment.

There were three petitions, and one of them was filed by Vic Rodriguez – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s former executive secretary and now an ally of Duterte.

In the ruling, the SC said it was too early – the petitions were premature – so it junked the cases. The decision also cited lack of legal standing or locus standi of the petitioners. A petitioner must have legal personality or a right to file a petition for a legal action to prosper in court.

The SC, at least based on the available briefer, did not dwell on the merits of the case. The petitions were dismissed on procedural grounds.

Rodriguez said he will appeal the ruling. He argued that the issue is not premature.

“Dito, hinog na hinog na ‘yong kontrobersiya. Bakit? Ginalaw na nga ‘yong ating saligang batas, nagkaroon ng amiyenda, illegal, unconstitutional. Hindi dapat hahayaan ng kataas-taasang hukuman,” Rodriguez said in a Facebook live. “But again, we still have 15 days from receipt of the resolution upang tayo ay maghain ng motion for reconsideration.”

(Here, the controversy is already ripe. Why? Because the Constitution has been amended – illegally and unconstitutionally. The Supreme Court must not let that happen. But again, we still have 15 days from receipt of the resolution to file a motion for reconsideration.)

Article XI, Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution states that a person may “be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate.”

When the Senate impeachment court adjusted this threshold, it stated that it will count only the vote of senator-judges who are “legally and factually capable” of participating in the proceedings at the time of the vote.

In his appeal, Rodriguez said he will reiterate his “intergenerational sovereignty” argument. This is his locus standi, according to him.

“Ibig sabihin po nito, ang bawat henerasyon ay may karapatan at kalayaang magpasya, magdesisyon para sa kanilang sarili sa kasalukuyang panahon, at hindi dapat igapos o limitahan ng mga desisyon no’ng mga naunang henerasyon,” the lawyer explained.

(This means that every generation has a right and freedom to decide for themselves at present, and cannot be bound by the decisions of the previous generations.)

“And this is precisely the locus stand or our legal personality when we filed the petition for certiorari,” he added.

Having locus standi was really the challenge in Rodriguez’s fight against the threshold. He had to prove, after all, that he has a personal interest in the case or is directly affected by it.

With respect to the camp of the Vice President, the party that may be affected by the adjusted threshold, it’s still uncertain when they will file a petition. But it’s still on the table, according to defense lawyer and spokesperson Michael Poa.

“Now, if you’re asking what about the defense if whether we will file, definitely that’s still on the table,” Poa said in a mix of Filipino and English on Thursday, October 1.

“We’re just talking if we really need to file and if we need to file, what would be the main arguments that we will raise. Because of course, we want that when we file with the Supreme Court, we also don’t want to waste the court’s time,” he added. – Rappler.com

World.title: Napolis provides silver lining with jiu-jitsu bronze after Ramirez, Custodio heartbreaks in Asian Games
World.content:
WIN. Jiu-jitsu athlete Kaila Napolis in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.

Kaila Napolis breaks through for the Philippine jiu-jitsu team in the 2026 Asian Games with a bronze medal after world champions Annie Ramirez and Kimberly Custodio suffered surprise early exits

MANILA, Philippines – Kaila Napolis somehow made up for the heartbreaking defeats of world champions Annie Ramirez and Kimberly Custodio as she salvaged a jiu-jitsu bronze medal in the 2026 Asian Games.

Napolis clinched what is so far the Philippines’ only jiu-jitsu medal in the continental meet in Nagoya, Japan, after a 2-0 win over Mongolia’s Tsagaanbileg Altangerel in the battle for the women’s 52kg bronze at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall on Friday, October 2.

A Southeast Asian Games champion, Napolis crashed out of gold-medal contention after a 3-2 loss to to Mongolia’s Mongoljin Ganbaatar in the quarterfinals, but she found her way to the podium by coming out triumphant in the repechage against Singapore’s Sofia Anabel Rivas and toppling Altangerel for the bronze.

“I really wanted to bounce back [and end] with the bronze medal. I wanna give it all. And thankfully, I pulled it off,” said Napolis in a mix of Filipino and English.

Napolis replicated her campaign in the 2023 edition in Hangzhou, China, where she also won bronze after losing in the semifinals.

Her podium finish came after the surprise exits of Ramirez and Custodio, who were tipped as strong gold-medal contenders following their triumphs in the Ju-Jitsu International Federation World Championships in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in August.

Eyeing a second Asian Games gold after ruling the women’s 57kg class in 2023, Ramirez lost her opening match as she competed in the lighter 52kg division, falling to Thailand’s Nuchanat Singchalad in the round of 16 on Friday.

The match ended in a scoreless tie, but Singchalad advanced by virtue of her two advantage points.

Meanwhile, Custodio — a four-time world champion in the women’s 45kg category — saw action in the heavier 48kg class, where she exited the round of 16 against UAE’s Balqees Abdulla on Thursday, October 1.

Similar to the fate Ramirez suffered, Custodio lost via advantage.

“We’re a bit sad, of course, for those who did not medal. But I’m still super thankful for the support,” said Napolis. – Rappler.com

World.title: Mangin, Barbosa fall short of more PH taekwondo golds in Asian Games
World.content:
KICK. China's Jingyue Ma in action during the taekwondo women's -49kg gold medal match against the Philippines' Tachiana Keizha Mangin (right) in the 2026 Asian Games.

World junior champion Tachiana Mangin and three-time Southeast Asian Games titlist Kurt Barbosa lose their respective title bouts as they add a pair of taekwondo silvers to the Philippines' haul in the 2026 Asian Games

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines missed out on two additional gold medals in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, after taekwondo jins Tachiana Mangin and Kurt Barbosa settled for a pair of silvers on Friday, October 2.

Barbosa and Mangin lost their respective title bouts at the Toyohashi Gymnasium as they fell short of delivering another gold in the sport after Jeus Gabriel Derick Yape ruled in the mixed individual virtual taekwondo earlier in the day.

Mangin saw her superb run come to a disappointing end at the hands of China’s Ma Jingyue, who pulled off a 2-0 victory in the women’s -49kg finale.

The two rounds each ended in a scoreless tie, but the Chinese won both by superiority to claim the gold medal.

Still, it was a promising campaign for Mangin as she won a medal on her Asian Games debut at just 18 years old.

A former world junior champion and a Southeast Asian Games titlist, Mangin beat Kazakhstan’s Rita Bakisheva in the round of 16, Chinese Taipei’s Wang Chieh-ling in the quarterfinals, and Japan’s Ruka Okamoto in the semifinals to get a crack at the crown.

Meanwhile, Barbosa absorbed a 16-14, 15-2 loss to Kazakhstan’s Tamirlan Tleules in the men’s -58kg final.

After losing a nip-and-tuck opening frame, Barbosa sought to pull level in the second round, but Tleules landed two straight head kicks to seal his golden victory.

Despite the defeat, the pride of Abra redeemed himself from his campaign in the 2023 edition in Hangzhou, China, where he lost his opening match in the round of 32. The Tokyo Olympian also bounced back from his failed four-peat bid in the 2025 Southeast Asian Games in Bangkok, Thailand.

Barbosa reached the final by stunning Asian champion Jafar Aldaoud of Jordan in the semifinals, following up on his victories over Saudi Arabia’s Abdullah Essa Almushraf in the round of 16 and Japan’s Hidetaka Maeda in the quarterfinals.

A win by either Mangin and Barbosa would have marked the first time the Philippines won at least five golds in an Asian Games edition since its seven-gold haul in 1962.

The country currently has four golds courtesy of Yape, gymnastics star Carlos Yulo (with two golds), and pole vault ace EJ Obiena. – Rappler.com

World.title: Fictitious name? The curious case of ‘Ang Hai Peng,’ Sara Duterte’s biz partner
World.content:
Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV alleges on October 2, 2026 that the name Ang Hai Peng in the corporate records of a company tied to Vice President Sara Duterte belongs to a person who does not exist.

Ask former senator Antonio Trillanes IV, and he will tell you it's a person who doesn't exist.

Who is behind the Chinese name that had appeared — but later disappeared — in the corporate records of Vice President Sara Duterte’s company?

Ask former senator Antonio Trillanes IV, and he will tell you it’s a person who doesn’t exist.

During his press conference on Friday, October 2, Trillanes put the spotlight on Ang Hai Peng, which Trillanes said appeared in the records of Timesquare Bee Foods, a company incorporated by Duterte, as per her assets list over the years.

Trillanes said the company’s corporate documents showed that Ang owned 60% of the company from 2013 to 2013. The company was later renamed Gencorp.

Gencorp’s records with the Securities and Exchange Commission didn’t bear Ang’s name beginning 2022. The top shareholder has become the JTC Group of Companies, owned by Jaime T. Cruz.

Cruz is a business partner of the Dutertes. His name appears in numerous corporate documents co-owned by the Vice President, her husband Mans Carpio, and her siblings Paolo and Sebastian Duterte.

Central to Trillanes’ allegation is that Peng does not have government records.

“They have no birth certificate, they have no passport, their TIN is fake, and, incidentally, their birthday is the same as Jaime T. Cruz’s,” Trillanes claimed.

“They are one person. I am one hundred percent person that [Ang Hai Peng] is nonexistent,” he added.

Play Video

We have emailed JTC Group of Companies’ email address for Cruz’s side of the story. We will update this story once we receive a reply.

Rappler first reported about Jaime T. Cruz in mid-September as part of our exposé on Gencorp and how it has bagged millions of pesos in contracts with Davao City Hall led by Mayor Sebastian since 2022. The arrangement raises conflict of interest and constitutional violation issues against the Vice President.

The prosecution’s team has zeroed in on Gencorp at the impeachment court, but it has yet to say whether it will actually call Cruz a witness.

With Trillanes no longer in prosecution’s witness lineup, it remains to be seen whether the issue he has raised will find their way somehow into the impeachment court. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Raffy Tulfo not arrested
World.content:
Senator Raffy Tulfo was present at the Senate impeachment court days after YouTube videos falsely claimed he had been arrested

Claim: An arrest warrant was issued against Senator Raffy Tulfo, who was then apprehended by the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP).

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The thumbnail of the YouTube video bearing the claim shows Tulfo alongside an image of a purported Supreme Court (SC) warrant and armed personnel from the AFP.

As of writing, the video posted on September 26 has 143,511 views, 3,800 likes, and 284 comments. Text on its thumbnail and its title read: “Raffy Tulfo may warrant! Utos ng Supreme Court sa AFP?”

(Raffy Tulfo has a warrant! Supreme Court order to the AFP?)

Another YouTube video uploaded by the same user on September 24 has 71,559 views, 2,300 likes, and 183 comments as of writing. Its thumbnail and caption state: “Raffy Tulfo inaresto ng AFP! Pinasok ang Senado?”

(Raffy Tulfo arrested by the AFP! Entered the Senate?)

The facts: Tulfo has not been arrested, and he continues to perform his duties as senator. No credible news reports, official notices from government agencies, or statements from Tulfo himself indicate that such an event happened.

Contrary to the claim, videos and live coverage show that he was present on Day 31 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 29, days after the first video claimed he had allegedly been arrested.

Neither YouTube video presents evidence of a warrant, court order, or any other official notice to support the claim. Instead, both contain unrelated political commentary on corruption, confidential funds, and voting in the 2028 elections.

Supposed SC warrant: The video does not identify any case that would have led to the issuance of an alleged arrest warrant against Tulfo. For a warrant to be issued, a case must first be filed before the proper court, after which trial court judges or justices determine whether probable cause exists to issue a warrant of arrest. (READ: Indicted? Charged? A guide to court jargon)

The Supreme Court primarily exercises original jurisdiction over certain cases and the authority to review, revise, modify, or affirm lower court decisions.

Publicly available Supreme Court records reviewed as of September 30 show no issuance that supports the claim. There are likewise no reports from credible media outlets about a warrant of arrest against Tulfo or his supposed arrest.

Tulfo’s role in Duterte’s impeachment trial: The false claim began circulating while Tulfo was serving as a senator-judge in the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

As a senator-judge, Tulfo previously questioned defense lawyer Michael Poa’s role as Duterte’s counsel, citing a potential conflict of interest following the relevation that Poa — previously an undersecretary and chief of staff of the Department of Education — had met with the Commission on Audit to discuss an audit query related to confidential funds.

Tulfo has also made statements about the Vice President’s alleged business involvements.

He was also among the 13 senator-judges who voted to lower the conviction threshold to 14 votes. His brother, senator-judge Erwin Tulfo, made the motion to bar absentee senators from voting in the trial.

Debunked: Rappler has previously fact-checked false claims about the Tulfo brothers:

– Agatha Gonzalvo/Rappler.com

Agatha Gonzalvo is a Research and Data volunteer intern at Rappler. She is a fourth-year Applied Economics student at De La Salle University Manila.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Who’s behind Trillanes’ trial withdrawal? He won’t say Escudero, but calls him out
World.content:
SPEAKING OUT. Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV holds a press conference at Club Filipino in San Juan City on October 2, 2026, where he presented his findings on the alleged ill-gotten wealth of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV doesn't explicitly disclose what he means when he says the prosecution is being pressured over his testimony, but he still can't resist taking a swipe at the trial's presiding officer

Listening to former senator Antonio Trillanes IV’s press conference is an exercise in reading between the lines.

Trillanes, fresh from his removal from the prosecution’s witness lineup in Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial, consistently faced questions from the media on the identity of the individuals who orchestrated his eventual withdrawal.

The veteran politician dodged these questions over and over, yet in the same breath repeatedly took a swipe at one person: presiding officer Chiz Escudero.

At first, Trillanes didn’t want to give reporters a juicy soundbite on the “pressure” subject.

“I would have wanted to address that, but it would be a distraction from the main issue that we want to discuss, which is more important,” Trillanes said in Filipino on Friday, October 2. When asked if the pressure was coming from the senator-judges, he quipped, “No comment.”

Relentless journalists didn’t drop the subject, prompting Trillanes to eventually take a swipe at Escudero, without explicitly naming him.

“It’s this simple: The prosecution requested that certain people be subpoenaed. My name was on the list. The subpoenas came back, and I was the only one missing. Does the impeachment court have that kind of power? Does the presiding officer have the power to say, ‘Not this one yet’? That is the question. They don’t have that power. Because this is the prosecution’s strategy,” Trillanes said.

“Let us suspend our judgment, but let’s call him out,” he added.

Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV holds a press conference at Club Filipino in San Juan City on October 2, 2026, where he presented his findings on the alleged ill-gotten wealth of Vice President Sara Duterte.

For the record, Escudero had suggested that the prosecution present witnesses from the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) and the banks first in their unexplained wealth case against the Vice President before calling Trillanes to the witness stand.

It was a peculiar week of the trial at the Senate, though, marred by a sudden cancellation of a trial day, deferment of the presentation of the AMLC witness, and lead prosecutor Jinky Luistro’s abrupt withdrawal of Trillanes’ name from its lineup, to the surprise of even some of her colleagues in the panel, based on our candid conversations with them.

Letting go of Trillanes has its pros and cons for the prosecution and even the former senator. It’s a risky move to present a witness who has a fraught history with senator-judges, although his testimony would have been potentially explosive and highly interesting to the general public.

For Trillanes, a court appearance may have limited what he could actually say due to — as he points out — the constant objections by the defense team. He argued the objections were unnecessary and could have been stopped by Escudero himself.

“If the person presiding over that were competent, the presentation of evidence should be liberal. Because what you want is the truth. This isn’t a criminal trial where someone gets sent to jail,” Trillanes said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan, Vatican Discuss Interfaith Cooperation and Protection of Children with Serious Illnesses
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan Vice President and Head of the Secretariat of the Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions Erlan Karin met with Cardinal George Jacob Koovakad, Prefect of the Holy See’s Dicastery for Interreligious Dialogue, on Oct. 2 to discuss interfaith cooperation and joint humanitarian initiatives.

During the meeting, the officials discussed cooperation within the framework of the Congress and the Joint Colloquium, as well as implementing joint humanitarian initiatives, reported Akorda.

Cardinal George Jacob Koovakad conveyed warm greetings from His Holiness Pope Leo XIV to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and his best wishes to the people of Kazakhstan.

Joint Colloquium on children’s rights

Following the meeting, Karin and Cardinal Koovakad attended the opening of the Second Joint Colloquium dedicated to protecting the life, health and dignity of children with severe and incurable illnesses.

The event brought together representatives of government bodies, religious organizations, medical and scientific institutions and experts.

Addressing the opening, Karin stressed that interfaith dialogue should produce concrete humanitarian outcomes. He also highlighted the political and socioeconomic reforms being implemented under Tokayev’s leadership.

According to Karin, improving citizens’ well-being remains the main objective of the reforms, while protecting children, notably those in vulnerable situations, remains a key priority of state policy.

Kazakhstan-Vatican humanitarian initiative

Participants discussed a draft Charter on the Rights of Children with Incurable Diseases, being advanced as a joint Kazakhstan-Vatican initiative.

Karin thanked the Dicastery and Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital for their contribution to preparing the document and highlighted the hospital’s cooperation with the University Medical Center corporate foundation.

World.title: Astana AI Film Festival Opens New Chapter For Cinema Industry
World.content:
ASTANA – Astana is emerging as a platform for exploring how artificial intelligence could reshape the industry, with the Astana AI Film Festival (AAIFF 2026) bringing AI-generated films from 125 countries to Kazakhstan. The festival received more than 8,000 applications with 25 selected for the final stage in Astana.

The AAIFF 2026 final program runs from Oct. 1-3 in Astana as part of AI Month and AI & Digital Bridge 2026. The finalists’ films are being screened publicly on Oct. 2-3, with the winners to be announced on Oct. 3.

The festival seeks to become more than a film competition. They want to turn it into an annual international festival in Astana and develop a dedicated streaming platform Mooncast.ai for AI-generated films, allowing works that did not make the final selection to reach a wider audience.

Beyond traditional cinema

For AAIFF 2026 Co-Founder and Creative Director Aizatulla Hussein, the more important question is what AI can do to cinema itself.

“Everyone is trying to repeat traditional cinema with the help of AI, but it seems that AI technology allows you to find some other forms of cinema,” Hussein told The Astana Times.

He sees the current generation of AI films as an experimental stage. Rather than simply reproducing the production methods and visual language of traditional cinema, creators can use AI to explore new approaches to storytelling, visual design and filmmaking.

The festival’s thematic category, “The Future Worth Living In,” was designed as a response to another familiar pattern in cinema: the way Hollywood often portrays the future as a dangerous place.

AI makes filmmaking easier, but not simple

While AI technologies help to overcome some technical barriers to visual production, the organizers mention that technology alone does not guarantee a strong film.

Hussain noted that many of the strongest submissions came from creators who already had experience in traditional filmmaking, including cinematographers, editors and directors.

“It’s not difficult to generate,” he said, referring to the technical process of creating AI content. The challenge, he suggested, lies in using the technology to create a coherent and compelling film.

The economics of film production are also an important consideration. According to the creative director of AAIFF 2026, producing a short AI film can cost between $3,000 and $5,000. The films submitted to the festival generally range from five to 20 minutes.

It means that AI is changing the filmmaking process without necessarily eliminating the need for creative expertise.

After reviewing more than 8,000 submissions, the jury chose approximately 200 works. They also launched Mooncast.ai, a streaming platform being developed specifically for AI-generated films to present other works. This would give AI filmmakers a distribution channel beyond individual competitions and could help build an international audience for a new category of film.

World.title: October Starts Here: Your Weekend Guide
World.content:
ASTANA — Unwind after a busy working week with inspiring concerts, thought-provoking exhibitions and captivating spectacles. There is something for everyone, whether you are looking to enjoy evenings with friends and spend quality time with family. The Astana Times editorial team has curated a selection of events to check out this weekend.

Astana

“Zhoshy Khan” performance, Oct. 4

The historical drama depicts the life of Zhoshy Khan, the eldest son of Genghis Khan and founder of the Zhoshy Ulus. The story explores his journey, leadership and role in the history of the steppe.

Venue: Kazakh National Musical and Drama Theater named after Kalibek Kuanishbaev; 8/1 Kalibek Kuanishbaev Street. Tickets are available here.

“Appak, The Kipchak Daughter”opera, Oct. 3

This opera tells the story of Appak, a young Kipchak woman whose life becomes connected with the renowned Azerbaijani poet Nizami Ganjavi. The production brings together history, love and dramatic events.

Venue: Astana Opera; 1 Konayev Street. Tickets are available here.

“The Universe of Hans Zimmer” concert, Oct. 4

Film music lovers can enjoy an evening dedicated to the works of Hans Zimmer. The programme features music from Interstellar, Dune, Gladiator, Inception, The Lion King and other well-known films, accompanied by live orchestra and choir.

Venue: Qazaqconcert; 10/1 Mangilik El Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

“Hollywood Soundtracks” concert, Oct. 3

Enjoy an evening of iconic movie music performed by a live orchestra. From thrilling adventures to heartfelt melodies, this concert captures the emotion and magic of Hollywood films, creating a memorable experience for cinema and music lovers alike.

Venue: Smart Space; 280 Baizakov Street. Tickets are available here.

“La Traviata” opera, Oct. 3

Verdi’s opera, inspired by Alexandre Dumas’ “The Lady of the Camellias,” caused a stir in the 19th century with its modern plot, costumes, and the bold portrayal of a “fallen woman.” The title, meaning “the one who goes astray,” highlights the tragic fate of the main character.

Venue: Abay Opera Theater; 110 Kabanbay Batyr Street. Tickets are available here.

“Swan Lake” ballet, Oct. 4

Experience the timeless beauty of Tchaikovsky’s “Swan Lake” in a breathtaking ballet performance. This beloved folk tale follows a maiden cursed by dark forces to live as a swan. Prince Siegfried vows to save her, but fate leads him to a tragic betrayal. A masterpiece of classical ballet, “Swan Lake” captivates both newcomers and longtime fans. With stunning grace and precision, the dancers bring this story of love and destiny to life.

Venue: Abay Opera Theater; 110 Kabanbay Batyr Street. Tickets are available here.

World.title: Tokayev Urges AI-Driven Industrial Transformation, Proposes ‘Washington Model’ for Global AI Governance
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called for a comprehensive AI-driven transformation of Kazakhstan’s industrial sector, urging the government and businesses to focus on measurable gains in productivity, technological modernization and high-value production.

Chairing the third meeting of the Council for the Development of Artificial Intelligence on Oct. 2, Tokayev said AI was becoming a key factor in global competitiveness, Akorda reported.

“Competition is going not only for natural resources, capital and markets, but also for the speed of increasing production efficiency,” he said, stressing that AI should become a key instrument for Kazakhstan’s industrial development.

AI in production

Tokayev said industrial production reached nearly 46 trillion tenge (US$102.5 billion) in January-August, while manufacturing grew by 8.4% year-on-year.

He instructed the government and Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund to identify enterprises where key production processes can undergo comprehensive AI-based transformation.

“Enterprises must review the entire production chain and determine where AI can provide the greatest increase in efficiency. The main criterion should be real results,” Tokayev said.

He also called for stronger links between science and industry, saying the Qazaq AI Research University should focus on applied research addressing real production challenges.

Scaling AI solutions

Tokayev called for a mechanism to accelerate the transition from effective industrial AI pilots to commercial implementation.

“Many promising solutions successfully pass the pilot project stage, but then become stuck due to additional approvals, repeated testing, overly complex procurement procedures and regulatory restrictions,” he said.

He also stressed the need for high-quality industrial data and common standards, while protecting commercial secrets and critical information.

‘Washington Model’ for global AI governance

In the final part of the meeting, Tokayev welcomed the voluntary agreement recently signed in Washington by U.S. President Donald Trump and leaders of major technology companies on the safe and responsible development of AI.

“I welcome this very important and timely initiative. It reflects a common understanding that the risks associated with artificial intelligence go beyond national borders and require coordinated action by both states and businesses,” he said.

Tokayev said the agreement could, after expert consideration, serve as a model for international AI governance.

“The ‘Washington Model’ could become the basis for an international treaty under the auspices of the United Nations. Kazakhstan supports the safe and responsible development of artificial intelligence. In this regard, we are ready to act as a platform for constructive international dialogue on these topics,” he said.

He instructed the AI Council to prepare concrete proposals for Kazakhstan’s international initiative, which he said it would present at the G20 Summit in Miami in December.

Tokayev proposed that the next Council meeting focus on AI in transport and logistics, saying its further transformation could increase efficiency and strengthen Kazakhstan’s transit potential.

World.title: CAMCA Forum Explores Prospects for Greater Regional Convergence
World.content:
BAKU – The CAMCA Regional Forum featured wide-range discussions on regional convergence on Oct. 1. Dr. Frederick Starr, the chairman of Central Asia-Caucasus Institute, introduced the topic by examining prospects for countries in the region to interact more closely and the barriers to deeper cooperation.

According to Zhandos Shaimardanov, director of Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, political dialogue within Central Asia and with other C5 partners is strong and Azerbaijan joining as a full-fledged participant was “very important and timely” last year.

“It’s not simply the transformation of C5 to C6. It gives the new Trans-Caspian dimension to the Central Asian vision. We should consider this new environment where Central Asia is being evolved toward. As we have stronger institutions now. We have different situations in the economy. And this gives us a different perception, both externally and internally, on the integration of Central Asia,” said Shaimardanov.

He elaborated on the concept of convergence, saying it doesn’t mean uniformity.

“How diverse we are, and we have so many commonalities and we should keep it as kind of a balance. I mean keeping this diversity. If we talk about integration, let me remind you of a musical metaphor. We are not the choir where each singer sings the same song, we are the orchestra where each player has its own musical instrument. Kazakhs have dombra, every other country has its own musical instrument. We should keep this ‘national favor’ and be synchronized with each other. We should advise each other on major topics like environmental issues, the economy, and the transport corridors. This is what makes us strong,” he explained.

Ambassador Eduards Stiprais, the EU Special Representative for Central Asia, said growing external challenges mean Central Asia countries feel an “absolute necessity to stick together and to support each other.”

He said the European Union sees growing integration as “a positive development” and is ready to share its experience if Central Asian countries “are willing to accept this experience and learn from it.”

Stiprais said Afghanistan should be part of this cooperation in the future, while noting that the process has been prevented from advancing.

“Azerbaijan de facto is a part of the consultative process. There are no formal sanctions, civil barriers, or even a formal legal basis for this sort of cooperation. The European position always was, and will continue to be, that this is a choice which must be made by countries themselves,” he said.

He said the EU sees Central Asia as a growing region.

“We already have 80 billion consumers and probably 100 billion by 2050. We are thinking about Central Asia as a source of raw materials, including the critical minerals, but also not just the raw materials, but we are looking at the possibility to develop the value-added chain within the region,” he said.

He described Central Asia as one of the few regions with a positive demographic development. The transfer of skills and knowledge to bring the region’s economy to a completely different level is vital, he said.

Dania Arayssi, assistant director at the New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy and Professor at Georgetown University, highlighted the unequal distribution of water resources in the region.

She said Central Asian countries have ambitious AI projects and that “a lot of these projects require tons and tons of water.”

“One of the suggestions that we have put forward is establishing an organization where all these think tanks, scholars can be working together, sharing data, sharing research together instead of being fragmented,” she added.

She also spoke about the New Line’s inaugural report about regional connectivity through the S7+ framework, which addresses the dual imperatives of internal integration among Central Asian states and connection to global markets. The report provides a basis for more effective U.S. engagement with the region.

Arayssi exclusively spoke about Kazakhstan’s AI ambitions, saying they are achievable but only if they are treated as a regional project rather than a national one. Data centers need reliable power and water, and both are shared resources and among the most pressing challenges facing Central Asia today.

“That is why multilateral cooperation among the Central Asian economies is essential. The smartest path is to tie AI investment to regional cooperation on electricity grids, renewable energy, and transboundary water management, which is exactly what the S7+ framework calls for. One concrete step, recommended in the New Lines Institute’s S7+ water report, is a regional water commission to manage these shared resources together. Done right, this turns a resource constraint into an engine for deeper Central Asian integration and stronger partnerships with the U.S. and Europe,” Arayssi told The Astana Times.

Farrukh Irnazarov, co-founder of Central Asian Development Institute, said convergence is “something that actually brings us together.”

Diplomacy is advancing much more rapidly than institutional cooperation. The question is “where we either see this opportunity, or we may lose” it.

“This is the heyday of countries’ cooperation. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan are developing Kambala-1, the water and energy development project. We see that Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan were able to settle the border issue in 2025, which was a very big issue, that peace somehow became an infrastructure for connectivity, for convergence, for integration,” he said.

“The region is converging,” Irnazarov said. “And at the same time, the most important thing, we see that the leaders of countries are meeting solo, which is an amazing human-to-human approach, where they develop trust, talk to each other, and sign lots of MOUs. The issue is infrastructure. There should be an opportunity for people of the CAMCA region to translate this infrastructure project into concrete projects.”

Baku hosted the annual the Central Asia, Mongolia, the Caucasus and Afghanistan (CAMCA) Regional Forum on Oct. 1-2. Established in 2014, it brings together leaders and experts from government, business, academia and civil society to discuss regional challenges and opportunities.

World.title: $344 Million Invested in Kazakhstan as Carlsberg Opens Beverage Plant in Almaty Region
World.content:
ASTANA – Carlsberg Kazakhstan has opened a new $344 million beverage production plant in Boraldai, the Almaty Region, expanding local production for Kazakhstan and the Kyrgyz Republic and strengthening the country’s position as a regional manufacturing hub.

The opening ceremony on Oct. 1 was attended by Kazakhstan’s Deputy Ministers of Foreign Affairs and Agriculture, Akim of Almaty Region Chingis Arinov, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen, and representatives of Carlsberg Group and PepsiCo, reported the company’s press service.

The project was implemented with the support of the Government of Kazakhstan, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, national company Kazakh Invest and the Akimat of Almaty Region.

Production for Kazakhstan and the Kyrgyz Republic

The new facility will manufacture PepsiCo beverage brands under license, with Kazakhstan serving as its primary market and the Kyrgyz Republic as an additional destination.

At full capacity, the plant is designed to produce approximately 1 billion litres of beverages annually. Phase 1 includes five production lines serving several beverage categories and packaging formats.

The facility is expected to create more than 230 direct jobs and generate additional economic activity in logistics, transportation, warehousing, distribution, packaging and related services.

The investment combines Carlsberg Kazakhstan’s local manufacturing and distribution capabilities with PepsiCo’s beverage portfolio, innovation expertise and international operating standards.

Expanding local production and suppliers

A key objective of the project is to increase local value creation and develop Kazakhstan’s domestic supplier base.

Local content currently accounts for 71.5% of Carlsberg Kazakhstan’s procurement. The company sources barley, wheat, aluminium cans, cardboard packaging and glass bottles from domestic suppliers and works with manufacturers across Almaty, Astana and Shymkent.

As production expands, Carlsberg Kazakhstan plans to increase the range and volume of materials sourced from Kazakhstan suppliers, supporting import substitution and creating additional opportunities for domestic producers.

The plant also incorporates technologies aimed at improving energy efficiency, recovering heat, reducing waste and supporting more sustainable packaging and production processes.

Leaders highlight long-term investment

Akim of Almaty Region Chingis Arinov said the project reflects the government’s focus on attracting investment and developing manufacturing in the regions. He said that President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev had set clear tasks for the government to ensure economic growth and improve citizens’ well-being.

“Economic development is first and foremost reflected in concrete projects being implemented in every region of the country. Therefore, developing production and attracting investment are among the important priorities for our region as well,” Arinov said.

According to him, the new facility will contribute to diversifying the regional economy, increasing investment activity and expanding the production of competitive goods.

Carlsberg Group CEO Jacob Aarup-Andersen described the opening as an important milestone in the company’s long-term commitment to Kazakhstan and its expansion in Central Asia.

“This is an important milestone in our long-term commitment to Kazakhstan, but it is also a major step in the development of our business across Central Asia. We are proud to work alongside PepsiCo, one of the world’s leading consumer goods companies,” he said.

Aarup-Andersen added that investments of this scale require confidence in long-term partnerships and stability.

Eugene Willemsen, CEO of International Beverages at PepsiCo, said the new plant demonstrates the company’s confidence in Kazakhstan’s growth prospects.

“Kazakhstan is a strategic growth market for our international beverages business, and today’s plant opening reflects the confidence we share with Carlsberg Group in its future,” Willemsen said.

He said the partnership would allow the companies to supply locally produced beverages to consumers and customers in Kazakhstan and the Kyrgyz Republic while supporting jobs and domestic supply chains.

Further investment by PepsiCo

The new plant adds to PepsiCo’s growing investment footprint in Kazakhstan.

In 2024, PepsiCo announced a $368 million investment in its first snack production facility near Almaty. The plant began producing Lay’s potato chips earlier this year and is expected to expand cooperation with local farmers and increase the share of locally supplied potatoes over time.

Carlsberg Kazakhstan is also among the country’s major foreign investors and taxpayers in the food and beverage manufacturing sector. In 2025, the company paid more than 37.5 billion tenge (US$83.6 million) in taxes and other mandatory payments to the state budget.

The opening of the $344 million beverage facility marks another major manufacturing investment in Kazakhstan and expands the country’s production capacity for the wider Central Asian market.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Denmark Set Course for Deeper Economic and Connectivity Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Denmark are moving to deepen economic cooperation through new institutional mechanisms, investment projects and expanded collaboration on the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, as President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen on Oct. 2.

The talks focused on strengthening political dialoguе, trade and economic ties, as well as regional and global topics and cooperation within the United Nations, reported Akorda.

New framework for economic cooperation

Tokayev described Denmark as a reliable partner in Northern Europe and the European Union, noting that the two countries will mark the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations next year.

“We regard Denmark as an authoritative and influential European country and a reliable partner. I am convinced that our relations have enormous potential that needs to be unlocked, provided that both sides work actively and purposefully in this direction,” he said.

Trade between Kazakhstan and Denmark reached $163 million in 2025, while cumulative Danish investment in Kazakhstan since 2005 exceeded $394 million, according to the Kazakh Foreign Ministry.

During talks between Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi and Rasmussen, the officials signed memoranda of understanding, including one on establishing a bilateral commission on trade, economic and investment cooperation.

The agreements followed the Kazakhstan-Denmark Business Forum on Oct. 1, which brought together more than 70 representatives of government agencies, development institutions and businesses. Kazakhstan highlighted opportunities for joint projects, production localization and technology transfer in logistics, water management, agriculture, pharmaceuticals and energy.

Investment and the Middle Corridor

A major example of bilateral investment cooperation is the Carlsberg Group plant producing PepsiCo non-alcoholic beverages in the Almaty Region, opened on Oct. 1.

The project represents $344 million in investment, with an annual production capacity of up to 1 billion liters and 230 jobs.

Transport and logistics were another priority. Kazakhstan and Denmark discussed cooperation with Danish logistics company Maersk to increase trade flows along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or the Middle Corridor.

The discussions built on a Sept. 30 roundtable in Almaty involving Maersk and Kazakhstan Temir Zholy, where container traffic and multimodal transport solutions were discussed.

Denmark’s growing interest in Central Asia

Rasmussen reaffirmed Denmark’s interest in expanding cooperation with Kazakhstan and highlighted Central Asia’s growing importance in Denmark’s foreign policy and economic agenda. The Danish side also pointed to the appointment of Lars Thuesen as Ambassador to Kazakhstan and Special Representative of the Danish Foreign Ministry for Central Asia.

Fabienne Bossuyt, associate professor and co-coordinator of the Ghent Institute for International and European Studies, said the visit reflected Kazakhstan’s growing importance for EU member states.

“An increasing number of EU member states, including Denmark and Belgium, which have traditionally not shown an interest in Kazakhstan, are now drawn to Kazakhstan for economic and investment cooperation opportunities,” Bossuyt told The Astana Times.

She attributed the heightened economic interest in Central Asia partly to the need to diversify economic partnerships amid a tense global economic environment, while noting that it remains to be seen whether stronger EU economic engagement will translate into greater political influence.

The officials also discussed cooperation in digital transformation, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, agriculture and water security.

Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Denmark and Sweden, Olzhas Suleimenov, previously told The Astana Times that the partnership was entering a more dynamic stage, focusing on translating political goodwill into concrete projects and investment.

World.title: Dastan Satpayev Becomes Kazakhstan’s Most Valuable Footballer
World.content:
ASTANA – Chelsea forward Dastan Satpayev, currently on loan at Burnley, has regained the top spot among Kazakhstan’s most valuable footballers, with his market value rising to a record €5 million (US$5.6 million), according to Transfermarkt.

The 18-year-old surpassed Kazakhstan national team teammate Maksim Samorodov, whose market value is €4 million (US$4.5 million). Satpayev’s valuation is the highest recorded for a young Kazakh footballer.

His market value rose after he adapted to English football and made his Championship debut. Satpayev is currently sidelined with a muscle injury and missed autumn UEFA Nations League matches, reported Kazinform.

Updated market values

Samorodov ranks second at €4 million, followed by Türkiye’s Beşiktaş midfielder Bakhtiyor Zaynutdinov at €3.5 million (US$3.9 million) and Russia’s Zenit defender Nuraly Alip at €3 million (US$3.3 million). RF Krylia Sovetov attacking midfielder Islam Chesnokov completes the top five with a market value of €1.2 million (US$1.3 million).

All five of Kazakhstan’s most valuable players currently represent clubs abroad.

Among players competing in Kazakhstan, Tobol midfielder Aleksandr Zuev has the highest market value at €1.2 million (US$1.3 million).

Sabah goalkeeper Stas Pokatilov, who has played for the Azerbaijan’ club since 2025, is valued at €600,000 (US$675,363).

World.title: Prisoner in Georgia accuses guards of sexual abuse. Penitentiary Service denies allegations
World.content:
Prison violence in Georgia

Prisoner Giorgi Davitadze said staff at Prison No. 6 in Rustavi subjected him to sexual abuse. He says the incident took place on 21 December 2025, when staff moved him to a de-escalation cell. According to Davitadze, ten people attacked him there.

The Special Penitentiary Service denied the allegations. It said its video of the incident shows no signs of violence.

What happened?

TV channel Pirveli published an audio recording of testimony Davitadze gave at the Court of Appeals. According to the prisoner, the alleged abuse took place within view of surveillance cameras. However, he says the staff positioned themselves in a way that prevented the cameras from fully capturing their actions.

“They took me to a de-escalation cell and raped me with their fingers and hands. […] Ten men raped me; a guard was also present, and the whole thing is visible on camera,” Davitadze said during the hearing.

The prisoner claims that staff subjected him to pressure after he demanded a forensic medical examination. He told the court that he had tried to take his own life because he could no longer bear staying near the same staff members he accuses of abuse.

Davitadze also said staff verbally abused him in the de-escalation cell. “I tell the man, ‘I was raped.’ And the representative of the Public Defender’s Office simply lowers his head,” he said. He questioned why the verbal abuse he described to the court could not be heard on the camera recordings.

Davitadze told the judges that he would go on hunger strike unless the guards involved in the incident faced prosecution. The judges asked representatives of the service whether an investigation had begun. The prosecutor confirmed that an investigation into the incident was under way.

What does the Penitentiary Service say?

According to the Special Penitentiary Service, video footage shows that Davitadze refused to undergo a mandatory search while staff were moving him to a de-escalation cell and insulted prison staff. The service says staff later conducted a forced search using a handheld metal detector as part of their official duties.

“No violence was used against Davitadze — let alone any sexual abuse,” the Penitentiary Service said.

The service explained that it had previously refrained from publishing the footage because authorities were investigating the incident. It did not want anyone to interpret the release as an attempt to put pressure on the investigation. The service said it decided to publish the footage because of the strong public reaction and what it described as deliberate attempts by the prisoner’s family to discredit the institution.

The Penitentiary Service also said it had archived continuous video footage of Davitadze’s movements around the facility from 3 March 2026 to the present. According to the service, it can provide these recordings to all interested parties in accordance with the law.

What does Davitadze’s family say?

Irma Davitadze, Giorgi’s mother, is calling for not only the guards involved in the incident but also Shota Trapaidze, head of Prison No. 6, to face prosecution. She said the family would continue its fight until those responsible for the abuse receive punishment. In particular, she mentioned prison employee Giorgi Kvaratskhelia, whom she alleges has links to the use of violence against prisoners.

According to Irma Davitadze, the family has also collected information about possible violations that occurred at the facility in the past. The Penitentiary Service rejects these allegations, saying investigators and a representative of the Public Defender’s Office have already examined the video footage and found no signs of a crime.

Giorgi Davitadze is the son of Avtandil Davitadze, a former member of the Tbilisi City Council. Avtandil Davitadze joined the city council in 2014 on the Georgian Dream coalition list and served in the Georgian Dream–National Forum faction.

World.title: How Armenia is reacting to export restrictions on Russia: farmers’ views and official statistics
World.content:
Reaction of Armenian exporters to Russia’s restrictions

Since May 2026, Armenian exporters have faced serious problems after Russia banned imports of many Armenian goods and food products. The restrictions initially targeted Jermuk mineral water and later certain alcoholic beverages. Russia’s Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Supervision then announced a temporary ban on imports of flowers and ornamental plants from Armenia.

The list expanded further in June. A new restriction came into force on Armenian products subject to quarantine controls. It covered around 130 types of goods, including fresh fruit and vegetables, flowers and other agricultural products.

Russia introduced the restrictions shortly before Armenia’s parliamentary elections. Local experts believed Russia was trying to support pro-Russian politicians taking part in the elections. For this reason, they and Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan expected the situation to gradually return to normal after the election.

However, no positive changes have emerged. The situation has become more difficult. At first, Russia justified the restrictions by citing the quality of Armenian products. It now openly says Armenia cannot use the Russian market because the country has chosen a path towards European integration.

Against the backdrop of Russian restrictions, the Armenian government has launched support programmes for Armenian exporters.

The programmes include subsidies and financial compensation, including compensation for export duties on other markets. In late September, the government allocated an additional 4.5 billion drams ($12.7 million) to help exporters offset their losses.

The measures aim to help businesses redirect their supplies from the Russian market to Europe and other countries. The country’s foreign ministry is providing the strongest support for this process. The government recently renamed it the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Trade to reflect this role.

Even so, the ban on exports to the Russian market has hit agriculture particularly hard. Armenian farmers had long considered Russia their main export destination.

A farmer on the situation and his plans

Six years ago, Argam Yerndjyan established cherry orchards in Armenia’s Ararat Province. Three years later, he harvested his first good crop and began exporting to the Russian market.

“This year was difficult. I sold about 80% of my crop on the local market, at a price that did not generate any profit. I sold it at cost. I decided that this year, at least, my people and local residents should be able to buy a high-quality product at a price they could afford,” he says.

As a result, the farmer was able to pay his employees and cover his bank interest payments. However, if the situation does not change next year, he plans either to sell the orchards or switch to another line of business:

“I supplied about 20% of my cherries to a company that prepares products for export to the European market. The exporting company has promised to buy more next year. But I am worried about the current situation and have many concerns. I am a responsible person. I have employees and I am responsible for them.”

Argam Yerndjyan believes Armenia should promote its products more aggressively in foreign markets.

“Business cannot handle this on its own. At the same time, businesses need advice. For example, I am wondering whether I should export not only fresh cherries but also dried fruit, compotes and jams. I am thinking about processing some of my products myself. We also need exporters to tell us what foreign markets are demanding. My partner is currently working to establish exports to countries in the Middle East. We will see how it goes.”

Political context and statistics

The restrictions Russia introduced in 2026 have not only created short-term problems for Armenian exports but have also pushed the country to accelerate efforts to diversify its foreign markets.

Against this backdrop, the European Union has reached out to Armenia. It has launched measures to support the Armenian economy and give exporters additional opportunities to access the EU market. In July, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced in Yerevan that the EU could introduce autonomous trade measures for Armenian goods:

“I am here today to state clearly: if Russia closes its market to Armenian products, the EU will open the doors of its consumer market to them, with 450 million people.”

The European Parliament and the Council of the EU have already approved a package of temporary trade preferences. The EU will suspend customs duties on a wide range of goods exported from Armenia for two years. The trade preferences will cover around 80% of Armenian exports. The proposed benefits for some groups of goods will be significant and will cover products previously exported to Russia, including:

99% of fresh agricultural produce,

91% of beverages.

In the first seven months of 2026, Armenia’s foreign trade exports totalled around $4.04 billion. Compared with the same period last year, total exports fell by 7.9%.

At the same time, Armenia’s export geography still includes both traditional and new markets.

From January to June this year, Armenian exports to EU countries exceeded $516 million. Compared with the same period last year, exports grew by more than 80%.

From January to July, exports of Armenian-origin goods to other major markets increased by:

100% to India,

66.8% to China,

4.2% to the United States.

Agricultural exports form a separate category. From June to August 2026, Armenia exported:

fruit to 24 countries,

vegetables to 16 countries,

flowers to 28 countries.

World.title: 14 years in power: how experts assess Georgian Dream’s rule
World.content:
14 years of Georgian Dream

On 1 October 2026, 14 years had passed since the Georgian Dream party came to power. Today, assessments of the party’s 14 years in power differ sharply from those voiced just five years ago.

Former government official Beka Natsvlishvili discusses the significance of the events that brought Georgian Dream to power, while representatives of civil society and the diplomatic community point to a critical situation in the country’s democratic development and foreign policy.

Sandro Baramidze, a representative of Transparency International Georgia and former deputy justice minister, believes that although the first years of Georgian Dream’s rule could be viewed positively, the country is now living under a “full-fledged dictatorship”, with democratic institutions no longer functioning properly.

Meanwhile, diplomat and former deputy foreign minister Gigi Gigiadze analyses the changes in Georgia’s relations with the European Union, NATO and Western countries since 2012.

How do they assess Georgian Dream’s 14 years in power, and what has changed in the country since 2012?

Sandro Baramidze

Sandro Baramidze: “Ultimately, the story of the past 14 years began with promises: protecting human rights, building an unprecedented democracy, ensuring Euro-Atlantic integration, promoting economic growth and so on. Bidzina Ivanishvili and Georgian Dream came to power with precisely these promises.

I would say that the first few years were normal. The government carried out certain democratic reforms, including attempts to introduce democratic changes to the judiciary. But gradually, everything first stalled and then changed course, especially after Russia launched its full-scale aggression against Ukraine.

The situation has changed dramatically, and today we are dealing with a full-fledged dictatorship — a dictatorship of one man who runs the country from behind the scenes through his associates. This system has no separation of powers or checks and balances. We have no independent judiciary, either in the ordinary courts or the Constitutional Court, while democratic institutions, civil society, political parties and the media face enormous pressure. Moreover, civil society, once active and strong, is now on the verge of collapse.

Not a single democratic institution functions properly: opposition parties face the threat of dissolution, some political leaders are in prison, while others face new charges that could lead to lengthy prison sentences based on completely absurd arguments. People are arrested every day simply for standing on a pavement or making a statement on Facebook…

In short, we are living under a full-fledged dictatorship. Ultimately, this will inevitably come to an end, although the nightmare they have subjected the country to continues for now.”

Gigi Gigiadze

Gigi Gigiadze: “In 2012, Georgia was one of the European Union and NATO’s closest partners, as well as one of the countries undergoing the fastest transformation. Georgia was a ‘top performer’ among the participants in the Eastern Partnership.

Georgia was more eager than any other country to join the EU and NATO as quickly as possible. It served as a reliable partner for the EU and NATO in the region and took an active part in military exercises and peacekeeping missions organised by both organisations. Moreover, Georgia stood out as the main beacon of hope in Eastern Europe among countries genuinely seeking to join the EU and NATO.

Today, however, the reality looks completely different: Georgia has fallen furthest behind and become the most isolated and distant from the European Union and the West. We are facing a situation in which Georgia has lost all the progress it had accumulated along the way. Georgia is no longer seen as a genuine candidate, a reforming country or a state at the forefront of progress.

Very tough sanctions and extremely negative decisions concerning Georgia are being announced almost every day. We are receiving very low scores on numerous indicators — and this is not new; it started a long time ago. We are witnessing significant regression.

A vacuum has emerged — a situation our country has never faced before. Georgia’s foreign policy had always been crystal clear, and the direction in which we were moving was clearly defined. Everyone knew this, including Iran. Until now, neither Iran’s ambassador nor any other representative of a [state] would have dared to use such rhetoric towards Georgia, make such statements or issue such threats.

Everyone knew exactly what position we held, who our partners were and which camp we belonged to. As Georgia became increasingly isolated and drifted catastrophically away from Europe, the European Union and the West, a natural vacuum emerged, which Iran is now trying to fill with its influence.

Iran understands perfectly well that this is a unique opportunity to strengthen its presence here.

The Iranian ambassador no longer holds back. He believes he can say and do whatever he wants, without feeling constrained by anything or accountable to anyone. This is a natural consequence of the policy pursued by Georgian Dream over the past 14 years.”

Beka Natsvlishvili

Beka Natsvlishvili: “[The victory of Georgian Dream] was not simply a case of the government handing over power as a result of an election. Rather, the United National Movement was forced to give up power while avoiding large-scale violence. I call it a ‘revolution at the ballot box’. In a sense, it was a revolutionary change. A revolution implies systemic change, but unfortunately, the systemic transformation we expected never took place.

The 1 October victory was certainly not solely Bidzina Ivanishvili’s achievement. After all, you cannot simply erase 2012 from Georgia’s history. I returned from abroad in 2006 and actively took part in street protests until 2012. The coalition included people with far more experience in political struggle than I had. The struggle continued regardless, but without Bidzina Ivanishvili’s arrival, it produced no tangible result. His emergence gave the struggle a powerful boost and created an opportunity for a decisive breakthrough. We cannot attribute this success unequivocally to the efforts of one person or any particular group.

1 October is an important date in Georgia’s history. I fully recognise that and am proud to have taken part in those events. When the first parliament was formed, it was a parliament of politicians. At the time, politicians felt much more accountable to society, and they were people with strong individual identities. Breaking their word or abandoning their promises was much harder for them. Later, everything changed.

Georgian Dream decided to build a monolithic party. From a pragmatic point of view, the plan to create a monolithic party made perfect sense. It is very difficult to govern a country when your team includes people with diametrically opposed ideological views. But what is the problem with that? [The problem is that] Georgian Dream never managed to truly unite as a party because it no longer had politicians. The people who had been hardened in the heat of political struggle left. Today, very few politicians remain there; perhaps only a handful are left in Georgian Dream. No one sees the current members of parliament as political figures. The leader of the ruling team is surrounded by close associates who simply make it onto the party lists and enter parliament. They hold political positions, but they are not politicians.”

14 years of Georgian Dream

World.title: Azerbaijan’s deputy prime minister visits Iran: what interests are bringing Baku and Tehran closer?
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s deputy prime minister visits Iran

At meetings in Tehran attended by Azerbaijani Deputy Prime Minister Shahin Mustafayev, the sides discussed electricity supplies, the development of border infrastructure and transport routes. Iran plans to increase its electricity purchases from Azerbaijan this coming winter. For Baku, meanwhile, the priorities include developing joint energy projects and expanding transit capacity.

However, these talks do not provide grounds to speak of restored political trust. Economic cooperation continues amid tensions stemming from the armed attack on the Azerbaijani embassy in Tehran and a drone incident in Nakhchivan in March this year.

What was discussed in Tehran?

On 29 September, Mustafayev met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. According to the Iranian side, Pezeshkian emphasised the importance of expanding road, air and rail links, as well as implementing agreements reached during talks with ministers.

A statement from the Azerbaijani Cabinet of Ministers also reported meetings with parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei, Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad and Energy Minister Abbas Aliabadi. However, the statement provided no details on the financial terms of the energy projects or specific deadlines for their implementation.

Transport issues featured more prominently during the visit. At a meeting with Iran’s Minister of Roads and Urban Development Farzaneh Sadegh, the sides discussed the capacity of the North-South Corridor, the expansion of the Astara border freight terminal and the Aghband-Kalaleh bridge. According to official information, construction of the bridge has been completed. However, the sides are still discussing the launch of the border-crossing infrastructure. Completing the bridge does not by itself mean that the entire border complex is already operational.

The sides also reviewed progress on agreements reached at the 17th meeting of the joint commission, which took place in Baku in February. This indicates that the September talks also aimed to speed up implementation of previously agreed commitments.

What is known about electricity imports?

According to Trend, citing Iran’s Energy Ministry, TAVANIR electricity company chief Mohammad Allahdad expressed hope on 28 September that Iran could increase electricity imports during the coming colder months. He made the comments at a meeting with Azerbaijani Deputy Energy Minister Elnur Soltanov.

The talks covered direct electricity supplies, the development of joint hydropower plants, and gas and electricity swaps — mechanisms for exchanging the two forms of energy. Allahdad said specialists from the two countries needed to examine the points where their power grids connect and assess their technical capacity before determining possible supply volumes.

The plans announced after the talks do not mean that the sides have already signed an agreement on additional electricity supplies. The published information does not specify supply volumes, prices or start dates. Iran’s intention to increase imports should therefore not be confused with an actual increase in supplies.

According to the Tehran bureau of APA, Soltanov also raised the implementation of the Khudaferin and Ordubad hydropower projects, as well as the participation of private Iranian investors in solar energy projects in Nakhchivan. These initiatives also remain under discussion.

For Azerbaijan, increased electricity exports could provide an additional source of revenue. However, without information on volumes, prices and technical conditions, it is impossible to assess the economic benefits of this cooperation.

The security dimension of the economic talks

The talks in Tehran also covered allegations that Azerbaijan’s territory had been used against Iran. According to Unikal, citing the Mehr news agency, Mustafayev rejected these allegations at a meeting with Mohsen Rezaei.

The fact that the sides raised this issue alongside economic matters shows that security concerns remain relevant.

Relations between the two countries deteriorated sharply after an armed attack on the Azerbaijani embassy in Tehran in January 2023 killed one person. Subsequent contacts helped ease tensions, but a drone incident in Nakhchivan in March 2026 triggered a new crisis.

Azerbaijani officials blamed Iran for the 5 March attack, which damaged an airport and other civilian facilities. Tehran denied any involvement. According to the Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that authorities were investigating the circumstances of the incident. Baku demanded an apology, an explanation and measures to prevent similar incidents in the future.

The suspension of cargo traffic during the crisis showed that a deterioration in security can immediately affect economic ties.

Why does Baku want to avoid further tensions?

In an analysis published on 16 March, Carnegie Endowment researcher Zaur Shiriyev described Baku’s decision to demand an explanation after the drone incident rather than launch a retaliatory strike as an attempt to prevent further escalation.

In his view, Nakhchivan’s vulnerable position was one reason why tensions eased quickly. Transit through Iran plays an important role in the autonomous republic’s land and air connections. Shiriyev also noted that a war in Iran would create risks for Azerbaijan, including a possible influx of refugees and higher prices for imported goods.

This assessment concerns the March crisis. Nevertheless, it helps explain why Azerbaijan seeks to avoid a sharp deterioration in relations with Iran.

The September talks show that Tehran wants to increase electricity imports, while both sides seek to expand cooperation in the energy and transport sectors. These mutual interests provide a basis for continued engagement. However, it would be premature to view the visit as evidence that political mistrust has been overcome.

The outcome of this cooperation will depend on whether the sides can turn their stated intentions into actual supplies, ensure that border crossings operate fully and implement the projects they have outlined.

Azerbaijan’s deputy prime minister visits Iran

World.title: Abkhaz opposition leader Adgur Ardzinba on ties with Russia and relations with Tbilisi. Video discussion
World.content:
Adgur Ardzinba on Georgia

In this episode of the Abkhaz Srez Podcast, hosts Georgy Berzenia and Alkhas Gagulia interview Adgur Ardzinba, chairman of the Abkhaz Popular Movement and a former presidential candidate in Abkhazia, about the key challenges facing the republic.

Key points:

Education should be the top long-term priority: the republic can be competitive only if it has a highly educated population.

the republic can be competitive only if it has a highly educated population. Defence and mobilisation readiness, along with food security, are essential amid regional instability.

are essential amid regional instability. Pragmatic approach to relations with Georgia: trade is possible provided there is equal and transparent partnership and Abkhazia’s independent status is respected.

trade is possible provided there is equal and transparent partnership and Abkhazia’s independent status is respected. Political fragmentation of society is unacceptable. Ardzinba describes himself as part of the systemic opposition, which has taken part in all political cycles.

Ardzinba describes himself as part of the systemic opposition, which has taken part in all political cycles. Strategic partnership with Russia: the politician points to positive momentum and new opportunities following an economic forum and visits by Russian officials.

the politician points to positive momentum and new opportunities following an economic forum and visits by Russian officials. Agriculture needs development: the executive authorities lack a clear plan for the sector. Agriculture requires a combination of research, market analysis and assessment of competitors, rather than simply distributing subsidies.

Full text version of the conversation:

Georgi Berzenia: Good evening. Our guest today is the chairman of the Abkhaz National Movement and former presidential candidate of the Republic of Abkhazia, Adgur Ardzinba. Good evening, Adgur Amiranovich.

Adgur Ardzinba: Good evening. Hello.

Georgi Berzenia: We are glad to see you in the Srez Podcast studio.

Adgur Ardzinba: I am glad to see you too. Thank you for the invitation.

Alkhas Gagulia: Good evening, Adgur Amiranovich. This is our first time in this studio, although we have had plans to shoot an episode with you for a long time. You have finally found the time.

Adgur Ardzinba: My turn has finally come.

Alkhas Gagulia: Either it was your turn, or the stars aligned somehow. In any case, we welcome you to this studio. As always, we hope for a candid conversation. I think it will be interesting.

Adgur Ardzinba: Possibly.

Alkhas Gagulia: We recently started a tradition… Usually, blitz questions are asked at the end. We decided to do it at the beginning. Can you name one Abkhazian politician whom you respect, despite internal disagreements or personal differences?

Adgur Ardzinba: I try to treat all politicians and all opinion leaders with respect. That is how I was taught and raised—to look for the good in people. So, I probably do not have the right to single out just one person.

Despite our internal contradictions, which have been clearly pronounced since 2004, we have a fairly competitive political environment. In this competitive environment over the past 20-plus years, many politicians of the older generation, as well as younger ones, have proven themselves. Currently, a lot of new people have joined. Each of them has their own strengths and weaknesses, just as I do. Therefore, I try to treat all politicians with respect.

Because to a greater extent—at least I want to believe so—people enter politics out of patriotic feelings, out of a desire to benefit society. It is a rather difficult endeavor. It might seem easy to someone looking from the outside until you immerse yourself in these processes. It is quite a difficult matter. It impacts your loved ones and your family members. It affects how your family and relatives perceive things, including the criticism that is always present in one way or another on social media or expressed openly. But it is not easy work. At the very least, it deserves respect for that alone.

Georgi Berzenia: What, in your opinion, should a political leader be like in today’s Abkhazia?

Adgur Ardzinba: Courageous.

Georgi Berzenia: Do you consider yourself to be such a leader?

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, I do not have the right to speak about myself in the third person right now, but I will say this: where the interests of our people are and were concerned, I have never hidden behind other people’s backs. I have always tried to express my point of view openly, and it seems to me that this point of view is supported by the majority of our citizens. Especially in our recent history, when it concerned critical issues like—as you remember—apartments and various anti-popular initiatives. We expressed our point of view openly and courageously.

Why can we talk about courage? Because I feel great gratitude toward our citizens, toward everyone who actively expressed their opinion. Such economic issues usually have certain people and certain interests behind them. Naturally, when someone’s economic plans crumble, no one says thank you for that. Therefore, standing up to these kinds of initiatives or groups of interested parties requires a certain level of courage. Once again, I want to say that I feel immense gratitude toward our citizens and our people.

We did not just settle things among ourselves; we also showed the whole world that without taking into account the fundamental interests of the Abkhazian people, it will be impossible to push through any initiatives here.

Alkhas Gagulia: Have you ever felt ashamed of your actions or words in politics? If so, could you give an example?

Adgur Ardzinba: A person should always be self-critical, and that is normal. Well, there were moments—without going into details now. I felt…

Again, as you move forward and look back sometimes, of course, you evaluate yourself when you had to come out with harsh criticism. Sometimes it concerned people who later proved themselves quite well. You feel a little ashamed before yourself for that. But then, I have never abandoned anyone. I have always had—again, as I was raised—the strength to approach someone, apologize, and say that I drew the wrong conclusions about them, that I was hasty. That is normal. Again, I believe every person should be critical of themselves. Then it becomes easier to build relationships.

Georgi Berzenia: Over the past year and a half, following the election period, have you ever thought about leaving politics permanently?

Adgur Ardzinba: Well, every person always has doubts. Anyone who says everything is absolute for them and so on is likely not telling the truth. Every person—especially when facing serious difficulties that affect not only you, but your family, your loved ones, and your children—naturally experiences doubts.

Human life is filled with these doubts and with struggle, primarily within oneself. Overcoming these doubts and all these difficulties, one must find the strength to press forward. That is why I am here today, and I have no intention of leaving Abkhazian politics. Well, at least for now, because I see the existing problems. I do not have the luxury to sit quietly on the sidelines and ignore what is happening.

I believe that the active life stance I have maintained for the past 15 years will continue in the interest of our citizens and our beloved Homeland. Therefore, we will keep going.

Alkhas Gagulia: Complete this sentence: the main problem or threat to Abkhazia today is…?

Adgur Ardzinba: There are many problems. In my view, the primary problem—even though other issues have become pressing now, and I will explain why I say this—is still the education system.

The education system is the main priority that must be placed at the core today.

Yes, the situation in the world today is very complex. Defense and security are coming to the forefront, along with several other issues, naturally. But if you broaden the horizon and think about the perspective of the coming decades, it is undoubtedly education. Today, the education system relies on the conscientious attitude of teaching staff, educators, and teachers who do their jobs for a pittance. But relying purely on enthusiasm is very difficult, Alkhas. I talk to these people, and the new Minister of Education is trying hard. I had a conversation with her. She approaches this matter with heart, so to speak. But what is needed here is state policy.
