All these misunderstandings taking place are simply part of the process. Just as there are mistakes on our side, there are mistakes on theirs as well.

I am confident that everything will be fine. The main thing is to remain vigilant. Times are very dangerous. I will repeat it endlessly: defense and security.

Alkhas Gagulia: Well, I want to say thank you for today’s broadcast, for coming to join us so that a thorough conversation could take place on all the questions that interested us. The only thing I would like to add, of course, is that while we spoke about priority tasks—about defense and education—all of this stems from a single overarching priority: our sovereignty and our independence. If that serves as the main guidepost, everything else is meant to serve that exact priority. There are no other options. You mentioned my age twenty times today; in any case, my generation accepts nothing less. We lost far too many people for this land, and it is thanks to them that we stand on this land today. That is what I want to say to every single politician, without exception, on both sides. Thank you for the broadcast and for coming. I look forward to our next meetings.

Adgur Ardzinba: Thank you, friends. I believe that while our conversation was lengthy, it was candid, and we answered a number of questions. If we missed anything, I think we will have another opportunity to meet. As for sovereignty, Alkhas, that concerns not only your generation. The younger generation and the youth—the rising generation with whom I interact—see no other path across all generations than the building of an independent, sovereign Abkhazian state in Abkhazia. If anyone thinks otherwise, that would be their mistake. All of us have stood, are standing, and will continue to stand for this. Fundamentally, our entire conversation has been dedicated to strengthening that sovereignty, to making our state less vulnerable.

Today, our state is vulnerable. Let us be frank. To eliminate these weak points, we need systemic work, the establishment of priorities, societal consolidation, and defense to preserve our territory, as well as our language—which you raised, Georgi—and our culture. All of this is vital, because knowing a language alone does not make you Abkhaz. The upcoming parliamentary elections are also crucial; the quality and substantive content of that body are of great importance. All of this, as was rightly stated, Alkhas, exists in order to preserve, strengthen, and pass down. Thank you.

Georgi Berzenia: Thank you for an engaging conversation.

World.title: ‘We will decide in the coming months’: Pashinyan on choosing model for Armenia’s new nuclear power plant
World.content:
Pashinyan on building a new nuclear power plant in Armenia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has announced a change in the government’s position on the technology and design of a new nuclear power plant.

“I have said dozens of times before that we do not need anything more [powerful] than a modular nuclear power plant. That was our position. But now we have to understand that a modular plant will most likely not be enough to meet our needs,” Pashinyan said.

He explained that the government changed its position because of the construction of AI factories. Armenia now needs to import electricity to meet their power requirements.

Discussions continue over which technology would best suit the new nuclear power plant. The Armenian government expects to make a decision on the issue by the end of 2027.

A day earlier, the prime minister met a delegation led by Alexey Likhachev, director general of the state-owned Rosatom corporation. They discussed proposals from the Russian side.

Armenia is currently working to extend the operating life of the Metsamor nuclear power plant until 2036. Russia has taken part in efforts to extend the plant’s operating life and modernise it throughout this period. The plant originally entered service in 1977.

At the same time, Yerevan is discussing the construction of a new nuclear power plant with several countries, including the US. The prime minister has repeatedly said in recent months that the nuclear power issue is not a geopolitical choice for Armenia: “We will choose the proposal that serves us best.”

Pashinyan does not rule out accepting the Russian proposal

Speaking about the upcoming decision on the technology for the new nuclear power plant, the prime minister stressed that before Armenia signed memorandums of understanding with the US on 8 August 2025, Armenia had a surplus of electricity.

“We had to think about where to direct this surplus energy. A year later, Armenia had become a country with an electricity deficit,” he said.

According to Nikol Pashinyan, this resulted from the construction of two AI factories in Armenia during that period:

“The point is that, given the scale of the investment projects already approved, Armenia has faced an electricity deficit. In other words, these projects are fully absorbing the surplus we have. So we need to decide what to do next.”

The prime minister said the government would make a decision in the coming months. Pashinyan also said that Armenia could accept the proposal put forward by Russia:

“It is quite possible that building a 1,000 MW plant will prove to be the most logical solution. However, I cannot say for certain at this stage because experts are still assessing the issue.”

“The unit should be at least one, with a capacity of at least 1 GW” — Likhachev

Rosatom director general Alexey Likhachev told journalists some details of Russia’s proposal after talks in Yerevan. Likhachev said Armenia would continue to rely on nuclear energy for decades to come. Russia therefore plans to “formulate the most competitive proposal” for building a new reactor unit in the coming months.

“And in our view, this unit should be at least one, with a capacity of at least 1 GW,” Likhachev said.

According to him, the proposal involves a VVER-1000 reactor, a pressurised water reactor with a capacity of 1,000 MW.

The head of Rosatom stressed that this proposal is “the best currently available on the global market”. He added that Rosatom has built and continues to build VVER reactors of this type in India and Iran:

“They combine very high economic efficiency, namely a low cost of electricity, with all the necessary Generation III+ safety systems.”

Details of talks with Rosatom director general in Yerevan

The Armenian prime minister’s office said Pashinyan and Likhachev discussed:

work to extend the operating life of the existing second reactor unit at the Armenian Nuclear Power Plant;

Russia’s proposals for building a new reactor unit.

At the same time, the prime minister told Likhachev that the Armenian government was continuing to consider proposals from other international partners.

Pashinyan stressed that the final decision would depend solely on economic considerations. These would include price, quality, safety, construction timelines and guarantees.

The statement also said Alexey Likhachev described cooperation with Armenian partners as constructive. The Rosatom chief also provided detailed information about the construction of not only large VVER reactors, but also small and medium-sized reactors.

Pashinyan on building a new nuclear power plant in Armenia

World.title: ‘Delicate issue’: how Abkhazia’s authorities are trying to ease situation of lawyer Irakli Bzhinava, arrested in Russia
World.content:
Abkhazia’s president, Badra Gunba, is discussing the fate of Abkhaz lawyer Irakli Bzhinava, who is being held in a Russian detention centre, with Moscow. Authorities have opened two criminal cases against him. Gunba says the issue requires a delicate approach.

At a meeting of the Consultative Council of political parties and civil society organisations, the president said Abkhaz authorities were working with their Russian counterparts on Bzhinava’s detention conditions. The foreign ministry and consular service are also providing the necessary support, including to his lawyers.

“State authorities are dealing with this issue. I personally discuss it with my colleagues through my own channels, and certain services are also involved,” the president said.

According to Gunba, the issue requires a delicate approach because it concerns another country’s laws. At the same time, he said, the Abkhaz side is not stepping back from the situation and continues to discuss it through various channels.

Irakli Bzhinava, who holds dual Abkhaz and Russian citizenship and lives in Russia, was detained on 5 February 2026 and has remained in pre-trial detention ever since.

According to the case materials, the authorities brought the charges over a social media post that Bzhinava published on 23 December 2022. The post concerned an agreement to transfer a famous state dacha in Abkhazia to Russia. Bzhinava criticised the agreement, arguing that it violated Abkhaz law.

Bzhinava initially faced charges of “criminal intent to make public calls for activities directed against the security of the Russian Federation”, which carries a prison sentence of up to three years.

However, in mid-September, Russia’s Investigative Committee opened a second criminal case against Bzhinava. The new charges accuse him of “publicly justifying the terrorist Shamil Basayev online” and carry a prison sentence of up to seven years.

Despite the more serious charges, Irakli Bzhinava was allowed to meet his mother for the first time in seven months in detention. According to civil society activist Kadir Argun, who is collecting signatures in support of Bzhinava, the meeting provided his family with “enormous support and moral strength during a difficult time”.

Irakli Bzhinava enjoys fairly broad support in Abkhazia, with local politicians and public figures regularly calling on the republic’s authorities to provide him with comprehensive assistance.

Abkhazia’s ombudswoman Anas Kishmaria has also formally appealed to her Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, asking her to help improve Bzhinava’s detention conditions and take personal oversight of the case.

World.title: Four Georgian citizens and people linked to country’s occupied regions hit by UK sanctions
World.content:
Georgian citizens under UK sanctions

The UK has announced a new package of sanctions against Russia, imposing restrictions on 31 individuals, organisations and vessels.

The UK has added four Georgian citizens to its sanctions list: journalist Nikoloz Mzhavanadze, who lives in Russia; pro-Russian businessman and Solidarity for Peace party chairman Mamuka Pipia; party member Giorgi Iremadze; and pro-Russian analyst Paata Abuladze. According to the British government, the sanctions target these individuals for spreading Kremlin disinformation.

The sanctions list also includes three people linked to Georgia’s occupied regions of Abkhazia and so-called South Ossetia. They are Marat Kambolov, the so-called president of the occupied Tskhinvali region; his predecessor Alan Gagloev; and Russian political strategist Sergei Tolmachev.

Media reports say Sergei Tolmachev helped run the election campaign of Badra Gunba, the so-called president of occupied Abkhazia.

According to the UK government, the sanctions target actions that threaten Ukraine’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence.

“Russia’s aggression against Ukraine forms part of a broader pattern of disregard for the sovereignty, territorial integrity and internationally recognised borders of neighbouring states. This includes Russia’s ongoing occupation of the Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

The UK condemns Russia’s attempts to cement its illegal control over Georgia’s occupied regions, including through the so-called ‘presidential elections’ held in South Ossetia on 18 September and subsequent steps towards de facto annexation.

The UK firmly supports Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders and continues to hold Russia accountable for its actions,” the statement says.

The broader package of sanctions announced on 1 October also targets Russian sources of revenue, including the so-called “shadow fleet” and Kremlin disinformation networks, as well as individuals involved in crimes against Ukraine’s civilian population.

World.title: EU Council delegation visits Azerbaijan’s Shusha (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 2. A delegation of the Eastern Europe and Central Asia Working Party (COEST) of the Council of the European Union visited Shusha on October 2.

Aydin Karimov, Special Representative of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the Shusha district, briefed the guests on the city’s history, its condition during the occupation and the reconstruction and redevelopment work carried out after its liberation.

The delegation’s tour of Shusha began with visits to the Lower and Upper Govhar Agha mosques.

The EU Council representatives then visited the bullet-scarred statues of prominent Azerbaijani figures Natavan, Bulbul and Uzeyir Hajibeyli in the central square of Shusha.

As part of the visit, the foreign delegates also toured the first residential complex in Shusha and familiarized themselves with the facilities there. Construction of the residential complex began in 2021, and it was inaugurated on May 10, 2024. All houses were built in Shusha’s traditional architectural style.

The 23-building residential complex has been equipped with all necessary facilities to ensure comfortable living conditions for residents. Former internally displaced persons have returned to their hometown and settled in the residential complex.

The guests also toured Shusha’s fortress walls and were briefed on the history of the city and the construction of the walls. Restoration work was carried out at the fortress after the liberation of Shusha from occupation.

The delegation was also briefed on the Gazanchi Church in Shusha.

World.title: Azerbaijan, World Bank discuss cooperation in financial access and transport (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 2. Azerbaijan and the World Bank have discussed cooperation in financial access and transport during a meeting today in Baku.

The discussion was held at a meeting between the First Deputy Minister of Finance of Azerbaijan, Anar Karimov and a World Bank delegation led by Regional Director for the South Caucasus Rolande Pryce, the Azerbaijani Finance Ministry told Trend.

The meeting addressed the key outcomes of the World Bank's Financial Inclusion for Jobs and Growth (FINGROW) and transport missions, future areas of cooperation, as well as strengthening coordination between the World Bank and relevant government agencies to accelerate project preparation and implementation.

Karimov highlighted the importance of partnership with the World Bank in supporting Azerbaijan's socio-economic development and implementing its reform agenda. He noted that there are broad opportunities to deepen cooperation in expanding access to finance, financing the private sector and developing transport infrastructure.

Regarding preparations for the FINGROW project, Karimov said work was continuing to establish the necessary financing and legal mechanisms for implementing the partial credit guarantee and equity financing components envisaged under the project, as well as to define the project's conceptual framework.

The sides also noted that the World Bank-financed Regional Roads and Development project was completed in March this year. It was reported that, as part of continued cooperation in the road sector, relevant measures are being taken to prepare the Reconstruction of the Bilasuvar-Astara Section of the M3 Highway project and secure World Bank financing and technical assistance.

In turn, Pryce expressed satisfaction with the development of cooperation between Azerbaijan and the World Bank based on mutual trust and effective partnership. She said the World Bank was ready to provide financial and expert support for initiatives aimed at expanding access to finance and developing transport infrastructure under the FINGROW project.

The sides stressed the importance of continuing cooperation in these areas and strengthening coordination.

World.title: Turkmenistan, Lithuania discuss trade, transport cooperation via Central Asia-EU format
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 2. Turkmenistan and Lithuania discussed opportunities to expand trade and economic cooperation, including transport and logistics links through the Central Asia-European Union format, during a meeting in Ashgabat.

This was reported in a press release issued by the Mejlis (Parliament) of Turkmenistan, following a meeting held on October 1 between representatives of Turkmenistan’s Mejlis and a Lithuanian delegation led by Dainius Varnas, chairman of the Lithuanian Seimas’ interparliamentary friendship group with Turkmenistan.

The sides discussed further development of bilateral cooperation, including in the trade, economic, cultural and humanitarian spheres.

According to the Mejlis, Lithuanian representatives said the Central Asia-European Union format provides opportunities to develop political dialogue and transport and logistics corridors between the countries of the region.

The sides also highlighted interparliamentary dialogue as an important component of bilateral cooperation, including the exchange of experience in legislative work.

Lithuania and Turkmenistan established diplomatic relations in 1992. Bilateral ties have since included political dialogue, trade and economic cooperation, as well as contacts in the transport, education and cultural spheres.

Trade between the two countries remains relatively modest but has included Lithuanian exports of machinery, electrical equipment, chemicals and other industrial goods. Lithuania has also sought to expand economic engagement with Turkmenistan through business delegations and bilateral contacts.

Transport and logistics have become an increasingly relevant area of cooperation. Lithuania, as an EU member and a Baltic state with access to the Baltic Sea, can provide a link between Central Asian markets and Northern Europe, while Turkmenistan is developing its position as a transport hub on routes connecting Central Asia with the Caspian Sea and beyond.

World.title: Nepal plans to drain four glacial lakes after flooding disaster
World.content:
Nepal will kick off a high-stakes effort to drain four glacial lakes perched high in the mountains, as it scrambles to reduce flood risks, officials said, after a recent disaster that killed more than 1,400.

"Our aim is to lower the risk of the lakes breaching their natural dams and reduce the risk of downstream floods," said Subash Tuladhar, an expert with a government research centre tasked with overseeing the new project.

Thick mud and debris left by the raging torrent that swept through Nepal have complicated recovery efforts. (Reuters: Tyrone Siu)

Canals will drain water into nearby rivers in a regulated way, he said, adding that workers faced health risks as a result of the lengthy periods of high-altitude work required, in addition to the dangers of sudden flooding.

Design work and detailed studies targeting the central and eastern lakes of Thulagi, Lower Barun, Lumding Tsho and Hongu II, will begin in the fiscal year that runs until mid-July 2027, authorities said.

The lakes, at heights ranging from 4,050m to 5,483m rank among Nepal's most potentially dangerous, the United Nations Development Programme and the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) said in a 2020 report.

Nepal had the skills and experience required for the $50-million project to be funded by the Green Climate Fund, the UNDP and the government, added Mr Tuladhar, of Nepal's Centre for Hydrology and Water Resources Research.

Draining project could take six years

The work of draining "through gated structures" will start after a detailed study, and could take up to six years to complete, said Sanjeeb Baral, the Centre's executive director.

It will encompass installation of sensors, a flood forecasting and warning system, and efforts to build downstream resilience and prepare communities for the risks.

In similar previous efforts, Nepal lowered by 3 m (10 ft) the level of the central Himalayan glacial lake of Tsho Rolpa by in 2000 and that of Imja in the vicinity of Mount Everest, the world's tallest peak, 10 years ago.

Urgency after recent floods

Nepal's disaster served as a warning to the world, Prime Minister Balendra Shah, 36, told the United Nations in an impassioned speech last month that blamed climate change despite his country's negligible emissions.

Retreating glaciers, unstable mountain slopes and increasingly unpredictable rivers showed Nepal was paying a heavy price, he added.

Life after disaster A month after catastrophic floods swept through Nepal's Nuwakot district, the town of Devighat is still reeling.

Nepal, which has reported about 26 glacial lake outburst flood events in the past four decades, loses more than 300 lives and property worth millions of dollars to extreme climate events annually on average.

The latest floods devastated a dozen hydro-electric plants, roads, bridges, farms and settlements. Cash-strapped Nepal would need billions of dollars for early recovery, officials have said.

Lowering the lakes by three metres would significantly reduce the threat, said Samjwal Ratna Bajracharya, a retired ICIMOD expert on glaciers, glacial lakes and outburst floods.

"They are growing fast, are high up in the Himalayas and could cause outbursts any time, due to earthquakes, avalanches, climatic conditions and unplanned human-induced activity," he told Reuters.

Immense DNA identification task continues

With thousands still missing and recovery crews facing mounting DNA profiles to process, fragmented remains and limited technical capacity experts warn matching bodies to families could take weeks.

Fighting for climate justice Can countries like Nepal use international law after natural disasters?

Just 112 bodies have been identified and returned to their families. A further 5,285 people are missing in Nepal, including hundreds of foreigners.

In China, the toll is 43 dead and 519 missing, according to state media -- taking the combined toll to nearly 1,500 dead and 5,800 missing.

REUTERS/AFP

World.title: Detailed plan led to murder of Hong Kong model Abby Choi, court hears
World.content:
The ex-husband and in-laws of a Hong Kong influencer and model crafted an elaborate plan that ended with her murder in 2023, prosecutors told the court Friday in the high-profile case.

Warning: this article includes graphic detail

Police discovered parts of 28-year-old Abby Choi's dismembered body at a suburban Hong Kong property in February 2023, in a case that stunned the financial hub.

Ms Choi's ex-husband Alex Kwong, 31, his father Kwong Kau, 68, and brother Anthony Kwong, 35, have pleaded not guilty to murder charges and have been on trial since Wednesday. They face life in prison if convicted.

Slain Hong Kong model’s in-laws, ex-husband detained Abby Choi's ex-husband and former in-laws were detained on murder charges. WARNING: graphic content.

Prosecution lawyer Charlotte Draycott said that days before Ms Choi was reported missing, the defendants bought equipment later used to cut up and dispose of her body including a mincing machine.

The court was played CCTV footage that prosecutors said showed Ms Choi, 28, getting into one of two vans used by the Kwongs in the afternoon on February 21, 2023.

Her last online activity was at 2:44pm.

Other footage showed the suspects parking the vans at a different location at around 3:20 pm the same day near the same property where police recovered her remains on February 24.

The three men were seen wearing face masks and were "not upset".

Police officers discovered missing parts of 28-year-old model Abby Choi's body in Hong Kong on February 28, 2023.

"It's what they expected," Ms Draycott told the court, saying that they had prepared a "cogitated plan" to kill Ms Choi.

On February 25, Alex Kwong -- who had two children with Ms Choi -- was arrested while planning to flee Hong Kong, a day after his father and brother were detained.

Prosecutors also displayed a hammer to the jury and cited a forensic report saying that the injuries on Ms Choi's skull, caused by a blunt instrument, matched the shape of the hammer.

Prosecutors told the jury earlier this week that Ms Choi and her ex-husband's family had financial disputes over a luxury property which she had paid HK$60 million ($10.98 million AUD).

The trial is expected to last at least until December.

AFP

World.title: Greens see red-hot anger as an opportunity to take on Hanson, Labor
World.content:
David Shoebridge has big ambitions for the Greens, but his party is still wrestling with how to turn voter disillusionment into greater support.

The new leader wants to harness the anti-establishment anger rife in Australia, declaring the Greens will fight and ultimately seek to "replace" Labor.

That won't be easy at a time when the populist right is capturing much of the voter anger here, though Shoebridge is not alone in seeing widespread economic frustration as an opportunity for the left.

Insurgent political movements in Britain, the United States and Germany have built support around everyday frustrations like rent, wages and living costs, and directed voters' anger toward inequality and concentrated wealth rather than the targets favoured by their opponents on the right.

Zack Polanski took the Green party in the UK and explicitly embraced "eco-populism" to achieve extraordinary membership growth and a surge in the polls.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani rode populist momentum into office. (AP: Angelina Katsanis)

In New York, Zohran Mamdani defeated an establishment Democrat and won the mayoral election by relentlessly translating socialism into rent, buses, childcare and groceries.

While a revitalised Die Linke party in Germany has almost doubled its vote through young supporters with a pitch on rent, wages and inequality.

All three have embedded climate, minority rights and other progressive causes inside a simple economic story.

Their circumstances and politics differ significantly, but each has demonstrated the potential for the left to turn economic dissatisfaction into electoral support.

If some of that sounds familiar, it's because the strategy is hardly new to Australians.

Long before Polanski or Mamdani became globally recognised names, the Greens here were trying to harness economic frustration with a pitch centred on inequality and the cost of everyday life.

Particularly under former leader Adam Bandt, the Greens consciously broadened beyond environmentalism.

Housing, inequality, free childcare, dental in Medicare, taxing billionaires and corporations and cost of living were all brought to the fore.

The strategy delivered the party four lower house seats and a 12.25 per cent primary vote nationally in 2022.

But three years later the Greens got a taste of just how fragile success can be.

Greens' changing strategy

The 2025 loss of three lower house seats — including Bandt's — showed the limits of a strategy that had produced spectacular gains, even as the party's national vote barely moved.

The Greens' attempts to extract concessions from the Albanese government on housing and climate were ultimately presented by Labor as blocking progressive outcomes rather than achieving them.

Former leader Larissa Waters focused on a constructive partnership with Labor. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

When Larissa Waters became leader of the party last year, she instead promised to be "firm but constructive" with Labor — to "get shit done".

The party's strategy basically went from "Labor isn't good enough so fight them and force them further left" to "Labor isn't good enough so negotiate and show voters what Greens leverage delivers".

But that leverage has yet to translate into a significant boost in the polls.

Shoebridge has now swung the emphasis back towards confrontation, though in a dramatically different political environment.

"We're not here to make the Labor Party any better. The Greens are here to replace them," he said.

He's also vowed to fight One Nation but blamed Labor for the rise of the populist right party.

Radical change, but how?

Meanwhile, Shoebridge's rivals for the leadership have ended this week emphasising markedly different priorities.

The rare, contested ballot against Mehreen Faruqi and Sarah Hanson-Young on Wednesday exposed a party still grappling with how to translate its ambitions into greater political power.

Move over, Hanson, Labor has a new thorn in its side David Shoebridge wants to hold Labor's feet to the fire. He will be a thorn in the party's side rather than a deal maker.

While they broadly share a vision of radical change, there is a live argument about who the Greens should fight and what voters should hear from them first.

Faruqi used a post-ballot statement to suggest she had not sought the deputy role so she could have the freedom to pursue "bold politics and radical action" from outside the leadership team.

Expressing her disappointment at the result, Faruqi appeared to imply she would have succeeded had the party held a membership-wide vote for the leader.

Her reaction contrasted starkly with Hanson-Young, who not only managed to congratulate Shoebridge but also kept her sights trained firmly on the populist right.

She cast the Greens as a progressive force to take on Pauline Hanson, rather than sharpen the fight with Labor.

It's been a week of free advice from outside the party room, too, with ousted MP Max Chandler-Mather also calling for a membership ballot — something Shoebridge has guaranteed would happen by 2028.

Meanwhile, Bandt told the Insiders On Background podcast the Greens could either choose "division and fear" or to "offer hope", working to "get good things done for people, for nature for climate".

When pushed on the idea that using the power of government to achieve those goals sounded "quite different" to the pitch from Shoebridge, Bandt replied, "well, that's right".

Loading

Opponents, allies and message

There is strong agreement inside the Greens about the problems they want to solve. But consensus on who exactly is their main opponent, which allies they need and what message will grow the party's support remains elusive.

For now, Labor and the Greens have a relatively reliable path to passing legislation through the Senate when they agree.

That arithmetic could look very different after 2028.

Shoebridge evidently believes there are gains to be made in chipping away at Labor, perhaps even more so if Labor is preoccupied fighting One Nation.

But it's unlikely Anthony Albanese would ever lose focus on a perennial political foe to his left.

That makes the Greens' message as important as the opponents they choose.

Each leadership hopeful offered a different strategy for success and while Shoebridge prevailed on the day, the battle for the future of the party is ongoing.

World.title: Indian 'Cockroach Party' protestors demand elections chief resign
World.content:
India's prime minister is facing renewed pressure as thousands led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and activist groups took to the streets demanding the resignation of the elections commission chief over a controversial voter roll revision.

Supporters of the CJP — which began in May as a satirical online movement — rallied in Mumbai's Shivaji Park, in their first protests since July, when their nationwide campaign helped oust the education minister.

Separately, hundreds of people gathered on roads around Jantar Mantar, a government-designated protest site in the heart of New Delhi, which was sealed off behind police barricades.

Police detained multiple protesters in Delhi, put them on buses and dropped them off elsewhere, but some returned to the Jantar Mantar site on foot.

India's opposition parties protest controversial electoral roll revision Critics and opposition leaders say the exercise will impact minorities the most, including Muslims, and disallow them from voting.

Student and civil society groups were prevented from gathering Friday at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in New Delhi, to also demand the commissioner's resignation.

Police detained some opposition leaders heading to the site, and mobile internet services were also suspended in the area.

The rallies are intended to kick off a new period of demonstrations nationwide.

Activist Vijeta Dahiya, who was involved in the previous "cockroach" campaign against the education minister, said that "no one wants to protest, but are forced to raise their voice when the government makes mistakes".

"Protest anywhere in the country," he said. "It is a matter of a right to vote."

India's opposition calls for election chief to be prosecuted

People detained by the police during a protest demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar. (Reuters: Adnan Abidi)

The protests mark the latest escalation in a dispute that has put unprecedented scrutiny on India's Election Commission, long regarded as one of the country's most trusted institutions.

The protesters' allege the commission manipulated voter rolls in ways that favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

"We have been asking and demanding for a change but nothing of that is going to happen, if our only tool that is left to change anything in our society 'the right to vote' is taken away from us," Saurav Das, CJP's convenor, told Indian news agency ANI on Thursday.

"We will only end the protest after Gyanesh Kumar resigns."

The main opposition Congress party has said Mr Kumar should be criminally prosecuted for treason.

The commission and the government have denied the allegations.

A woman is detained during a protest demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner. (Reuters: Adnan Abidi)

Pressure on Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar intensified last month after the Indian Express newspaper reported the election chief's two deputies had formally raised concerns at least 14 times over the past 10 months over voter-list revisions, registration procedures and the commission's digital systems.

The Election Commission has said differing views are a normal part of internal deliberations and that all its actions were lawful.

Voter verification controversy

Political analysts estimate that 130 million names have been struck off the voter list since the latest round of revisions began last year.

Nearly 650 million people voted in the last national election in 2024.

The commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate, deceased or ineligible voters and ensure the accuracy of electoral rolls.

Political scientists Rahul Verma told ABC's The World there was "no doubt" the majority of those deleted were deceased or moved away.

Protesters detained by police during a protests in New Delhi.

But he said people were "suffering" because of the amount of documentation needed to prove why they should remain registered.

Mr Verma said he has not seen this level of mass outrage among general voters since the controversial revision process started in 2025.

India began verification of its voter rolls of elections in the eastern state of Bihar. The review has now covered the majority of Indian states.

While voter roll revisions are routine, this round became controversial after large numbers of voters in states such as Bihar and West Bengal found their names missing from electoral rolls and were unable to cast ballots.

"While the chief commissioner and election commission may have its own explanation for why things were happening the way they have been happening, the trust in [the] election commission at this moment has taken a hit," Mr Verma said.

Cockroach Janta Party's sway

Activists shout slogans during a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Mr Verma said the only way for the chief commissioner to be removed is through parliamentary impeachment but it was unlikely to happen because the opposition does not have the numbers to force such a move.

But he did not rule it out because the CJP spearheaded mass protests earlier this year over unemployment and leaked examination papers triggered the resignation of India's education minister, one of Mr Modi's most significant political setbacks in recent years.

Headed by Abhijeet Dipke, the CJP is a youth movement that emerged earlier this year and has become an unexpected political force.

While education and employment was an "emotive" issue that cut across all young people, Mr Verma was skeptical the electoral roll revision would carry the same sway.

"Whether this movement or organisation has ability to mobilise again and again is at this moment difficult to say."

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Man City appeals guilty findings of breaking EPL's financial rules
World.content:
Manchester City has filed an appeal against an independent commission ruling that found the club guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules, seeking to overturn the verdict and avoid potentially severe sanctions.

The league said on Tuesday that ​City had used "sham" commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than £900 million ($1.71 billion) over nearly a decade.

City was found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the league's financial rules over nine seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as three out of four charges concerning failures to cooperate with the investigation.

The club has denied wrongdoing throughout the process.

"Manchester City Football Club can confirm that at 7pm on Thursday 1st October 2026 the Club lodged its comprehensive Appeal against the opinion of the Premier League Commission, in relation to the Premier League disciplinary matter," the club said in a statement.

"The Club's firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case."

The appeal will be heard by an independent three-member appeal board appointed by the chair of the league's Judicial Panel.

"The club lodged the appeal to the Chair of the Judicial Panel," the league said in a statement.

"The independent Appeal Board hearing will remain private and confidential until publication of the outcome is permitted."

Appeal decision is final

The Premier League's rules state that an appeal hearing should be held within 12 weeks of an appeal being lodged, with a decision due within 30 days of the hearing concluding.

The appeal will take place in private, as did the original hearings. The board will review the commission's decision, but will not conduct a full rehearing of the case.

The board can dismiss the appeal, allow it, refer the case back to the commission for further consideration or alter any sanction or compensation order imposed.

A decision by the appeal board is final and cannot be challenged further except in limited circumstances that permit a subsequent arbitration process.

With potential sanctions including heavy fines, points deductions and other sporting penalties, and with relegation or the removal of titles also discussed as possible outcomes, the case could have consequences across the league.

City can also separately appeal against any sanctions. It remains unclear whether sanctions will be announced before the appeal is heard, and whether they would take effect immediately.

A league representative told Reuters they could not discuss the process for confidentiality reasons.

While the fate of the case remains unresolved, the season will continue, with leaders City looking for their sixth straight league win when they visit Liverpool on October 11.

Reuters

World.title: Healthcare workers killed in Ledcourt triple-fatal had a 'bright' future in Australia
World.content:
Friends and colleagues have paid tribute to two Chinese nationals who were victims of a crash in Victoria's west that claimed three lives.

Michael Zheng, 38, and his wife Angela Wang, 31, died at the scene after their car was involved in a collision with a Mitsubishi Triton and a truck at Ledcourt about 6.45pm on September 27.

Tenesha Fieldsend, 14, a passenger in the Mitsubishi, driven by a learner driver, later died at hospital.

The couple, who recently celebrated their fifth wedding anniversary, had been living in the town of Horsham, approximately 300 kilometres west of Melbourne.

Friends have described them as two "wonderful people" with "so much hope for their future in Australia".

Mr Zheng had recently been promoted as the manager of the Horsham Dentist Group, while Ms Wang was a nurse at Grampians Health.

JingJing Tang got to know the couple last year when she was helping them look for their missing dog.

" Perhaps because we were all Chinese living here, there was naturally a sense of closeness between us, and they would affectionately call me 'jie', which means 'older sister' in Chinese. "

Ms Tang said they were a lovely young couple.

"They had been granted Australian permanent residency last year, and I remember how happy and hopeful they were about building their life here," she said.

Angela Wang and Michael Zheng met while living in Africa. (Facebook)

Ms Tang last spoke to Mr Zheng and Ms Wang a few months ago, when they came to Ms Tang's newly opened takeaway restaurant for a meal.

"The shop wasn't busy, so we sat together and talked for quite a long time," she said.

"I could never have imagined that would be the last time I would see them.

"Looking back now, that ordinary and happy conversation has become a very precious memory for me."

During that conversation, Ms Tang said the couple had spoken about their new home being built in Ballarat, and their hopes for the future — including having a baby one day.

"I could see how excited they were about the life they were building together, they had so many hopes, plans and dreams ahead of them," Ms Tang said.

"It's heartbreaking that their journey ended. I hope they are together in heaven now … continuing the dreams and beautiful life they had planned together."

Michael Zheng and Angela Wang enjoyed living in Australia. (Facebook)

A heartbreaking wait for friends

Simon Yan, one of Mr Zhang's colleagues, said he was always quick to reply, even on weekends, so the team was shocked when they hadn't heard from him on Monday.

"We tried to follow up with him after work, that's when I think the first news of the car crash came out," Dr Yan said.

A few of Ms Wang's friends had stopped at the couple's house to check on them, he said.

"The fact that they hadn't been identified for quite a long time, it was torturous … just thinking that it could possibly be them, but even just the tiniest glimmer of hope that it wasn't them, that was what we were just clinging onto."

Dr Yan said he had been a "wreck" since the news broke.

"It's been hard going to sleep and everything … I wake up during the night," he said.

Dr Yan said Mr Zheng, who had been at the dental clinic since March last year, had made his mark as a "lovely and warm" person whom the team viewed as family.

"He was always there for us, supported us through everything, he was our sounding board, he was our rock … It's hard to imagine going on without him."

Clinic owner and dentist Catherine Feng said the entire team was devastated.

"When we saw the description, our hearts sank … that's when we knew," she said.

"I was in shock, in disbelief, especially after holding out hope about the unidentified people in the car … We all broke down crying when we found out."

Colleagues said he was a dedicated manager and loved by everyone.

"We are just struggling to come to terms that he's gone. Every day we come to work … you just expect to see him [there] smiling like every other single day," Dr Feng said.

"The team respected him a lot, and we all miss him a lot right now … the clinic feels a little bit emptier without him."

She said while they had never met Ms Wang, her husband would always talk about her fondly.

More tributes for teenage victim

Earlier this week, the volleyball coach of Tenesha Fieldsend paid tribute to the "bubbly, bright and energetic" teenager.

Tenesha Fieldsend died in the same multi-vehicle crash. (Supplied: Sale Catholic College)

Tenesha, who was from Sale, east of Melbourne, had been returning from a volleyball tournament in Horsham with her family when the crash took place.

She had represented LaTrobe Valley Volleyball at the Victorian junior country championships, where her team won bronze in the under-17 girls division.

In a statement posted online, Tenesha's school, Sale Catholic College, said she was a valued member of the year 8 cohort and that her loss had been deeply felt by her friends, classmates, teachers and the wider school community.

"During this difficult time, we stand together as a community supporting one another with compassion, kindness and care, while remembering the joy and memories Tenesha brought to those around her," the statement read.

Victoria Police said the investigation into the crash is continuing.

World.title: Flydubai 'hero' pilot says praying gave him courage
World.content:
The "hero" Indian pilot who fought off a mid-flight attack from his co-pilot has described the harrowing ordeal from hospital in a talk with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Captain Smit Machchhar, appearing from an Abu Dhabi hospital bed, told Mr Modi that he opened the cockpit door while he was still being attacked on the floor.

Captain Smit Machchhar has worked in the airline industry for more than a decade, according to his LinkedIn profile. (Supplied: Israel Foreign Ministry)

"I had so many wounds. I had fallen down," he said from the hospital, his head bandaged and tubes in his nose, before breaking down as he recalled the attack in a nearly 10-minute-long video released by the prime minister's office on Friday, local time.

"I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn't get up … then passengers would lose their lives," he told Mr Modi.

"I knew that the aircraft was going down … I had fallen to the ground. I told myself that the door is right there, just open it. I managed to do it and people entered."

Mr Machchhar was stabbed by his co-pilot in an alleged attempt to crash the flydubai plane on Wednesday.

The jet plunged nearly 14,000 feet (4,267 metres) in less than 30 seconds in the incident.

The flight bound for Tel Aviv was carrying 174 people and was forced to divert to Tabuk in north-western Saudi Arabia for an emergency landing.

Mr Machchhar said that during those difficult moments, he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a Hindu devotional hymn dedicated to Lord Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.

"Lord Hanuman gave me courage," he told Mr Modi.

Co-pilot attempted to crash plane from Dubai to Tel Aviv, Netanyahu says The plane was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

United Arab Emirates presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said the incident was a "terrorist act", as he praised the courage of the captain attacked by his co-pilot.

Mr Gargash said on X that Mr Machchhar was a "true hero" and deserved "every appreciation, for in confronting a serious terrorist act and a potential disaster, he embodied the true meaning of courage and responsibility".

Mr Machchhar, who is married and has two children, has worked for flydubai for about four years, according to his LinkedIn profile.

Before joining the airline, he spent 11 years with SpiceJet, an Indian low-cost carrier, where he served as a senior commander and line training captain.

He logged more than 9,750 flying hours with SpiceJet.

Israel's flag carrier El Al earlier announced repatriation flights from Dubai had been cancelled as Emirati authorities had not given landing permission for the two special flights that were announced late Thursday, local time.

ABC/AP/REUTERS

World.title: Former Liberal politician Bruce Baird dies aged 84
World.content:
Former Liberal politician Bruce Baird has died aged 84.

Mr Baird was father to former New South Wales premier Mike Baird, journalist Julia Baird and son Steve.

In a post on social media, Ms Baird said he died suddenly on Friday morning, and the family was still in shock.

"It feels like an eclipse, when your father dies. Everything suddenly black, then sore eyes and the world cast in another kind of light," she wrote.

She described him as a character, a fit, extroverted man, who was full of life, who loved ocean swimming, had lots of friends and was "fond of a gossip and a yarn".

"He taught the three of his kids to be bold, to step with certainty and to dream big, 'You go for it', he'd say.

"He was married to Judith, his first girlfriend and great love, for more than half a century."

She added that outside of politics, he was a "bon vivant who loved parties — all and any parties — champagne, airport lounges and dodgy jokes".

The NSW Liberal Party paid tribute to Mr Baird in a statement.

"Bruce was a party stalwart and a greatly respected politician, serving the people of NSW in the state and federal parliaments," a spokesperson said.

"We offer our deepest condolences on behalf of all members to his family at this difficult time."

While he was the NSW minister for Transport, Roads and Tourism, Mr Baird played a key role in securing the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney.

Road to politics

Political figures have paid tribute to Baird and his contribution to Australia. (AAP: Tracey Nearmy)

Speaking on a podcast in 2024, when asked what made him enter politics, he attributed it to the Vietnam War and a talk by an American priest.

"In my teenage years I loved to party, and I loved to surf. I went to uni and not much more was happening," he said at the time.

"The Vietnam War made me think about issues, political issues and later, when I was in New York, I had a consul general there when I was Australian trade commissioner who suggested to me that I should think about going into politics.

"Later, I heard a talk by an American Episcopalian priest on 'God has a plan for your life', and it was about committing the talents that we have to him and just see what happens. And it wasn't that long after that that I was pre-selected for a seat in Northcote in NSW politics and things went from there."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Australia had lost "a real gentleman and a true parliamentarian".

"Bruce had the uncommon distinction of serving his nation as a Liberal member at both the state and federal level," he said in a statement.

"In whichever role he served, whether it was in Parliament or leading bodies including the Tourism and Transport Forum and the Refugee Resettlement Advisory Council, he served with distinction, and he served with principle and unwavering humanity.

"Tellingly, the respect and admiration for Bruce knew no political boundaries. Our hearts go out to his adored children Julia, Steve and Mike."

'A mentor and a friend'

After a career in state politics, Mr Baird went on to represent the federal seat of Cook in the Sutherland Shire in NSW from 1998 to 2007.

The seat was later won by former prime minister Scott Morrison.

In a statement, Mr Morrison described Mr Baird as a "giant, a mentor and a friend".

"Bruce had a tremendous sense of humour and a wonderful heart," he said in the statement.

"He was a magnificent witness and role model, who showed the way to serve as a Christian in politics.

"Bruce leaves behind a rich legacy in his family, who he loved and was so proud of, speaking constantly about all of them any chance he could, as well as all those he encouraged and supported, which I was privileged to have been one."

NSW Liberal leader Kellie Sloane said Mr Baird's contribution to NSW and Australia was "extraordinary".

"Throughout his public life, Bruce was driven by a strong sense of service, conviction, and compassion, earning the trust and respect of people regardless of their political affiliation," she said in a statement.

"Ever jovial and encouraging, Bruce was often the life of the party."

The ABC's Global Affairs Editor and former press gallery member, Laura Tingle, described Mr Baird as one of the "world's most decent human beings".

"One of the rare politicians who I regarded as a friend, along with his beloved wife Judy," she said.

In referencing his time in federal politics, Tingle added, he was one of a small group of traditional "small L" Liberals to last into the Howard government.

"That meant he represented a tradition of economic conservatism, but socially moderate policies in a party which had become increasingly hardline on social issues from welfare to immigration," she said.

"Along with Petro Georgiou, Russell Broadbent and Judi Moylan, he defied and challenged John Howard's push for the detention of asylum seekers and to send all asylum seekers arriving in Australia by boat offshore for processing."

Mr Baird's contribution to NSW and Australian has been described as "extraordinary". (AAP: Alan Porritt)

In 2008, he was appointed as the chair of the Refugee Resettlement Advisory Council by the Rudd Labor government.

Former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull said Mr Baird was "a genuine liberal, motivated by love, not hate”.

"He was never dull and had a mischievous sense of humour," he said.

"He was a courageous politician who, in federal parliament, often in league with Petro Georgiou, put his own compassionate principles ahead of personal advancement."

Mr Baird retired from politics before the 2007 general election, when he expressed his disappointment that he was never made a minister in the Howard Liberal government.

"I have no regrets, and in politics you have to learn to roll with the punches," he said at the time.

Mr Baird was appointed a Member of the Order of Australia in 2010.

World.title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil to combat soaring fuel prices
World.content:
The Group of Seven industrial nations have agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel after the fuel recently hit record high prices in the United States, where President Donald Trump said the diesel release would happen “immediately”.

Trump and his Republican Party face pressure to address surging prices ahead of November’s midterm elections. Trump announced the action on Friday (US time) on social media, saying, “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately.”

French President Emmanuel Macron and US President Donald Trump, pictured at the G7 summit in June, spoke on the phone before the meeting was convened. Getty

The president faces lagging approval ratings as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased US prices for oil and other goods.

Gas prices in the US and abroad have soared during the eight-month-long war, a cost Trump has repeatedly said is worth it for making sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons. Trump has insisted prices will come down after the war, though there’s no end in sight.

World.title: AFLW round eight: Prespakis, Morrison grow partnership as Cats too good for Tigers; Mystery surrounds Dees skipper’s neck injury
World.content:
Georgie Prespakis and Nina Morrison set them up then Chloe Scheer kicked them home as Geelong bounced back from a scrappy first half to comfortably beat Richmond by 34 points at Ikon Park on Friday night.

World.title: In search of the Herald’s voices of the future
World.content:
NationalNSWNote From The Editor In search of the Herald’s voices of the future Jordan Baker October 2, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Memories can be slippery, particularly as you get older. Some things linger, many more fade, and there appears to be no rhyme or reason to what sticks and what disappears. When I think back to the lessons from my journalism traineeship, some are cemented in my cerebral cortex. When you leave a voice message, always repeat your number in case they don’t get it all down the first time (still handy advice, even in this era of text). Use “more than” rather than “over” when talking about quantities. And never forget the “rule of three” (use three examples, as per this paragraph), which gives writing a stronger cadence. Other lessons from that time have been built on and developed – and some forgotten, probably to my detriment – but that early training laid the foundation for everything I’ve done since, and I could not be more grateful for it. The Herald’s class of ’24 trainees, from left: Daniel Lo Surdo, Kayla Olaya, Nick Newling, Frances Howe, Penry Buckley and Cindy (Xunzhi) Yin. Louise Kennerley This week, the Herald put out a call for smart, curious, talented aspiring journalists to join our 2027 trainee program. The announcement generated great excitement here, because we love the enthusiasm and talent trainees bring to the newsroom, and we love watching them grow as journalists.



I remember when Natassia Chrysanthos joined the newsroom in the trainee class of 2018. I knew she’d flourish, not only because she was a strong writer with a great news instinct, but because she was empathetic and curious, and enjoyed interacting with people. Reporters must be able to pick up the phone, rather than text; they need to be able to have real-life conversations – to listen, ask questions and empathise. Natassia did this from day one. Natassia Chrysanthos will be the Herald’s next South-East Asia correspondent. Wolter Peeters This week, the we announced that Natassia would be the Herald’s next South-East Asia correspondent. She will head to Jakarta early next year. She believes the traineeship was crucial to her development as a journalist. “Your writing gets cleaner, your questions get sharper, your contact list expands, your confidence builds,” she told me. Traineeships are a great way to learn, but they’re also great fun. “Some nights were spent at the Sydney Theatre Company after interviewing the country’s best playwrights, others learning the rules of AFL from the media box at Blacktown Stadium while profiling the league’s female players,” Natassia says. “I covered my first HSC as a cadet, driving to schools across the city and sharing students’ pre-exam jitters, before becoming an education reporter. One month after ending the program, we were racing down the Princes Highway to cover the Black Summer bushfires.” Michael Koziol was a trainee in the class of 2014; now, he’s the Herald’s North America correspondent. He recalled his trainee experience en route to Mexico this week, where he covered the tragic story of two Australian brothers who were murdered in Baja California during a surfing trip.





Applications are open now. Sharp, curious individuals with exceptional writing skills, strong news judgement and a passion for Herald journalism are invited to apply. Applications will be open until just before midnight on Sunday, October 18, and the traineeships will begin in February next year. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil to combat soaring fuel prices
World.content:
The Group of Seven industrial nations have agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel after the fuel recently hit record high prices in the United States, where President Donald Trump said the diesel release would happen “immediately”.

Trump and his Republican Party face pressure to address surging prices ahead of November’s midterm elections. Trump announced the action on Friday (US time) on social media, saying, “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately.”

French President Emmanuel Macron and US President Donald Trump, pictured at the G7 summit in June, spoke on the phone before the meeting was convened. Getty

The president faces lagging approval ratings as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased US prices for oil and other goods.

Gas prices in the US and abroad have soared during the eight-month-long war, a cost Trump has repeatedly said is worth it for making sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons. Trump has insisted prices will come down after the war, though there’s no end in sight.

World.title: ‘The club is innocent’: Manchester City appeal against Premier League ‘sham’ contracts ruling
World.content:
SportSoccerPremier League ‘The club is innocent’: Manchester City appeal against Premier League ‘sham’ contracts ruling Lori Ewing October 2, 2026 — 11:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Premier League with 4K on Stan Sport. Every match, live & on demand. Stream now

Manchester City have filed an appeal against an independent commission ruling that found the club guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, seeking to overturn the verdict and avoid potentially severe sanctions. The league said on Tuesday that ​City had used “sham” commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than £900 million ($1.7 billion) over nearly a decade. Manchester City’s Etihad stadium. AP Photo/Jon Super City were found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the league’s financial rules over nine seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as three out of four charges concerning failures to cooperate with the investigation. The club, who had until the end of the day on Friday to appeal, has denied wrongdoing throughout the process.



With potential sanctions including heavy fines, points deductions and other sporting penalties, and with relegation or the removal of titles also discussed as possible outcomes, the case could have consequences across the league. “Manchester City Football Club can confirm that at 7pm on Thursday 1st October 2026 the Club lodged its comprehensive Appeal against the opinion of the Premier League Commission, in relation to the Premier League disciplinary matter,” the club said in a statement. Related Article Premier League Manchester City found guilty in biggest scandal in Premier League history “The Club’s firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe. “The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.”



The appeal will be heard by an independent three-member board appointed by the chair of the league’s judicial panel. “The club lodged the appeal to the Chair of the Judicial Panel,” the league said in a statement. “The independent Appeal Board hearing will remain private and confidential until publication of the outcome is permitted.” A billboard in Manchester after City had been found guilty of all charges. Getty Images The Premier League’s new fast-track rules state that an appeal hearing should be held within 12 weeks of an appeal being lodged, with a decision due within 30 days of the hearing concluding. Some legal commentators expect City to argue that those rules did not exist when the club were originally charged in February 2023.



The appeal will take place in private, as did the original hearings. The board will review the commission’s decision, but will not conduct a full rehearing of the case. The board can dismiss the appeal, allow it, refer the case back to the commission for further consideration or alter any sanction or compensation order imposed. A decision by the appeal board is final and cannot be challenged further except in limited circumstances that permit a subsequent arbitration process. City can also separately appeal against any sanctions. It remains unclear whether sanctions will be announced before the appeal is heard, and whether they would take effect immediately.



A league representative told Reuters they could not discuss the process for confidentiality reasons. Related Article Manchester City Manchester City found guilty of 114 financial charges in seismic Premier League ruling While the fate of the case remains unresolved, the season will continue, with leaders City looking for their sixth straight league win when they visit Liverpool on October 11. In its first public statement since the commission’s findings were announced, the Football Association (FA) said on Friday it was closely monitoring the case. “The Independent Commission’s decision has significant implications for the integrity of the game,” the FA said in a statement.



“We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate.” The repercussions facing City could extend beyond football. On Thursday, the chair of parliament’s Treasury Committee Meg Hillier asked Britain’s tax authority ​HMRC what action it was taking in response to the commission’s findings. Hillier said she had written to HMRC Permanent Secretary JP Marks following the publication on Tuesday of the independent commission ruling that the club had committed “well over 100 individual breaches ​of the Premier League Rules across the course of many seasons”. Some sports lawyers have predicted years of further litigation as rival clubs, players and agents assess whether they may have grounds to pursue compensation claims connected to the case.

Georgie Prespakis and Nina Morrison set them up then Chloe Scheer kicked them home as Geelong bounced back from a scrappy first half to comfortably beat Richmond by 34 points at Ikon Park on Friday night.

World.title: A healthy environment is a healthy nation
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters A healthy environment is a healthy nation October 2, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. As one involved in their formation, I must say that the Australian Greens were not started to supplant a party of the left, as the new leader has stated (″⁣New Greens leader sends a shot across the bow of Labor″⁣, 1/10). The original concept was to move from the destructive narrow-minded left-right economically based spectrum of politics ie, socialists v capitalists. The idea was to replace this decrepit self-serving notion with one based fundamentally on a healthy environment. Without environmental protection and nature conservation as a foundation principle, society was perceived, as the evidence of the past 50 years has shown, to be spiralling into economic and social chaos. Unfortunately, the election of yet another NSW-based leader in love with politics rather than outcomes means that many of us electors are left with voting at the next election for the least worst party. What a sorry outcome for anyone deeply concerned about the natural environment in Australia – the fundamental basis for a healthy, fair and just society.

Geoff Wescott, Northcote Die may already be cast for next election

Waleed Aly is surely correct when he identifies the potential for a Greens resurgence under new leader David Shoebridge (Comment, 2/10). But the key electoral movers for 2028 are already locked in. A combined One Nation/Coalition vote has more potential to replace Labor, based purely on the numbers. Our preferential system creates immense advantages to parties that preference each other, and at present the biggest bloc of votes sits on the right. It’s true that Greens voters generally follow the card, meaning their votes eventually find their way to Labor. But we’ve never had a situation where the Liberal vote is going to flow, en masse, to another party, due to its woeful primary position. Liberal voters, like Greens voters, follow the card ensuring a swag of seats can fall to One Nation. This doesn’t require a formal preference deal, but does anyone believe that the Coalition will preference Labor over One Nation? I think not.

Greg Gardiner, Brunswick The new idea is the new radicalism

Now is the time for a leader to inspire us with a vision of a better Australia. Their speeches will be about how to re-energise the economy and to ameliorate climate change. It will not be about bagging the other parties. One wonders whether someone like David Shoebridge is such a person. His opening salvo is about radicalism. His burden is to defeat the perception that the past Greens history under Adam Bandt was about seeking the perfect over the good. In devising policies to increase Australia’s productivity, which is much needed, and to show leadership on dealing with climate change, perhaps we need a bigger vision. This may involve working with parties because it is doubtful any one party will have an outright majority. Concentration on original and new ideas is the true radicalism.

Jan Marshall, Brighton



THE FORUM The cost of business

I was left scratching my head recently after hearing a retailer complain about the negative impact of removing card surcharges. He argued that people paying cash would now be subsidising card users, who would no longer pay the typical 1.6 per cent fee. This overlooks a few important points. First, it was the banks and financial institutions that steered us away from cash, closing branches and removing ATMs. Second, legitimate dealings in cash are not cost-free. There are labour and other costs involved in counting, sorting, bagging, securing and transporting cash to an ever-diminishing number of deposit facilities, where it must then be processed again and credited to the merchant’s account. Cards and computers are convenient, but they reduce many of the costs and inconveniences associated with handling cash. People should not have to pay an additional fee simply for paying for a product or service. The cost of accepting payment, by whatever reasonable means, is simply part of the cost of doing business and should be reflected in the price. Profit takes care of the rest.

David Fox, Beaumaris Transport priorities

My husband recently had to take the airport bus from Southern Cross to Tullamarine and was very impressed. A bus left every 10 minutes and they all seemed to be full. It was easy to catch a train to Southern Cross and connect with the bus. We fail to see how a very expensive train line to the airport is going to improve on this experience. Surely there are far more important public transport projects that are needed in our outer suburban areas?

Anne Maki, Alphington E-bike risks

My sympathy to Margaret Throsby (″⁣Throsby faces new injuries after e-bike collision″⁣, 2/10). As a now elderly pedestrian, I’m far more concerned about e-bikes and scooters than I am about cars for the risk to my safety. A long time ago, to ride my slower and noisier moped in London, I had to be at least 17, have a licence, the moped had to be registered with a number plate, and I had insurance.

It’s not unreasonable to require the same for these electric projectiles.

Adam Thomson, Collingwood A botched killing

If the botched execution attempt of Christa Pike in the US doesn’t have us comprehend what a grisly practice state-sanctioned murder is, nothing will.

John Rawson, Mernda



Ideas of entitlement

And I thought I was the only one fed up with noisy children disrupting the quiet of a public library (Letters, 1/10). Yes, they’re just being children, but their behaviour is the responsibility of the parent. The problem is another example of people believing they’re ″⁣entitled″⁣. They’re entitled to let their children ″⁣just be children″⁣ in a library. Dog owners are entitled to leave their dogs tied up outside the supermarket where they can ″⁣just be a dog″⁣, barking intrusively.

Brian Thorpe, Northcote Climate blind spot

Recent Treasury modelling of the cost of no further action on net zero found that Australia’s GDP could be 14 per cent lower by 2050, equivalent to an estimated $6.8 trillion reduction in GDP over the next 25 years. Yet the Coalition wants to scrap net zero.

We also learn it wants to scrap the trade deal with Europe because it could ″⁣lock Australia into legally binding action on climate change″⁣ (″⁣European envoy warns of $10 billion hit if trade deal fails″⁣, 2/10). Even former Coalition finance minister Mathias Cormann, now in his second term as Secretary-General of the OECD, warns against scrapping the deal. It seems the self-labelled best economic managers still have a blind spot when it comes to climate.

Ray Peck, Hawthorn Out of control

I welcome columnist Cherie Gilmour’s timely reminder to “Beware lifestyle creep turning little luxuries into staples″⁣ (30/9). This comfort or ″⁣lifestyle creep″⁣ quietly emerges with oat lattes,Uber eats and streaming services as an increasing number of small comforts ″⁣now feel like entitlements″⁣. Perhaps like governments, we barely notice that ″⁣our discretionary spending had gotten out of control″⁣?

Kevin Burke, Sandringham Recognising reality

Josh Burns accuses David Shoebridge of causing social division between Australian Jews because he acknowledges that many fervently support Israel, in spite of its genocidal actions in Gaza, while others strongly oppose its policies. That is not causing division, or being prejudiced, it is recognising reality when it stares you in the face. The government’s reluctance to sanction Israel for war crimes and to continue sitting on the fence while international law is continually flouted, does not help matters. Shoebridge has the courage of his convictions, would that Anthony Albanese had.

Lorel Thomas, Blackburn Why no Green wave?

Like Waleed Aly, I have been trying to understand why there has not been a Green wave in Australia (Comment, 2/10). It may be that the Greens receive relatively little media attention. In an era of growing distrust of institutions, it may also be that voters perceive the Greens to be part of the political establishment.

Yet the Greens could hardly be more different from the major parties. Uninfluenced by corporate lobbyists, they consistently argue that public policy should put people ahead of large multinationals. Whether on housing, healthcare, inequality or climate action, they seek to make Australia fairer and more sustainable for all.

Perhaps the real question is not why there hasn’t been a Green wave, but why so many Australians have overlooked the party most committed to confronting the challenges ahead.

Amy Hiller, Kew



Services and spending

Calls for the government to cut spending to control inflation are not new, but there seems to be a public disconnect between government spending and services. Necessary cuts to the NDIS to control spending were met with protest. Cuts to veterans’ access to allied health had to be reversed. Removal of tax breaks for investors was subject to a concerted campaign of misinformation.

Instead of spending cuts, people want more government spending – higher pay (deserved) for nurses, teachers, doctors, more police, more public transport, more hospitals, better schools etc. There are areas in which I think the government can cut spending – stop funding rich private schools with their multi-million-dollar sports centres being one – but many would disagree with me.

Higher taxes on companies and extremely wealthy individuals may take some heat out of the economy if banked, not spent, but the resulting protests would be vicious.

The arithmetical impossibility of cutting spending and at the same time maintaining or increasing services is rarely recognised.

Louise Kloot, Doncaster Rise of the machine

As I read of our fears of AI, I am reminded of The Sorcerer’s Apprentice, whose moral is “never invoke powers or tools that you do not fully understand or cannot control”. That it was written in the 2nd centur, reminds us that the weakness in the AI revolution is not the technology, but humans who have changed very little since Lucian’s time. For Donald Trump to suggest that we should now refer to the technology as super intelligence rather than artificial intelligence, is implying that it is no longer a tool, but already its own entity.

Kevan Porter, Alphington Perambulation shock

Your correspondent (Letters, 2/10) writes about prams left outside shops in England. We all did it, the prams were big, beautiful, bulky and impossible to get into or out of shops. As a new (very tired) mother, I once forgot my baby in the pram and walked away, until I almost had a heart attack and went back to get her. I still shudder at the memory.

Myra Fisher, Brighton East Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING



Artificial intelligence

Is Donald Trump calling himself a very stable genius an indication of the presence of artificial intelligence?

Gerry Lonergan, Reservoir Does AI have the potential to cause more chaos than Donald Trump?

Peter Carlin, Frankston South Perhaps we have forgotten Asimov’s three laws of robotics. A robot cannot injure a human or allow one to come to harm through inaction. A robot must obey human orders unless they conflict with the First Law. A robot must protect its own existence, provided it doesn’t conflict with the first two laws. He wrote them in 1942.

Lesley Taskis, Kingsbury Is there any AI programmed to give the greatest good to the greatest number of people?

Chonyi Taylor, Inverloch Furthermore

Your correspondent (Letters, 1/10) was lucky, my bank manager rang me and said mine was going to 19.5 per cent!

Peter Thomas, Barwon Heads



China’s push for electrification looks stronger than ever as Donald Trump sinks into a swamp of his own making.

Paul Chivers, Box Hill North What about the staff of the facilities and airlines at Tullamarine? A train line would help provide public transport to their work. It’s not just about going on a holiday.

Ruth Berkowitz, Kew East Re annoying kids and dogs (Letters, 1/10), why have them?

Margaret Skeen, Ocean Grove Is Greens leader David Shoebridge calling out genocide in Gaza antisemitic?

Hans Paas, Castlemaine Did the Greens just clone Adam Bandt? Perhaps leadership is also part of their recycling policy.

Don Phillips, Fitzroy Finally

I have a new idea (Letters, 30/9). Put the letters on the front page; they’re enlightening, sometimes amusing and food for thought. Add the brilliant cartoons and we’ve intellectual stimulation for the day.

Jane Ross, San Remo

World.title: Magnitude 5.3 earthquake strikes 25km east of New Plymouth
World.content:
A magnitude 5.3 earthquake has struck the North Island this morning, waking thousands of New Zealanders.

GeoNet reported the quake, which struck at 2.57am, was 25 kilometres east of New Plymouth and at a depth of 11km.

More than 7000 people reported feeling the quake, with about 4000 feeling moderate to strong shaking.

Fire and Emergency said it had not received any callouts relating to the tremor.
