RNZ listeners have described how it felt at their homes in various parts of the country.

Richard said there was strong shaking at his home in central New Plymouth: "Haven't felt one like that for a long time. Was getting ready to drop, cover and hold. No damage but internet was offline for 15-20 mins."

Also in Ngamotu/New Plymouth, Rob said it was "a huge shock".

"A few big thumps (loud bangs, complaints from the building) and then gentle shaking as it died away. That's the biggest quake I've felt in ages."

A listener based in Kaimata, a small rural settlement near the quake's epicentre, said pictures and pot plants fell and smashed at their home.

Meanwhile, a couple of Golden Bay listeners reported "light shaking" and "a gentle sway".

In Raetihi, in the Manawatū-Whanganui region, Tina reported a small shake, adding that it was great to get an alert on her phone before the quake began.

World.title: Tip Top recalls batch of Jelly Tip ice creams
World.content:
Tip Top is recalling a batch of its Jelly Tip ice creams due to the possible presence of a bacteria which can cause severe gastrointestinal illness.

The recalled ice creams were sold in a six-pack cardboard box and had a best-before date of 30 September, 2028.

Food Safety deputy director-general Vincent Arbuckle said the product, sold at Woolworths supermarkets in the North Island, had been removed from shelves.

"The concern with these products is that they could contain the bacteria Bacillus cereus, which can cause severe gastrointestinal illness," he said

"They should not be eaten. You can return them to the place of purchase for a refund. If that's not possible, throw them out."

Bacillus cereus in milk products usually causes diarrhoea, with symptoms typically appearing one to six hours after eating the contaminated food. Most people recover within a day.

Arbuckle said the agency hadn't received any reports of people getting sick.

World.title: Christopher Luxon walks back 'bizarre claim' about the Greens
World.content:
Christopher Luxon has walked back claims made by one of his ministers about the Greens, before then suggesting - wrongly - that they originated from the media.

Trade Minister Todd McClay, on Wednesday, accused the Green Party of "joining with foreign actors to attack New Zealand" in regards to a climate change complaint lodged with the European Commission.

The Greens quickly denied any involvement and McClay provided no evidence.

Asked for evidence on Friday, Luxon put the responsibility back on reporters to investigate whether the Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick had any involvement.

"That'd be up for you guys to accertain whether she has or hasn't," he said.

Luxon then suggested that the media had first raised the possibility of Swarbrick's involvement.

"I'm just saying that's not appropriate if that's the case. But equally, I'm sure she hasn't done that."

Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick. RNZ / Nick Monro

Told that the Green Party had not been involved, Luxon replied: "Great, great. That's good to hear. That's good that you've bottomed that out. Well done, well done... Good job."

In a statement, Swarbrick said McClay had provided "zero evidence" to support his "bizarre claim". She said Luxon's government was blaming everybody else for the consequences of its policy to "shred climate action".

"The worst absurdity of all of this is that the most fired up the government has got on climate action is trying to cover their tracks by attacking everyone else, instead of doing the responsible thing."

RNZ has asked McClay's office for evidence for his claim.

Trade Minister Todd McClay. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Luxon said he was not worried about the international complaint because New Zealand upheld its free trade obligations.

"It's very disingenuous to suggest otherwise. We take that incredibly seriously. We are a free trading nation. We respect our FTA agreements and what's in them, and we'll continue to do so.

"When any other country gets to 96.3 percent renewable electricity, then you might want to throw some stones at us.

"But until then, I'm not that interested in what Laura Clarke or anybody else says, frankly."

World.title: One person dead after falling from cliff at popular Coromandel beach
World.content:
One person has died after an incident at Cooks Beach on Friday afternoon.

Emergency services were called to Purangi Road about 5.50pm after a report that someone had fallen from a cliff.

In a post on social media, Cooks Beach Volunteer Fire Brigade said they immediately started medical treatment when they arrived.

"Our combined Cooks and Hahei crews worked extremely hard in very difficult and dangerous conditions, with ambulance crews, westpac and Police.

"Unfortunately, the person is deceased and our thoughts go out to the family," chief fire officer Brayden Jack said

A witness saw a rescue helicopter drop off a crewmember before returning 10 minutes later to airlift a stretcher from the base of Shakespeare Cliff.

St John had sent two local first response units, a helicopter, and a manager to the beach.

Cordons remain in place while emergency services personnel work at the scene.

The death will be referred to the Coroner.

World.title: Review into OmniHealth clinics launched after staff resignations
World.content:
The Primary Health Organisation (PHO) says a review into OmniHealth clinic services is being launched after seven staff resigned from Pahīatua Medical Centre.

The staff, who included a doctor and nurses, resigned in September claiming overwhelming workloads in a ballooning safety crisis.

OmniHealth is the parent company behind 16 medical centres and owns Tararua Health Group. It also provides services at Dannevirke Community Hospital, but it's currently on notice after a spot audit found the hospital was unsafe for patients due to staff shortages.

Audio player for " Sixteen OmniHealth clinics under review " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/health/1685958%2Freview-into-omnihealth-clinics-launched-after-staff-resignations

Sixteen OmniHealth clinics under review Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

There's currently a 30-day freeze on any patient admissions, and Omni has a deadline to get more staff.

PHO chief executive Tony Wai told Checkpoint the a review was being done to ensure the concerns from Pahīatua Medical Centre were not "existing in other areas".

"I know there's been some staffing shortages which have been announced, but we recognise as well that like other clinics around the country, there are a number of staffing shortages, but we took prudent measures now to just do a review."

"At a minimum service level, we do see that they have to be open, they have to be seeing patients, they have to see patients within a certain timeframe, they have to maintain certain standards actually in there."

The staff that have resigned from Pahīatua Medical Centre have said they would not return unless OmniHealth was out of the picture.

Wai said OmniHealth was "taking some steps at the moment and there are other parties involved".

"It's not my role to say what will happen with those parties and what they will look to do. But we recognise that our role is to ensure that the clinic is safe for the meantime and that the changes are actually made to continue to issue on."

Wai said the review is to be done by a PHO team and will look at the Omni Health clinics within the PHO network.

He also acknowledged that OmniHealth chief executive Mark Wills was on the PHO board but said they had taken steps to ensure Wills was not part of any conversations that relate to the review.

"He is stood down from those matters as it relates to anything in relation to Omni or in relation to Tararua Health Group.

"We have asked him and each of the clinics that he's involved in to get the information back. So he is aware that the review's there and he's in no way influencing that part of it."

Once the information is received an internal assessment would take place but Wai said the review would likely not be publicised.

"Largely because this is about an assurance level for us and the individual providers."

World.title: 'Shedding tears for you': Tributes to late MP Adrian Rurawhe at tangi in Whanganui
World.content:
Audio player for " Some MPs pause campaigning to attend former Speaker's funeral " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics/1686307%2Fshedding-tears-for-you-tributes-to-late-mp-adrian-rurawhe-at-tangi-in-whanganui

Some MPs pause campaigning to attend former Speaker's funeral Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Politicians, whānau and iwi leaders have come together to pay their respects to former Labour MP and Speaker of the House Adrian Rurawhe.

Gathering for his tangi at Whangaehu Marae in Whanganui on Friday afternoon, a 100-strong delegation of political leaders from across the motu remembered Rurawhe as a "huge leader within Parliament", who conducted himself with "quiet resolve and real dignity".

Rurawhe's death was confirmed by his family on Wednesday.

Iwi leaders and Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po were welcomed to the marae first, followed by the political delegation led by Speaker Gerry Brownlee.

That delegation also included Labour leader Chris Hipkins, deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni and Māori caucus chair Willie Jackson. Te Pūoho Katene, who is contesting Te Tai Hauāuru - the seat Rurawhe held - also attended.

Shane Jones and Jenny Marcroft represented New Zealand First, Rawiri Waititi and John Tamihere attended on behalf of Te Pāti Māori, and Todd Stephenson attended on behalf of ACT.

Waititi speaks at the tangi. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

Former MPs Trevor Mallard, who Rurawhe succeeded as speaker, as well as Nanaia Mahuta and Poto Williams attended.

Following kōrero in te reo Māori, politicians from both sides of the House paid tribute to Rurawhe.

Hipkins said Rurawhe had not told Labour he was ill, because "he didn't want to get in the way".

"That's made the shock that much harder for many of our team," Hipkins said.

Brownlee paid tribute to Rurawhe as a speaker with "quite a different approach".

Brownlee told the tangi that Rurawhe had left a strong legacy. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

"He was able to use his gentle persona to terrify people," he joked.

"Adrian, your legacy is a strong one."

Jackson said he was a "quiet achiever" whose strength was underrated.

"He had lovely skills, in terms being calm and cool. But his big strength was he could... do the business. I mean, he kicked me out of the House, and that was one of the biggest shocks I got from him. I thought, 'what the heck's happened here?'"

Adrian Rurawhe quit politics earlier this year. VNP / Phil Smith

Jackson said Rurawhe was "almost universally" rated or loved across the House.

"He'd always stand his ground, if he knew he was right. He was terrific, incredibly underrated, undervalued at times. But to become the Speaker of the House, and then to become a great Speaker of the House, even better."

Katene said the party was searching for who would follow in Rurawhe's footsteps.

"Tēnei tō Pāti Reipa e tangi hotuhotu ana mōu," Katene said.

"Here is your party, the Labour Party, shedding tears for you."

Davidson attends Rurawhe's tangi on Friday. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

Green MP and Assistant Speaker Teanau Tuiono recalled that Rurawhe had ejected Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson from the House twice.

"Nōku anō te hē engari nōku te hōnore," Davidson said.

World.title: Going for gold: World panning championship takes over Cromwell
World.content:
Audio player for " Dozens of gold prospectors flock to Otago for world champs " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/regions/1686301%2Fgoing-for-gold-world-panning-championship-takes-over-cromwell

Dozens of gold prospectors flock to Otago for world champs Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

More than 150 high-speed prospectors have converged on Central Otago to prove their weight in gold.

The 49th annual World Gold Panning Championship is being held at Cromwell Racecourse, with competitors putting a centuries-old goldfields skill to the test.

Panners from more than 20 countries have been facing off over troughs of water and buckets of gravel, racing to extract minuscule flakes as accurately as possible.

Event coordinator Terry Davis said international visitors had embraced everything on offer, from fierce competition to warm spring weather and tours of local mining history.

An immense amount of work had gone into hosting the event, not least sourcing 20 tonnes of gravel and building water troughs that adhered to strict World Gold Panning Association codes, he said.

New Zealand's Sally Beverley competes in the panning with an unusual object event using a pāua shell. Katie Todd/RNZ

"It was a huge logistical nightmare getting it all together. There were a lot of things had to come together and they did come together," he said.

Event organiser and New Zealand competitor Megan Ide said the tournament had attracted top-tier international talent.

"It's a very high calibre of competitors. We've got a panner here, Ken Carlson, who actually designed the speed pan. I had a chat to him yesterday to get a few tips off him. He's won 39 championship medals in his panning career," she said.

The New Zealand competitors were putting on a powerful performance, Ide said.

"We've managed to qualify for quite a few semi-finals and finals, so the Kiwi contingent is holding their own."

A judge inspecting a competitor's vial of gold flakes at the World Gold Panning Championship. Katie Todd/RNZ

Davis said the week's festivities had included an opening parade, movie night and markets, and would finish with a hoedown.

Many of the competitors were camping at the racecourse, where there had also been novelty competitions such as "panning with an unusual object" - a pāua shell, he said.

Canadian competitor Jonathan Garner, who was attending his fifth world championship, said the event was as much about the global community as it was about panning.

"It's a good way to see the world and you have friends everywhere you go," he said.

"This year has been awesome. This is a little smaller and so it's given me a chance to meet many of these people who I've met before but get to know them on a more intimate basis."

World Gold Panning Association (WGA) president Sanjay Singh praised the execution of the New Zealand event.

World Gold Panning Association president Sanjay Singh travelled to Cromwell as part of the South African contingent. Katie Todd/RNZ

"From the proceedings, the processes and managing of the rules of the WGA, I can say the competition will get a tick from the rules committee," he said.

Singh, who travelled to the competition as part of a 19-person South African delegation, said he had been marvelling at the Kiwi hospitality.

"The reception, from the time we got to the airport up to now, has been phenomenal. People ask me which is the best part for me - the best part besides the competition is my interaction with New Zealand people."

The championship was due to conclude on Saturday with the finals and an afternoon medal ceremony.

World.title: Christchurch residents told to rely on instincts not sirens for tsunami evacuation
World.content:
Audio player for " Christchurch tsunami sirens to be removed " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/regions/1686212%2Fchristchurch-residents-told-to-rely-on-instincts-not-sirens-for-tsunami-evacuation

Christchurch tsunami sirens to be removed Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

New Brighton beach-goers have expressed concerns about Christchurch City Council moves to remove tsunami sirens but emergency managers say people must rely on their instincts rather than waiting for someone else to sound the alarm.

From 6 October Canterbury's city and district councils will move from the current three tsunami evacuation zones - red, orange and yellow - to a single blue tsunami evacuation zone.

The 45 sirens between Brooklands and Taylors Mistake will also be removed, with the city council instead urging people to rely on their own judgement in an emergency, and mobile phone alerts.

New Brighton's beach and playground was busy with people enjoying the warm spring weather on Friday but none of the dozen people spoken to by RNZ knew that the sirens were being removed and most did not understand the rationale.

Carol Williams, who works in New Brighton and lives nearby, said she was particularly concerned for the elderly and people who did not have a cellphones.

"I don't think its right. We have a large population down here of elderly people who might not have cell phones and they won't get their emergency alerts. Sirens need to stay," she said.

New Brighton visitor Pauline King shared Williams' concerns.

Nicole Hibbs and Pauline King often visit New Brighton, but had heard nothing about the tsunami sirens being removed. Pauline says she thinks they are important for anyone who doesn't have a cell phone. Rachel Graham/RNZ

"I don't think its a good idea because of the old people. The old people really need to hear the sirens. I think the sirens should go to let people know," King said.

Sam, who lives near the beach in North Canterbury, said she did not know whether to evacuate during the 2016 Kaikoura earthquake.

"I was back in bed and it wasn't until I heard the sirens I thought, 'oh we need to go', and at that point we also had people knocking on our doors. I'd probably urge them to keep it."

Christchurch City Council emergency manager Brenden Winder said an independent review of tsunami alert methods showed that sirens were not the best option.

"The sirens are being removed because they are unreliable. They rely on power, they are no good in the wind and people don't know what to do when they hear them. Our reports told us very clearly it was time to get rid of the sirens and be consistent with the rest of the country," he said.

"People will use the reminder - long and strong get gone - and they can receive emergency mobile alerts on their cellphone too."

Brenden Winder, Christchurch City Council Emergency Manager, says the tsunami sirens are now outdated. Rachel Graham/RNZ

Winder said the council would also put up signs in tsunami evacuation zones and embark on a public information campaign.

In April 2025 the bi-annual test of Christchurch's tsunami sirens did not happen because the person in Auckland who was supposed to activate them was waylaid by a car crash.

Winder said that was not the reason the sirens were reviewed but did point to a weakness in the system.

"While that was regrettable, in some ways it just reminded us of how fragile the system was. We certainly didn't plan for that to happen," he said.

"While the guy in Auckland was doing the right thing in the moment, it didn't help with the testing of the sirens but it did highlight the larger fragility of the arrangements that were in place."

Winder said technology has improved since the sirens were first introduced in 2016 and the mobile emergency alerts offered more comprehensive cover.

"The sirens met a need for a time but they were never across the whole region. They are only in Christchurch, not Banks Peninsula, so there are some equity challenges there. They are also costly and had coverage issues too, so it was time for the sirens to go."

Winder said the council had decided to remove the sirens altogether to ensure the message was simple.

World.title: NRLW needs its own CEO, says legend Ali Brigginshaw
World.content:
In her final press conference before retirement, rugby league legend Ali Brigginshaw has called on the NRL to create a separate chief executive for the women's game.

As she prepares for a fairytale finish hoping to win back-to-back premierships with Brisbane, Brigginshaw knows the NRLW still has much growing to do.

At today's official pre-grand final press conference, the Bronco was asked to put herself at the desk of newly crowned executive chairman Peter V'landys.

"If there's someone in charge of the [women's] game, maybe someone that plays the game, not me, maybe Millie," Brigginshaw joked about her fellow retiring grand finalist, the Roosters' Millie Elliott.

"Just someone that knows the game and what we've been through.

"We try to shape our game exactly [how] the men do, but there's nothing saying we have to just follow in those footsteps.

"We can go in a different direction, we can do what we want to do and what's best for the [NRLW] players and the staff."

Ali Brigginshaw was given a guard of honour for Brisbane's last home game. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

The women's game is currently managed by the chief executive of the NRL. In contrast, the AFLW has always had its own dedicated leadership, currently headed by Laura Kane.

It was not the only major innovation suggested at today's fan event, with tributes to Brigginshaw also on the agenda.

"She will be remembered in the game for such a long time, and I really hope that they name an award after Ali," Broncos coach Scott Prince said.

The 2020 Dally M medallist has captained her state and country and now leaves behind a legacy that even her fiercest rivals admire.

"Ali's been a pioneer of our game for a very long time now, and I've been really lucky to know Ali for a number of years and play with her and experience her as a leader as well," Roosters captain Isabelle Kelly said.

Roosters captain Isabelle Kelly paid credit to the retiring Ali Brigginshaw. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

She also shared plenty of praise for her own retiring teammates Corban Baxter and Elliott, the 2022 Dally M medallist.

"[Millie] never stops; she's always putting her best foot forward. She promotes the game in such a positive and respectful light that so many young girls look up to.

"Corban, she's the most humble, beautiful human that I think has just put such a landmark on this game."

Meanwhile, the Roosters will make a last-second decision on winger Jayme Fressard as she races the clock to have her shoulder right for grand final day.

The Blues representative picked up a shoulder injury in last week's win over Canberra and did not return to the field after half-time.

A final decision will be made after the captain's run tomorrow, with coach John Strange rating Fressard a "50-50" chance of playing.

"A little niggle, a few fitness tests to still get through, but hopefully looking good," Strange said.

"I just really want to be present this week and do everything that I need to do to be the best athlete as possible."

AAP

World.title: Amy Shark to lead NRL grand final musical tribute to Jai Arrow
World.content:
An all-star ensemble of Australian musicians is set to take part in this weekend's NRL grand final pre-game entertainment.

Pop sensation Amy Shark is leading the performance, alongside members from Newcastle favourites and Better hit-makers The Screaming Jets, electronic duo Peking Duk, plus rock groups Grinspoon, and Teen Jesus and the Jean Teasers.

The all-Australian supergroup will soundtrack an on-ground tribute to South Sydney Rabbitohs player Jai Arrow, who told ABC earlier this week he knew "nothing" about plans for him to take a lap of honour around Stadium Australia on Sunday.

The ABC understands that Shark, who performed at the 2020 NRL grand final, and company will perform a series of cover songs, including the Gerry and the Pacemakers' song and Liverpool FC anthem You'll Never Walk Alone.

Each musician's appearance fee is reportedly being donated to motor neurone disease causes.

The Screaming Jets were among the acts speculated by fans to replace Tones And I. (Supplied: The Screaming Jets)

News of the supergroup musical tribute comes after the NRL's negotiations to secure Tones And I fell through, leaving the grand final without a pre-match entertainment headliner.

Why Tones And I won't appear at grand final Tones And I has broken her silence after the NRL declared it will forego a grand final tradition of pre-match entertainment.

The Sydney Morning Herald reported that the issue centred on the NRL's insistence that she perform her 2019 mega-hit Dance Monkey, which she had refused to do.

However, the musician's team confirmed that prior commitments touring with Macklemore in the US left her unable to accept the offer when it was made in September.

"Nothing was signed or confirmed in writing," Tones and I's management said.

"Due to the last-minute nature and prior commitments by Tones, we were unable to accept the offer."

It sparked speculation over potential replacements for pre-match entertainment, including Silverchair frontman Daniel Johns ruling out rumours that the band would be reuniting to cheer on their home team, the Newcastle Knights

Jai Arrow was awarded the Provan-Summons Medal at the 2026 Dally M Awards for embodying the spirit of the game. (Getty Images: Don Arnold/WireImage)

Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC the money spent on pre-match entertainment — running close to $1 million — could be put to better use.

"I'd prefer to see 20,000 underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league play rugby league, rather than spend $1 million on 11 minutes of a musical performance," he said.

"You spend money to get outcomes, and I think it's a better outcome to get kids that can't afford to play with their mates, gear etc, to play rugby league."

Peter V’landys said money set aside for pre-match entertainment would be invested in junior rugby league. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

V'landys also said the league would be donating $100,000 to Arrow's family, following the Rabbitohs player's departure from the NRL earlier this year after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease.

The grand final has regularly featured pre-match entertainment, including international pop star Teddy Swims last year, and previous acts such as Billy Idol and Tina Turner.

"Our game sells itself," said V'landys.

"People come to watch rugby league. They don't come to watch a pop concert."

World.title: How Assefa ran third fastest marathon ever despite 'destroyed' Achilles
World.content:
Right up until the 40km mark of the Berlin Marathon at the weekend, Tigst Assefa was well on track to regain her world record.

After 10km, the Ethiopian star was already over a minute in the lead of a race that quickly became a challenge between her and the clock.

By the 30km mark, the noted fast-finisher was running inside world record pace and flying.

"She was on [target] to run 2:09:30, 2:09:40," Assefa's representative Gianni Demadonna told The Associated Press on Tuesday.

Tigst Assefa was flying through the first 30km of the race, running well under world record pace. (Getty Images: Maja Hitij)

Official World Marathon Majors social media accounts were excitedly posting "this is on" with Assefa 20 seconds under the existing world record time, set by controversial Kenyan Ruth Chepng'etich.

Chepng'etich's record is 2:09:56 from the 2024 Chicago Marathon, but she hasn't raced since July 2025 after admitting to a doping violation.

She is currently serving a three-year ban. There is no suggestion that Chepng'etich doped in Chicago and that record still stands.

Assefa was within touching distance of eliminating Chepng'etich from the record books.

But, within sight of the Brandenburg Gate at just 2 kilometres remaining, Assefa began to grimace, then started to limp and hobbled to the line.

She eventually finished 68 seconds shy of Chepng'etich's record.

Assefa suffered 'complete rupture of the right Achilles tendon'

Assifa's finishing time of 2:11:04 was the third-fastest in history and gave the Olympic silver medallist her third career victory in Berlin, in a new course record.

But incredibly, it was later revealed that the 29-year-old had suffered a "complete rupture of the right Achilles tendon" and has since undergone surgery.

According to her team, Assefa had felt pain in her Achilles from the 31st kilometre, but pushed on regardless, before complete disaster struck with just 2km to go.

Tigst Assefa was unable to stand after crossing the line. (Getty Images: picture alliance/Andreas Gora)

The Achilles tendon connects your calf muscles to your heel bone and lifts the heel when the calf muscle contracts.

"Your Achilles is basically a spring to propel yourself forward," Zoe Russell, a specialist sports and exercise physio as awarded by the Australian College of Physiotherapists, told ABC Sport.

"It transfers your load to propel you forward.

"Tendon experts around the world sort of suggest that a painful tendon doesn't often rupture because it just can't sustain the load.

"You don't typically hear this story of how they're running along, they're sore and then it pops."

How can you run with a ruptured Achilles?

Associate Professor Peter Malliaras, a physiotherapist and clinical researcher at Monash University, told ABC Radio National's Health Report in 2022 that an Achilles tendon rupture "is quite a catastrophic injury".

"It will prevent you from pretty much doing everything in your daily functions; including walking, running, driving, for a fair period of time," he said.

Tigst Assefa could barely struggle to her feet. (Getty Images: Anadolu/Halil Sagirkaya)

Demadonna claimed that Assefa "completely destroyed the tendon" by the end of the race, running the final 500 metres without it.

"She was no longer able to run, because when she was going to put her foot on the ground she had no power," Demadonna said.

Adidas one-run-and-done shoe sets new mark in sport's arms race Adidas's new running shoe helped Ethiopia's Tigst Assefa take more than 2 minutes off the marathon world record in Berlin at the weekend — but if you want to get hold of the one-run-and-done shoe, you'd better start saving.

Yet Assefa was still able to finish the race, running along at a fair lick too, despite being unable to push off with her forefoot.

One reason for her ability to keep moving forward could be found in the super shoes she was wearing, with the integrated carbon plate essentially providing some of the spring instead.

"It could have helped her keep going, yes," Russell suggested.

"Those carbon plates will allow you to transfer your load a bit easier."

Nevertheless, Assefa collapsed soon after crossing the line in clear distress before support arrived, including Ethiopian long-distance running legend Haile Gebrselassie.

Quick surgery vital

She was immediately flown to Munich by private jet courtesy of her sponsor, Adidas, where Demadonna said she underwent "very complex surgery" on Monday.

Without knowing the exact details of the rupture, or the exact surgery technique used, Russell said a time frame for a return would be impossible to guess, but noted that quick surgery was essential.

"Things can move quickly, really quickly in elite sport," she said.

"I've had athletes get an appointment with a surgeon within 20 minutes, half an hour of the injury.

Tigst Assefa was aided by four-time Berlin winner Haile Gebrselassie to leave the finishing area. (Getty Images: Maja Hitij)

"When you've got means and connections at the elite level, things can move very quickly — and you do want to move fairly quickly with an Achilles rupture because it is constantly under tension. When it ruptures, it actually retracts back.

"So if you're waiting weeks for surgery, it means that your muscles actually start to suffer the effects of de-conditioning and it retracts, which makes for a technically harder surgical process because you've got to pull it and put it all on tension and then stitch it up.

"For an elite athlete, you'd want to get it in two or three days, whereas in the general population, you'll probably get away with getting it within a week."

In a statement, Assefa's coach Gemedu Dedifo said that she "successfully underwent surgery" within 24 hours.

"Tigst is a champion," the statement read.

"We believe in her strength, courage and determination.

"We look forward to seeing her recover and return to the track and roads."

Assefa vows to return

Assefa sent a message from her hospital bed via the Berlin Marathon organisers, defiantly promising to return to break the record.

"My surgery went well," she said in a statement.

"I am overwhelmed by the tremendous support I have received from all over the world. From the bottom of my heart, I would like to thank everyone for their incredible support and concern.

"I will definitely come back to Berlin, and then I will break the world record."

Tigst Assefa holds the women's only world record. (Getty Images: Xinhua/Li Ying)

No marathon has seen more world records than Berlin, with 13 set at the race since 1974 thanks to its largely flat profile with just 73 metres of elevation gain and 79 metres of elevation loss over the 42km.

Assefa set one of those world records in 2023, running 2:11:53 to become the first woman to set a record on the course since Sydney Olympic champion Naoko Takahashi did so in 2001.

Assefa already holds the women's only world record, having run 2:15:41 to win the 2026 London Marathon in April.

Races where men and women start at the same time, as is the case in Berlin, tend to be faster for women, who are able to benefit from male pacemakers who can block the wind and reduce fatigue earlier in the race.

World.title: Roosters blow as Watson ruled out of NRL grand final
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters have suffered a significant blow ahead of the NRL grand final, with hooker Connor Watson ruled out of the match.

In a cruel blow, Watson will miss Sunday's decider against his former club Newcastle and become the first player to sit out a grand final as a result of a concussion.

Watson was dazed and was taken from the field moments after coming on in the Roosters' preliminary final win over the Dolphins.

Under the NRL's protocol, players diagnosed with a category-one concussion, as Watson was, face a mandatory stand-down period of 11 days.

The Roosters had indicated that Watson was testing well leading into Thursday when the 30-year-old met with an independent specialist.

But on Friday the club confirmed the utility had failed to receive clearance to line up in the grand final.

The outcome means Watson has played his last game for the Roosters with the popular utility heading to St George Illawarra next season before linking up with the PNG Chiefs in 2028.

Connor Watson has played 127 games for the Roosters in the NRL. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Watson's absence likely forces Roosters coach Trent Robinson's hand when it comes to his bench, with hooker Benaiah Ioelu the most obvious man to come into Easts' 19-man squad.

Five things to know ahead of the NRL and NRLW grand finals The final day of the NRL and NRLW season is almost here, with the grand finals being held this Sunday. Here's everything you need to know.

Ioelu has played mostly off the bench through his 17-game NRL career, starting just once in five appearances this season, and would act as cover for Reece Robson.

"I don't think it takes too much to work out what plan B is, but we have got some really good hookers," Robinson said on Thursday.

"Benaiah Ioelu played some great footy for us this year. He brings a lot of energy to us as well so he will come into consideration then."

Newcastle, meanwhile, are also expected to face a tough decision leading into Sunday's decider as they weigh up a replacement for suspended number nine, Phoenix Crossland.

Harrison Graham has excelled as a bench option at hooker for the Knights, but coach Justin Holbrook, who doesn't have to name his final team until 90 minutes before kick-off on Sunday, has the option of also starting Thomas Cant or Diesel Hagan.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Neale switches to Collingwood, Greene joins Cats in AFL free agency
World.content:
Lachie Neale has sealed his high-profile switch to Collingwood, with Brisbane teasing the dual Brownlow medallist on his way out the door.

The AFL approved Neale signing a three-year deal with the Magpies on Friday afternoon, closing out the first day of free agency.

The 33-year-old ball-winner leaves as an unrestricted free agent after the Lions clinched a third-straight flag with their stunning seven-point grand final victory over Fremantle.

Brisbane chairman Andrew Wellington poked fun at Neale's switch to the "dark side" at the club's best and fairest event, where he finished third behind Will Ashcroft and Josh Dunkley.

"Take a last look at Lachie, because he's going tomorrow to have some teeth removed and a bit more ink," Wellington joked on Thursday night, drawing laughter from the crowd.

Departing coach Chris Fagan hailed Neale's perseverance after stepping down as captain in January following the public breakdown of his marriage and almost missing the grand final through suspension.

"As we all know, he's been under a fair bit of pressure, but it's never shown out on the field," Fagan said.

"[We] wish you all the best at your new club and with the rest of your life and whatever happens to you."

The Lions have been handed a second-round draft compensation — currently pick number 39 — with Neale reportedly raking in about $900,000 a season.

Toby Greene has signed a three-year deal with Geelong. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Jason McCawley)

Earlier, Toby Greene became the first major AFL free agency domino to fall, with Greater Western Sydney to receive a second-round draft pick for losing their former captain to Geelong.

The Cats lodged paperwork on Friday to land the inaugural Giant as an unrestricted free agent.

Greene, a triple All Australian and dual club champion, booted 450 goals across his 15-year, 282-game tenure for GWS.

The 33-year-old cited family reasons for returning to his native Victoria and reuniting with his close mate and former Giants forward Jeremy Cameron at the Cattery on a lucrative three-year deal.

The Giants will receive a second-round draft selection as compensation, currently slated at number 26.

Earlier, key forward Joel Amartey's switch from Sydney to Carlton was confirmed as the free agency period opened.

The Swans will receive draft compensation for losing the unrestricted 27-year-old, who was an emergency during finals after failing to convince coach Dean Cox following a partial Achilles tear.

Melbourne's 2021 premiership vice-captain Jack Viney is poised for a move with two years remaining on his contract after meeting with West Coast.

After being sidelined through injury for all but one game this season, the 32-year-old was told by coach Steven King there would likely be limited opportunities for him in the Demons midfield.

"Footy's gone that way mate," Viney told 10 News at Perth Airport on Thursday.

"So took a bit to process early days, but we're here now, so we'll make the best of the opportunity … it [a deal] will get done."

Neale set to join Magpies Collingwood says it "looks forward" to Lachie Neale joining the club in 2027 after it is announced he is leaving the Brisbane Lions.

Young Hawthorn forward Calsher Dear, meanwhile, has opted to stay at the Hawks on a two-year deal after weighing up a potential move to the Dees.

The 21-year-old, son of late 1991 Norm Smith medallist Paul Dear, burst onto the scene in his debut season with 25 goals from 17 appearances in 2024.

But the emerging tall has struggled to hold his spot through injury and internal competition, adding just 14 games in 2025 and 2026.

"We are very excited about what the future holds for Calsher with a strong pre-season under his belt and greater continuity into 2027 and beyond," Hawks list manager Mark McKenzie said.

Hawthorn's key forward selection squeeze is set to worsen in 2027, with Gold Coast's restricted free agent Ben King expected to join Jack Gunston, Mitch Lewis, Mabior Chol and Dear.

AAP

World.title: NRLW grand final marks end of era
World.content:
One year after the greatest and most controversial grand final in the NRLW, we're right back where we were 12 months ago.

Once again the Roosters will face Brisbane, with the Broncos all that stands between the Tricolours and a perfect season.

But while the season seems to be ending in the same place, the changes in the two sides, plus those that loom in the near future, make this game feel like the end of an era.

Controversial try decides NRLW premiership Brisbane and the Roosters played one of the greatest games in NRLW history, but the controversial winning try to Mele Hufanga shapes as a football mystery that might never be solved.

Roosters Millie Elliott and Corban Baxter will retire after the match, while New South Wales Origin prop Rima Butler is bound for Wests Tigers.

But where they limped into the decider last year, without injured halfback Tarryn Aiken and winger Taina Naividi after she broke down at the club's final training session, this time they're fully loaded.

The Broncos have not quite been the dominant force they were last year but they showed their class downing the Gold Coast in last week's preliminary final and have extra motivation of their own.

Ali Brigginshaw, one of the icons of the NRLW's early years, will be playing her last game before hanging up the boots.

Throw in lingering feelings from last year's 22-18 Broncos victory, which was sealed by a contentious try to Brisbane centre Mele Hufanga with three minutes left, and the stakes could not be higher.

The Roosters are determined to run towards the bad memories, having watched a replay of the match together before the season began.

"We're building on the feelings from last year," five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher said.

"It was a big theme of our pre-season camp.

"We watched it all together and it was really hard. There were a lot of people getting emotional but it was dead silent. It was so eerie.

"We all feel the hurt and the pain from last year. We won't let it happen again. We've worked so hard to fix those little things that went wrong last year."

After another undefeated regular season, that grand final loss is the only time the Roosters have had their colours lowered in the past two years, giving them 30 wins from their last 31 starts.

The Roosters have humbled their opponents this year. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

It meant they'd forgotten what defeat could even feel like. While they'll keep talk about it to a minimum this week, there's no doubt it hangs over them like a spectre.

"At the time, it was a weird feeling because the result was disappointing, but there was a lot of things in the lead-up that didn't go our way," hooker Keeley Nizza said.

"That's rugby league though and we still had the opportunity to win it but we didn't. The way we rallied together and played well regardless of the result, it brought us closer together.

"We won't speak about it too much, so it won't need to be brought up. It's always with us. Every year there's a new squad and a new feel, but we won't forget."

That possibility of a new squad in 2027 is why the match feels like the end of something.

Elliott is a Test and Origin mainstay, Baxter has played for the club since 2019, Butler has blossomed since joining Newcastle, and each of them leaves a serious hole in the roster with their departure.

Millie Boyle is one of three key players appearing in their last game for the Roosters. (Getty Images: Matt King)

The Roosters have done an excellent job identifying and progressing talent through their women's program, but all three are exceptionally difficult to replace.

While the club will be a premiership threat for some years to come, this game could mark the end of the club as a historically dominant force.

The combined impact of the departing trio makes them just a little more like everyone else, which could make this their last chance at the elusive perfect season.

Brisbane have already felt the pinch hurting the Roosters now. They have eight changes from last year's grand final, including Hufanga, who left for the Warriors.

But they did welcome in Blues halfback Jesse Southwell, and with her and Brigginshaw calling the shots, the Broncos attack is sure to fire.

Plus the defending premiers boast newly minted three-time Dally M and two-time Karyn Murphy Medal winner Tamika Upton, who's won three of the past four premierships across two different clubs.

Brigginshaw's last 'last' in NRLW grand final Ali Brigginshaw and fellow OGs Julia Robinson and Chelsea Lenarduzzi are hoping to join Broncos royalty with a fifth NRLW premiership.

Given her record in big matches, she's sure to put her stamp on the game and is good enough to win it almost on her own, meaning the result is well and truly up for grabs.

The Roosters were in imperious form to end the regular season, winning their last four regular season games by a combined total of 200 points to 34, but any thought of catching them complacent was ended in the preliminary final against Canberra.

The gallant Raiders gave a fine account of themselves in an intensely physical encounter, and the 20-10 Roosters win has them primed to hit their straps when it matters most.

"That's the sorest I've felt all year," Kelleher said.

"We absolutely bashed each other up on that field for 70 full minutes."

"We showed our mindset, that we could go through the grit and the arm wrestle. It's the perfect lead in to a grand final."

World.title: Piastri likens track to 'sandpaper' as F1 returns to Malaysia
World.content:
Formula 1 is heading back to Malaysia's Sepang International Circuit after a nine-year hiatus this weekend, with more than half the drivers on the grid unfamiliar with a track that is hosting the rescheduled Bahrain Grand Prix.

After making its first appearance on the calendar in 1999, Sepang has not hosted a Formula 1 race since 2017 after the Malaysian government said it could no longer justify the costs given the declining returns.

But it is making its F1 comeback after owners Liberty Media said it would host the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, relocating the race from Sakhir due to the Iran war and the situation in the Middle East.

Russell wins Azerbaijan GP after Piastri disaster in Baku George Russell has claimed a nail-biting victory in Baku, holding off Max Verstappen by just 0.196 seconds to secure his third victory of the season.

The 5.543-km long circuit combines long straights with several high-speed corners, with this week's race set to be held over 56 laps.

Only 10 of the 22 drivers have previously raced in Malaysia, leaving world champion Lando Norris and his McLaren teammate Oscar Piastri among those who will be learning the track for the first time.

Tyre supplier Pirelli has warned teams to expect challenging conditions, describing Sepang's surface as "relatively abrasive" with roughness comparable to Bahrain.

Piastri said the track "looks like sandpaper" and he too expected a lot of tyre degradation.

"I don't know how much racing or track running there's been recently. And anything that has been, the rain probably washes it off every afternoon anyway," Piastri said.

"So it's going to be a pretty tough weekend for everyone."

Thunderstorms are far from unusual in Malaysia, where the tropical climate regularly produces heavy afternoon showers and lightning storms.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli said Sepang's notorious abrasive surface could prove a welcome surprise should F1 finally get its first wet race of the season in Malaysia.

The young Italian, who has enjoyed a charmed run of dry conditions throughout his title charge, reckons the Malaysian circuit's rough tarmac would make it the ideal venue to test the sport's 2026 cars in challenging weather.

"I think this track will be quite OK in the wet … The surface is so open, there's actually not a lot of standing water unless it pours down," Antonelli told reporters, adding that it was the "roughest track tarmac" he had ever seen.

"But if it rains normally, then it would probably be the best track to try these cars for the first time in the rain because the tarmac is so open that the water just doesn't sit on top of the surface. It actually goes in between the stones. So it makes less risk of aquaplaning."

Reuters

World.title: Australia calls Maddinson and Harper into Test squad
World.content:
Nic Maddinson is within touching distance of a remarkable return to the Test team, after Cameron Green's abdominal strain left him in doubt for the series opener against South Africa.

Selectors confirmed on Thursday night that Maddinson had been called into the Test squad after not featuring in Australia's red-ball side for almost 10 years.

Sam Harper has also been drafted in as a back-up wicketkeeper, with a finger fracture now officially ruling Josh Inglis out of the first Test in Durban starting next Friday.

Inglis was hurt while playing in the series-opening ODI against South Africa last week, with further scans back home in Perth revealing a fracture.

Cameron Green is in doubt for the first Test after being injured in the Potchefstroom ODI against South Africa. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

There are now similar concerns around Green following the third ODI in Potchefstroom on Wednesday after he hurt his abdomen trying to pull a ball while batting in Australia's dead-rubber win.

Australian medical staff will now keep close watch on the allrounder, who will be "assessed further" in the coming week.

Regardless, the latest abdominal injury will raise question marks over Green's ability to bowl, after having not done so yet in a game on this tour.

The one bit of good news for Australia is opener Matt Renshaw has been cleared of a wrist injury after being hurt while fielding in the final ODI.

But the injuries do leave Australia's line-up for the first Test largely up in the air with up to two spots in the top-six unclear if Green is not fit.

Inglis had stood a chance of coming into the side for Marnus Labuschagne if selectors had opted to drop the Queenslander for the series opener.

Australia Test batter Nic Maddinson reveals testicular cancer diagnosis Former Australia batter Nic Maddinson has revealed he underwent chemotherapy for testicular cancer.

Maddinson could now fill one of those roles, with Cooper Connolly the other reserve batter in the Test squad.

Maddinson last played a Test on Boxing Day in 2016, and has since overcome a battle with testicular cancer to restart his cricket career.

The 34-year-old did not play a first-class match last summer, but struck 126 for NSW in a one-day match against Victoria last week.

Harper looms as another option, after being called into his first Australian squad at age 29.

The Victorian was the second-leading run-scorer in last summer's Sheffield Shield with 677 at 35.63 and is fresh off hitting a century for Australia A against India A in Pudcherry.

"Sam gives us wicketkeeping cover as Josh continues his recovery, while Nic provides flexibility throughout the batting order," chief selector George Bailey said.

Australia will play an intra-squad warm-up match in Potchefstroom this weekend, before moving to Durban on Monday to commence preparations for the first of three Tests.

AAP

Tech.title: Tesla will now let you drive off mid-charge if there’s an emergency
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Tesla introduced a new feature to enable drivers to escape quickly while charging their vehicles in response to a mass shooting at a Supercharger location in Idaho in August that left seven people wounded and four dead.

When a Tesla vehicle is charging, the plug is locked to the charging port and driving is disabled. To put the car in drive, a charging cable has to be manually released from the vehicle’s charging port. Since the shooting in Twin Falls, Idaho, Tesla owners have been requesting a quick-release mechanism that would allow them to escape in the event of an emergency. This week, Tesla responded with a software update that responds to those concerns.

The new “emergency drive away” feature allows vehicle owners to override the charging lock and drive away while the handle is still attached. Shifting into drive will activate an emergency drive away alert that asks the driver to confirm they need to get away. The handle will break away and fall to the ground and, unfortunately, both the vehicle and the charging handle will sustain some damage in the process, which underscores why this feature should only be used in an emergency.

“Deliberate misuse will invoke additional penalties,” Tesla said on X, without specifying what kind of penalties. The feature is only available in the US, where an estimated 500 million firearms are owned by private citizens, “for now.”

Tesla didn’t mention the mass shooting in its announcement, but it’s not hard to draw a connection. A Tesla owner who was charging his vehicle was among seven people wounded by the 24-year-old gunman, who later took his own life.

Some aftermarket companies have tried selling their own breakaway adapters for electric vehicles, including Tesla. In 2024, a startup called EVject built a breakaway adapter designed to let you drive away from a Tesla Supercharger (or other station) without getting out of your car in case of a dangerous situation. However, Tesla sued the company after the automaker’s testing found that the adapter could overheat. Tesla eventually dropped the case later in the year, and EVject maintains that its product is safe.

Tech.title: Keurig’s new machine uses plastic-free compressed coffee pucks
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Keurig’s new single-serve coffee machine delivers the same convenience that helped popularize its appliances but without the use of recyclable pods made from plastic and aluminum. The company first showed off its Keurig Alta machine two years ago while introducing the puck-shaped pod replacements called AltaRounds that wrap pressed coffee grounds in a plant-based coating derived from seaweed. The pucks are 100 percent compostable, and while they currently come in plastic wrappers to keep them fresh, the company is working to transition to paper wrappers, according to CNET.

The Keurig Alta is now available for preorder for $499.99 with shipping expected to start on October 21st. Color options include graphite, sandstone, and sandstone mixed with a “satin stainless” gray finish. The Alta is currently only offered as part of a bundle that includes a collection of glassware and six boxes of the AltaRounds. At launch there will be six caffeinated varieties of AltaRounds available with light roast, medium roast, and flavored options.

The new AltaRounds are made from fine coffee grounds wrapped in a plant-based coating derived from seaweed. Image: Keurig

The Alta is one of Keurig’s most expensive consumer-focused machines because in addition to traditional brewing methods it doubles as an espresso maker. Hot water is pushed through the AltaRounds at high pressure after the puck has been punctured by an array of spikes and finished with milk foam whipped up by a built-in frother.

The Keurig Alta can make coffee or espresso and includes a built-in milk frother. Image: Keurig

Despite the added capabilities the Alta is designed to be as easy to use as Keurig’s older machines. You don’t need to use a grinder or even know what a tamper is. The AltaRounds are each printed with a QR code ready by the machine that specifies brewing instructions including what pressure and temperature are needed. Manual adjustments aren’t needed but the Alta features a large touchscreen display where different drink recipes can be selected. The machine is also Wi-Fi connected so as more varieties of AltaRounds are released it can be updated to include more recipes and options.

Tech.title: Paramount’s Warner Bros. megamerger will just be called Skydance
Tech.content:
What once was the peak, is now just the beginning.

Paramount and Warner Bros. shaped over a century of culture. By combining them, we aren’t rewriting history — we’re equipping these iconic studios with a more powerful engine. Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for bold, quality storytelling.

We chose this name for a few important reasons. First and foremost, as we bring Paramount and Warner Bros. together, we wanted to preserve what has made each of these studios iconic. Both have distinct identities, extraordinary legacies and brands that have resonated with audiences for generations. We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one. Instead, we wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. — and all our extraordinary brands — to remain in the spotlight.

We have big goals for Skydance, and we intend to pursue them with passion, imagination and a willingness to take smart risks. At the same time, we will honor what makes Paramount and Warner Bros. special — giving both studios the opportunity to grow, tell more great stories and bring those stories to even broader audiences around the world, powered by the scale and capabilities of Skydance.

I couldn’t be more excited about what we’re going to build together.

Tech.title: Tesla’s recovery hits a speed bump
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Tesla sold fewer vehicles in the third quarter than it did a year ago, when consumers rushed to cash in on expiring federal tax credits for electric vehicle purchases. But the company still beat estimates from Wall Street, suggesting that it’s recovery was still on track.

Tesla said that it produced a total of 464,391 vehicles between July and September of this year, including 457,387 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles, as well as 7,004 “other vehicles” like the Cybertruck, Cybercab, and Tesla Semi. (The company discontinued the Model S and X earlier this year.) That represents about a 3.8 percent increase compared to the third quarter of 2025, when the company produced 447,450 vehicles.

Tesla also said that it delivered to customers a total of 486,532 vehicles, including 481,166 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles, as well as 8,295 other vehicles — about a 2.1 percent decrease compared to the blockbuster third quarter of 2025, when it delivered 497,099 vehicles. (For a direct-to-consumer company like Tesla, deliveries are a proxy for sales.)

The drop in sales was widely expected thanks to the expiration of the $7,500 federal tax credit for electric vehicles on September 30, 2025. Elon Musk himself said that the company was in for “a few rough quarters” thanks to the expiring incentive and other macroeconomic factors.

But Musk also said he believes that Tesla will rebound as its AI plans come to fruition, including robotaxis and humanoid robots. We saw how that might play out, with the July launch of the steering-wheel and pedal-less Cybercab in Austin. Even so, Musk predicted that 50 percent of the US population will have access to Tesla’s robotaxis by the end of 2025 — which of course turned out to be very wrong.

Last quarter, Tesla said its sales were up 25 percent year over year. Wall Street investors were expecting Tesla to report sales of 463,000 vehicles for the second quarter. The company-compiled sell-side analyst consensus estimated 461,974 vehicle deliveries for Q3. Today’s report represents a clean beat of those expectations.

The report comes amid a tumultuous time for Tesla — which always seems to be the case for any company with Elon Musk at the helm. The company scored some good headlines — the re-launch of the Semi and Cybercab, European sales rebound, a boost in EV market share stateside — and was rocked by a few bad ones — the delay of the next-gen Roadster reveal and a federal investigation into the Cybercab launch.

Tech.title: Home Assistant says ‘Big tech ruined the cloud, so we’re out’
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

All the smart home news, reviews, and gadgets you need to know about

The open-source smart home platform Home Assistant is kicking the cloud to the curb — in name at least. “We are renaming Home Assistant Cloud to Home Assistant Link, because we hate clouds,” founder Paulus Schoutsen told The Verge in an interview ahead of today’s announcement. “Big tech ruined the cloud, so we’re out.”

The move is part of a long-term strategy Schoutsen and his team have been pursuing to make Home Assistant a mainstream smart home platform. Schoutsen says most users find the powerful platform after hitting the limits of mainstream options like Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and Apple Home. But it has a steep learning curve, and that’s what he’s looking to change.

I spoke with Schoutsen at the Z-Wave Summit in Boca Raton, Florida, this week about the changes and Home Assistant’s future plans, which include lowering barriers to entry by developing simpler dashboards, making setup more intuitive, and using generative AI to reduce complexity. He also said they plan to launch a new hub next year that’s more user-friendly. “We’re growing up.”

“You don’t have to trust me not to misuse your data because I just don’t have your data.” — Paulus Schoutsen

Renaming Home Assistant Cloud to Link is mostly symbolic. The features stay the same, aside from some back-end improvements to speed and reliability. The new name also tries to address a concern some new users had that it meant Home Assistant ran in the cloud, says Schoutsen. Home Assistant runs on local hardware and controls your smart home locally, but this means once you leave your home network, you can’t control anything.

For $6.50 a month or $65 a year, Home Assistant Link gives you a convenient way to access your Home Assistant instance from anywhere, alongside the option to enable other internet-dependent features such as integration with Alexa and Google voice control, text-to-speech, speech-to-text, and encrypted backups.

Nabu Casa published this graphic to explain its perspective on the differences between Home Assistant Link and other cloud services. Image: Nabu Casa

The move addresses an awkward dynamic for the platform. Schoutsen and his team have spent years campaigning against proprietary cloud ecosystems, which he believes hurt the smart home, and encouraging people not to buy cloud-dependent products, all while offering a service with “cloud” in the name. However, unlike some cloud services, Home Assistant Cloud was never mandatory, and you could always replicate everything it provided with other methods; the same remains true for Link.

Schoutsen says Link is also different from many cloud services because it has no access to your data. Link is run by Nabu Casa, Home Assistant’s commercial partner, and all Link traffic is encrypted. “We can’t see it, and we don’t want to,“ he says. “You don’t have to trust me not to misuse your data because I just don’t have your data.” The service provides a revenue stream to fund the platform’s development, with 60 percent of the profit going to the non-profit Open Home Foundation that runs Home Assistant.

Home Assistant had its first ever booth at a trade show this year, attending the IFA consumer technology conference in Berlin in September. Image: The Open Home Foundation

For Home Assistant, cloud-dependent products are a hard no. “The cloud is ruining how people think of the smart home,” says Schoutsen, pointing to the recent examples of Nest shutting off the cloud for its early thermostats, smart TVs sending your data to the cloud without you knowing, and Weber sunsetting the June Oven’s servers. “Now you have a dumb oven that cost $1,500. It’s crazy,” he says. “People get so used to it and get so disappointed by it.”

The cloud isn’t all bad, Schoutsen concedes. Speech-to-text, backups, and AI work better online, but the problem is products that stop working without it. He wants product manufacturers to commit to offering local control by default, using open standards (Matter, Zigbee, Z-Wave, MQTT, ESPHome), never locking basic features behind a cloud, and allowing users to control their own data.

“I’d love to see a nutrition label on boxes showing if a product is cloud-dependent or not,” he says, adding that they’re building a database to help consumers find products that aren’t fully reliant on the cloud.

This stance against the cloud is likely to appeal to consumers who are increasingly concerned about who has access to their data. But Home Assistant still has a long way to go before it becomes mainstream. Schoutsen says Home Assistant is installed in an estimated 2.7 million homes, but that’s still a fraction of the reach of Amazon Alexa, Google Home, Samsung SmartThings, and Apple Home. Winning over mainstream users will be hard.

The Home Assistant Green hub is one way to get started with the smart home platform. You can also use your own hardware. Image: Home Assistant

The biggest barrier to entry is complexity. Home Assistant does a lot, meaning you have a lot of choice, which can be overwhelming. “If you want to try something with Home Assistant, the answer is never no,” says Schoutsen. “We want everything to be possible, which means that the UX is more complicated, and that scares people.” In comparison, “You open Apple Home, and there’s like nothing you can do,” he says.

Over the last few years, the team has been working to remove those barriers without taking away functionality. “We’re looking to lower the floor without lowering the ceiling,” he says. There are plans to launch a successor to the Home Assistant Green hub that will be easier to set up. “We want to make it more like onboarding a Philips Hue hub,” says Schoutsen.

They are also working to make the UX easier and will integrate the HACS community store — where users find and install community-built integrations — into Home Assistant next month. This should make integrations easier to find and set up. “If people haven’t tried Home Assistant in over a year, they should give it a shot,” he says.

“We’re looking to lower the floor without lowering the ceiling.” — Paulus Schoutsen

Another big push that could turn into a major selling point for the platform is a “No Device Left Behind” program. Nabu Casa is developing devices that will more easily bring people’s existing analog or legacy tech into the platform — such as old receivers, AC units, solar panel inverters, even TVs — using technology such as serial, IR, and Modbus.

Schoutsen sees AI as a big driver for Home Assistant. “AI is going to solve the complexity problem, and our biggest weakness is becoming our biggest strength,” he says. As a broad, open platform that can bring together data and controls from across your smart home, Home Assistant could provide a useful foundation for AI agents.

I used Claude to set up Home Assistant last year, and it was a big improvement over trying to figure out what on earth YAML was. “Soon you’re just going to have your agent configure your software for you,” he says. “Because people don’t want the software, they just want the solution that comes out of it.” Schoutsen acknowledges that agents raise obvious privacy concerns, but says Home Assistant keeps your data at home and you can choose which agent to trust with it, including one that runs locally.

Ultimately, Home Assistant may not need to reinvent itself to win over the mainstream if it can become the foundational layer that lets your home talk to your AI agent or platform of choice. “If you just have a box in your house that runs Home Assistant that connects all your data to your agents or to, say, Apple Home, that’s great,” he says. “That’s a win for Home Assistant.”

Tech.title: The Pocket Advance nearly perfects my favorite Nintendo handheld
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Although I count the original Game Boy as one of my first tech obsessions, I still consider Nintendo’s Game Boy Advance to be my favorite console of all time thanks to its more comfortable horizontal design (for my big hands) and its expansive catalog of excellent 32-bit and 16-bit games. Ayaneo isn’t the first company to attempt to modernize the GBA, but its Konkr Pocket Advance does it best. The handheld strikes a near perfect balance between authentically re-creating the GBA’s design while updating its hardware with new controls, a much better screen, and the flexibility of Android at a price that feels like a bargain.

As much as I still adore the GBA, I’ve eagerly embraced upgrades to the aging console over the years. First it was the clamshell GBA SP that finally delivered a frontlit screen I could actually see without a lamp over my shoulder, and later it was aftermarket upgrades like a backlit LCD display and a rechargeable battery that vastly improved Nintendo’s original hardware. Two years ago, I eagerly purchased Anbernic’s GBA-inspired RG34XX, but all of those have now been replaced by the Konkr Pocket Advance.

It’s my first handheld from Ayaneo, and I’ve been pleasantly surprised to find the hardware feels on par with Nintendo’s. The Pocket Advance is an all-plastic affair but with a satisfying heft thanks to extra internal hardware including a cooling fan for its MediaTek Helio G90T processor and a 4,000mAh battery. I opted for the cheaper $109 version with 3GB of RAM and 32GB of storage, which is expandable with a microSD card, but for $129, you can get 4GB of RAM with 64GB of storage built-in.

The Pocket Advance (left) with its larger screen and extra controls next to an upgraded original Game Boy Advance (right).

It’s not an exact copy of the GBA, but the Pocket Advance’s dimensions are close enough to fit all the cases I’ve somehow preserved for the past 25 years. Where Ayaneo’s remake really diverges from the original is with eight additional buttons including X and Y action buttons plus four extra shoulder buttons on the top edge. I’m a big fan of the larger D-pad Ayaneo has included, but some retro gaming purists may not be fans of how soft and squishy the Pocket Advance’s buttons all feel. I’ve had to learn to mash the action buttons just a little harder to ensure presses are always registered, but I don’t necessarily think the button feel is a downside because they’re also satisfyingly quiet.

The D-pad on the Pocket Advance (right) is larger than what the original GBA (left) featured and feels better under my larger thumb.

The Pocket Advance’s 3.5-inch LCD touchscreen with a glass cover is an excellent upgrade, but it does cater to GBA games with a 3:2 aspect ratio and a 960x640 resolution allowing them to be perfectly scaled at 4x. (The GBA had a 240x160 screen resolution.) Unless you’re a monster who can tolerate playing games that have been stretched vertically or horizontally to fill a screen, emulating games from other systems will result in letterboxing or pillarboxing on the sides, and potentially some visual artifacts from scaling when the math isn’t perfect.

The Pocket Advance includes a headphone jack and features a small dial for adjusting volume instead of buttons.

Most similarly sized and similarly priced handhelds run some variation of Linux. There’s a thriving community of developers creating and porting a large assortment of emulators, games, and apps to Linux, but installing, configuring, customizing and updating software is not always a user-friendly process, especially for novices who may only be familiar with using plug-and-play game carts. The Pocket Advance instead comes with Android 12, and while that version feels a little dated, setting up the handheld will feel a little more familiar to anyone with smartphone experience.

Ayaneo Konkr Pocket Advance $ 109 $ 109 An authentic but upgraded clone of Nintendo’s Game Boy Advance that can play more than just GBA games using emulation. Read More $109 at Ayaneo

Getting the Pocket Advance up and running was relatively easy thanks in part to Ayaneo’s custom launcher called AYASpace that makes it easier to install various emulators. But the handheld also has access to the Google Play Store, or you can install Android apps or add-ons downloaded directly from a website.

I’m a big fan of a clean and simple launcher for Linux handhelds called MinUI, so instead of AYASpace, I installed an alternative Android launcher called Cannoli on the Pocket Advance that brings the same aesthetics with several emulators preinstalled and preconfigured. The flexibility of Android means I can set the Pocket Advance to load Cannoli by default, but I have the option to switch back to AYASpace at any time, or install and jump between multiple alternatives.

Unlike the original GBA (left) and handhelds like the Analogue Pocket, the Pocket Advance (right) isn’t compatible with original game cartridges.

When it comes to emulation capabilities, you’ll want to keep your expectations limited to “retro” gaming. The Pocket Advance’s seven-year-old processor is powerful enough to handle many titles from the PS2 and GameCube, but the handheld is better equipped to emulate the PS1 and Sega Dreamcast, and you’ll have the best experience with games from even older consoles like the Super Nintendo and Genesis. An easy-access quick settings menu that slides in from the right lets you quickly customize and reconfigure the handheld including boosting its performance (at the cost of battery life) to handle more intensive games, but another thing preventing the Pocket Advance from playing more modern games is its lack of analog thumbsticks.

On the top edge of the Pocket Advance, you’ll find three pairs of shoulder buttons alongside a power button and an additional one that’s customizable.

Performance and compatibility will also vary with native Android games and apps. I’ve had a lot of fun playing through Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder’s Revenge once again, but while the Pocket Advance is a passable way to stream Netflix, I can’t get it to play any Disney Plus content without the app crashing out.

The Pocket Advance (bottom) is similar to Anbernic’s RG34XX (top,) but feels like a higher quality handheld overall. The Pocket Advance (left) runs Android 12 while the RG34XX (right) is based on Linux, making it a little more complicated to install, customize, and update apps.

Anbernic’s $69.99 RG34XX is still cheaper than the Pocket Advance and may seem like a better alternative, but I think Ayaneo’s is absolutely worth the extra $40. It’s a more powerful and capable handheld with a higher-res display, and I much prefer the Pocket Advance’s larger D-pad and shoulder button arrangement. I also find the quality of Anbernic’s hardware to be hit and miss. Similar to what others have reported on Reddit, I’ve experienced intermittent issues with the responsiveness of the RG34XX’s D-pad. I haven’t had the motivation to crack it open to attempt a DIY fix, and with the Pocket Advance now in my collection, it’s doubtful I ever will.

Even with buttons that feel very soft, the Pocket Advance is easily the best GBA clone currently available.

The Pocket Advance is one of the best retro handhelds currently available and not just because of its nostalgic retro design. As long as you temper your gaming expectations and won’t be frustrated by what it can’t play, it’s an excellent way to revisit and enjoy games from Nintendo’s earlier handheld era.

Photography by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge

Tech.title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer is my childhood podracing dream come true
Tech.content:
The podracing scene in The Phantom Menace is one of my favorite movie sequences ever. It’s just so dang cool: The futuristic racers tear over treacherous Tatooine terrain while various Star Wars aliens bark at each other in incomprehensible sci-fi languages. Eventually a young Anakin Skywalker proves his mettle by clawing his way from the back of the pack to win the race, which left an impression on me when I first saw it at 10 years old. I always wished I could pilot a podracer myself. Over the past several days, I’ve been able to live out that dream thanks to Star Wars: Galactic Racer, which takes everything from that brilliant scene and packs it into a thrilling video game.

In Galactic Racer’s campaign, you play as Shade, a cargo pilot who gets a shot at racing in the underground Galactic League circuit to eventually challenge the smarmy champion Kestar Bool. The game is basically a roguelike. You start a run (called a “tour”) by picking between a few different vehicles — though you don’t get to drive a podracer until partway through the campaign — and selecting various perks that can influence your style of play. Races themselves take place across a few planets, including the desert Jakku planet from The Force Awakens, and you’ll pick different events to participate in from a branching map screen. After each race, you’ll get rewards to help craft your build, and along the way, you’ll also play brief sections where you walk around as Shade, talk with other characters, and upgrade your vehicle.

This is Shade, the customizable player character. Characters make fun of their helmet, which I always found funny. Image: Secret Mode

It’s all standard roguelike stuff, but the familiar format lets me better focus on the races themselves, which are really intense. Turns and obstacles that look far away come up in the blink of an eye, forcing you to react in an instant. Two different kinds of boosts mean you’re constantly surging forward in some way. And all the while, other racers are on the hunt, often ramming your craft or targeting you with weapons. I nearly always felt like I was just on the cusp of losing control, and a split-second mistake usually results in a crash. (When you crash, the whole game also briefly stops to showcase your wreckage flying across the track, which is satisfying in its own way.) Things get even more intense when you finally get into an actual podracer.

It’s extreme in the way that I imagined racing a vehicle in the Star Wars universe would actually be. There’s more to that feeling than the races themselves, though as developer Fuse Games — a relatively new studio with former staffers of Need for Speed, Burnout, and Star Wars Battlefront maker Criterion Games — makes the whole experience feel authentically Star Wars. The speeders and vehicles are grungy and worn, and your fellow racers constantly bicker at each other. (You’ll hear a lot of Huttese.)
