There are wipe transitions between scenes and bombastic, John Williams-esque music. My favorite touch might be the brief scene before each race where you press different buttons to prepare your vehicle, like what the racers do in The Phantom Menace.

Many races force you to drive through cramped caverns, which can be terrifying at high speeds. Image: Secret Mode

That intensity also means that the campaign can be frustrating. I crashed a lot, often because I couldn’t see an obstacle in front of me until far too late, and the opposing racers can be extremely aggressive. I sometimes wished I actually had the reflexes of a Jedi to be able to keep up. A run can take a long time — late in the game, they can exceed two hours — which makes a late loss exasperating. Between tours, you can permanently boost your vehicle’s stats to make the next run easier, though that wasn’t always enough to make the pain of a loss worth it. Occasionally, I turned down the difficulty so that I could play without as much pressure.

Even after a brutal tour, though, I kept finding myself thinking about when I could carve out the time for another run. Galactic Racer isn’t the first Star Wars racing title, but it feels like the best realization yet of a game that embodies what made The Phantom Menace’s racing scene so memorable. I know I’ll never actually get to pilot a podracer, but Galactic Racer is close enough for me to live out my childhood dream.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer launches on October 6th on PC, PS5, and Xbox.

Tech.title: AI hallucinations are making entitled customers even worse
Tech.content:
Madison, a server in New York City, greets every table by asking about each diner’s allergies. Lately, there have been some close calls. “Sometimes people will tell me they have a shellfish allergy, and I’ll come back, and they won’t ask me any questions,” says Madison, who asked that her last name be withheld to protect her identity. “And they’ll order a fish dish that comes with a broth that is made of shellfish.”

When she tells them a dish contains an allergen, she’s had guests push back, saying ChatGPT disagrees. “They just want to talk to ChatGPT,” Madison explains. “You’re allergic to shellfish, and ChatGPT says there’s no shellfish in this, and we are telling you, yes there is!”

Mass adoption of generative AI tools is rewriting the old adage that has long been a thorn in the side of restaurant and retail workers: “The customer is always right.” But what happens when the customer expects you to play along with something AI made up?

Beyond ignoring her warnings about allergens, Madison has noticed an increased reliance on generative AI among patrons at the Michelin-recommended Italian restaurant where she worked until recently. “The amount of times I’ve suggested, ‘Let me grab the sommelier for you,’ and they say, ‘No, I’ll just ask ChatGPT,’ or somms have been dismissed from the table because the guest has a preference for ChatGPT, that has been increasing quite a bit,” she says. She’s had customers request bottles that the restaurant doesn’t carry — or, in some cases, that don’t exist at all.

For Madison, these AI hallucinations exacerbate some people’s preexisting anxieties about wine. “Some people have always had an issue with sommeliers, thinking ‘These people are like used car salesmen trying to get us to spend way more than we want to on a bottle of wine,’” she says, “or there are people who get in their heads and think, ‘The sommelier is going to think I’m stupid.’” To “soften the blow” of AI hallucinations, Madison and her colleagues will say things like, “We have this really hyper-specific wine list, maybe it’s showing you a French wine, and we don’t carry French wine,” instead of telling the customer their AI chatbot completely made up a wine brand.

You’re allergic to shellfish, and ChatGPT says there’s no shellfish in this, and we are telling you, yes there is!

The AI creep is seemingly ubiquitous in customer service jobs now. The launch of Muse, Meta’s new AI agent, will likely exacerbate the issue — and the headaches for workers who have to field customers’ occasionally nonsensical requests. In reporting this story, I heard from movie theater workers, baristas, and Apple Store employees, all of whom have had customers ask for products or features that don’t exist. On Reddit and X, customer service workers are complaining about customers who take ChatGPT’s word as gospel.

Jason, a river ranger who works on federal lands in the Mountain West, says he’s noticed an increase in visitors arriving to the park with nonsensical AI-generated itineraries.

“My colleagues and I have explained that the AI hallucinated campsites or scheduled things out of geographical order, so the group would have to row their boats upstream some days (not possible) and float with the river current other days,” says Jason, who asked to be referred to by a pseudonym because he’s a federal employee. “The craziest part is that even with a ranger explaining this while pointing at a map, we’ve had multiple groups remain skeptical. A certain type of AI user is inclined to trust ChatGPT over rangers, maps, and printed guidebooks.”

Casey, an after-school program teacher in New York who asked to be referred to by a pseudonym, says she’s noticed many students’ parents, nannies, and other caretakers are now turning to ChatGPT or Claude for their questions on childhood development.

“We had one family that consulted ChatGPT to come up with a bedtime routine and sleep schedule for their kid, but their kid wasn’t getting quite enough sleep,” Casey says. Based on his behavior in the program, Casey estimated that the child needed two to three more hours of sleep a night, and told his parents this. “The parents just insisted that their ChatGPT was telling them that their schedule was fine.”

Some parents, she says, now see generative AI tools as experts whose knowledge surpasses that of childcare professionals. “It can be really hard to talk with somebody who has made their mind up,” Casey says, “because they trust this outside entity as being invaluable.” She’s also noticed more anodyne uses of the technology, like kids coming in with AI-generated coloring sheets.

Lauren Wilford, who has worked in food service for 15 years, has noticed AI creeping into her recent interactions with guests as well. It started with the menu: Someone would upload a photo of it to ChatGPT or Claude and ask it what to order, or for guidance on a wine pairing, instead of asking the server.

But now, it appears, some customers have dropped the intermediary altogether. Over the past year, Wilford’s restaurant has been getting calls and emails from agents trying to make reservations on users’ behalf. The rise of agentic AI makes these interactions that much more confusing.

Wilford was surprised when a hands-off client suddenly became demanding on the eve of a big event, making last-minute requests for podiums and AV equipment — neither of which were readily available at the Providence, Rhode Island, restaurant she manages — and eleventh-hour changes to the catering menu. But Wilford was even more taken aback when the clients arrived the next day and didn’t mention any of it. Though she can’t prove it, Wilford believes the requests may not have come from anyone at the company at all; she suspects they were the work of an AI agent.

“I’m sympathetic to the reasons people use AI agents,” Wilford says, especially for bureaucratic and administrative tasks. “But anything where there’s value to two humans seeing each other and working something out together, I think we’re not sensitive to what might be lost if we try to skip all of that stuff.”

Tech.title: Slovenia’s .si domain sees a surge in registrations after Trump’s ‘super intelligence’ order
Tech.content:
In not-so-surprising news, the .si domain name is seeing unprecedented demand after President Trump signed an executive order mandating all government agencies to refer to “AI” and “artificial intelligence” as “SI” and “super intelligence.” It echoes what happened at the start of the AI boom, when interest in the .ai domain name—associated with the country Anguilla—spiked and brought in millions for the island territory.

Now it’s .si’s turn in the spotlight. The domain name was commonly associated with Slovenia, where, ironically, First Lady Melania Trump is from. Klara Herman, a spokesperson at Registry SI, the official organization that manages Slovenia’s domains, told the BBC earlier this week that there was a 2,199% increase in .si domain name purchases in September. However, she was cautious about linking the boost only to President Trump.

Still, the Registry noted 11,000 new addresses recorded on September 30th, the day after President Trump signed the executive order, and almost 13,000 new .si domain names were registered in the past 24 hours.

We reached out to a few other web hosting sites to see if they had seen similar trends. GoDaddy said they don’t yet host the .si domain, and Squarespace hadn’t yet responded as of the time of publication. Wix, interestingly enough, said that they weren’t seeing any “meaningful uptick” on their end, and that it’s been minimal on the site since September 29th. “It’s still early so that could change,” a Wix spokesperson said.

But web hosting platform Hostinger told me that .si is now its second most popular domain extension, right after .com. It found that among its customers, almost 4,300 registered .si on September 30th and about 5,400 on October 1st; more than three-quarters of all .si domains registered since September 23 came in the last two days. It found that more than half the buyers were coming from the U.S. and India.

Curiously enough, on Hostinger, only around 3% of the .si domains are explicitly related to AI, it said. Most are “unclassified,” — meaning their names don’t match any specific category. It said that most of those registering the .si domain name seem to be people and businesses, though there is a speculative element, in that people could be buying the domains to resell them later.

Upon hearing this, my first thought went back to what a founder messaged me earlier this week, noting that .si domains were reselling for over a million dollars. Kim Than, CEO of Genius PR, who specializes in working with AI and crypto founders, told me that he already bought the .si version of his company name “to protect the brand in case this takes off like .ai.” And did so because it was cheap, so he figured he might as well “secure it now than potentially pay a lot more later.”

Than sees domain names as digital collectibles and wants to pick up a few more while the price is still good, and he might resell them later; one can also tokenize domains, he said, and trade them on the blockchain, though he’s not sure if .si is supported just yet. “A few founder friends are buying too cause we think it’s the new AI boom,” he continued. “Who knows how far it goes, but I’m happy to take a bet.”

There is a chance that .si could become pretty popular. President Trump’s executive order said that “the capabilities of today’s frontier systems do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence,” and that they “increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence but a new super intelligence.”

Klaudijus Januitis, head of domains at Hostinger, told me that he expects the demand for .si to keep growing, though he doesn’t see that domain as replacing .ai anytime soon. Instead, as noted by that founder and his friends, Januitis said .si is right now a more available and a “more affordable second option.”

“Slovenia will not see what Anguilla saw,” he said, noting that, for one, Anguilla charges a “premium” to use .si and that money goes straight to the government, while .si is a fraction of the cost and goes to the registry rather than the treasury. For example, on Hostinger, .si costs around $12 dollars a year while .ai goes for $90 and requires a two-year commitment. “For Anguilla, .ai became a second economy. For Slovenia, .si is a nice bonus.”

Tech.title: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Clay’s Kareem Amin on the rise of the GTM engineer
Tech.content:
Two years ago, most companies didn’t have a GTM engineer. Now the role is showing up across tech, with practitioners using AI and automation to build revenue systems that once required multiple people, tools, and manual processes.

What changed — and what does it mean for the way companies find customers and grow?

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Clay co-founder and CEO Kareem Amin will take the AI Stage for “The GTM Engineer: How AI Created Tech’s Next Big Job Category.” He’ll trace how AI has changed the traditional go-to-market stack and helped create a new discipline in its place, giving attendees a look at what AI-native GTM looks like in practice and how it’s changing company growth.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

AI is giving go-to-market teams new ways to research prospects, work with data, personalize outreach, and automate workflows that once moved between separate tools and teams. As those capabilities converge, companies are rethinking not only their GTM technology, but who builds and manages the systems behind growth.

If you’re building a company or rethinking how your team approaches sales, marketing, and growth, this is a new role worth understanding. Secure your Disrupt pass and see where GTM engineering fits into the next generation of go-to-market. Get a second pass at a 50% discount, and more savings for groups of four or more.

What does a GTM engineer actually do?

Traditional go-to-market work can involve hours of researching accounts, cleaning data, qualifying leads, preparing outreach, and moving information between systems. GTM engineering uses AI, data, and automation to turn more of that work into repeatable systems.

Clay coined the role in 2023. Its own GTM engineering guide describes GTM engineers as practitioners who build automated revenue workflows rather than executing individual GTM tasks by hand. The company says roughly 100 GTM engineering job listings are now appearing each month, including roles at companies such as Cursor, Lovable, and Webflow.

For founders and GTM leaders deciding where to put their next dollar or whether to make their next hire, this session offers another way to think about growth. Do you add more people to execute the existing process, or build systems that let the people you already have execute differently?

At Disrupt, Amin will put the shift into context and explore what AI-native GTM looks like in practice. Get your ticket to Disrupt to understand a role that barely existed a few years ago but could change how your next sales, marketing, or growth team operates.

Clay puts AI to work across the GTM stack

Clay started in Brooklyn in 2017 with a goal: give more people access to the power of programming. Its original spreadsheet let users connect information and automate work without writing code. When salespeople, growth teams, and agencies began using it to find and reach customers, Clay followed them into go-to-market.

Today, the company provides infrastructure for GTM teams to access data, run agentic workflows and launch campaigns. Its OpenAI-powered agent, Claygent, automates research and outreach for sales, marketing and recruiting teams.

That evolution has been accompanied by rapid growth. TechCrunch reported in February that the company had tripled annual recurring revenue to $100 million in a year and announced an employee tender offer at a $5 billion valuation. Clay has continued growing since then, announcing a $115 million Series D in September at a $7.1 billion valuation.

Clay is also investing directly in the job category at the center of Amin’s Disrupt session, announcing a $1 million scholarship fund in September to train GTM engineers.

For companies trying to determine where AI can make a meaningful difference in revenue operations, add Amin’s session to your Disrupt agenda and see how one company is putting that model into practice.

From product leader to a new GTM approach

Kareem Amin co-founded Clay in 2017 and serves as its co-founder and CEO. Before Clay, he was VP of product at The Wall Street Journal and co-founded collaboration startup Frame, which Sailthru acquired in 2012.

Amin started Clay around the idea of putting programming capabilities into more people’s hands. AI eventually gave that idea a new application: enabling GTM teams to build systems that automate research, data enrichment, and outreach without relying on traditional engineering resources for every workflow.

Tech.title: Tesla sustains its EV sales momentum despite US troubles
Tech.content:
Tesla sold more than 480,000 EVs in the third quarter, as the company continues finding ways to move new cars despite its troubles in the U.S. market.

It was the second strong quarter in a row for Tesla after a somewhat rough start to the year. The sales figure easily beat out consensus estimates from Wall Street and topped even the most optimistic view for the company, which made its 10 millionth vehicle earlier this year.

The company said Friday morning that it built 464,391 vehicles in the quarter and delivered more than 486,532. That’s an increase of roughly 6,000 vehicle deliveries compared to the second quarter. But sales were still down from the same period last year, when Tesla delivered 497,000 vehicles. That quarter — Tesla’s best ever — was helped by a rush of U.S. buyers who were looking to take advantage of an expiring federal tax credit.

Before Friday’s numbers were released, Tesla’s sales were down nearly 20% year-over-year in the U.S. market, according to Cox Automotive.

That drop has been the result of a number of factors. Tesla has not released any new consumer models in years — with the exception of the Cybertruck, which has been a commercial flop. Potential buyers have also balked because of Elon Musk’s personal support of Donald Trump’s presidential campaign and his role overseeing the Department of Government Efficiency, which laid off thousands of workers and canceled international aid funding.

Tesla has looked to other markets to make up for lost U.S. sales. The company’s sales are on the rise again in Europe, where EVs are more widely adopted and supported by tighter emissions regulations. Tesla is reportedly expanding capacity at its factory in Germany to meet that demand. The company has also seen continued strong sales out of its factory in China despite competition in the region, with some of those sales driven by Tesla looking to newer markets like Japan, Australia, and Lithuania.

Despite the rebound in overall momentum, sales have become something of a taboo subject for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who is increasingly focused on the company’s other efforts. Perhaps the biggest example is the Cybercab, which Tesla started putting on the roads of Austin, Texas in recent weeks. The two-seater EV has been giving autonomous rides to passengers despite having no driver, steering wheel, or pedals.

Tesla also recently launched the production version of its electric big rig, nearly a decade after it was first introduced. The company aims to make roughly 50,000 Tesla Semi vehicles per year.

Other new efforts are in the works, but don’t have firm commercial timelines. The second-generation Roadster is set to be re-revealed on October 15 after years of delays, though it’s not clear when it will get built. Tesla is also developing the Optimus humanoid robot, but has repeatedly pushed back its timeline. Earlier this week, Tesla announced it had secured up to $30 billion in new lines of credit to support these projects.

Tech.title: Medical records giant Epic pauses product development to fix security bugs that risk patients’ data
Tech.content:
Epic, the software technology giant that makes the widely used MyChart software for accessing patients’ medical data, has paused most of its product development as the company works to protect its software and systems from cyberattacks.

Judy Faulkner, the founder and chief executive of Epic, told Modern Healthcare last month that the pause would likely last six weeks while work continues on “safeguarding” the company’s products, after a deployment of Anthropic’s frontier cybersecurity model Mythos unearthed security flaws that could allow access to patients’ data.

The company has not disclosed the nature of the bugs, but its chief security officer Stirling Martin told The New York Times that some customer configurations of MyChart could allow outsiders to access patient records without recording any intrusion in the software’s logs.

Martin, who did not return TechCrunch’s request for comment, told the Times that the AI model did not say if the bug could be exploited to alter patient records without detection, but argued it was enough of a risk to remediate the issues.

Epic’s widely used MyChart software is used to maintain over 320 million patient records across hospitals and doctor’s offices across the United States. Epic says it does not have access to customers’ medical data: that responsibility falls on healthcare providers like hospitals and doctor’s offices. But a bug unknown to Epic could allow hackers to compromise multiple MyChart affected systems located across the United States and raid the data stored within.

It’s rare for a company to pause development to fix security bugs, but the advent of AI tools capable of rapidly finding and exploiting security vulnerabilities has led to concerns that attackers could have an easier time at stealing data.

Healthcare breaches are increasingly common as hackers seek access to highly sensitive health and medical data, under the assumption that providers would pay to prevent hackers from publishing the information online. A 2024 ransomware attack on Change Healthcare, a health tech company owned by insurance giant UnitedHealth tasked with handling payments and billing for most Americans, allowed hackers to steal health data on more than 192 million people, the majority of people in the United States. The company paid the hackers twice not to publish the stolen data.

This year, a string of back-to-back data breaches at healthcare and tech companies have affected tens of millions of Americans. This includes medical records stolen during a breach at electronic health data storage giant CareCloud, millions of rows of patient data from pharmaceutical distributor McKesson, and an unspecified amount of stolen data from U.K.-based health tech company Craneware, whose software is used across North America.

The Department of Health and Human Services currently lists a breach at dental insurance company DentaQuest affecting 15 million people as the largest healthcare-related data breach of 2026 so far.

Tech.title: Rivian’s R2 just helped it set a new sales record
Tech.content:
Rivian sold more electric vehicles than ever in the third quarter, thanks in large part to the launch of its new, more affordable R2 SUV.

The company said Friday morning that it built 19,751 vehicles and delivered 19,248. That’s roughly 45% more than it delivered in the same period last year.

While Rivian didn’t break out how many of those were R2 SUVs, this was the first full quarter of sales of the new vehicle after it launched in June. The company said Friday that it will release its full third-quarter financial results on October 29.

Rivian has big plans for the R2, which currently starts at just under $60,000. The company is betting that it will sell between 20,000 to 25,000 R2 vehicles by the end of the year, which would make it one of the fastest-selling EVs in U.S. history — second only to Tesla’s Model Y. Rivian also plans to make cheaper models available that will cost as low as around $45,000.

If Rivian hits those numbers, the company believes it can sell between 65,000 and 70,000 vehicles this year, including its R1 lineup of vehicles and its commercial electric van. That would be its best sales year ever, as the company has spent the last few years stuck at around the 50,000-vehicles-sold mark.

Rivian is currently building the R2 at its factory in Normal, Illinois, where it recently expanded the production space to accommodate the new SUV. But Rivian is also building a brand new factory outside Atlanta, Georgia, where it expects to be able to build as many as 300,000 vehicles per year in the near future, with the option to expand that capacity down the road.

Rivian needs the R2 to sell well in order to staunch years of heavy losses, due in part to the company’s expensive infrastructure required to support this mass-market vehicle. But Rivian has also signed a deal with Uber to make robotaxi versions of the R2 SUV. Rivian believes robotaxis represent such a big potential market that, in March, the company pushed back its goal of reaching profitability in 2027 to invest more money into autonomy.

Tech.title: Trump’s Crazy AI Rebrand Was a Loyalty Test for Tech Execs—and It Worked
Tech.content:
Seventy years ago last summer, a group of scientists met at Dartmouth College to discuss a wild idea—that machines might one day be capable of human-like thought processes. One of those scientists, John McCarthy, had suggested a name for the new field: artificial intelligence. It stuck. When you search Google Scholar for “artificial intelligence,” approximately 7,420,000 results appear. The term is utterly ubiquitous. Everyone understands it. Even for people who despise AI, the least of their worries is what we call it.

Well, not everyone. Somehow, President Donald J. Trump developed a distaste for the term, and when he doesn’t like something, he feels free to issue an edict against it. In a September 23 speech at the United Nations, he hinted that he might want to do away with the term “artificial intelligence.” His rant seemed like bluster, even for someone with a penchant for renaming gulfs, lakes, and centers for the arts. Renaming an entire field of study and America’s most pivotal industry? This week, at a White House lunch with top AI leaders, he actually pulled the trigger with an executive order declaring that “artificial intelligence” was now a verboten coinage. Instead, the government will call it “Super Intelligence.” Clearly the president expects the private sector to follow suit.

To their shame, the lords of AI meekly acquiesced. From this point on, they will presumably be known as the lords of SI.

One can’t help but see this as the ultimate presidential flex—for all the executives’ trillions of dollars and all their actual intelligence, the alpha in the room was the guy with the orange skin. Changing a name might seem like a minor matter compared to the enormity of constraining a potentially catastrophic technology. But to this crowd, artificial intelligence is much more than a bunch of letters strung together. It’s their foundation. Their identity. When they were kids reading science fiction books under the covers, the term ignited their imaginations.They built or transformed their companies in service of AI, and it's just about all they’ve talked about for the past four years.

Yet when the president used his lunch soiree to win their approval for his wacky idea to undo 70 years of history, apparently not a single person in the room expressed an objection. Not Jeff Bezos, Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Greg Brockman, Alex Karp, or Elon Musk.

Jacob Weisberg, author of the recent book Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era, views the episode as a classic Trump loyalty test, meant to assess if otherwise powerful people will demean themselves to curry the president’s favor and avoid his wrath. If you pass the loyalty test, you fail the backbone test. “The only way to resist this kind of thing is by acting collectively,” says Weisberg. “If all of those guys had just said, ‘We'll agree to the terms of the self-regulation, but we don't accept [the name change], what would he have done?”

Tech.title: Amazon Says It’s No Longer Using NDAs for Data Centers
Tech.content:
Amazon has made a series of new public commitments to communities where it’s building data centers, including making an official announcement that it no longer uses nondisclosure agreements in its arrangements with county officials.

In a blog post published Friday, CEO Matt Garman detailed the steps the company says it’s already taking around data centers. In addition to stopping the use of NDAs, Garman says $1 billion will be invested over the next five years in communities that house the company’s data centers. The money will go toward free community college programs, workforce training, and energy efficiency upgrades for schools, homes, and community buildings.

In the post, Garman acknowledged how the fierce backlash against data centers across the country is hampering the AI buildout.

“Right now there are over 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the country,” he wrote. “If these measures are enacted, the US could be writing its own losing ticket to [the AI] race, and the consequences would last generations. As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

Nondisclosure agreements have become a key point of contention amid the massive data center buildout. Typically, local officials who sign NDAs with data centers looking to develop projects in their area are unable to share information with the public, including the energy and water use of certain projects. Many NDAs bar officials from revealing even basic information—like the tech companies involved in building out the data center. In July, the New York Times reported how secret agreements at all levels of government were crucial in building out plans for Hyperion, its massive data center in Louisiana.

Tech.title: Best Smart Cat Trackers of 2026: Fi Mini vs. Tractive
Tech.content:
However, note that all tested models rely on GPS for location tracking. This means that if the satellite signal is spotty—a common issue in rural areas and other settings—you may not know your cat's precise location. Some Reddit and Amazon reviewers complain that Tractive's location tracking is less accurate in areas with dense vegetation.

Tractive app via Molly Higgins

In setting up each tracker's connected app, you can designate specific mapped areas as safe or danger zones, and the app will notify you when the pet enters or exits these zones. Basil is an indoor cat, but with all three trackers, my apartment was too small to create a virtual fence around the perimeter, so I had to expand it to an area outside my apartment. That means if Basil got out but stayed nearby, I wouldn't get an alert.

In the Tractive app, after you create a profile, you'll get personalized daily activity goals for your cat based on statistics from other cats of similar age and weight. The app assigned Basil 120 to 230 minutes of daily activity and later reported that he was consistently more active than 70 percent of similar cats. I felt at peace knowing I'm keeping him on the move in my small apartment.

At the end of each day and week, the app provides activity averages and daily calorie estimates, calculated using factors like pet type, weight, and size, and compared with activity output.

Tractive's sleep-tracking feature monitors sleep duration, breaking it down into categories of night sleep, day sleep, and calm. Because it tracks sleep length and cycle phases based on movement patterns and time of day, the data is more general than precise. In general, I found the information in Tractive's app more useful and easier to analyze than in Fi.

Best Battery Life, Charging, and Size

Testing these trackers made me realize the importance of basic features like battery life and ease of removing the tracker from the collar for charging. This is where the Fi Mini shines. (Read my full review here.)
