One bonus for Fi users with an Apple Watch: You can add the Fi app to your watch to monitor your pet’s location and activity and enter “Lost Mode” without a phone, which is especially helpful if your cat has escaped while you're away from your phone.

Tech.title: Your Driverless Cab Is Spying on You
Tech.content:
One afternoon this past summer, a self-driving Waymo pulled into a parking lot in San Mateo County, California, and stayed there until the police arrived. Local cops had gotten a 911 call from Waymo staffers—humans, it should be said—who were viewing the car’s passengers through cameras installed inside the vehicle. It looked like two teens were shooting a black handgun out the window of the vehicle, playing with it and drinking between shots, a police report said.

The story has a happy(ish) ending: The gun was shooting water-filled Orbeez, not bullets. But the incident drew attention to Waymo’s surveillance system. The cars are equipped with automated tech that can flag the presence of a firearm inside, the company said.

The outsides of self-driving cars are studded with cameras, which help them “see” the world around them. (Most also use other sensors, including radar and lidar.) Less appreciated are the cameras inside the vehicles, which companies say are essential to keeping riders safe and enforcing their rules. Earlier this year, Waymo said it used its cabin cameras to do both after some California passengers, many in their twenties or older, reported that Waymo employees suddenly took over the vehicles’ intercoms mid-ride to make sure they were old enough to ride on their own. (One 35-year-old told WIRED he thought his backpack sent up red flags.)

Still, robotaxi privacy policies can be broad. They suggest that footage captured inside vehicles can be used for many innocuous and commonsense reasons—to check cleanliness between rides, to detect lost items—but also to improve their products or services. These catch-all terms could cover many uses. Experts say that in the US, few clear rules govern this sort of surveillance, especially because riders often must agree to lengthy “terms of service” printed in minute fonts before they use ride-hailing apps. That leaves riders to trust that the companies are handling their information responsibly.

“We are being essentially abandoned by our lawmakers when it comes to consumer privacy and what companies can do with information after they’ve collected it,” says Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, where he works on surveillance and policing issues. His advice? “Just because you’re alone in the car doesn’t mean you’re alone in the car. You should behave as if there’s a jumpy person in the front seat.”

In general, robotaxi companies including Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla say that human staff view interior cameras only when needed. All say personal data, including recordings, may be sent to law enforcement or regulators. (A Waymo support page says that government agencies seeking data “are directed to follow valid legal processes in making such request.”)

Tech.title: Election Deniers Think the GOP’s Terrible Midterm Polling Is a ‘Psyop’
Tech.content:
Taking their lead from president Donald Trump, election deniers have dismissed the GOP’s terrible polling numbers by claiming the polls themselves are fake, a psyop, or a ploy to stop Republicans from turning out to vote in November.

Kevin Roberts, president of the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, told Fox News that midterm election polling is a “psyop…to depress conservative turnout.”

“The midterms are near,” Phillip Buchanan, the election denier and MAGA troll known online as Catturd, wrote to his four million followers on X. “The laughable fake polls are rolling out.”

For over a decade, Trump has claimed without evidence that American elections have been impacted by fraud. In the wake of his loss in 2020, an entire online community and ecosystem of election denial groups sprung up to push the baseless allegation that former president Joe Biden stole the election from Trump. These claims have become central to the Republican Party’s belief system, to the point where hundreds of GOP candidates for federal and statewide elections in November have expressed doubts about the integrity of US elections.

And now, multiple polls have shown Trump’s approval rating at historic lows with Democrats leading in Senate races across the country in states Trump won easily in 2024. Reuters reported this week that Republicans are now pouring money into dozens of races they considered safe.

Tech.title: A Flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac App Could Have Let Hackers Grab Sensitive Data
Tech.content:
Hardly a day goes by lately without news of AI agents autonomously hacking websites or AI tools being used by cybercriminals and scammers. But a recently patched vulnerability in the macOS version of OpenAI’s ChatGPT underscores the potential value to attackers of compromising AI software itself as these apps proliferate more and more.

The bug could have been exploited to essentially take over ChatGPT on a victim’s computer, giving an attacker access to all the chat logs and other data stored by the app, as well as interconnections like browser sessions. Discovered by researchers at the Objective-See Foundation, the vulnerability illustrates the deep system access and trust that AI platforms are afforded in order to work—and the target that this puts on their backs.

“Agents need a lot of access to do their job,” says Objective-See Foundation software analyst and longtime macOS researcher Patrick Wardle. “They are like the building manager who has access to the keys to all the rooms. So if they can be corrupted or subverted, that’s super problematic. It can mean that unprivileged code could then potentially have access to all the things.”

OpenAI publicly acknowledged the security flaw and fix in its system change log on September 25. “We continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster,” OpenAI spokesperson Shane Bauer told WIRED in a statement.

The ChatGPT macOS app includes multiple components that communicate with each other securely by checking for digital signatures. The idea is to confirm with these validity checks that both processes are OpenAI components and not outside, potentially malicious software making a request. And the system design goes so far as to require these signature checks at three layers of remove from the request, to ensure that malicious software isn’t somehow directing an OpenAI component to be a proxy and make a seemingly trusted request.

Tech.title: Health Care Workers Are Tired of Cleaning Up Palantir’s Mess
Tech.content:
Over the past four months, Amber Retzloff, a critical care nurse in Florida, requested to work 50 specific 12-hour shifts. But over half the time, she says her hospital’s Palantir-powered scheduling software assigned her to different shifts, often putting her on back-to-back-to-back days and leaving her mentally drained. Retzloff doesn’t expect to always get the slots she wants, but by her count the tool does a far worse job honoring her preferences than managers did when they assigned shifts by hand.

Retzloff’s experience mirrors that of other nurses across HCA Healthcare, the largest hospital chain in the US. Since 2023, HCA has rolled out an AI scheduling tool it co-developed with Palantir called Timpani at roughly 130 of its 190 locations. Retzloff’s hospital adopted it nearly two years ago.

“No one is happy with Timpani,” says Retzloff, echoing what five nurses at other locations reported in interviews with WIRED. “Everyone complains all the time.” Other purported HCA workers have expressed similar gripes about the tool on platforms like Reddit.

The nurses who spoke with WIRED allege that Timpani has potentially harmed patients by causing care teams to be understaffed, imbalanced, and exhausted. Operating with minimal oversight, they say the tool routinely schedules too few nurses or not enough experienced veterans during shifts, particularly on Sundays. It also frequently ignores nurses’ stated preferences for spacing out shifts, working nights and weekends, or taking specific days off.

As a result, nurses say they are being forced to waste more time trying to trade shifts or appeal their schedules than prior to the arrival of the software. They also believe colleagues are increasingly calling out, using paid or unpaid time to skip assignments, though doing so more than a few times annually puts them at risk of termination.

Retzloff, 34, a National Nurses United labor union leader with a decade of bedside experience, recalls recent shifts where all four of her colleagues were junior. Because she was the only senior nurse working, Retzloff says she had to delay care for the sickest patients to guide the novices through milder cases.

HCA is “letting AI dictate,” Retzloff says. “We are overriding clinical judgment and the human-to-human piece of health care with an app.”

Previously, managers handled scheduling manually and generally consulted nurses well in advance when overriding requests. With Timpani, nurses report needing to make alternative arrangements on shorter notice and an increase in temporary reassignments to different teams. “I can’t remember any issues before,” says a non-union nurse in Texas who asked to remain anonymous out of fear of retaliation from HCA. “Everything came out on time.”

Tech.title: 31 Best STEM Toys for Kids (2026): Learning Made Fun
Tech.content:
There’s something super-satisfying about these tactile building blocks. They come in a range of appealing colors and have a slightly squishy form that makes them delightful to build with and pull apart. Because the pieces are all the same, children don’t have to spend ages searching for a specific block as they do with Lego. They can pick by color or just experiment, and it’s as easy to create bracelets and headbands as it is to construct robots and bridges.

These building blocks were very popular in the classroom with 7- and 8-year-olds. Some kids had fun just playing without something specific in mind, while others planned scenes and put their engineering skills to use to realize them. There are also some instruction booklets with suggestions.

For kids aged 5 years and up.

Tech.title: Reddit Is Choking Off RSS and Open Web Access to Keep AI Bots Out
Tech.content:
People who post on Reddit often love to complain, especially if it’s about Reddit itself. Now they have a legit reason to do so.

The massive network of online discussion forums and social news aggregator has announced a timetable and details regarding its new antibot and data-scraping measures, which include discontinuing support for RSS feeds on Nov. 13.

The platform, which boasts over 500 million monthly active users, first hinted at these changes in early August and outlined measures it said were to protect the site from spam and to make moderation easier. But subsequent updates left users with lingering questions about when restrictions on public APIs — the rules that allow interaction between software programs — and changes to the site’s Old Reddit version would take effect.

More from CNET

Under the new policy, access to Old Reddit will be restricted to individuals who have used the legacy interface within the last six months. Many users still prefer this classic layout because it features fewer ads and loads faster due to its text-heavy design. As user shillyshally writes, “No geegaws, just straight up info and ads that are unobtrusive text only.”

As for slamming the door on RSS feeds, the company said those feeds have become a huge attack surface for “large-scale scraping and automated abuse,” though it will support moderators who need that option for subreddits through its developer platform. RSS is an open-web standard that lets users consume content on their own terms, without targeted ads, tracking cookies, sponsored posts or engagement-based algorithms that steer what you see.

And while it previously mentioned limiting its public API, Reddit now says it will move all public API access to its developer platform, Devvit, effectively closing the open web “front door.” That means any third-party developer accessing Reddit will need to be inside the site’s tightly controlled sandbox, barring any off-the-books workarounds or hacking.

The company said in a post on Wednesday that it’s easing the transition to its developer platform by working directly with creators to migrate over 14,000 registered apps, close technical capability gaps and help communities find new owners for abandoned bots.

A representative told CNET in an email that the company had no comment beyond the updates it had posted publicly.

Reddit vs. Reddit

Reddit frames the move as a necessary defense against abuse and theft by unauthorized AI scrapers, but some critics view it as a deliberate strategy to force users into its proprietary ecosystem. By killing open RSS feeds and shutting down public APIs, Reddit appears to be closing off ad-free, third-party alternatives that have allowed people to easily access and sort large volumes of news and messages.

While Reddit points moderators toward internal tools like the Discord Relay app for alerts, the company says that general users relying on RSS feeds for reading Reddit content beyond moderation are out of luck: “If you use RSS for feeds outside of a community you moderate, there is no replacement. RSS has been a beloved part of the open web for a long time, and we’re grateful to everyone who used it to stay connected to Reddit.”

Many have been quick to point out that eliminating open standards will break independent workflows and result in total platform enclosure. Users will be funneled directly into the official app and modern desktop site, where Reddit can capture ad impressions, collect usage data and ensure that its vast data — composed of many human conversations — is reserved exclusively for high-value corporate AI licensing deals with partners like Google and OpenAI.

Some users complained that Reddit’s current app and design are why they use a third-party app or still use Old Reddit. “old.reddit.com was first created in 2018,” said da_chicken, “and new reddit is still worse in every way except the lack of dark mode. You can’t compete with your own design from almost a decade ago.”

Not surprisingly, many on the RSS subreddit said they’re done with X (formerly Twitter) once RSS goes away. “I follow about 20 subs, and have nested posts/threads I subscribe to if I find something interesting and want to see replies. Without RSS, I don’t see how the site is even usable,” wrote way-too-lazy.

One user suggested reaching far back into internet history to replace Reddit. “Maybe we should go back to DIGG. Are they still around?” asked OneCalledWell.

Tech.title: Audible Will Soon Let You Use AI to Talk to a Book Character
Tech.content:
Audible is making audiobook listening more immersive. The Amazon-owned streaming service launched three new AI-powered features on Thursday to expand the book-listening experience. You’ll be able to explore character guides, interact with stories and access bonus content to learn more about cities and landmarks referenced in the book you’re listening to.

Yes, this means the ability to hold a conversation with a book’s character is on the horizon. Generative AI is the tool that’s powering the Interactive Story feature. Users will soon be able to engage, for instance, with Count Dracula’s rat-eating manservant, Renfield, through a new interactive story.

According to Audible, the interactive nature of this feature is guided by the creators and publishers of the titles it’ll be featured on, thus keeping the narrative grounded and believably connected to the events in the book. (Audible didn’t say who guides the feature on books by dead authors like Dracula’s Bram Stoker.)

More from CNET

“The character speaks first, assigning the listener a role, goal, and stakes; the listener responds in their own words, and the character reacts in real time,” Audible explains.

Audible’s new interactive AI features — Interactive Story, Character Guide and Visual Explorer — will expand your audiobook listening experience. Audible

I went looking for this interactive story as a chapter in Dracula, a new Audible Original that premiered Thursday, but Renfield on the Run was nowhere to be found. Perhaps the rollout of this feature will take some time for users to access with this title. I’m on an Android phone, so that may also be an issue.

The press release says these new AI features are in beta testing and will be rolling out in a limited capacity for customers in the US and UK.

An Audible spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to our request for further comment.

What I did find in Dracula, though, was the newly launched Character Guide feature, which tracks the speaking character in real time and offers an information card with details about the performer playing the role. It’s all on the player page, minimizing distractions.

The character guide feature is now available for George Orwell’s 1984 and will be part of Audible’s upcoming original audiobook Exoplanet, written by Benjamin Percy and executive-produced by Project Hail Mary author Andy Weir. Audible plans to expand this feature to let listeners interact with the guide and ask questions as the story progresses.

Visual Explorer has yet to launch, but this feature will provide listeners with additional imagery and visual context for locations and important moments featured in a given narrative.

“These new features invite listeners into a story in ways that simply weren’t possible before, marking the latest step in our nearly 30-year journey to push audio storytelling forward,” Audible’s Chief Content Officer Rachel Ghiazza said in a statement.

Tech.title: Trading In Your Smartphone During Holiday Sales? Our Readers Recommend This Brand for Your Next Upgrade
Tech.content:
Early holiday sales are coming up. Whether you’re considering one of the newest smartphone models like the Pixel 11, Samsung Galaxy S26, one from the iPhone 18 lineup or one of the older models, now could be a good time to get a new phone without paying full price. You may choose to stay loyal to the phone brand you’ve stuck with for years, or you could use the upgrade as a chance to try a new one.

CNET readers shared what they think about their smartphone in our People’s Picks survey to help you narrow down your choice before the sales start. We asked about the phone features and buying factors that matter most, such as battery life, price-to-value and durability. Readers boiled their favorites down to four big-name brands, but there’s one winner that may surprise you. Spoiler alert, it’s not Apple.

Overall winner: Google

Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

Google is the overall winner for CNET’s People’s Picks for Phones. CNET averaged the scores across three categories to determine the overall satisfaction rating, which includes customer satisfaction, battery longevity and price-to-value.

More from CNET

Google wins with a score of 4.52 out of 5, while Motorola trails closely behind with 4.45.

“It’s no surprise to me that Google and Motorola scored top marks because both sell some of the most affordable phones that people can buy. Motorola’s Moto G series costs hundreds of dollars less than Apple’s cheapest iPhone,” said CNET Director of Content Patrick Holland. “At $500, Google’s Pixel 10A is one of the best values that you can buy today, especially as phone prices spike due to the ongoing RAM shortage caused by AI and data centers. It just goes to show that in 2026, you can spend less than $500 and still have a great phone that lasts you years.”

On the other hand, Samsung and Apple trail behind with scores of 4.19 and 3.87, respectively. Both brands have evolved in the smartphone space with AI-powered features, upgraded cameras and thinner phone designs, but fell short in this category.

“There are a few factors at play here, most notably that Google and Motorola ship a fraction of the phones that Samsung does — so Pixel and Razr buyers are a more devoted core of customers than the many who buy Galaxy phones,” said CNET Managing Editor David Lumb. A Counterpoint Research report on phone shipments in the first quarter of 2026 noted that Google (3% of the US market) and Motorola (10%) combined accounted for half of Samsung’s market share (26%).

The other thing to remember is that Google sells mostly premium phones.



“Aside from the Pixel 10A as a midrange device, Motorola and Samsung have wider ranges of more affordable and cheap phones, so I’d guess there’s less consumer fondness at the lower end of the device price scale,” Lumb said.

Apple’s fourth-place spot is a tougher nut to crack. Perhaps consumers haven’t seen as many upgrades in successive years as they would like in new iPhones, or they’re miffed at the higher prices Apple’s phones sell for. What’s most likely the case, Lumb suggested, is that there are simply more people buying new iPhones. In the Counterpoint report above, Apple handsets accounted for 58% of all phones shipped in the US.

AI features

AI features like photo editing, live translation and AI-powered summaries are becoming the focal point for new smartphone models. But what matters more is how much you’ll use those built-in features. Google Pixel wins with 88% of its users saying their phone’s AI features are essential and occasionally useful.

“Out of the four brands, only one is a true AI company, and that’s Google,” Holland said. In fact, Google’s Gemini AI can run on phones from all four brands, including the iPhone via an app. The Gemini Assistant can be used on Motorola and Samsung phones.”

Lumb added that Google has led the charge in both including and promoting AI features in its Pixel phones that people actually use, like Magic Eraser and live translation.

“Pixel owners have been using AI features for years, and combined with Google aggressively inserting its Gemini assistant throughout the phone, it makes sense that Samsung Galaxy owners would feel a lesser impact from AI,” he said.

Samsung has made plenty of AI advancements, like a health assistant and browser upgrades, but it falls behind, with only 64% of its users saying the same. Apple and Motorola trail behind with 14% and 8% each. Most Motorola users say the phone lacked built-in tools or ignored them.



What few AI features are available on iPhones were introduced more recently, so it’s unsurprising that their owners wouldn’t consider them essential to daily use, Lumb said. While Gemini continues to evolve, Apple’s advanced AI Siri was delayed for years and finally arrived with iOS 27.

Battery life

Ties with Motorola



For a phone’s battery to exceed expectations, it must last a day or more. Motorola and Google tie in this category, with 74% saying their phones’ batteries exceed expectations by lasting a full day or longer without needing to be charged. Comparatively, Samsung and Apple fall behind, with only about half (52%) saying their phones’ batteries exceed expectations, while others say they just meet expectations. Apple finishes last, with only 31% reporting the same for their iPhones’ batteries. Most said their phone needed to be charged midday.

“The No. 1 factor for battery life is how you use your phone. And I think this result speaks volumes about how much iPhone owners are on their phones,” Holland said.

CNET’s phone battery testing found that Apple’s phones had the longest battery life, with OnePlus placing second and Motorola third. However, the test doesn’t account for how you use your phone specifically each day – everyone is different. If you’re hyper-connected and your default is scrolling through social media apps or streaming videos, even the best battery life won’t be enough for you, Holland said.

“Thankfully, Google, Motorola and Samsung, along with Apple, have all increased the charging speeds on their handsets to at least make topping them off less of a pain,” he said.

Motorola

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Value

Motorola wins in price-to-value, with 82% of its readers saying it offers exceptional value by delivering more than its price suggests. Only 4% rate the brand as overpriced.

“Before Motorola brought back the Razr as a foldable phone, its most popular handsets were its Moto G line that start as low as $200 and top out at $350,” Holland said. “Motorola has deep, long-term relationships with phone carriers, which often sell these phones at a discount.”

Compared with other brands, 45% of Pixel owners say Google’s phone offers exceptional value, and 35% of Samsung users say the same.

The surprising fact is that Apple places fourth in this category, with 58% of iPhone users saying it’s overpriced. Only 12% find the phone’s value exceptional. However, many tech brands are raising prices due to the RAM shortage, which makes it tough to determine what’s worth the high cost.

Apple

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Durability

Choosing a phone that doesn’t shatter, crack or leave you with a broken camera can make a big difference when you need one to last a few years. Some phones are more durable than others. Apple wins this category with 78% of readers saying it’s highly durable against drops and daily use with minimal to no damage. The remaining 22% either deal with normal wear and minor scuffs over time, report their phone as fragile or always have a heavy-duty case to protect it.

Holland said that when Apple released the iPhone 12 in 2020, it was the first to have a flat, dense build with squared-off sides to increase durability. In the years following, Samsung followed suit, adopting a flat build for its Galaxy S and S Plus models, and Google implemented a similar design with its Pixel phones.

Google follows closely behind with 72% saying their Pixel smartphone is highly durable, while 28% say it’s moderately durable.

Not as many readers with a Motorola say the phone is highly durable (65%), but even fewer readers with a Samsung (58%) phone say the same. Samsung users say their foldable phone and screens are fragile and only moderately durable. Some readers criticize the brand for the phone’s fragility and susceptibility to damage from drops.

Brand retention and loyalty

Despite Apple falling short in several categories, 86% of Apple users said they’re extremely likely to buy the same brand next time.

“Apple’s most popular product is the iPhone, but its iPhone-only features like iMessage and FaceTime, not found on Android, that keep people tied in,” Holland said. “Also, if you want to learn about how to use your iPhone or get it fixed, you can go to the Apple Store and talk with an actual human – I think those retail stores are Apple’s secret weapon.”

Whereas 79% of Samsung owners share the same sentiment for the brand. Over half of Google Pixel owners (58%) would buy a Google phone again, but only 42% of people with Motorola phones would. Other Motorola owners are using competitor research to determine their next phone purchase.

Did you agree with these findings? CNET’s People’s Picks is community-driven and helps us spread the word about the tech and services you love. Take our ongoing privacy and security apps survey to tell us what you love about yours.

Methodology

CNET commissioned Alchemer to conduct the People’s Picks survey to compile data. The survey was carried out online, and all figures are from Alchemer. The total sample comprised 1,107 adults. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus). Fieldwork was undertaken from July 1 to July 28, 2026.

Tech.title: Ninja’s New Chopper Is Like Nothing I’ve Tested (Just Don’t Call It a Food Processor)
Tech.content:
It often seems as though Ninja has some sort of Bat Phone to the patron saint of small kitchen appliances. Every new product they introduce is fundamentally different and quite often superior to everything else in its category, making us wonder how we ever lived without that functionality.

SharkNinja Ninja Prepi 8.4 See at Ninja Pros & Cons Modular design for easy component storage

Two bowls of different sizes for true food prep versatility

Lids for bowls allow them to also be used for storage

Bowls are different sizes but have same diameter so lids are interchangeable

Lightweight but powerful motor pod that snaps in and out

Snap-off lid easy to remove for scraping down sides

3-part feed chute is versatile for components of various sizes

Dicing Kit accessory for additional functionality Snaps to lock lid can be fussy

Bowl shape can allow small pieces to stay unblended

Numerous components don’t store as compactly

Bowls don’t include handles, which can make scraping challenging

Components can get stuck in the dicing kit system

From blenders to air fryers to coffee makers, Ninja regularly lands a top spot in CNET’s “best of” lists, and with its latest release, is shaking up the food processor game. Because it’s Ninja, though, and with never-before-seen versatility and design, it also comes with a twee product name. Enter: Ninja Prepi.

Ninja doesn’t call the Prepi a food processor, but rather a meal prep system, and for good reason. One of Ninja’s hallmarks is its modular design, which lets it function as an appliance and a storage or serving vessel, and the new Ninja Prepi system offers exactly that.

More from CNET

Prepi does much of what a food processor does, but it bills itself as a meal prep system.

Instead of a heavy base with a motor that you stack with a food-processing bowl and blade, the Ninja Prepi flips the script: a motor pod snaps onto the lid, similar to the vibe of the Ninja Crispi air fryer, and then sits on a utilitarian bowl. So let’s get into it.

Ninja Prepi at a glance

Style: modular food processor/food prep system with two bowl sizes, lids, and a separate motor pod. Includes slicing and crinkle-cut discs, and an optional Dicing Kit accessory is available either as part of the Ninja Prepi package or as a separate purchase.

Dimensions (when assembled with larger bowl): 7.38” L x 10” W x 15.56” H

Watts: 500

Weight: 10.6 pounds

Price $180

Ninja Prepi setup

If you’re already familiar with a food processor, the Ninja Prepi is simple to set up, even though it’s somewhat upside down compared with other food processors. The chopping/puree blade sets onto a spindle centered in the bowl. (A smaller spindle is included for the smaller bowl.) The lid, which includes a three-part feed chute, locks onto the top of the bowl with two side snaps. The motorized pod snaps intuitively into place on the lid and includes an obvious eject button that easily pops it back out.

Both included discs (slice/shred and crinkle cut) fit on either spindle, while the optional Dicing Kit sits inside the larger bowl, no spindle needed.

Either included disc—slice/shred or crinkle cut—fits onto the top of either spindle, and the optional $60 Dicing Kit fits inside the top of the larger bowl without the spindle. A dial on the front of the motor has chop, pulse, low, high and disc settings, plus a stop/start button that illuminates only when the motor pod is snapped in correctly.

Ninja Prepi operation

Although the Ninja Prepi is upside down compared with typical food processors, the operation is standard. Set the dial on the front of the motor pod to the desired function or speed, then use the stop/start button to begin or pulse as needed.

You can change the mode and speed with the circular control. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Even with the motor pod snapped into place, you can unclip the entire lid of the Ninja Prepi system from the bowl and place it on the smaller bowl. Once prep is done, you can remove the blades and spindles and use the functional plastic bowls to serve or top with the included rubber lids for storage.

The chute built into the lid disassembles for maximum control in inserting components of varying thicknesses, allowing for three different widths.

What I liked about Ninja Prepi

Like the Foodi, the separate bowls let you switch the motor between projects. Pamela Vachon/CNET

The Ninja Prepi’s dual-bowl versatility is its main selling point, and calling it a Meal-Prep System, rather than a food processor, is a smart move by the brand. The system doesn’t have the largest volume or the most powerful motor, but no other food processor makes it as easy to run multiple components or recipes at once without emptying and cleaning the bowl first.

The plastic bowls aren’t anything fancy, but they’re perfectly innocuous serving vessels that don’t require an extra dish, and the included lids add storage functionality that basically no other food processor can claim. If my main requirement for a food processor was to chop individual components for meal prep throughout the week, this would be a game changer.

The motorized pod snaps intuitively into place on the lid and includes an obvious eject button that easily pops it back out.

While food processors are generally not that heavy, the motorized pod is the only substantial part of the Ninja Prepi system and is extremely compact, making it easy to move around and to store. Because it operates top-down, gravity works in the Prepi’s favor, so it doesn’t require a weighted base. All of this makes for a system that doesn’t require much vertical storage space, and that is also relatively portable.

Everything but the pod can go in the dishwasher, which makes cleanup easier than most standard food processors; even without a dishwasher, the atypical bowl shape the Ninja Prepi features is much easier to hand-wash.

The Best Food Processors We Tested See at CNET

While the Prepi’s $179 price is a little higher than the average food processor of similar volume, I believe the value it offers is fair and doesn’t come close to the price of a high-end system. It would be a solid investment for those who can put its exceptional versatility to good use.

What I disliked about Ninja Prepi

To create a meal prep system, however, the Ninja Prepi had to make some food-processor sacrifices, which shouldn’t be discounted. My main complaint is the lack of a handle on either bowl. I understand the choice, since it needs to function as a potential serving or storage vessel, but as someone whose main use of a food processor is to make a melange such as hummus or pesto, I want something more secure to hold onto when scraping it out. Is this a deal breaker? No. Is it still annoying? Yes.

Pamela Vachon/CNET

The clip-on lid can also be a little fussy, and with the motor pod clipped in, I felt like there were several instances where I had to keep adjusting the fit to get the clips to clamp down correctly. This is a necessary safety feature, which I appreciate, but it doesn’t make it any less annoying when you have to fuss with it.

Because the Prepi has a bowl shape, rather than the straight-sided walls of a typical food processor, I also found that components could sometimes be out of reach of the blade. It’s nothing that pausing and scraping down wouldn’t fix, which you’d be doing with a typical food processor anyway, but it was enough to warrant a mention. Again, not a deal breaker, especially if the slice/shred/crinkle cut discs are your main event.

The Prepi has a lot of components, for better or worse. Pamela Vachon/CNET

While the Prepi breaks down more thoroughly into its component parts than other food processors, requiring less vertical space for storage, unlike the functionality with the Ninja Crispi they don’t stack as easily. Both bowls included in the system have the same mouth diameter, which lets the chute lid and storage lids work with both, but they don’t nest inside each other. Unless you’re holding onto the box, there are a lot of individual pieces to keep track of here, even more so if you’re also invested in the optional Dicing Kit.

Final verdict on Ninja Prepi

As a food processor, the Ninja Prepi isn’t the most powerful or the best value for its size, but as a meal prep system with multifunctional, simultaneous capabilities, it’s in a class of its own. If its versatility compels you, then the $180 price tag shouldn’t be a barrier.

Tech.title: I Tested the Galaxy S26 Ultra Cameras Against the Pixel 11 Pro: One Captures Vibes Better
Tech.content:
September just ended, but I’m still reminiscing over my end-of-summer trip to Cape May. It was the perfect weekend getaway to the southernmost town of New Jersey, where the sun beamed through voluminous clouds and the streets were bustling — I even remembered to fold the bed sheets that first morning.

This was also the perfect opportunity to test and compare the camera quality of the $1,299 Google Pixel 11 Pro XL and the now-$1,400 Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, two of the best Android phones we’ve tested at CNET.

This year’s flagship models feature iterative hardware updates, with the most notable changes being modifications to camera sensor architectures that allow for more light and, therefore, detail to be captured. This was mostly expected, as my colleague Jeff Carlson found last year’s Samsung and Google models already quite adequate.

More from CNET

Instead, both companies leaned more into image processing and how their respective AI models could detect and modify subjects to get you an “ideal” shot. Below, I’ll walk you through a gallery of photos I captured throughout my trip that I took under various lighting conditions and with moving subjects to help you determine which phone camera is best for you.

Note that all of these photos were captured using each phone’s native camera settings and were not modified after the fact, except for straightening in Adobe Lightroom.

Pixel 11 Pro XL vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra: Ultrawide

Let’s begin with ultrawide shots I took before driving through the Garden State Parkway. The first difference I noticed between the Pixel’s 48-megapixel sensor and the Samsung’s 50-megapixel sensor was how they process colors. The Pixel portrays trees, roads and the sky in more neutral, realistic tones, whereas the Samsung leans toward more vibrant, saturated tones.

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

The better camera ultimately comes down to the flavor of green and blue you prefer, but if I had to pick a phone based on its color science alone, I would choose the Pixel, as it appears less modified.

One camera is decisively better when you look at the details of the clouds. Samsung wins here with a more balanced exposure and highlights, depicting the ever-random, cotton-ball shapes of clouds. You can clearly distinguish how each cloud merges with another. On the Pixel, however, the clouds are blown out, appearing as a single white blob.

Generally speaking, the Pixel captures photos with a warmer color temperature, as you can see the difference in my wife’s sleeves and the surrounding tree leaves as we walked through the Cape May Zoo.

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

If you prefer something cooler, like on the Samsung, you can always tweak things in post or through the new Camera Looks introduced with the Pixel 11 lineup. They’re effectively real-time filters that apply to the phone’s imaging pipeline, giving you creative control before the phone even processes the image.

In the same photos above, notice how the edges of the ultrawide angle are blurrier on the Samsung. This can be chalked up to a slower shutter speed or less effective stabilization, though it can also be interpreted as giving the photo a more dynamic feel. I would still pick the Pixel in this case.

Pixel 11 Pro XL vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra: Telephoto

The far-distance, telephoto comparison may be the biggest toss-up between the two phones. On paper, Samsung should have the advantage, with an extra 10-MP telephoto (for 3x optical zoom) to accommodate the 50-MP telephoto (for 5x optical zoom). Google, on the other hand, uses a main sensor crop for close-up shots, then switches to its single 48-MP 5x telephoto for longer distances.

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

In practice, the quality of both phone cameras is quite good, with natural-looking bokeh (background blur) and separation between the subject and what’s behind it. When we walked by a crocodile lounging by the fence, it was a great opportunity to see how well the sensors captured the textures of its rough skin while gradually smoothing out the grass behind the animal.

My ideal shot is somewhere in the middle. I like how natural the colors and background blur on the Pixel, but I prefer the contrast levels on the Samsung, which give the crocodile more depth and detail. For some, Samsung’s output may almost be too sharp. But if what you’re after is as much detail as possible from far away, it’s the superior camera system.

In the middle of the walk, we stopped by a gift shop for souvenirs and snacks. (I also stopped by for the abundance of colors in the room, but that’s between you and me.) I picked up a name tag, swiped over to portrait mode on both phones, then snapped a picture.

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

The result is the Pixel producing an ever-warmer photo with a generous amount of bokeh and smoother edges around the name tag, while the Samsung produces one with sharper edges and subject isolation, but worse blurring. You can see the artificial processing overworking in Samsung’s photo, with the two B’s in “ABBY” slightly blurred.

The portrait mode effect can be toned down in both the viewfinder and the gallery afterward, but as I mentioned earlier, I am only comparing photos straight out of the camera’s default settings here.

Pixel 11 Pro XL vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra: Main camera

For lunch, we settled on a Cape May classic: the Lobster House. The half-century-old institution, which is docked by the harbor, is best known for its fresh seafood, including lobster, oyster and fish. And the dim-lit ambiance, an old-school maritime theme with fishing ropes and wooden planks made for a good test of the phones’ dynamic range.

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

In this first shot at the table, I’m very impressed with the sharpness and contrast from the Samsung. The highlights are managed well, too, with noticeable detail in the ships parked outside. The Pixel’s image is flatter, with just about everything appearing too smooth, and shadows that would otherwise make things more dramatic are lifted.

After the meal, we wandered through Cape May to view the iconic Victorian houses, with their high-gabled roofs and distinctive color schemes that would fit any Roald Dahl movie. In this scenario, both phones produced great-looking photos, juggling the various lines and textures of the houses with the bright sky and commendably well-maintained lawns.

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

If there’s one comparison where the difference truly comes down to color fidelity, this is the one. Take your pick.

Pixel 11 Pro XL vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra: Moonshot

A few years ago, a big controversy surrounded the Samsung Galaxy S21 Ultra and its seemingly unimaginable ability to capture clear, detailed photos of the moon. The company reportedly used AI to detect when a moon was in the camera frame, then enhanced the image to fill in details such as craters. Apparently, that’s still a thing, and Google is in on the artificial magic, too.

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

Compared with Samsung’s 100x Space Zoom, the Pixel’s 120x Pro Zoom produces a brighter image, though not as detailed. There’s simply more surface clarity of the Moon in the Samsung image, likely due to the underexposure. By reducing the overly bright planet at night, the Samsung camera renders its textures more accurately. By the way, I took both of the shots with the devices held in hand, so the electronic stabilization on both devices helped a lot.

There’s no easy way to validate the results of both images, but if I had to choose one for a moonshot, I would pick Samsung.

Which is the better camera?

In most cases, the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra is the better, more capable camera phone for me. I also prefer a camera that produces social-ready imagery, so the touch of saturation and sharpness makes Samsung’s output more ideal.

While I based the comparison on camera samples shot with default settings, know that both devices offer creative tools to tweak how images are captured. The Pixel 11 Pro’s Camera Looks, for example, lets you modify colors, tones, and sharpness in ways that can dramatically transform the expression of shots. CNET’s Andrew Lanxon put it to the test during a stay in Paris.

And as you saw above, the better camera phone ultimately comes down to your own preferences for color fidelity, detail, depth and bonus features. The undeniable truth is that you can’t go wrong with either phone.

Tech.title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer Review: A Fantastic Burnout Successor From a Galaxy Far, Far Away
Tech.content:
It pains me to say it, but Star Wars’ cultural staying power has taken a massive blow in recent years – and for pretty good reason. Most of the Disney Plus shows have flopped, and the franchise’s return to cinema, The Mandalorian and Grogu, performed worse than any other theatrical release in the series’ history. Despite my lifelong fandom, I cast my eye upon the current state of the sci-fi space opera and feel a sense of apathy.

But Star Wars video games have remained consistently impressive in recent years – the Soulslike Jedi Fallen Order and Survivor duology and the turn-based Star Wars Zero Company were engaging entries in the canon, prioritizing fun gameplay over anything else.

Developer Fuse Games has continued this string of bangers across wildly different genres with Star Wars: Galactic Racer, an arcade-y game with speedy ships, plenty of underhanded action and a refreshingly self-contained story. It’s F-Zero meets Burnout, and it’s one of my new favorite racing games.

More from CNET

A classic underdog sports story with Star Wars set dressing

From the outset, I was uncertain if a plotline about a Star Wars racing league would remain narratively engaging over the course of an entire game — its spiritual predecessor, the 1999 podracing classic Star Wars Episode 1: Racer, didn’t bother with one. Once I found out Star Wars: Galactic Racer takes place between Return of the Jedi and The Force Awakens, I was even more skeptical – the sequel timeline hasn’t been an era for consistently engaging stories, after all.

It was a pleasant surprise, then, to discover that Galactic Racer tells a mostly novel story about a small corner of the universe coming to terms with a new normal after the downfall of the Galactic Empire. As it turns out, there’s not much time to engage with speeder racing when entire worlds are buckling under the tyranny of space fascism, so everything has to be put together again from the ground up.

Racing promoter Darius Pax has a passion for high-speed sports, and he’s wrangling sponsors for a new league by pulling in some of the best talent from across the galaxy. That includes shady characters like ex-TIE Fighter pilot Griff Halloran and kindhearted thrillseekers like old Soren Zaks. The most talented racer is nepo baby Kestar Bool, who is using his family’s riches to fund top-tier racing machines and initiate a hostile takeover of Pax’s assets.

Players can choose among agile skim speeders like the one shown here, bulkier landspeeders or nimble speeder bikes. Fuse Games

To stave off the imminent threat of Bool seizing the league, Pax enlists the help of main character Shade and their happy-go-lucky mechanic Hibi to win the league championship and keep the sport pure. Shade has a devil-may-care attitude and a mysterious vendetta against the egoistic antagonist, so they’re happy enough to sign on to the competition.

The setup is your classic sports underdog story where you’re looking to score petty vengeance against your sneering opponent. There’s no high-stakes galaxy-level threat – this is a story about outperforming one bad guy on the most dangerous racetracks in the universe, and it rules.

Fuse Games describes the campaign structure as “runs-based,” which essentially means it plays out like many other roguelikes, where random rewards build up your kit as you progress up a procedurally generated tournament bracket. I’m not entirely sold on the integration of this concept for an arcade racer, but I appreciate how crashing out and losing too many events essentially scraps your vehicle and causes Shade and Hibi to begin anew. Shade is supposed to be a scrappy upstart, so losing your parts and upgrades and needing to retune the whole racing kit feels like it serves a narrative purpose.

The game features returns of some classic characters, and special modes where you can race their vehicles. Fuse Games

Galactic Racer does indulge in a little bit of nostalgia – Anakin’s podracing rival, Sebulba, appears as a washed-up legend, while the antagonistic Bool family apparently built a large chunk of its wealth running part of the empire’s slave trade. There are plenty of cameos and one-off dialogue lines that will tickle lore nerds pink.

Still, there’s more restraint in this game’s storytelling than in most Star Wars projects, and the narrative is better off for it. I think fans want to explore new corners of the galaxy rather than follow the same handful of bloodlines – I know I do – and Galactic Racer debuts plenty of fun characters that don’t connect to high-stakes galaxy-ending plotlines.

The seedy underbelly of the Star Wars universe is perhaps the space opera at its most entertaining, even if that wretched hive of scum and villainy is largely composed of comically evil mobsters and smugglers. It’s great fun to explore that side of the sci-fi world without forcibly including a legacy character like Han Solo or Boba Fett.

Scrappy, speedy and strategic playstyles are equally viable

There’s a surprising amount of depth to Galactic Racer’s build system. Before you even start a run, you need to decide whether you’re flying a versatile landspeeder, risky speeder bike or graceful skim speeder – each vehicle has different acceleration speeds, turning rates and drifting capabilities.

You’ll start a campaign tournament with mostly stock equipment, but each race won provides credits and upgrades that will help you prepare for the knockout championship event. Different parts provide passive bonuses on the track, and active abilities let you expend the vehicle’s energy at key moments to score advantages in a race.

As with any roguelike, I found a build type that worked for me: I routinely invest in my speeder’s afterburners and its volatile ramjet engine, picking up parts that permit boosting in the dangerous redline zone for longer before worrying about blowing up my craft. There’s still an appreciable level of friction that forces players to make hard decisions – you’re not guaranteed to find parts or abilities you like to use, and crashing or corroding your ship during races can do damage that carries debuffs over to the next event.

More kinetic abilities that encourage brawls with other racers are probably going to be fan favorites, because Galactic Racer has a sickly satisfying takedown system ripped straight out of the old Burnout games. Brushing up against other speeders and watching the sparks fly feels intense, and slamming into an opponent will reward you with a crash cam as they go careening off the track. This type of carnage may not win every run, but building a resilient chassis or dropping bombs to cause mayhem is absolutely cathartic.

That’s not to say that I’m completely in love with every ability you can pick up in the game. The addition of an autopilot is particularly silly to me, especially since drifting around sharp turns and racing clean lines feels gratifying. Worse, while it might buy a couple of seconds to activate traps or fix malfunctioning parts, the ability could just as easily betray you by ending right before you speed directly into a wall. It just isn’t particularly well-implemented – but that’s one of the exceedingly few balancing missteps I discovered.

Lots of thought was put into the roguelike structure of Galactic Racer, and it feels like there’s a viable path for every type of racer to win – whether you enjoy running clean lines or using underhanded tactics to force opponents off the track.

This arcade racer can go the distance

There’s plenty of content for budding racers to take on once they’ve taken Kestar Bool down a few pegs in Galactic Racer’s story mode. The game features arcade time trials, multiplayer races, podracing events and more cosmetic rewards than you can shake a rathtar tentacle at. These are genuinely challenging races that could take hours to score a gold medal on, and I started to feel like a bit of a masochist after half a dozen attempts to master the ramjet-themed arcade event.

A notable pain point is the lack of an AI quick race – it seems like a massive oversight that there’s no mode where you can hop on, pick a track and difficulty and duke it out in a single match against some bots. This is something that I hope gets rectified soon.

A few flaws notwithstanding, it’s obvious that the development team at Fuse Games has an earnest love for this storied universe, and it shows through plenty of little tidbits and extra flourishes that flesh out the gameplay experience. Runs build into their own diegetic narratives as players crash out opponents and form rivalries that last throughout multiple races.

Characters react to your skill (or lack thereof), challenging Shade to one-on-one knockout races and proposing lucrative sidebets before each event. It makes sense that any headstrong individual willing to strap themselves into a speeder bike and speed through the wreckage of a downed Star Destroyer would arrogantly put their money where their mouth is, and it makes the world feel alive.

Many of those elements carry over to the multiplayer tours, where players are able to gamble among themselves with credits earned in previous races – I can foresee this potentially getting a tad toxic in a public lobby, but in my experience, it was a great way for emergent narratives to form and made the mode feel all the more meaningful.

I can’t imagine this game will make many critics’ GOTY lists, especially when so many blockbuster projects have already been released. But Star Wars: Galactic Racer is easily one of my favorite games of 2026 – and not just because its gameplay loop had me inadvertently staying up for “one more run” at 3 a.m.

Among its many virtues, the game reminded me that there’s still value in a galaxy far, far away. Over breakneck races and loving details, my apathy for the series melted away, returning a childlike spark of awe and wonder for this sci-fi universe. I doubt a game like this will dictate the future creative direction of a juggernaut franchise like Star Wars, but Galactic Racer is surely something special for anyone who wants to ride their ramjet from Crait to Tatooine.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is set to be released for PlayStation 5, Windows and Xbox Series X/S on Tuesday.

Tech.title: Welcome to Opt Out October: It’s Time to Ditch Unwanted Subscriptions and AI Spies
Tech.content:
Tired of companies constantly updating their terms and conditions to train their AI with your data, recruit your personal info for their own ends, or charge ever-higher fees? On Thursday, the Electronic Frontier Foundation launched its 2026 Opt Out October guide, urging people to retake control of their data and devices.

If you’ve been wanting to change your privacy settings, stop social media from looking over your shoulder and avoid age verification requirements, this is the guide to start with. The EFF guide walks through all the toggles to flip and the platforms or services you should outright avoid, suggesting better alternatives where available.

The EFF notes on its blog that it will update the guide’s instructions and details if anything changes.

More from CNET

A representative from the EFF didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

What should I be opting out of?

Find privacy suggestions and alternatives to common choices. Screenshot by Stephen Shankland/CNET

EFF’s Opt Out October focuses on services that have been shown to treat your personal data poorly, and there are a lot of options.

My personal favorite is the AI tools section, which teaches you how to stop chatbots and platforms like Twitch and Snapchat from training on your data.

If you’re frustrated with social media’s use of your personal data, its obnoxious ads or its face-analyzing age verification, the guide also includes a list of alternative social media. If you want to move away from Chrome’s activity tracking or find a free, user-friendly design tool beyond Adobe, this is the place to stop and plan your exit. And if you’ve finally had it with Windows cramming ads and AI into everything, the guide discusses how to get started with Linux instead.

More privacy guides

Ring offers a lot of AI options, including some you’re going to want to turn off. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Your social media and AI tools are good places to start, but there’s much more you can do for your personal privacy.

First, check out our list of the best VPN services this year, which offers plenty of options to encrypt your internet data, hide what country you’re connecting from and more.

Physical privacy is important, too. My guides on checking your home privacy online and wiping your home address off the internet are great places to get started.

If you have smart devices or just want to improve your home’s privacy and safety, I’ve also got tips on the best privacy habits for your home and the tech you may be using inside it.

You may also appreciate guides for the best privacy settings for specific devices you use. Here are changes you may want to make to Alexa to improve the voice assistant’s privacy, and here are settings for Ring security devices you may want to turn off when using its video doorbells or security cameras.

Tech.title: McDonald’s and Walmart Are Part of the Widening Fray Over Surveillance Pricing
Tech.content:
The debate over whether companies can set prices based on information they have about individual customers continues to grow. So-called surveillance pricing is in the news again on reports that Walmart patented technology for dynamic AI pricing about six months after filing for patents related to digital shelf labels.

Walmart, faced with a backlash, has been trying to assure the public that different customers will see the same digital shelf label prices and that its backend AI systems won’t engage in discriminatory pricing. “Your income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay won’t change the price,” Walmart CEO John Furner wrote in a Sept. 25 letter to customers. “And whether you’re buying groceries or electronics on a hot afternoon or in a sudden rush for an item, it’s never a reason to charge you more.”

Reached for comment, a representative for Walmart pointed CNET to the web page and letter to customers regarding pricing.

More from CNET

“Walmart does not set different prices based on who you are or the time of day, and we won’t,” the representative said in an email. “A patent does not define Walmart’s pricing practices or intent.”

But the backlash may continue if customers aren’t convinced. One consumer advocate, Jeff Rossen, went as far as to suggest in a recent video that Walmart customers should leave their phones in the car when they shop in order to avoid being datamined.

Separately, but in a similar vein, McDonald’s has been the target of media coverage over its shift to AI systems that could mean different prices for different burgers at different restaurants for different customers. The company has bristled at some of that coverage, calling it “speculative and misinformed,” but it hasn’t stopped reporters from asking why burger prices can vary from neighborhood to neighborhood as part of the company’s technology makeover.

A representative for McDonald’s didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Two of the largest American brands are now caught in the publicity crossfire over a topic that is drawing attention from lawmakers, the Federal Trade Commission and consumer advocacy groups: how companies are using AI to set prices and whether those practices may harm certain shoppers or even break the law.

The state of surveillance pricing

Surveillance pricing, which is often conflated with the terms “dynamic pricing” or “algorithmic pricing,” is a broad term that includes something that’s been happening for decades: prices set automatically based on supply and demand (say, gasoline prices). For years, shoppers also heard about “surge pricing,” such as the cost of an Uber ride increasingly dramatically during spikes in activity or around big events.

But as AI has gone mainstream and more companies have access to an array of information collected about their customers — whether it’s through apps, loyalty programs or just website tracking — it’s increasingly likely that those companies can set different prices for different shoppers based on that information.

It may not always be personal: In June, a lawsuit was filed in California claiming gas stations were inflating the price of fuel illegally due to AI software used by thousands of gas stations. But lawmakers in states are concerned about more personalized dynamic pricing. This summer, New Jersey passed a law set to go into effect in 2027 banning the use of personal data to set prices; the law primarily targets grocery stores.

Walmart’s new digital shelf labels, like these seen in Albany, New York, can update prices automatically. Consumers are worried that means prices can change unexpectedly based on who’s shopping. Larry Rulison/Albany Times Union/Getty Images

Last year, shoppers in New York began seeing warnings on product pages due to new laws mandating that customers let people know when shopping prices were set using personal data in an algorithm.

According to the Electronic Privacy Information Center, for instance, personal data and market data are being used by retailers to determine the highest price a customer is willing to pay, leading to higher prices.

In a report released in August, the Consumer Federation of America called out retailers, hotel booking sites and airlines for engaging in practices like raising prices based on things like how much AI determined they’d be willing to pay, their income or their proximity to a store.

What the FTC is doing

The Federal Trade Commission said in August that it’s looking for public comment on policy around surveillance pricing, but it has implied that it may not be able to do much to stop companies by enforcing rules; its approach appears to be geared toward helping consumers be more aware of potential surveillance pricing and requesting that those engaging in this kind of pricing be transparent about it.

That’s not enough, according to consumer advocates like the CFA, which responded to the FTC’s proposal with a letter demanding it do more than promote transparency.

“Not even the most detailed disclosure of what information they’re using to hike your prices will change the fact that those prices are still going up,” said Emily Peterson-Cassin, director of competition and market fairness at the CFA, told CNET in an email. The CFA argues in its letter that surveillance prices can be based on proxies for protected characteristics like race or age and are likely to disproportionately hurt low-income and working families who can’t easily comparison shop.

“To put it bluntly, the more vulnerable you are, the harder you stand to get hit,” Peterson-Cassin said. “If companies know you must have, for example, baby formula, they are more likely to charge you a higher price for it. “
